options.rationale: One hundred minutes is short of 150, and strengthening is missing.

options.text: Brisk 30-minute walks 5 days a week, strength exercises 2 days
options.rationale: Thirty minutes on 5 days is 150 minutes of moderate activity, with strengthening on 2 days.

options.text: Slow 10-minute strolls every day, stretching 2 days
options.rationale: Seventy minutes of slow strolling is neither enough time nor moderate intensity, and stretching is not strengthening.

questions.takeaway: Adults: at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week, such as brisk walking, plus muscle strengthening on 2 or more days.
questions.strategy: Multiply minutes by days for each option, then check for strengthening on 2 days.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Brisk walking is moderate. A slow stroll is not.
Two or more.

elimination.verdict: 30 minutes on 5 days plus strength on 2 days.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old with no health problems describes his new jogging routine to the clinic nurse. Which part of the routine does the nurse correct?

options.text: Walks slowly for 5 to 10 minutes before each jog
options.rationale: Correct. A 5 to 10 minute warm-up sends blood to the muscles and helps prevent injury.

options.text: Stops at the end of the jog and sits down at once
options.rationale: There is no cool-down. Five to 10 minutes of cool-down exercise helps the body recover.

options.text: Stops and rests if he feels pain
options.rationale: Correct. Activity stops with pain, fatigue or discomfort.

options.text: Spreads his sessions across the week
options.rationale: Correct. Activity can be spread across the week.

questions.takeaway: An exercise session has a 5 to 10 minute warm-up and a 5 to 10 minute cool-down around the activity.
questions.strategy: Walk through one session from start to finish and find the missing piece.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: You want the part to fix.
He warms up 5 to 10 minutes.
He stops abruptly with no cool-down.

elimination.verdict: Stopping and sitting at once. Add a 5 to 10 minute cool-down.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old with a left ankle fracture practices going down stairs with crutches, one hand on the handrail. Which observation needs correction?

options.text: Steps down with the right leg first, crutch left on the upper step
options.rationale: The order is wrong. Going down, the crutch and then the affected leg go first while the strong leg bends to lower him.

options.text: Stands close to the edge of the top step before starting
options.rationale: Correct starting position.

options.text: Lowers the crutch to the step below, then the left leg
options.rationale: Correct. The crutch and the affected leg lead on the way down.

options.text: Goes down one stair at a time
options.rationale: Correct. One stair at a time.

questions.takeaway: Down stairs on crutches: crutch down first, then the affected leg, then the strong leg. The affected leg leads going down.
questions.strategy: Ask which leg does the work of lowering the body. That leg stays on the upper step until last.

steps.detail: You want the error.
The strong right leg bends to lower him, so it moves last.
One option leads with the crutch and left leg, the other with the right leg.

elimination.verdict: Leading with the right leg. The crutch and the affected leg go first.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old with a right knee injury uses axillary crutches and is taught to sit down in a chair. Which observation needs correction?

options.text: Backs up until her legs touch the chair
options.rationale: Correct. She stands at the center front of the chair with the backs of the legs touching it.

options.text: Holds both crutches in her left hand
options.rationale: Correct. Both crutches go in the hand opposite the affected leg.

options.text: Keeps a crutch under each arm while she lowers herself
options.rationale: Both crutches are moved to one hand before sitting. Crutches left under the arms leave no free hand for the chair and press into the axillae.

options.text: Grasps the chair arm with her free hand
options.rationale: Correct. The free hand takes the chair arm as she lowers herself.

questions.takeaway: Sitting with crutches: back up until the legs touch the chair, both crutches in the hand opposite the affected leg, free hand on the chair arm, then lower.
questions.strategy: Follow the crutches. Before she sits they both have to end up in one hand.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three observations are correct steps.
Both in the left hand, opposite the right knee, is correct.
A crutch under each arm leaves no hand for the chair.

elimination.verdict: Sitting with a crutch under each arm.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old must keep all weight off the left foot after surgery and is fitted with axillary crutches. Which gait does the nurse teach?

options.text: Right crutch, left foot, left crutch, right foot
options.rationale: This is a four-point gait. It puts weight on the left foot.

options.text: Left crutch with right foot, then right crutch with left foot
options.rationale: This is a two-point gait. It needs at least partial weight on each foot.

options.text: Both crutches forward, then both feet swung up to land together
options.rationale: Both feet land and take weight, including the left.

options.text: Both crutches forward with the left foot off the floor, then the right foot
options.rationale: This is the three-point gait. Weight goes on both crutches and then on the uninvolved leg, and the affected foot stays off the ground.

questions.takeaway: No weight on one leg: three-point gait. Weight is borne on both crutches, then on the unaffected leg.
questions.strategy: Read each pattern and ask one question: does the left foot ever take weight?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No weight on the left foot.
Three patterns put the left foot down.

steps.action: Keep the one that does not
steps.detail: Crutches, then the right foot.

elimination.verdict: Three-point gait: both crutches, then the right foot.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old on bed rest in leg traction will begin crutch walking in 5 days. Which exercise does the nurse teach now to prepare his arms?

options.text: The nurse moves each arm through its full range
options.rationale: Passive range of motion keeps joints flexible and does not build strength.

options.text: Tighten the upper arm muscles against a fixed surface, hold, relax
options.rationale: Isometric exercise of the biceps and triceps prepares a client for crutch walking. Resistance and hold time are increased gradually.

options.text: Pump both ankles up and down each hour
options.rationale: Ankle pumps help venous return in the legs. They do not prepare the arms.

options.text: Rest both arms on pillows until the crutches arrive
options.rationale: Rest builds nothing, and crutches need a great deal of upper body strength.

questions.takeaway: Isometric exercise of the biceps and triceps prepares a client for crutch walking. Passive range of motion does not build strength.
questions.strategy: The goal in the stem is arm strength. Ask which option makes the arm muscles contract against resistance.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Arm strength for crutches.

steps.action: Cut what does not load the arms
steps.detail: Passive range, ankle pumps and rest.
Tighten against a fixed surface, hold, relax.

elimination.verdict: Isometric biceps and triceps exercise.

questions.stem: The nurse watches assistive personnel help a steady client stand from a chair and walk with a gait belt. Which action needs correction?

options.text: Hauls the client up from the chair by the belt
options.rationale: A gait belt steadies a client. It is not used to lift or carry a client by the waist.

options.text: Grasps the belt firmly with one hand at the client's back
options.rationale: Correct. One hand holds the belt firmly to steady him.

options.text: Places the other hand under the client's flexed elbow
options.rationale: Correct placement for the second hand while walking.

options.text: Walks at the client's side
options.rationale: Correct. The helper walks alongside the client.

questions.takeaway: A gait belt gives a hand hold to steady a client. It is never used to lift or carry the client by the waist.
questions.strategy: Ask what the belt is for. Three options use it to guide and one uses it to lift.

steps.detail: You want the misuse.
Steadying and guiding.
Pulling him up by the belt.

elimination.verdict: Lifting the client by the belt.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old with weak legs and poor balance tires quickly from lifting her standard walker and stops walking. Which device does the nurse discuss with the physical therapist?

options.text: A four-wheeled rollator
options.rationale: A rollator suits higher-functioning clients with good balance. It can roll forward when weight is applied, and her balance is poor.

options.text: A two-wheeled rolling walker
options.rationale: A two-wheeled walker is easier to move for a client who has difficulty lifting and advancing a walker without wheels.

options.text: Axillary crutches
options.rationale: Crutches take a great deal of upper body strength and are rarely used by older adults.

options.text: A straight cane
options.rationale: A cane is for minor problems with balance. She has poor balance and two weak legs.

questions.takeaway: A two-wheeled rolling walker is for clients who cannot lift a standard walker. A four-wheeled rollator needs good balance because it rolls forward under weight.
questions.strategy: List her limits: weak legs, poor balance, cannot keep lifting the walker. Each wrong device fails one of them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weak legs, poor balance, tires from lifting.
A cane and crutches give less support or need more strength.
Four wheels need good balance. Two wheels do not need lifting.

elimination.verdict: Two-wheeled rolling walker.

questions.stem: The day after abdominal surgery, a 77-year-old who can bear weight will move from lying in bed to a chair for the first time. Which steps does the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed 30 to 45 degrees before sitting her up
options.rationale: Raising the head 30 to 45 degrees first brings her partway up before she sits at the edge.

options.text: Have her dangle her legs for 1 to 2 minutes before standing
options.rationale: Dangling 1 to 2 minutes helps prevent a sudden drop in blood pressure on standing.

options.text: Stand her as soon as her feet touch the floor
options.rationale: Standing at once skips the dangle and invites a drop in blood pressure.

options.text: Place her feet flat on the floor, hips and knees at 90 degrees
options.rationale: Feet flat with hips and knees at 90 degrees gives her a stable base to stand from.

options.text: Put nonskid shoes or socks on her
options.rationale: Nonskid footwear prevents slipping on the floor.

options.text: Pull her upright by lifting under both arms
options.rationale: Lifting under the arms can injure her shoulders and the nurse. She pushes up while the nurse steadies her with a gait belt.

questions.takeaway: First time up: head of bed 30 to 45 degrees, sit at the edge, dangle 1 to 2 minutes, feet flat with hips and knees at 90 degrees, nonskid footwear.
questions.strategy: Take each step alone and ask whether it is safe on a first time up. Do not count how many you have picked.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dangle 1 to 2 minutes and stand at once cannot both be right.
Head of bed 30 to 45 degrees, feet flat at 90 degrees and nonskid footwear are all taught steps.
Pulling under the arms is unsafe handling.

elimination.verdict: Raise the head of the bed, dangle, feet flat at 90 degrees, nonskid footwear.

questions.stem: An alert 77-year-old with 3 days of diarrhea became dizzy the last time she stood. She now asks to walk to the bathroom. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Measure lying, sitting and standing blood pressures now
options.rationale: Tempting because it is an assessment, but she already showed you she gets dizzy on standing. Standing her for a reading repeats the risk.

options.text: Have her sit at the bedside, then stand with help
options.rationale: She is about to get up now, and a slow position change with assistance prevents the fall.

options.text: Offer a glass of oral rehydration solution
options.rationale: Right treatment for an alert patient who can swallow, but it does not make this trip to the bathroom safe.

options.text: Request a prescription for IV fluids
options.rationale: She is alert, so oral fluids would be tried first, and it does nothing for the next two minutes.

questions.takeaway: Low volume plus a position change equals a fall. Slow the change and stay with her before you treat the volume.
questions.strategy: The stem already gives the assessment: she is dizzy when she stands. The question is what keeps her safe right now.

steps.detail: Dizziness on standing is in the stem, so more assessment adds nothing.
She is getting up now, so the action must work now.
Fluids fix the cause later. The slow, assisted position change prevents the injury.

elimination.verdict: Sit her at the bedside first, then stand with help.

questions.stem: Potassium chloride prescribed at 5 to 10 mEq per hour is running at 10 through a forearm IV. The patient reports burning. The site is soft, pale and has a brisk blood return. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Stop the infusion and restart it in the other arm
options.rationale: Tempting because potassium can damage tissue. This site is soft with no redness and a good blood return, so the catheter is in the vein and a new stick is not needed.

options.text: Continue at 10 mEq per hour and recheck in an hour
options.rationale: Burning is common with potassium, but leaving the rate unchanged ignores her pain and keeps irritating the vein.

options.text: Slow the infusion to 5 mEq per hour
options.rationale: Burning with an intact site is vein irritation. A slower rate inside the prescribed range eases it and keeps the replacement going.

options.text: Apply a cold compress over the site
options.rationale: Cold narrows the vein and does nothing about the rate that is irritating it.

questions.takeaway: IV potassium irritates veins. Burning with a soft site and a blood return means slow it; burning with redness and swelling means the site has failed.
questions.strategy: Stopping and slowing are both real responses to a burning potassium site. The site findings in the stem decide which one fits.

steps.detail: Soft, pale, brisk blood return. The catheter is still in the vein.
Stopping is for a failed site. Slowing treats irritation in a working one.
5 mEq per hour is inside the prescribed range, so the nurse can make the change.

elimination.verdict: Slow the infusion to 5 mEq per hour.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old taking furosemide has a potassium of 2.6 mEq/L. Which finding does the nurse act on first?

options.text: Abdomen distended with absent bowel sounds
options.rationale: Serious. A silent, swollen belly suggests paralytic ileus, and it still ranks behind failing breathing.

options.text: Leg cramps and weakness when she stands
options.rationale: Expected at this level. Manage it with fall precautions.

options.text: Flat T waves with a regular rhythm
options.rationale: An expected ECG change. The rhythm is regular, so keep watching the rhythm while you deal with breathing.

options.text: Respirations shallow at 8 per minute
options.rationale: Severe low potassium weakens the breathing muscles. Slow, shallow breaths mean ventilation is failing now.

questions.takeaway: Low potassium weakens every muscle, including the ones that breathe. Shallow, slow respirations outrank the gut and an ECG change with a regular rhythm.
questions.strategy: Three options are alarming. Rank them with airway, breathing, circulation, and notice the rhythm is still regular.

steps.detail: Cramps and weakness are the usual picture.
Ileus, flat T waves and shallow breathing.
The rhythm is regular, so breathing is the failing system.

elimination.verdict: Shallow respirations at 8. Breathing first.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old taking a thiazide has a sodium of 124 mEq/L, a weak thready pulse and dry mucous membranes. Which prescription does the nurse clarify with the provider?

options.text: Fluid restriction of 1,000 mL per day
options.rationale: Restriction is for low sodium from too much water. Her pulse and mouth show she has lost volume, so this would make her worse.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride IV at 125 mL per hour
options.rationale: Fits. She lost sodium and water, and isotonic saline replaces both.

options.text: Seizure precautions
options.rationale: Fits. A sodium of 124 puts the brain at risk.

options.text: Hold hydrochlorothiazide
options.rationale: Fits. The diuretic is the likely cause of the sodium loss.

questions.takeaway: Low sodium has two opposite treatments. A thready pulse and dry mouth mean loss, so she needs saline, not restriction.
questions.strategy: Fluid restriction is a correct hyponatremia order for a different patient. The pulse and mucous membranes tell you which patient this is.

steps.detail: You are looking for the order that does not fit.
Thready pulse and dry mucosa mean low volume.
Saline fits low volume. Restriction fits excess water.

elimination.verdict: Clarify the fluid restriction.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with 2 days of vomiting had a blood pressure of 92/58 and urine output of 15 mL per hour. After 1 L of 0.9% sodium chloride, which finding best indicates the bolus was effective?

options.text: Weight is 1 kg higher than on admission
options.rationale: Tempting, since 1 kg is 1 L. It only shows the fluid went in, not that the organs are perfused.

options.text: Reports feeling less thirsty
options.rationale: Subjective, and it lags behind what the vessels are doing.

options.text: Urine output is 45 mL per hour
options.rationale: The kidneys are being perfused again. Output above 30 mL per hour shows the vessels are refilled.

options.text: Urine is dark amber
options.rationale: Still concentrated, which means the deficit is not corrected.

questions.takeaway: To judge fluid replacement, look at perfusion. Urine output is the fastest honest sign that vascular volume is back.
questions.strategy: Weight and urine output both look like good news. One shows fluid was given; the other shows it worked.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the finding that shows failure
steps.detail: Dark amber urine is still concentrated.
Thirst is not a reliable measure.
Weight records what was infused. Output shows the kidneys are perfused.

elimination.verdict: Urine output of 45 mL per hour.

questions.stem: A patient with a magnesium of 1.1 mEq/L has been receiving IV magnesium sulfate for 90 minutes. Which finding requires the nurse's follow up?

options.text: Patellar reflexes are 2+, down from 3+
options.rationale: This is the goal. Reflexes were hyperactive and are now normal.

options.text: Respirations are 16 per minute
options.rationale: Normal. Toxicity slows breathing below 12.

options.text: Reports feeling warm during the infusion
options.rationale: A common, harmless effect of IV magnesium.

options.text: Urine output is 22 mL per hour
options.rationale: The kidneys clear magnesium. With low output the drug builds up and toxicity follows.

questions.takeaway: Magnesium leaves through the kidneys. Normal reflexes and breathing are reassuring now, and low urine output warns of what is coming.
questions.strategy: The reflexes and breathing are the usual toxicity checks and both are fine. Look for the finding that predicts trouble.

steps.detail: Reflexes present and respirations 16. No toxicity yet.
Warmth is common with the infusion.
Output below 30 mL per hour means magnesium is not being cleared.

elimination.verdict: Urine output of 22 mL per hour.

questions.scenario: A 70-year-old with heart failure ate a salty holiday dinner yesterday. Today his weight is up 2.3 kg. He is short of breath lying flat and has new crackles in both lung bases.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed
options.rationale: He is short of breath lying flat. Sitting him up eases breathing right away.

options.text: Give furosemide as prescribed
options.rationale: A loop diuretic removes the extra fluid before it becomes pulmonary edema.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids
options.rationale: He already has too much fluid.

options.text: Start 0.9% sodium chloride as prescribed
options.rationale: Isotonic fluid stays in the vessels and adds to the overload.

options.text: Fluid overload with early pulmonary edema
options.rationale: Sudden weight gain, orthopnea and new crackles after a sodium load.

options.text: Isotonic dehydration
options.rationale: Dehydration brings weight loss and clear lungs.

options.text: Hyponatremia from sodium loss
options.rationale: He took in extra sodium, and nothing in the scenario shows a loss.

options.text: Hypokalemia
options.rationale: May follow the diuretic later. It does not explain today's findings.

options.text: Lung sounds
options.rationale: Crackles clearing or spreading tells you which way the lungs are going.

options.text: Daily weight
options.rationale: The best indicator of fluid status, measured at the same time on the same scale.

options.text: Chvostek sign
options.rationale: A calcium and magnesium check.

options.text: Skin turgor over the sternum
options.rationale: A dehydration check, and he has the opposite problem.

questions.takeaway: A sudden weight gain with new crackles is overload heading toward pulmonary edema. Sit him up, remove fluid, then track lungs and weight.
questions.strategy: Decide the direction first. Every wrong option belongs to a patient who is dry.

steps.detail: Weight up 2.3 kg overnight with crackles means too much fluid.

steps.action: Choose actions that help breathing and remove fluid
steps.detail: Head of bed up, then the diuretic.
Lung sounds and daily weight.

elimination.verdict: Fluid overload; raise the head of the bed and give furosemide; lung sounds and daily weight.

questions.stem: A patient taking lisinopril and spironolactone has a potassium of 5.4 mEq/L and receives diet teaching. Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I'll have orange juice and a banana with breakfast every morning."
options.rationale: Both are high in potassium, which he needs to limit.

options.text: "I'll read the label on my salt substitute before I use it."
options.rationale: Many salt substitutes are potassium chloride. Checking the label shows he knows the hidden source.

options.text: "I'll skip the spironolactone on days I feel weak."
options.rationale: He should report weakness, not change his own doses.

options.text: "I'll switch to baked potatoes instead of fries."
options.rationale: Sounds healthier, and potatoes are a high potassium food either way.

questions.takeaway: Both of his drugs hold on to potassium. Salt substitutes are the source patients do not suspect.
questions.strategy: Three statements either add potassium or change a prescription. One shows he can find potassium that is not obvious.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Juice, bananas and potatoes all add potassium.
Stopping a drug on his own is not safe self care.
It targets a hidden potassium source.

elimination.verdict: Reading the salt substitute label.

questions.stem: A patient with a calcium of 7.2 mg/dL had hand spasms when the blood pressure cuff inflated. After IV calcium, which finding indicates the treatment was effective?

options.text: No hand spasm occurs when the cuff is inflated
options.rationale: The Trousseau sign is gone, so the nerves are no longer overexcitable.

options.text: Tingling has moved from the fingers to the mouth
options.rationale: Tingling that is still present, and now around the mouth, means the calcium is still low.

options.text: Patellar reflexes are absent
options.rationale: Absent reflexes point past normal toward too much calcium.

options.text: Bowel sounds are hypoactive
options.rationale: A slowed gut is a high calcium finding, not a sign of recovery.

questions.takeaway: Judge the treatment by the sign that showed the problem. A negative Trousseau means the calcium is doing its job.
questions.strategy: Less tingling and no spasm both sound like improvement. Only one of them is a finding that has fully resolved.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Absent reflexes and a slow gut belong to high calcium.
Tingling that remains is still a symptom.
The cuff no longer triggers a spasm.

elimination.verdict: No hand spasm with cuff inflation.

questions.stem: An alert 86-year-old resident who swallows safely has a sodium of 149 mEq/L and says she is never thirsty. Which intervention does the nurse add to her plan?

options.text: Remind her to ask for water when she is thirsty
options.rationale: Her thirst signal is weak, so she will not ask.

options.text: Limit high sodium foods at meals
options.rationale: Tempting, since restricting sodium is a real treatment. Her problem is too little water, and this adds none.

options.text: Offer fluids every hour while she is awake
options.rationale: Older adults lose the thirst drive. Scheduled fluids replace the water she is not asking for.

options.text: Request a prescription for IV 0.45% sodium chloride
options.rationale: She is alert, swallows safely and is only mildly high, so the oral route comes first.

questions.takeaway: When thirst cannot be trusted, put water on a schedule. Use the least invasive route that works.
questions.strategy: Her own words are the cue. A plan that depends on her thirst will fail.

steps.detail: She is never thirsty, so waiting for thirst is out.
The sodium is high because water intake is low.
She can drink, so oral fluids come before IV.

elimination.verdict: Offer fluids every hour while awake.

questions.stem: A patient with a sodium of 116 mEq/L had a seizure and is receiving 3% sodium chloride. Two hours later, which finding best indicates the therapy is working as intended?

options.text: Sodium is 134 mEq/L
options.rationale: Tempting because it is nearly normal. A rise of 18 in 2 hours is far too fast and can injure the brain.

options.text: She is awake and follows commands
options.rationale: The brain is the organ at risk, and improving alertness shows the swelling is easing.

options.text: She reports a new headache and nausea
options.rationale: A new neuro symptom during treatment needs follow up.

options.text: Urine output is 35 mL per hour
options.rationale: Adequate output. It says nothing about whether the brain swelling is easing.

questions.takeaway: With sodium, the brain tells you how treatment is going. A number that jumps fast is a problem even if it looks normal.
questions.strategy: The near normal lab looks like success. Check how fast it got there.

steps.action: Cut what does not show the goal
steps.detail: A new headache with nausea needs a call, and urine output is not the target.

steps.action: Do the math on the sodium
steps.detail: From 116 to 134 in 2 hours is too rapid.
Awake and following commands is the goal.

elimination.verdict: Awake and following commands.

questions.stem: A patient with a magnesium of 0.9 mEq/L and a prolonged QT interval asks to come off the cardiac monitor to shower. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: Remove the monitor for a 10 minute shower
options.rationale: Tempting because it respects his wishes and is brief. A prolonged QT can turn into a lethal rhythm in seconds.

options.text: Remove the monitor and have a nursing assistant stay nearby
options.rationale: Someone nearby cannot see a rhythm change.

options.text: Offer a shower after tomorrow's magnesium level
options.rationale: Reasonable sounding, but it leaves today's hygiene need unmet when a bedside wash solves it safely.

options.text: Keep the monitor on and help him wash at the bedside
options.rationale: Keeps him monitored while the magnesium is low and still meets his hygiene need.

questions.takeaway: Low magnesium with a prolonged QT is a dysrhythmia risk every minute. Meet the patient's need without giving up the monitor.
questions.strategy: Two options honor his request and two keep him monitored. Find the one that does both jobs.

steps.detail: Prolonged QT with low magnesium can become a fatal rhythm.

steps.action: Cut options that remove the monitor
steps.detail: Short time and a helper do not replace telemetry.

steps.action: Choose the option that still serves him
steps.detail: A bedside wash meets the need safely.

elimination.verdict: Keep the monitor on and help him wash at the bedside.

questions.stem: The day after major abdominal surgery, a patient has puffy hands and face, a blood pressure of 90/54 and urine output of 20 mL per hour. Which problem does the nurse address first?

options.text: Low volume in the blood vessels
options.rationale: Low pressure and low urine output show the vessels are underfilled. Fluid has moved into the tissue, and organs are not being perfused.

options.text: Excess fluid in the tissues
options.rationale: Tempting because the swelling is what you see. Treating it as overload would empty the vessels further.

options.text: Risk for skin breakdown over swollen areas
options.rationale: A real risk, and a potential problem comes after an actual one.

options.text: Risk for falls when getting out of bed
options.rationale: A real risk with low pressure, and it is still a potential problem.

questions.takeaway: A patient can be swollen and still dry in the vessels. Blood pressure and urine output tell you about the plasma; edema does not.
questions.strategy: The edema and the low pressure point in opposite directions. Ask which finding describes the compartment that perfuses organs.

steps.detail: Puffiness is interstitial. Pressure and urine output reflect plasma.
Skin and fall risks have not happened yet.
Underfilled vessels threaten the kidneys now.

elimination.verdict: Low vascular volume comes first.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old taking prednisone long term has a potassium of 2.9 mEq/L and weak legs. Which actions does the nurse include in the plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place her on a cardiac monitor
options.rationale: Low potassium can cause fatal dysrhythmias.

options.text: Give oral potassium with meals
options.rationale: Food reduces the nausea oral potassium causes.

options.text: Start fall precautions
options.rationale: Weak legs make a fall likely.

options.text: Limit potatoes, oranges and spinach
options.rationale: These are potassium rich foods. She needs more of them, not fewer.

options.text: Watch breathing depth and oxygen saturation
options.rationale: Severe low potassium weakens the breathing muscles.

questions.takeaway: Low potassium: watch the heart, replace potassium safely, protect from falls and keep an eye on breathing.
questions.strategy: Decide the direction of the imbalance first. Then test each action: does it fit a patient who needs more potassium and has weak muscles?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 2.9 is low, and corticosteroids waste potassium.
Monitor, fall precautions and breathing checks.
Limiting potassium foods belongs to high potassium.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and E.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old with chronic hypocalcemia from kidney disease needs to be moved up in bed. Which instruction does the nurse give the assistive personnel?

options.text: Have her pull up using the overhead trapeze
options.rationale: Tempting because it builds independence. Her bones are fragile, and pulling her weight on them risks a fracture.

options.text: Use a lift sheet with two people and support her limbs
options.rationale: Chronic low calcium thins the bones. A lift sheet moves her without pulling on arms or legs.

options.text: Lift her under the arms with one person on each side
options.rationale: Pulling under the arms loads fragile shoulders and ribs.

options.text: Reposition her only once a shift to limit handling
options.rationale: Less handling sounds protective, but it trades fracture risk for skin breakdown. Gentle is the answer, not seldom.

questions.takeaway: Long standing low calcium means fragile bones. Move the patient gently, with the sheet carrying the load.
questions.strategy: Independence is usually the better answer. Here the chronic low calcium changes what is safe for her bones.

steps.action: Link the lab to the bones
steps.detail: Chronic low calcium pulls calcium from bone.

steps.action: Cut options that load her bones
steps.detail: The trapeze and pulling under the arms both do.
Not repositioning causes other harm.

elimination.verdict: Lift sheet, two people, limbs supported.

questions.stem: A patient on a continuous insulin infusion for 6 hours has new leg weakness and a U wave on the monitor. The last hourly glucose was 164 mg/dL. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Recheck the fingerstick glucose now
options.rationale: Tempting with insulin running. The last hourly check was 164, and weakness with a U wave is not how low glucose presents.

options.text: Request a serum calcium level
options.rationale: Low calcium causes tingling, spasm and a long QT, not weakness with a U wave.

options.text: Slow the insulin infusion by half
options.rationale: Changing the rate is the provider's decision, and it does not tell you what the potassium is.

options.text: Request a serum potassium level
options.rationale: An insulin infusion moves potassium into cells. Weak legs and a U wave are the picture of low potassium.

questions.takeaway: Insulin carries potassium into cells along with glucose. Weakness and a U wave during an insulin infusion mean check the potassium.
questions.strategy: Insulin makes you think glucose. The stem already gives a safe glucose, so ask what else insulin moves.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Use the glucose in the stem
steps.detail: 164 at the last hourly check rules out low glucose as the cause.
A U wave belongs to low potassium.
Insulin shifts potassium into cells.

elimination.verdict: Request a potassium level.

questions.scenario: A patient with a potassium of 2.8 mEq/L from diuretic use has received IV and oral potassium for 12 hours. On admission he had hypoactive bowel sounds, leg strength of 3 out of 5 and a U wave on the monitor.
questions.stem: For each reassessment finding, indicate whether it shows he is improving or requires follow up.

rows.text: Bowel sounds are active in all four quadrants
rows.rationale: The gut is waking up as potassium returns.

rows.text: Tall peaked T waves on the monitor
rows.rationale: This is the high potassium pattern. Replacement may have overshot.

rows.text: Leg strength is 5 out of 5
rows.rationale: Muscle strength has returned.

rows.text: New tingling in the hands with watery diarrhea
rows.rationale: Early signs of high potassium, the opposite imbalance.

rows.text: The U wave is no longer visible
rows.rationale: The low potassium ECG sign has resolved.

rows.text: Heart rate is 50, down from 82
rows.rationale: A slowing heart during potassium replacement suggests the level is now too high.

questions.takeaway: When you treat an imbalance, watch for the opposite one. Improvement is the admission signs resolving; trouble is the other imbalance appearing.
questions.strategy: Compare each row with the admission findings. If it reverses one of them, he is improving. If it is a new finding, ask whether it fits high potassium.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Bowel sounds, leg strength and the U wave have all reversed.
Peaked T waves, tingling with diarrhea and a slow heart rate.
The new findings are high potassium.

elimination.verdict: Improving: r1, r3, r5. Follow up: r2, r4, r6.

questions.stem: A patient with a potassium of 3.2 mEq/L takes oral potassium chloride before breakfast and is nauseated after each dose. He is not vomiting. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the next dose with his breakfast tray
options.rationale: Oral potassium irritates an empty stomach. Giving it with food reduces the nausea and keeps the replacement on track.

options.text: Hold the next dose and report the nausea
options.rationale: Tempting because a side effect is being reported. His potassium is still low, and a simple change in timing solves the problem without a missed dose.

options.text: Request a change to IV potassium
options.rationale: IV potassium carries more risk. He is not vomiting, so the oral doses stay down and the less invasive route stays.

options.text: Have him take the dose at bedtime
options.rationale: Bedtime is usually an empty stomach too, which irritates just as much, and he would be lying down with it.

questions.takeaway: Oral potassium goes with food. Fix a tolerable side effect with the smallest change before you stop or escalate a replacement the patient still needs.
questions.strategy: Holding the dose sounds like the safe choice. Ask whether the patient still needs the drug and whether a smaller change removes the problem.

steps.action: Check whether he still needs it
steps.detail: 3.2 is low, so the replacement should continue.

steps.action: Find the cause of the nausea
steps.detail: The dose is going onto an empty stomach.
Food with the dose, before a held dose or an IV.

elimination.verdict: Give the dose with breakfast.

questions.stem: A malnourished patient with alcohol use disorder still has a potassium of 3.0 mEq/L after 2 days of IV replacement. His reflexes are hyperactive. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Ask to raise the IV potassium rate
options.rationale: Tempting because the level has not moved. More potassium will not hold while the cause is untreated, and faster rates are unsafe.

options.text: Recheck the potassium the next morning
options.rationale: Waiting does not explain why two days of replacement failed.

options.text: Request a serum magnesium level
options.rationale: Malnutrition and alcohol use drain magnesium, hyperactive reflexes fit low magnesium, and potassium often will not correct until magnesium is replaced.

options.text: Ask to change to oral potassium
options.rationale: A different route does not fix the reason the potassium is not holding.

questions.takeaway: Low magnesium rides along with low potassium. When potassium will not come up, check and correct the magnesium.
questions.strategy: Two options push more potassium. Ask why the first two days did not work, and use the reflexes as the clue.

steps.detail: Three keep working on potassium alone.
Hyperactive reflexes are not a low potassium finding.
Malnutrition and alcohol use point to low magnesium.

elimination.verdict: Request a magnesium level.

questions.stem: A patient on a psychiatric unit drinks water constantly. This afternoon he has a headache and is newly confused. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the as-needed acetaminophen for headache
options.rationale: Treats a symptom and hides a neurologic change that needs explaining.

options.text: Request a serum sodium level
options.rationale: Constant water drinking dilutes sodium. Headache and new confusion mean brain cells may be swelling.

options.text: Measure lying and standing blood pressures
options.rationale: An assessment, and a tempting one. It looks for a fluid deficit, and his problem is too much water.

options.text: Offer a sports drink in place of water
options.rationale: Still adds fluid to a patient who is already water loaded.

questions.takeaway: Psychiatric polydipsia causes water intoxication and dilutional hyponatremia. A headache with new confusion is the brain's warning.
questions.strategy: Two options gather data. Pick the one that tests the problem his intake predicts.

steps.action: Name the risk from the cue
steps.detail: Too much water dilutes sodium.
Acetaminophen answers the headache and nothing else.
Orthostatic pressures look for low volume. Sodium looks for dilution.

elimination.verdict: Request a sodium level.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients with fluid or electrolyte problems. Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: Fluid overload, crackles in both bases, sitting upright after furosemide
options.rationale: Tempting because it is breathing. The crackles are expected for overload and treatment is already working on them.

options.text: Potassium 3.2 mEq/L on furosemide, pulse newly irregular
options.rationale: A new irregular pulse means the low potassium has reached the heart. It is the only finding that is new and not yet treated.

options.text: Calcium 7.8 mg/dL, tingling fingers, IV calcium now infusing
options.rationale: Tingling is the expected early sign and the treatment is running. No airway or spasm finding is reported.

options.text: Fluid deficit, heart rate 112, first fluid bolus now infusing
options.rationale: A fast heart rate is the expected response to low volume and the bolus is addressing it.

questions.takeaway: Rank by what is new and untreated. An expected finding under treatment waits behind a change in heart rhythm.
questions.strategy: All four sound unstable. Ask of each one: is this what the condition normally looks like, and is something already being done?

steps.detail: Crackles in overload, tingling in low calcium, a fast pulse in fluid deficit.
Furosemide, calcium and the bolus are all running.
A pulse that became irregular with a low potassium.

elimination.verdict: The patient with the newly irregular pulse. A rhythm change is circulation and it is new.

questions.stem: After IV furosemide for fluid overload, a patient's crackles have cleared and his weight is down 2.5 kg. He felt lightheaded when he sat up. His next dose is due in 6 hours. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Encourage extra oral fluids for the rest of the shift
options.rationale: Tempting because it treats a deficit. It guesses at the problem in a patient who was just treated for overload.

options.text: Document the clear lungs and weight loss as the expected response
options.rationale: Two findings fit a good result. The lightheadedness does not, and charting past it misses a possible overshoot.

options.text: Ask the provider to lower the furosemide dose
options.rationale: May be the outcome. The provider will ask for the pressures, and the nurse has time to get them before the dose is due.

options.text: Measure his blood pressure lying, sitting and standing
options.rationale: Lightheadedness after a 2.5 L loss suggests he may now be dry. Orthostatic pressures turn a vague report into a finding the nurse can act on and report.

questions.takeaway: A treatment can overshoot. When one finding does not fit a good result and nothing is urgent, measure it before you treat or call.
questions.strategy: Two findings say improved and one does not fit. Nothing in the stem is an emergency and the next dose is hours away, so there is time to assess.

steps.detail: Lightheaded on sitting up does not belong with a good result.
No finding in the stem is an emergency and the dose is 6 hours away.

steps.action: Choose between treating, calling and measuring
steps.detail: Fluids and a dose change both assume a deficit. Orthostatic pressures confirm it.

elimination.verdict: Measure orthostatic blood pressure first, then report.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure taking furosemide had an intake of 1,400 mL and a recorded output of 2,300 mL yesterday. On the same scale before breakfast, he weighs 1.2 kg more than yesterday. Which conclusion guides the nurse?

options.text: He is retaining fluid despite the recorded output
options.rationale: A 1.2 kg overnight gain is about 1.2 L of fluid. Weight measured the same way each day is more reliable than an intake and output record.

options.text: The furosemide is working because output exceeded intake
options.rationale: This is what the numbers on the record say. Records miss intake such as IV flushes and food fluids, and the scale contradicts them.

options.text: The scale reading is likely an error, so reweigh tomorrow
options.rationale: Reasonable if the method had changed. The stem says same scale, before breakfast, so the reading stands.

options.text: The gain reflects food and stool and is expected
options.rationale: Solid weight does not change by more than a kilogram overnight. A sudden change is fluid.

questions.takeaway: Daily weight is the best single measure of fluid status. When weight and the intake and output record disagree, believe the weight.
questions.strategy: Two measures conflict. Decide which one is more reliable, then check whether the stem gives any reason to doubt it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Output higher than intake, yet weight is up.
Same scale, before breakfast. No reason to doubt it.
1.2 kg is about 1.2 L retained.

elimination.verdict: He is retaining fluid. The scale outranks the record.

questions.stem: A patient with kidney disease who missed dialysis reports leg weakness and tingling. The monitor shows tall peaked T waves. The potassium result is pending. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Hold his scheduled lisinopril and spironolactone doses
options.rationale: Correct, since both raise potassium. Holding them prevents more rise and does nothing for the heart right now.

options.text: Ask the laboratory to run the potassium result first
options.rationale: Tempting because the number is not back. The ECG has already shown the effect on the heart, so waiting for the number delays treatment.

options.text: Report the rhythm now and prepare IV calcium
options.rationale: Peaked T waves are the heart's response to high potassium. The cue is enough to act on, and calcium protects the heart while the level is lowered.

options.text: Give the prescribed patiromer earlier than scheduled
options.rationale: A binder removes potassium over hours. It is part of the plan and too slow for an ECG change.

questions.takeaway: An ECG change from potassium is treated as an emergency on the cue, without waiting for the lab value.
questions.strategy: Every option belongs in this patient's care. Ask which one protects the heart in the next few minutes.

steps.detail: Missed dialysis, weakness, tingling and peaked T waves point to high potassium.

steps.action: Decide whether more data is needed
steps.detail: The monitor already shows cardiac effect.
Holding drugs and binders work over hours. Calcium works in minutes.

elimination.verdict: Report the rhythm and prepare IV calcium. Circulation first, the cause after.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old with fluid volume deficit has received 2 L of 0.9% sodium chloride. Blood pressure rose from 88/50 to 112/68, urine output is 50 mL per hour, and she has a new cough. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Continue the current rate until the bag is finished
options.rationale: The pressure and urine output say the deficit is corrected, which is the reason to stop pushing fluid.

options.text: Slow the infusion and listen to her lungs
options.rationale: A new cough after 2 L in an older adult is an early sign of overload. The goal is met, so reduce the fluid and assess breathing.

options.text: Stop the infusion and remove the IV catheter
options.rationale: Tempting because the fluid is the cause. She has not been assessed yet, and removing the catheter gives up the access she may need for a diuretic.

options.text: Request a chest x-ray before changing the rate
options.rationale: Imaging may follow. The nurse can slow the fluid and auscultate now without waiting for a result.

questions.takeaway: When the goal of fluid replacement is met, the next risk is too much. In older adults a new cough is the quiet first sign.
questions.strategy: Two findings show the therapy worked. One small finding is new. Ask what that finding means in someone who just received 2 L.

steps.detail: Pressure up, urine above 30 mL per hour.
Fluid moving into the lungs in an older heart.
Slowing cuts the fluid and keeps the line. Then the lungs tell you what comes next.

elimination.verdict: Slow the infusion and listen to her lungs.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old using a morphine pump after surgery is drowsy with respirations of 10. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.31, PaCO2 54 mm Hg. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Wake him and coach slow deep breaths
options.rationale: He is retaining carbon dioxide because he is breathing too little. Rousing him and deepening each breath blows the carbon dioxide off, which is the only thing that fixes this pH.

options.text: Apply oxygen by nasal cannula
options.rationale: Tempting because he is breathing slowly. Oxygen raises the saturation and does nothing to remove carbon dioxide, so the acidosis continues.

options.text: Request a sodium bicarbonate prescription
options.rationale: Bicarbonate treats a metabolic problem. His acid is carbon dioxide, and the lungs remove it.

options.text: Repeat the blood gas in one hour
options.rationale: The gas already shows the problem. Waiting an hour lets the carbon dioxide climb.

questions.takeaway: Respiratory acidosis is a ventilation problem. Move more air to remove carbon dioxide; oxygen alone does not correct it.
questions.strategy: Read the gas for its cause: a high PaCO2 means too little breathing. Pick the action that increases breathing, not the one that only adds oxygen.

steps.detail: Low pH with a high PaCO2 in a drowsy patient on an opioid.
Repeating the gas changes nothing.
Oxygen treats saturation. Deep breaths treat carbon dioxide.

elimination.verdict: Wake him and coach deep breaths.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old seen after a car crash is breathing 32 times per minute and reports tingling lips and fingers. pH is 7.52 and PaCO2 is 29 mm Hg. Which interpretation guides the nurse's plan?

options.text: Low oxygen is irritating the nerves
options.rationale: Fast breathing raises oxygen; it does not lower it. Nothing in the stem shows hypoxia.

options.text: A neck injury is compressing nerves
options.rationale: Reasonable to consider after a crash, but lips and both hands together with this blood gas point to a chemical cause.

options.text: Fast breathing has lowered usable calcium
options.rationale: Blowing off carbon dioxide makes the blood alkaline, and alkalosis lowers the calcium available to nerves. Slowing the breathing reverses it.

options.text: Fear has shifted potassium into cells
options.rationale: Alkalosis can lower potassium a little, but low potassium causes weakness, not tingling around the mouth.

questions.takeaway: Alkalosis is a cause of low calcium signs. In hyperventilation, fix the breathing and the tingling goes away.
questions.strategy: Tie the symptom to the blood gas you were given. High pH with a low PaCO2 came from the breathing rate, so the answer names the breathing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: pH up, PaCO2 down: respiratory alkalosis.

steps.action: Cut what the stem does not support
steps.detail: No low oxygen. Potassium loss causes weakness.

steps.action: Weigh the injury against the chemistry
steps.detail: Tingling in the lips and both hands fits low usable calcium.

elimination.verdict: Fast breathing lowered usable calcium.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes is vomiting and breathes deeply at 30 per minute. pH is 7.22 and bicarbonate is 12 mEq/L. IV fluids and insulin are prescribed. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Coach her to slow her breathing down
options.rationale: Tempting because the rate looks abnormal. Her lungs are removing acid; slowing them lets the pH fall further.

options.text: Start the fluids and let her breathe as she is
options.rationale: The deep fast breathing is compensation for a metabolic acidosis. Treating the cause with fluids and insulin is what ends it.

options.text: Request a sedative to ease her breathing
options.rationale: Sedation depresses the breathing that is holding her pH up.

options.text: Delay the insulin until her breathing has settled down
options.rationale: The breathing will not settle until insulin stops the acid production.

questions.takeaway: Deep rapid breathing in metabolic acidosis is the body's compensation. Leave it alone and treat the cause.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the abnormal finding is the problem or the body's fix. A low bicarbonate with fast deep breathing means the lungs are helping.

steps.detail: Low pH with low bicarbonate: metabolic acidosis.

steps.action: Group the options that suppress breathing
steps.detail: Coaching, sedating and waiting all treat the breathing as the problem.

steps.action: Keep the one that treats the cause
steps.detail: Fluids and insulin.

elimination.verdict: Start the fluids and leave the breathing alone.

questions.stem: After four days of gastric suction a patient had a pH of 7.50, bicarbonate of 33 mEq/L and respirations of 11. After a day of IV sodium chloride with potassium, which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: He says he is less thirsty than yesterday
options.rationale: A comfort gain that reflects volume. It does not show the acid base problem is correcting.

options.text: Suction drainage is 900 mL this shift
options.rationale: Ongoing loss of stomach acid is what caused the alkalosis. Large drainage means the cause continues.

options.text: Oxygen saturation is unchanged at 96%
options.rationale: Saturation was never the problem and it has not changed.

options.text: Respirations have risen to 17 per minute
options.rationale: He was breathing slowly to hold on to carbon dioxide. A rate back to normal means the body no longer needs to compensate.

questions.takeaway: In metabolic alkalosis the lungs slow down to keep acid. When the breathing returns to normal, the alkalosis is resolving.
questions.strategy: Evaluate with the finding that was abnormal because of the problem. Slow breathing was the compensation, so watch the rate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Respirations of 11 were compensation.
Heavy suction drainage keeps removing acid.

steps.action: Rank comfort against the compensation sign
steps.detail: Less thirst is volume. The breathing rate reflects the pH.

elimination.verdict: Respirations back to 17.

questions.stem: A patient with SIADH is on a 1,200 mL daily fluid restriction and says he is thirsty all evening because his fluids are gone by midafternoon. Which plan does the nurse make?

options.text: Divide the allowance across the day and evening
options.rationale: The total stays the same and he has fluid available when he is thirsty. Involving him in the schedule improves adherence.

options.text: Offer ice chips freely throughout the evening hours
options.rationale: Tempting as a comfort measure. Ice melts to about half its volume in water and counts toward the restriction.

options.text: Request a larger fluid allowance for evenings
options.rationale: The restriction is the treatment for his diluted sodium. Poor planning is the problem, not the limit.

options.text: Give the full allowance with his three meals
options.rationale: This leaves nothing for medications or thirst between meals and repeats today's problem.

questions.takeaway: A fluid restriction works when it is planned: spread the allowance over the waking hours, and count ice as fluid.
questions.strategy: When a patient struggles with a needed restriction, look for the option that keeps the limit and changes how it is delivered.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The limit corrects his sodium, so the larger allowance goes.
Free ice is uncounted fluid.
Meals only leaves the evening dry again.

elimination.verdict: Divide the allowance across day and evening.

questions.stem: A patient with fluid overload is on a 1.5 L fluid restriction and IV furosemide. Which task does the nurse assign to the assistive personnel?

options.text: Grade the ankle edema each shift
options.rationale: Grading edema is assessment and stays with the nurse.

options.text: Explain why salty foods are limited
options.rationale: Teaching needs nursing judgment about what the patient understands.

options.text: Measure and record each voided amount
options.rationale: A routine measurement with a clear result. The nurse still interprets the totals.

options.text: Decide which fluids to remove from trays
options.rationale: Tempting because the assistive personnel handle the trays. Planning the restriction is a nursing decision.

questions.takeaway: Assistive personnel collect and record data such as intake, output and weights. Assessing, teaching and planning stay with the nurse.
questions.strategy: Sort each option into measure, assess, teach or plan. Only measuring a stable patient can be delegated.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Grade is assess. Explain is teach. Decide is plan.
Measure and record is data collection.
Handling trays is not the same as planning the restriction.

elimination.verdict: Measure and record each voided amount.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old with a draining abdominal fistula is assessed at noon. Which finding is the earliest sign that she is losing too much fluid?

options.text: Her eyes look sunken in their sockets
options.rationale: Tempting because it looks like dehydration. Sunken eyes appear after a large loss, so they are a late finding.

options.text: Blood pressure is lower when she lies flat
options.rationale: Pressure that is low lying down is a late sign. The body holds pressure up until compensation fails.

options.text: She says she does not feel thirsty
options.rationale: Older adults have a weak thirst signal, so its absence tells you nothing.

options.text: Heart rate is 106, up from 78 this morning
options.rationale: The heart speeds up to keep pressure normal when volume falls. A rising rate comes before a falling pressure.

questions.takeaway: A rising heart rate is the early sign of volume loss. Low blood pressure and sunken eyes come late, and thirst is unreliable in older adults.
questions.strategy: The word earliest asks for the body's first compensation. Remove the unreliable finding, then order the rest from first to last.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Thirst is weak in older adults.
Heart rate rises first; lying blood pressure and sunken eyes come late.
78 to 106 in a few hours is a change.

elimination.verdict: Heart rate up from 78 to 106.

questions.stem: A patient with a potassium of 6.1 mEq/L and peaked T waves received sodium polystyrene sulfonate six hours ago. Which finding best indicates the drug has been effective?

options.text: She has had three loose stools
options.rationale: Tempting because the binder leaves in the stool. Stools show the drug is moving, not that enough potassium left with it.

options.text: T waves on the monitor are normal height
options.rationale: The peaked T wave was the heart's response to the potassium. Its return to normal shows the level has fallen where it matters.

options.text: Urine output is 35 mL per hour
options.rationale: Adequate output, but the binder removes potassium through the gut, not the kidneys.

options.text: She reports less nausea than before
options.rationale: Nausea is not specific to potassium and does not show the level changed.

questions.takeaway: Judge hyperkalemia treatment by the heart. A drug's expected side effect is not proof that it worked.
questions.strategy: Separate what shows the drug acted from what shows the patient improved. The outcome is the sign that made the potassium dangerous.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the danger sign in the stem
steps.detail: Peaked T waves.
The binder does not work through urine.
Stool is the mechanism. The T wave is the result.

elimination.verdict: Normal T waves.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old admitted with fluid volume deficit from fever and poor intake has had IV and oral fluids for 24 hours. Which findings indicate her fluid balance is improving? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pulse is 86, down from 110 on admission
options.rationale: The heart no longer has to race to hold blood pressure up.

options.text: She stands at the bedside without dizziness
options.rationale: No orthostatic symptoms means the vessels are filled well enough to tolerate standing.

options.text: Weight is up 0.7 kg since admission
options.rationale: In a patient who was dry, a modest gain over a day is replaced water.

options.text: Her tongue and mouth are moist
options.rationale: Mucous membranes are a reliable hydration sign in older adults.

options.text: Her eyelids and hands look puffy
options.rationale: New edema is fluid collecting in the tissues. It suggests too much fluid, not a return to balance.

options.text: She sleeps most of the day and is slow to wake
options.rationale: Tempting to read as rest. Lethargy is a neurologic finding that needs assessment, not a sign that fluid balance is returning.

questions.takeaway: Fluid replacement is working when the deficit signs reverse: pulse slows, standing is tolerated, weight returns and the mouth is moist. Edema or lethargy is a different problem.
questions.strategy: For each option ask whether it is an admission sign going away or a new finding. Only signs that are going away count as improvement.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pulse, standing, weight and mouth all move back toward normal.
Puffiness and lethargy are not deficit signs going away.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and D.

questions.stem: A patient with hypovolemia from vomiting has a prescription for a 500 mL bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride. Place the nurse's actions in the order they are performed.

options.text: Listen to the lungs and measure blood pressure and pulse
options.rationale: A baseline comes first. Without it you cannot tell whether the bolus helped or overloaded the patient.

options.text: Start the bolus on the infusion pump
options.rationale: With a baseline recorded, give the prescribed volume at a controlled rate.

options.text: Repeat the lung sounds and vital signs during the bolus
options.rationale: Reassess while the fluid is running so new crackles are caught early.

options.text: Measure the urine output for the next hour
options.rationale: Urine output shows whether the added volume reached the kidneys. It takes time to change.

options.text: Report the response to the provider
options.rationale: Report last, when there is a complete before and after picture to give.

questions.takeaway: A fluid bolus runs through the nursing process: baseline, give, reassess during, measure the outcome, report.
questions.strategy: Place the baseline first and the report last. The middle steps follow how fast each finding changes: lungs and pulse during, urine after.

steps.detail: Baseline before fluid; report after the outcome is known.
Lungs and vital signs change in minutes. Urine output needs an hour.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old on continuous tube feeding has a sodium of 153 mEq/L. She is newly agitated, with twitching in both hands. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Review the water flushes prescribed with her feeding
options.rationale: Formula without enough free water concentrates the blood. Agitation and twitching are the high sodium showing in nerve and muscle, so the fix starts with her water.

options.text: Apply mitts so she cannot pull out the feeding tube while agitated
options.rationale: Tempting for an agitated patient with a tube, but it restrains a symptom and skips less restrictive steps.

options.text: Request an as-needed sedative for the agitation
options.rationale: Sedation hides the neurologic sign you need to track and leaves the sodium untouched.

options.text: Slow the tube feeding to half the current rate
options.rationale: Cuts her calories and also cuts the water the formula itself supplies.

questions.takeaway: Agitation and twitching with a high sodium mean brain and muscle cells are losing water. Give back free water before you treat the behavior.
questions.strategy: Do not treat the agitation as a behavior problem. Ask what the sodium is doing to her cells and what she is missing.

steps.action: Link the cue to the lab
steps.detail: Twitching and agitation are irritable nerve and muscle from high sodium.

steps.action: Cut the options that mask it
steps.detail: Mitts and a sedative manage behavior only.

steps.action: Pick the one that adds water
steps.detail: Flushes are how a tube fed patient gets free water.

elimination.verdict: Review the water flushes.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old with late-stage kidney failure is assessed at 0800. Which finding tells the nurse his fluid overload is getting worse?

options.text: Pitting edema of 2+ at both ankles and shins, the same as it was yesterday
options.rationale: Abnormal but unchanged, so it does not show a trend.

options.text: Neck veins newly distended with the head of bed at 45 degrees
options.rationale: Veins that stay full when he is upright mean the vascular space is overfilled now, and the lungs are next.

options.text: Urine output of 280 mL in 24 hours, his usual amount
options.rationale: Low, but expected for his kidneys and it is his baseline rather than a change.

options.text: Skin on the lower legs that is pale and cool
options.rationale: A finding of edema that goes along with the swelling he already has.

questions.takeaway: Edema tells you fluid is in the tissues. Distended neck veins and a bounding pulse tell you the vessels are overfilled, which is what leads to pulmonary edema.
questions.strategy: All four fit kidney failure. Look for the one that is new and that sits closest to the heart and lungs.

steps.detail: Edema and low output are his usual.
Neck veins reflect pressure in the central circulation.
Overfilled vessels push fluid into the lungs.

elimination.verdict: Distended neck veins at 45 degrees.

questions.stem: A patient with a potassium of 6.2 mEq/L and a wide QRS received IV calcium. Ten minutes later the QRS is narrower and the repeat potassium is 6.2 mEq/L. Which conclusion guides the nurse?

options.text: The calcium did not work, so a repeat dose is needed
options.rationale: The rhythm improved, which is exactly what calcium is for.

options.text: The calcium worked, and the potassium still has to be lowered
options.rationale: Calcium steadies the heart muscle and does not move potassium. Insulin with dextrose and a binder still have to bring the level down.

options.text: The repeat sample was probably hemolyzed and should be redrawn
options.rationale: Tempting when a lab does not move, but an unchanged value is the expected result here.

options.text: The remaining treatments can wait because the rhythm has improved
options.rationale: The protection is short lived. The potassium is still dangerous.

questions.takeaway: IV calcium protects the heart and does not lower potassium. An unchanged level after calcium is expected, and the lowering treatments still come next.
questions.strategy: Two results look like they disagree. Ask what each drug is supposed to change before calling it a failure.

steps.detail: It stabilizes the myocardium.
No shift or removal has happened yet.
A better rhythm on calcium is borrowed time.

elimination.verdict: It worked on the heart. Now lower the potassium.

questions.stem: A patient with kidney failure who makes no urine has a magnesium of 4.2 mEq/L and is hard to arouse. IV calcium has been given. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate next?

options.text: IV furosemide with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: The usual way to flush magnesium, but it works only through kidneys that make urine. Here it adds volume he cannot remove.

options.text: Oral magnesium binder with meals
options.rationale: Not a treatment for a high magnesium level, and he is too drowsy to swallow safely.

options.text: Hemodialysis to remove the magnesium
options.rationale: With no urine output, dialysis is the only route left to remove the magnesium.

options.text: A repeat magnesium level in 12 hours
options.rationale: Monitoring alone leaves a patient who is hard to arouse with a rising risk of respiratory failure.

questions.takeaway: Fluids and a loop diuretic remove magnesium only if the kidneys work. In kidney failure, stop the source, give calcium and expect dialysis.
questions.strategy: The usual answer is fluids and furosemide. Check the stem for the detail that takes that option away.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He makes no urine.

steps.action: Test the standard treatment against it
steps.detail: A diuretic has nothing to act on.

steps.action: Pick the route that still works
steps.detail: Dialysis removes magnesium directly.

elimination.verdict: Hemodialysis.

questions.stem: A patient with hyperparathyroidism and a calcium of 13.1 mg/dL had a heart rate of 102 this morning. Which afternoon finding most concerns the nurse?

options.text: No bowel movement for three days
options.rationale: Expected with high calcium because the gut slows. It needs a plan, not an urgent response.

options.text: Knee reflexes weaker than this morning
options.rationale: Also expected. High calcium makes nerve and muscle harder to excite.

options.text: Reports feeling thirsty and urinating often
options.rationale: A common effect that calls for fluids.

options.text: Heart rate of 48 with cool, pale feet
options.rationale: Early high calcium speeds the heart. A slowing rate with poor perfusion means it is now depressing the heart.

questions.takeaway: In hypercalcemia the heart rate rises early and slows when the level is severe or prolonged. A falling rate with poor perfusion is the dangerous turn.
questions.strategy: Three options are expected for this condition. Find the one that shows a change in the organ that can kill.

steps.detail: Constipation, weak reflexes and thirst all fit.
102 down to 48 is a change in direction.
Cool pale feet mean perfusion is falling.

elimination.verdict: Heart rate 48 with cool, pale feet.

questions.stem: Assistive personnel report that an 85-year-old's skin stays tented on the back of her hand and suggest she needs more fluids. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Check turgor over the sternum and look at her mouth
options.rationale: Hand skin tents in most older adults because it has lost elasticity. The sternum and the mucous membranes give a reading you can trust.

options.text: Start an hourly oral fluid schedule for the shift
options.rationale: Reasonable if she is dry, but you would be treating on a finding that is unreliable at her age.

options.text: Request a prescription for IV 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Jumps to treatment with no valid evidence of a deficit.

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel to recheck the other hand
options.rationale: Repeats the same unreliable site and hands an assessment to someone who cannot interpret it.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, assess skin turgor over the sternum and confirm with mucous membranes. Tenting on the hand proves nothing.
questions.strategy: Before acting on a reported finding, ask whether that finding is reliable in this patient.

steps.detail: Hand turgor is unreliable after about age 65.
Oral or IV fluid needs a valid assessment first.
Assistive personnel collect, the nurse interprets.

elimination.verdict: Check the sternum and the mouth.

questions.stem: A patient with kidney disease has a sodium of 151 mEq/L, a bounding pulse and edema to both knees. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Furosemide with a sodium-restricted diet
options.rationale: His sodium is high because the kidneys are holding sodium and water together. Remove both and stop adding sodium.

options.text: A fluid restriction of 1 L per day
options.rationale: Tempting because he is overloaded, but taking away water alone concentrates the sodium further.

options.text: A 300 mL bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Adds sodium and volume to a patient who has too much of both.

options.text: Oral water every hour while awake
options.rationale: Right for a dry patient with high sodium. He already has excess volume.

questions.takeaway: High sodium does not always mean a dry patient. Read the volume status: with a bounding pulse and edema, the plan is a diuretic and less sodium.
questions.strategy: The sodium number points one way and the pulse points the other. Volume status decides the treatment.

steps.detail: Bounding pulse and edema mean excess.
Bolus and hourly water both do.
Restricting water raises sodium. A diuretic with less sodium fixes both.

elimination.verdict: Furosemide and sodium restriction.

questions.stem: A postoperative patient's pump has run at 250 mL per hour for four hours instead of the prescribed 75. His pulse is bounding, his lungs are clear and he breathes easily. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Request a prescription for IV furosemide
options.rationale: May well be needed, but the extra fluid is still running in while you make the call.

options.text: Reset the pump to the prescribed rate
options.rationale: Stops the cause at once. He is breathing easily, so removing the source comes before anything else.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and apply oxygen
options.rationale: The right first move if he were short of breath. He is not.

options.text: Complete an event report for the rate error
options.rationale: Required, and it comes after the patient is safe.

questions.takeaway: When a treatment is causing the problem, correct the source first, then assess and report.
questions.strategy: The stem already gives you the assessment. Ask which action stops more harm in the next minute.

steps.detail: Bounding pulse, clear lungs, easy breathing.
Each minute adds more fluid.
Reassess, report, then document.

elimination.verdict: Reset the pump to 75.

questions.nursesNote: 1400: 58-year-old with diabetes and kidney disease, takes lisinopril. Serum potassium 5.8 mEq/L. Reports tingling around the mouth and in both feet since noon. Legs now feel heavy when he walks. Three loose watery stools this shift, bowel sounds hyperactive. Apical pulse 52 and irregular. Fingerstick glucose within his usual range. Skin warm and dry. Reports a good appetite at lunch.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow-up because of his potassium level.

segments.text: Reports tingling around the mouth and in both feet since noon
segments.rationale: Tingling and twitching are the early nerve signs of high potassium.

segments.text: Legs now feel heavy when he walks
segments.rationale: Weakness that starts in the legs and moves upward is the next stage.

segments.text: Three loose watery stools this shift, bowel sounds hyperactive
segments.rationale: High potassium speeds the gut. It is easy to blame food or a virus.

segments.text: Apical pulse 52 and irregular
segments.rationale: A slow irregular pulse means the heart's conduction is affected. This is what kills.

segments.text: Fingerstick glucose within his usual range
segments.rationale: Normal for him and not a potassium finding.

segments.text: Skin warm and dry
segments.rationale: Normal.

segments.text: Reports a good appetite at lunch
segments.rationale: Normal, and not related to the potassium.

questions.takeaway: High potassium: tingling first, then weakness that climbs, a fast gut, and a slow irregular heart. Check the pulse and rhythm before anything else.
questions.strategy: The diarrhea looks like a separate stomach problem. With a high potassium it belongs to the same picture.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 5.8 with kidney disease and an ACE inhibitor.

steps.action: Collect nerve, muscle, gut and heart
steps.detail: Tingling, heavy legs, watery stools, slow irregular pulse.
Glucose, skin and appetite.

elimination.verdict: Tingling, heavy legs, watery stools and the pulse.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with a potassium of 3.0 mEq/L has a prescription for 40 mEq of potassium chloride diluted in 1 L of 0.9% sodium chloride through a forearm IV. Which setup does the nurse use?

options.text: On an IV pump at 20 mEq per hour
options.rationale: Right device, wrong rate. 20 mEq per hour is double the 5 to 10 mEq per hour limit and can trigger a dysrhythmia.

options.text: On an IV pump at 10 mEq per hour
options.rationale: Diluted, on a pump, and inside the 5 to 10 mEq per hour limit.

options.text: By gravity with a roller clamp at 10 mEq per hour
options.rationale: Right rate, wrong device. Gravity tubing can run fast if the arm moves, and IV potassium must be on a pump.

options.text: On an IV pump at 40 mEq per hour
options.rationale: Right device, wrong rate. The whole dose in one hour is four times the limit.

questions.takeaway: IV potassium is diluted, on a pump, at 5 to 10 mEq per hour. It is never pushed.
questions.strategy: Check each setup for two things: a pump and a rate of 5 to 10 mEq per hour.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gravity tubing fails. Potassium needs a pump.
20 and 40 mEq per hour are over the limit of 10.

elimination.verdict: Pump at 10 mEq per hour.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old who takes furosemide has a potassium of 3.1 mEq/L, eats a regular diet and has an IV pump at the bedside. Which prescription does the nurse question?

options.text: Potassium chloride 20 mEq by mouth with breakfast
options.rationale: Oral potassium with food is correct. Food reduces the nausea.

options.text: Potassium chloride 20 mEq in 250 mL IV over 4 hours
options.rationale: Diluted and 5 mEq per hour, which is inside the 5 to 10 mEq per hour limit.

options.text: Potassium chloride 20 mEq IM in the ventrogluteal site
options.rationale: Right drug and dose, wrong route. Potassium is a severe tissue irritant and is never given IM or subcutaneously.

options.text: Spironolactone by mouth in place of furosemide
options.rationale: A potassium sparing diuretic in place of a loop diuretic is a listed change for low potassium.

questions.takeaway: Potassium goes by mouth or diluted IV on a pump. Never IM, never subcutaneous, never IV push.
questions.strategy: You are hunting the unsafe order. Read the route of each one before the dose.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Do the math on the IV order
steps.detail: 20 mEq over 4 hours is 5 mEq per hour. Safe.
Oral and diluted IV are allowed. IM is not.

elimination.verdict: The IM order is the one to question.

questions.stem: An alert 80-year-old has a sodium of 153 mEq/L after 3 days of fever and poor intake. The provider prescribes a hypotonic IV fluid to replace free water. Which bag does the nurse hang?

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride on a pump
options.rationale: Hypotonic. Water moves into the shrunken cells, and the pump keeps the correction gradual.
