options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride on a pump
options.rationale: Isotonic. It stays in the extracellular space and is not the hypotonic fluid prescribed.

options.text: 3% sodium chloride on a pump
options.rationale: Hypertonic. It pulls more water out of cells and raises the sodium further.

options.text: Lactated Ringer's on a pump
options.rationale: Isotonic, like 0.9% sodium chloride. It does not match a hypotonic order.

questions.takeaway: 0.45% sodium chloride is hypotonic, 0.9% sodium chloride and lactated Ringer's are isotonic, 3% sodium chloride is hypertonic.
questions.strategy: All four are on a pump, so the pump is not the decision. Sort the bags by tonicity and match the order.

steps.action: Name the tonicity of each bag
steps.detail: Two are isotonic, one is hypertonic, one is hypotonic.
The order says hypotonic, for a sodium above 145.

elimination.verdict: 0.45% sodium chloride.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old starts potassium chloride at 10 mEq per hour through a peripheral IV on a pump. Which site monitoring plan does the nurse follow?

options.text: Check the site every 4 hours and ask about burning
options.rationale: Right questions, wrong interval. Four hours lets phlebitis or tissue damage go unseen.

options.text: Check the site once each shift and ask about burning
options.rationale: Right questions, wrong interval. Once a shift is far too long for a tissue irritant.

options.text: Check the site when the pump alarms for an occlusion
options.rationale: A pump alarm is not an assessment. Burning and irritation come before an occlusion.

options.text: Check the site every hour and ask about burning or pain
options.rationale: IV potassium irritates the vein, so the site is assessed hourly and the client is asked about burning or pain.

questions.takeaway: During IV potassium, assess the IV site every hour for burning, pain or irritation.
questions.strategy: Three options share the same check and differ only in how often. Pick the interval that matches a tissue irritant.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Waiting for an alarm is reacting, not assessing.
Hourly is the taught interval. Every 4 hours and once a shift are too long.

elimination.verdict: Every hour, asking about burning or pain.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews morning results for four clients on a medical unit. Which result does the nurse report to the provider?

options.text: Receiving 0.9% sodium chloride: sodium 144 mEq/L
options.rationale: Within 135 to 145 mEq/L.

options.text: Taking furosemide: potassium 3.6 mEq/L
options.rationale: Within 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L. Close to the low end, so it is trended, and it is still normal.

options.text: Taking calcium with vitamin D: calcium 10.4 mg/dL
options.rationale: Within 9.0 to 10.5 mg/dL.

options.text: Taking a daily magnesium antacid: magnesium 2.9 mEq/L
options.rationale: Above 1.3 to 2.1 mEq/L. High magnesium depresses reflexes, breathing and the heart, and the antacid is a source.

questions.takeaway: Sodium 135 to 145 mEq/L. Potassium 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L. Calcium 9.0 to 10.5 mg/dL. Magnesium 1.3 to 2.1 mEq/L.
questions.strategy: Hold each number against its range. Values near an edge are still normal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 144, 3.6 and 10.4 all sit just inside their ranges.
2.9 is well above 2.1.

elimination.verdict: Magnesium 2.9 mEq/L.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old reports tingling lips the evening after a thyroidectomy. The nurse checks for Trousseau sign. Which technique does the nurse use?

options.text: Inflate a blood pressure cuff on the arm and watch the hand
options.rationale: Trousseau sign is a spasm of the hand and fingers when the cuff is inflated.

options.text: Tap the cheek over the facial nerve and watch the face
options.rationale: Correct technique for Chvostek sign, which is a different test.

options.text: Inflate a blood pressure cuff on the arm and watch the face
options.rationale: Right tool, wrong place to look. The spasm appears in the hand.

options.text: Tap the patellar tendon and watch the lower leg
options.rationale: This tests a deep tendon reflex, not Trousseau sign.

questions.takeaway: Trousseau: inflate a cuff on the arm, the hand spasms. Chvostek: tap the cheek over the facial nerve, that side of the face twitches.
questions.strategy: Two options use the cuff and two use tapping. Match the tool, then match where you look.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Trousseau uses the blood pressure cuff.
The hand and fingers, not the face.

elimination.verdict: Cuff on the arm, watch the hand.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with a magnesium of 0.9 mEq/L starts IV magnesium sulfate. A student nurse describes the monitoring plan. Which statement needs correction?

options.text: "I will keep the infusion on the pump at the prescribed rate."
options.rationale: Correct. A pump controls the rate of a high risk infusion.

options.text: "I will keep her on the cardiac monitor while it runs."
options.rationale: Correct. Low and high magnesium both cause dysrhythmias.

options.text: "I will check her knee jerk reflex once, after the infusion ends."
options.rationale: Right assessment, wrong timing. Reflexes are checked often during the infusion, because a fading reflex is the warning of toxicity.

options.text: "I will watch her breathing and alertness while it runs."
options.rationale: Correct. High magnesium causes drowsiness and respiratory failure.

questions.takeaway: During IV magnesium, check deep tendon reflexes often while it infuses. A fading reflex means stop.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement where the right check is done at the wrong time.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pump, monitor and breathing checks are all correct.
A single reflex check after the infusion cannot catch toxicity during it.

elimination.verdict: The once after the infusion statement.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old with kidney disease has a potassium of 6.6 mEq/L. The provider prescribes a treatment to shift potassium from the blood into the cells. Which setup does the nurse prepare?

options.text: Regular insulin IV with no dextrose
options.rationale: Right drug, missing its partner. Insulin without dextrose shifts the potassium and drops the glucose.

options.text: Regular insulin IV given with dextrose
options.rationale: Insulin moves potassium into the cells and the dextrose prevents hypoglycemia.

options.text: IV calcium given with dextrose
options.rationale: Calcium protects the heart. It does not lower or shift potassium.

options.text: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate given by mouth
options.rationale: A binder removes potassium through the GI tract. It does not shift it into cells.

questions.takeaway: Hyperkalemia: IV calcium protects the heart, regular insulin with dextrose shifts potassium into cells, binders remove it.
questions.strategy: Match each drug to its job: protect, shift or remove. The order asks for shift.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Calcium protects. The binder removes. Insulin shifts.
Insulin is given with dextrose to prevent hypoglycemia.

elimination.verdict: Regular insulin with dextrose.

questions.stem: The nurse totals the urine output of four clients being treated for dehydration. Which total does the nurse report as concerning?

options.text: 1,400 mL over the past 24 hours
options.rationale: Well above 500 mL per day.

options.text: 700 mL over the past 12 hours
options.rationale: On pace for 1,400 mL per day.

options.text: 380 mL over the past 24 hours
options.rationale: Below 500 mL per day. The kidneys are still holding on to water.

options.text: 1,100 mL over the past 24 hours
options.rationale: Above 500 mL per day.

questions.takeaway: In dehydration, urine output under 500 mL per day is concerning.
questions.strategy: Put every total on the same 24 hour scale before you compare.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 700 mL in 12 hours is about 1,400 mL in a day.
Only 380 mL falls below it.

elimination.verdict: 380 mL in 24 hours.

questions.stem: The day after a thyroidectomy, a 38-year-old has a calcium of 6.8 mg/dL, painful hand spasms and a prolonged QT interval. Which prescription fits this client?

options.text: Oral calcium with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Right monitoring, wrong route. Oral calcium is for mild or chronic low calcium, not tetany.

options.text: IV calcium with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Severe, symptomatic low calcium is replaced IV, and the QT change is watched on the monitor.

options.text: Oral vitamin D with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Vitamin D improves absorption over time. It does not stop tetany.

options.text: IV magnesium sulfate with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Treats a different electrolyte. The stem gives a low calcium, not a low magnesium.

questions.takeaway: Oral calcium for mild or chronic hypocalcemia. IV calcium for severe hypocalcemia or acute tetany.
questions.strategy: Every option has the monitor, so the monitor is not the decision. The spasms tell you how fast the calcium is needed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 6.8 mg/dL with spasms and a long QT is severe and acute.
Acute tetany gets IV calcium.

elimination.verdict: IV calcium on the monitor.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with SIADH has a sodium of 126 mEq/L, a bounding pulse and a weight gain of 2 kg. Which prescription does the nurse question?

options.text: Restriction of oral fluids
options.rationale: Correct for low sodium from excess water.

options.text: Tolvaptan by mouth
options.rationale: A vasopressin antagonist makes the kidneys lose water. It is listed for SIADH.

options.text: Daily weight on the same scale
options.rationale: Correct monitoring for fluid excess.

options.text: Continuous 0.45% sodium chloride IV
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid adds free water to a client whose sodium is low because of excess water.

questions.takeaway: Low sodium with fluid excess: restrict fluids and use a vasopressin antagonist. Do not add hypotonic fluid.
questions.strategy: The bounding pulse and weight gain tell you the sodium is diluted. Find the order that adds water.

steps.detail: Bounding pulse and a 2 kg gain mean fluid excess.

steps.action: Find the order that adds water
steps.detail: Three orders remove or track water. One adds it.

elimination.verdict: The 0.45% sodium chloride infusion.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old's 0.9% sodium chloride with 20 mEq potassium chloride runs at 75 mL per hour. The potassium returns at 6.1 mEq/L. The provider says to stop potassium and continue IV fluid. Which setup does the nurse use?

options.text: Plain 0.9% sodium chloride at 75 mL per hour
options.rationale: Removes the potassium source and keeps the fluid going as directed.

options.text: The same bag slowed to 40 mL per hour
options.rationale: Still delivers potassium. The source is slowed, not stopped.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride with 10 mEq potassium chloride at 75 mL per hour
options.rationale: Less potassium is still potassium.

options.text: The same bag at 75 mL per hour until it empties
options.rationale: Finishing the bag keeps giving potassium to a client above 5.0 mEq/L.

questions.takeaway: Potassium above 5.0 mEq/L: stop every potassium infusion and supplement first.
questions.strategy: Three setups still contain potassium. One does not.

steps.action: Look for potassium in each bag
steps.detail: Slowed, halved or finished, three options still give it.
The provider wants IV fluid continued, without potassium.

elimination.verdict: Plain 0.9% sodium chloride at the same rate.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old admitted with dehydration has received IV fluids for 24 hours. Which result tells the nurse the fluid deficit is not yet corrected?

options.text: Serum osmolarity of 325 mOsm/L
options.rationale: Above 270 to 300 mOsm/L. The blood is still concentrated.

options.text: Serum osmolarity of 288 mOsm/L
options.rationale: Within 270 to 300 mOsm/L.

options.text: Serum sodium of 140 mEq/L
options.rationale: Within 135 to 145 mEq/L.

options.text: Serum potassium of 4.2 mEq/L
options.rationale: Within 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L, and potassium does not measure hydration.

questions.takeaway: Normal osmolarity is 270 to 300 mOsm/L. A higher value means the blood is still concentrated.
questions.strategy: Two options give the same lab with different numbers. One of them is likely the answer.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 288 is inside 270 to 300. 325 is above it.
Sodium and potassium are both in range.

elimination.verdict: Osmolarity of 325 mOsm/L.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old with a sodium of 162 mEq/L is receiving 0.45% sodium chloride with a goal of lowering the sodium gradually. Which reassessment requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: After 8 hours: sodium 159 mEq/L, more alert
options.rationale: A small drop with better alertness is the gradual correction intended.

options.text: After 6 hours: sodium 160 mEq/L, asking for water
options.rationale: A small drop, and thirst is expected while the sodium is still high.

options.text: After 4 hours: sodium 161 mEq/L, easy to wake
options.rationale: Slow, and moving in the right direction with no new neurologic change.

options.text: After 4 hours: sodium 150 mEq/L, new headache and drowsiness
options.rationale: A drop of 12 mEq/L in 4 hours is far too fast. Water rushes into brain cells and causes cerebral edema.

questions.takeaway: High sodium is lowered gradually. A rapid drop causes cerebral edema.
questions.strategy: Compare how fast each sodium fell, then look at the brain.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Compare the size of each drop
steps.detail: 1 to 3 mEq/L over 4 to 8 hours versus 12 mEq/L in 4 hours.
Only one client has a new headache and drowsiness.

elimination.verdict: The sodium of 150 after 4 hours.

questions.scenario: The charge nurse reviews actions taken for six clients with fluid or electrolyte problems.
questions.stem: For each action, indicate whether it is correct or needs correction.

rows.text: Dehydration with orthostatic hypotension: the client is helped to sit on the edge of the bed before standing
rows.rationale: Slow position changes are a listed safety measure for dehydration.

rows.text: Fluid overload, taking furosemide: output is charted as "voided several times" without measuring
rows.rationale: Fluid overload calls for accurate intake and output, which means measured volumes.

rows.text: Potassium of 2.8 mEq/L: the client is placed on a continuous cardiac monitor
rows.rationale: Low potassium causes dysrhythmias, so the heart is monitored.

rows.text: Potassium of 6.3 mEq/L: telemetry is removed because the client has no chest pain
rows.rationale: High potassium needs continuous telemetry. Dysrhythmias are its most common cause of death and do not wait for chest pain.

rows.text: Chronic hypocalcemia, calcium 8.0 mg/dL: scheduled oral calcium with vitamin D is given
rows.rationale: Mild or chronic low calcium is replaced by mouth, and vitamin D improves absorption.

rows.text: Fluid overload, on a fluid restriction: the bedside water pitcher is refilled every shift
rows.rationale: A full pitcher within reach defeats the restriction. Fluids are measured and counted.

questions.takeaway: Dehydration: slow position changes. Overload: measured intake and output and a counted fluid restriction. Potassium high or low: cardiac monitor. Chronic low calcium: oral calcium with vitamin D.
questions.strategy: Name the imbalance in each row first, then ask whether the action matches its rule.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low and high potassium both need the monitor.
Unmeasured output and a refilled pitcher both break accurate intake and output.
Slow position changes and oral calcium with vitamin D follow the rules.

elimination.verdict: Correct, needs correction, correct, needs correction, correct, needs correction.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old with presbycusis does not respond when the nurse gives discharge instructions from the doorway. His reading glasses are at home. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Sit facing him at eye level with the light on the nurse's face
options.rationale: Correct. He needs to see the speaker's face, and this fixes the distance and the lighting at once.

options.text: Hand him the printed discharge instructions to read
options.rationale: Tempting, because written information is a real strategy for hearing loss. Without his reading glasses he cannot use it.

options.text: Repeat the instructions from the doorway in a louder voice
options.rationale: Shouting distorts speech and raises the pitch he hears worst.

options.text: Give the instructions to his daughter by telephone
options.rationale: This goes around him. Hearing loss is a barrier to communication, not to learning, and the nurse has not yet communicated the right way.

questions.takeaway: Hearing loss: get close, face the client, put the light on your face, speak slowly in a lower pitch.
questions.strategy: Written material is a good answer only when the client can see it. The missing glasses are the detail that decides.

steps.action: Cut the option that goes around him
steps.detail: The phone call to the daughter leaves him out.
Shouting distorts sound.
No reading glasses removes the printed sheet.

elimination.verdict: Sit facing him at eye level in good light.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old who works at a computer all day has burning eyes and blurred vision by midafternoon on workdays. Her eye exam last month was normal. Which instruction does the nurse give?

options.text: Raise the screen brightness and sit closer to it
options.rationale: More brightness and a shorter distance add to the strain.

options.text: Every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds
options.rationale: The pattern fits digital eyestrain, and the 20-20-20 rule rests the focusing muscles through the day.

options.text: Schedule another eye exam to check for new glasses
options.rationale: Tempting because blur suggests a refractive change, but her exam a month ago was normal.

options.text: Wear tinted glasses indoors during the afternoon
options.rationale: Tinted lenses do not rest the eyes from close focus.

questions.takeaway: Eyestrain that follows the workday and clears with rest is managed with the 20-20-20 rule.
questions.strategy: Use the timing. Symptoms that build over a day of screen work and a normal recent exam point to habit, not disease.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Workdays, midafternoon, screen job.
A repeat exam would find nothing new.

steps.action: Pick the measure that rests the eyes
steps.detail: Regular distance breaks.

elimination.verdict: The 20-20-20 rule.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old on bed rest for 8 days became confused about the date. The nurse added a large clock, family photos and scheduled visits. Which finding shows the plan is working?

options.text: He lies quietly and has stopped using the call light
options.rationale: Looks calm, but a quiet client who stops calling may be withdrawing further.

options.text: He watches television from breakfast until bedtime
options.rationale: More stimulation is not the same as meaningful stimulation, and it does not show orientation.

options.text: He names the day and the people in the photos
options.rationale: Orientation has returned and he is responding to stimuli that mean something to him.

options.text: He follows directions when the nurse repositions him
options.rationale: He could do that while still disoriented to time.

questions.takeaway: Sensory deprivation is treated with meaningful stimuli. You evaluate it by orientation and engagement.
questions.strategy: Match the outcome to the problem. The problem was confusion about the date, so look for the option that shows orientation.

steps.detail: Disorientation from too little meaningful input.

steps.action: Cut calm that is not engagement
steps.detail: Lying quietly and following directions do not show orientation.
A television left on is quantity, not quality.

elimination.verdict: Names the day and the people in the photos.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old with new vision loss in both eyes has stopped going to her card group and has tripped twice this week on her back step. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Refer her to a low vision support group
options.rationale: Helpful for isolation, and it can follow once she is safe at home.

options.text: Explore how she feels about losing her sight
options.rationale: Therapeutic and important, but feelings rank below an injury that is already happening.

options.text: Arrange a ride so she can rejoin the card group
options.rationale: Addresses socialization, which is a real problem and not the most urgent one.

options.text: Mark the step edge and have a handrail secured
options.rationale: She has already tripped twice, so the fall hazard is an actual problem and safety comes first.

questions.takeaway: With sensory loss, risk for injury outranks socialization and coping. An actual hazard is fixed first.
questions.strategy: All four help her. Ask which problem has already caused harm this week.

steps.detail: Isolation, grief and falls.
Two trips on the same step.
Contrast on the edge and a secure rail.

elimination.verdict: Mark the step and secure a handrail.

questions.stem: An 85-year-old with a hearing aid has answered several questions incorrectly this morning. Which task does the nurse assign to the assistive personnel?

options.text: Clean the hearing aid, check the battery and reinsert it
options.rationale: Correct. Routine care of an assistive device is a standard task with a predictable result.

options.text: Find out why the client is answering incorrectly
options.rationale: Working out the cause is assessment, which stays with the nurse.

options.text: Teach the client how to tell when the battery is low
options.rationale: Teaching is the nurse's responsibility.

options.text: Decide whether a writing board would work better for this client
options.rationale: Choosing a communication method takes nursing judgment.

questions.takeaway: Assistive personnel care for the device. The nurse assesses, teaches and decides.
questions.strategy: Look at the verbs. Find out, teach and decide belong to the nurse. Clean and check can be delegated.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find out, teach and decide are judgment.
Cleaning and checking a battery follows fixed steps.

elimination.verdict: Clean the aid, check the battery and reinsert it.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old with diabetic retinopathy lives alone and can no longer read the markings on her insulin syringe. She wants to keep managing her own insulin. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Arrange for a neighbor to draw up and give each dose
options.rationale: This is safe, and it takes away the independence she asked to keep.

options.text: Teach her to use an insulin pen with audible dose clicks
options.rationale: Correct. It replaces the lost visual cue with sound, so she stays safe and stays independent.

options.text: Have her daughter prefill a week of syringes on each visit
options.rationale: Tempting and sometimes used. She still depends on someone else and cannot adjust a dose herself.

options.text: Advise her to use a brighter overhead kitchen light
options.rationale: More light can add glare and does not make fine markings readable with retinal damage.

questions.takeaway: Adapt the task to the senses that still work. Keep the client as independent as safety allows.
questions.strategy: Two options are safe. The stem says she lives alone and wants to do it herself, and that picks the one that keeps her in charge.

steps.action: Cut the option that does not fix the problem
steps.detail: Bright light does not restore fine vision.
A neighbor or daughter makes her dependent.
She wants to manage her own insulin.

elimination.verdict: The insulin pen with audible clicks.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old says she cannot tell where her feet are when she walks to the bathroom at night. Which statement shows the home safety teaching was effective?

options.text: "I keep the hall dark so I fall back asleep faster."
options.rationale: In the dark she loses the one sense that can stand in for position sense.

options.text: "I wear thick cushioned socks so my steps are softer."
options.rationale: Sounds protective, but padding dulls what her feet can still feel and socks slip.

options.text: "I walk there quickly so I am up for less time."
options.rationale: Tempting as less time at risk. Hurrying with poor position sense makes a misstep more likely.

options.text: "I leave a hall light on and hold the handrail."
options.rationale: Position sense declines after 60, so she replaces it with vision and a secure rail.

questions.takeaway: When a sense declines, safety depends on replacing it with another cue, such as light and a handrail, not on being careful with the sense that is fading.
questions.strategy: Ask of each statement: does it give her another way to know where her feet are?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Position sense in the feet, an expected change after 60.
A dark hall and padded socks.
Speed does not replace a sense.
Light and a handrail.

elimination.verdict: The hall light and handrail statement.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with chronic pain on a step-down unit is restless and cannot focus. Staff enter hourly at night for separate vital signs, laboratory draws and repositioning. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Request a prescription for a medication to help him sleep
options.rationale: Tempting, because he is not resting. A drug adds another factor that alters perception and leaves the cause in place.

options.text: Request transfer to a private room at the end of the hall
options.rationale: Tempting, because it lowers noise. The interruptions come from the care schedule and would follow him.

options.text: Combine the night tasks and schedule protected rest periods
options.rationale: Correct. The stem names the cause, hourly separate entries, and clustering care removes it.

options.text: Reorient him to place and time at every entry
options.rationale: Reorientation helps confusion. Doing it at every entry adds more stimulation.

questions.takeaway: Sensory overload: combine activities, schedule rest, set quiet time. Fix the environment before adding a drug.
questions.strategy: Find the cause in the stem. It is the schedule, not the room and not the client.

steps.detail: Hourly separate entries at night.
Reorienting at every entry is more stimulation.

steps.action: Test the room and the drug
steps.detail: Neither one changes how often staff walk in.

elimination.verdict: Combine the tasks and protect rest periods.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old with macular degeneration says she manages her medications fine at home. Which assessment best tells the nurse whether that is safe?

options.text: Have her read a pill bottle label and set up a dose
options.rationale: Functional ability is judged by watching the task itself, here reading a label and preparing a dose.

options.text: Measure her visual acuity with a Snellen chart
options.rationale: Gives a number for distance vision, which does not show whether she can read a label.

options.text: Ask her daughter how she has been managing her pills at home
options.rationale: Useful background, but it is secondhand and the client is able to show the nurse directly.

options.text: Review the eye clinic's most recent examination
options.rationale: Describes the disease, not how she functions with it.

questions.takeaway: Assess function by watching the client do the task. A chart result or a report from someone else does not replace that.
questions.strategy: Three options describe her vision. One tests the thing the nurse needs to know.

steps.detail: Can she take medications safely?
Acuity, records and family report.
Label and dose in front of the nurse.

elimination.verdict: Watch her read the label and set up a dose.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old carpenter has ringing in his ears after work, and testing shows mild high frequency hearing loss. He says the damage is already done. Which teaching is the priority?

options.text: Have his hearing tested again each year
options.rationale: Tempting and worthwhile, but testing only measures loss. It does not prevent it.

options.text: Wear ear protection every time the saws are running
options.rationale: Noise damage is permanent and keeps adding up, so protection at every exposure prevents further loss.

options.text: Ask about a hearing aid for the loss he has
options.rationale: Mild loss does not need a device yet, and an aid does not stop more damage.

options.text: Rest in a quiet room for an hour after every work shift
options.rationale: Eases the ringing without reducing the exposure that causes it.

questions.takeaway: Noise related hearing loss cannot be reversed. The nurse's priority is prevention of more loss with consistent protection.
questions.strategy: Screening and prevention both sound right. Ask which one changes what happens to his hearing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: More exposure means more loss.
A yearly test only records it.
Protection at each exposure.

elimination.verdict: Ear protection at every exposure.

questions.stem: The nurse taught the wife of a 66-year-old with expressive aphasia how to communicate with him. Which observation shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: She finishes his sentences when he pauses
options.rationale: This takes away his chance to speak and raises frustration.

options.text: She speaks louder and repeats each question twice
options.rationale: Expressive aphasia is a problem producing words, not hearing or understanding them. Volume does not help him speak.

options.text: She asks whether he wants tea, then waits for his nod
options.rationale: Correct. A yes or no question with time to answer lets him communicate with what he still has.

options.text: She points to objects and asks him to name each one
options.rationale: Naming on demand is the hardest task for him and turns conversation into a test.

questions.takeaway: Expressive aphasia: listen patiently, ask yes or no questions, use a board, allow time.
questions.strategy: Ask which option lowers the amount of speech he has to produce and gives him time.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the options that speak for him
steps.detail: Finishing his sentences.

steps.action: Cut the options that treat the wrong problem
steps.detail: Loud speech treats hearing loss.
Naming objects demands the skill he lost.

elimination.verdict: A yes or no question, then waiting.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old who wears contact lenses was taught lens care after an eye irritation. Which statement shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I rinse them with tap water if I run out of solution."
options.rationale: Tap water is not sterile and carries organisms to the cornea.

options.text: "I top off the solution in the case each night."
options.rationale: Sounds thrifty and careful, but old solution loses its disinfecting effect.

options.text: "I keep them in if my eye is only a little red."
options.rationale: A red eye is the signal to remove the lenses, not to wait.

options.text: "I take them out before I sleep or swim."
options.rationale: Removing lenses for sleep and water keeps organisms from being trapped against the cornea.

questions.takeaway: Proper contact lens care is prevention. Lenses come out for sleep, water and any redness.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that reduces contact between the cornea and organisms.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Tap water rinse.
Topping off.
Redness means remove them.

elimination.verdict: Out before sleep or swimming.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old arrives on the unit at night, and the emergency department reports him as confused because he answers questions inappropriately. His daughter is at the bedside with his belongings. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Start a bed alarm and move him near the nurses' station
options.rationale: Tempting, because safety matters for a confused client. The cause is not known yet, and the answer may be in the bag of belongings.

options.text: Ask the daughter whether he uses hearing aids or glasses
options.rationale: Correct. Establishing the baseline comes first, and an uncorrected hearing deficit looks like confusion.

options.text: Request a prescription for a urinalysis and blood work
options.rationale: Reasonable if the confusion is real. A quick baseline check comes before testing.

options.text: Reorient him to place and time every hour
options.rationale: Reorientation does not help a client who cannot hear it.

questions.takeaway: In acute care, establish the baseline. Know whether the client already has a deficit before you label the behavior.
questions.strategy: Here the assessment is not done. The daughter and the belongings are the stem's way of telling you where to look.

steps.detail: Only that his answers do not match the questions.
Asking about hearing aids and glasses.
Alarm, laboratory work and reorientation all assume the confusion is real.

elimination.verdict: Ask the daughter about hearing aids and glasses.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old received his first hearing aid. Which statement shows he understood the teaching?

options.text: "At bedtime I will take it out, turn it off and open the battery door."
options.rationale: Correct. This saves the battery and lets moisture dry out.

options.text: "I will leave it in while I shower so I can hear the smoke alarm."
options.rationale: Water damages the aid. A flashing alert system covers alarm safety.

options.text: "I will put it in before I use hairspray so it stays in place."
options.rationale: Spray clogs the microphone. It goes in after hair products.

options.text: "If it whistles I will turn the volume up until it stops."
options.rationale: Whistling means poor fit or too much volume. Turning it up makes it worse.

questions.takeaway: Hearing aid care: keep it dry, off and open at night, in after hair products, reseat it if it whistles.
questions.strategy: Test each statement against two enemies of a hearing aid: moisture and blockage.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The shower.
Hairspray on the aid.
More volume increases feedback.

elimination.verdict: Out, off and battery door open at bedtime.

questions.stem: An 87-year-old with cataracts becomes agitated at dusk and tries to climb out of bed. The room is dim and her glasses are on the windowsill. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Turn on the bed alarm and raise all side rails
options.rationale: Tempting, because she is trying to get up. An alarm reports the attempt and does nothing about why she is frightened, and four rails act as a restraint.

options.text: Request a prescription for a sitter overnight
options.rationale: A sitter may be needed later. A simpler step has not been tried.

options.text: Turn on soft lighting and put her glasses on
options.rationale: Correct. Aging pupils and cataracts need more light, and the stem shows both the light and the glasses are missing.

options.text: Request a prescription for a low dose sedative
options.rationale: A sedative adds fall risk and clouds perception further.

questions.takeaway: Older eyes adapt poorly to the dark. Correct the light and the device before using alarms, sitters or drugs.
questions.strategy: Use the least restrictive fix that matches the cause. The stem gives the cause in its second sentence.

steps.detail: Dim room, no glasses.
Light and glasses, then alarm, then sitter, then sedative.

steps.action: Start at the bottom of that list
steps.detail: It also treats the cause.

elimination.verdict: Soft lighting and her glasses.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old with muffled hearing and ear fullness had impacted cerumen removed by irrigation. Which finding best shows the treatment was effective?

options.text: He denies pain in the ear
options.rationale: Pain was not the problem being treated. This shows no harm, not benefit.

options.text: He reports no dizziness or nausea after the procedure
options.rationale: This means he tolerated the irrigation. It says nothing about his hearing.

options.text: The return fluid ran clear at the end
options.rationale: Clear return suggests the wax is out. It does not confirm that function returned.

options.text: He repeats words the nurse whispers from 2 feet away
options.rationale: Correct. The problem was conductive hearing loss, so restored hearing is the outcome that counts.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate by the problem you treated. Cerumen impaction is a correctable conductive loss, so check hearing.
questions.strategy: Separate three ideas: the procedure went safely, the wax came out, the hearing came back. The question asks about the third.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Muffled hearing.
No pain and no dizziness.
Clear return is about the wax. Whispered words are about the client.

elimination.verdict: He repeats whispered words.

questions.stem: An 89-year-old began an opioid and a sleeping pill 2 nights ago. She now misjudges the distance to her chair and reaches for objects that are not there. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Request an eye examination for new glasses
options.rationale: Tempting because the problem looks visual, but vision does not change in two nights without a cause.

options.text: Review the two new medications with the provider
options.rationale: The change is new and began with drugs known to alter perception, so the cause is addressed first.

options.text: Place a clock and calendar and reorient her
options.rationale: Right for deprivation. Her cues began with new medications, not with too little stimulation.

options.text: Explain to the family that perception declines with age
options.rationale: A new change is not assumed to be aging.

questions.takeaway: Opioids and psychotropic drugs can impair perception. A new sensory change is traced to its cause before it is called aging.
questions.strategy: Use the timing. What started 2 nights ago?

steps.detail: Two nights, not years.
Opioid and sleeping pill started then.

steps.action: Cut the fixes for other causes
steps.detail: Glasses, reorientation, reassurance.

elimination.verdict: Review the new medications with the provider.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old with both eyes patched after a chemical splash is admitted. His hearing is normal. Which actions does the nurse include in his care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Describe the room layout and let him touch the call bell
options.rationale: Touch and description replace sight. He must be able to find the call bell without help.

options.text: Keep his water, tissues and telephone in the same places
options.rationale: A consistent layout is what lets him move safely on his own.

options.text: Say who you are on entering and say when you are leaving
options.rationale: He cannot see who came in or whether anyone is still there.

options.text: Speak louder and more slowly than usual
options.rationale: His hearing is intact. Speak in a normal voice.

options.text: Move the furniture each shift to suit the staff workflow
options.rationale: Every change in layout erases the map he has learned.

questions.takeaway: Sudden vision loss: orient fully, keep things in the same place, announce yourself, speak normally.
questions.strategy: Judge each option alone. Ask whether it helps a person who can hear and cannot see.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Touch, description, announcing and a fixed layout.

steps.action: Cut the option that treats the wrong sense
steps.detail: Loud, slow speech is for hearing loss.
Moving furniture.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C.

questions.nursesNote: 0900: 82-year-old admitted 2 days ago with heart failure. Needs a brighter lamp to read the menu. Has trouble telling the blue cup from the green one. Misses high pitched voices in conversation. Says the left ear "went quiet" when she woke today. Started IV furosemide yesterday. Unsteady when standing this morning, steady yesterday.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow-up and should not be attributed to aging.

segments.text: Needs a brighter lamp to read the menu
segments.rationale: Aging pupils dilate less, so more light is needed. Expected.

segments.text: Has trouble telling the blue cup from the green one
segments.rationale: Blue and green discrimination declines with age. Expected.

segments.text: Misses high pitched voices in conversation
segments.rationale: High frequencies are lost first in presbycusis. Expected and gradual.

segments.text: Says the left ear "went quiet" when she woke today
segments.rationale: Sudden hearing loss in one ear is new, not aging. It needs prompt evaluation.

segments.text: Started IV furosemide yesterday
segments.rationale: A loop diuretic is ototoxic, and the timing fits the new hearing loss. The provider needs to know.

segments.text: Unsteady when standing this morning, steady yesterday
segments.rationale: A new balance change with an ear change raises fall risk and points to the inner ear.

questions.takeaway: Gradual and both sides is aging. Sudden, one sided or new since yesterday is reported, and you look for an ototoxic drug.
questions.strategy: For each finding ask whether it came on slowly over years or appeared since admission.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: More light, blue and green, high pitches.
The left ear and the new unsteadiness.
The diuretic started the day before.

elimination.verdict: Left ear went quiet, IV furosemide, new unsteadiness.

questions.scenario: A 61-year-old in the emergency department observation unit for 30 hours was restless and anxious with racing thoughts. The nurse lowered alarm volumes, combined care tasks and set quiet time. Six hours later the nurse reassesses.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether the plan to reduce sensory overload was effective or not effective.

rows.text: Naps for 90 minutes without interruption in the afternoon
rows.rationale: Protected rest is the goal of clustered care and quiet time.

rows.text: Picks at his IV dressing and tubing
rows.rationale: Playing with tubes and dressings is a behavior of overload that is still present.

rows.text: Follows a 10 minute teaching session and asks relevant questions
rows.rationale: Attention is no longer scattered.

rows.text: Needs reorientation each time staff enter
rows.rationale: Constant reorientation shows his brain is still not sorting the input.

rows.text: States the alarms no longer startle him since the volume was lowered
rows.rationale: The stimulus was reduced and he reports the change himself.

questions.takeaway: Overload resolves as rest, focused attention and leaving equipment alone. Picking at tubes and repeated reorientation mean it continues.
questions.strategy: Compare each finding with how he looked before: restless, anxious, scattered. Better or the same?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Mark rest and focus as improvement
steps.detail: The nap, the teaching session and his own report.
Picking at tubing and needing reorientation.

elimination.verdict: Effective, not effective, effective, not effective, effective.

questions.stem: A clinic nurse reviews four messages. Which client does the nurse call first?

options.text: Cataract surgery yesterday, eye itchy with slightly blurred vision
options.rationale: Itching and mild blurring are expected early; best vision takes weeks.

options.text: Meniere disease, vomiting during a spinning attack since morning
options.rationale: Dramatic and miserable, and expected for an attack. She needs safety and antiemetics, not emergency care.

options.text: Cataract surgery yesterday, worsening pain in that eye with nausea
options.rationale: Pain with nausea after eye surgery suggests rising pressure in the eye and must be reported at once.

options.text: Open-angle glaucoma, halos and narrowing side vision for months
options.rationale: Real damage, and gradual. It is chronic and needs follow-up, not a call first.

questions.takeaway: After eye surgery, pain with nausea is never expected. Acute and unexpected beats chronic and dramatic.
questions.strategy: Two clients had the same surgery. Compare their symptoms against what is expected the day after.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Months of halos is not new.
Vomiting with vertigo fits Meniere disease.
Itching is expected. Worsening pain with nausea is not.

elimination.verdict: The surgical client with worsening pain and nausea.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old with expressive aphasia grimaces and holds his abdomen. An as-needed analgesic is prescribed for his knee pain. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the as-needed analgesic and reassess within the hour
options.rationale: Defensible because he is clearly in pain. The site is new and unassessed, and the drug was ordered for his knee.

options.text: Ask his wife what she thinks he is feeling
options.rationale: A family member's guess replaces his own report. Expressive aphasia leaves understanding intact, so he can still answer yes or no.

options.text: Wait at the bedside until he finds the words
options.rationale: Patience is part of aphasia care. On its own it delays assessment of a new pain.

options.text: Ask yes or no questions about the pain with a board
options.rationale: The assessment is not done yet. Yes or no questions and a board let him tell the nurse where and what the pain is.

questions.takeaway: Aphasia changes how you assess, not whether you assess. Use yes or no questions and a board before treating a new complaint.
questions.strategy: Treating the grimace feels kind. Check whether the nurse knows what is being treated.

steps.detail: Abdomen now, analgesic ordered for the knee.
Location and type of pain are unknown.

steps.action: Pick the method that fits aphasia
steps.detail: Yes or no questions and a board.

elimination.verdict: Assess the pain with yes or no questions and a board.

questions.stem: An older adult with long-standing cataracts and presbycusis ate from only the right half of his tray at lunch and walked into the left door frame. Yesterday he did neither. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Assess him now for other new changes
options.rationale: A one-sided change since yesterday is new and unexplained, so the nurse assesses before adapting the room.

options.text: Brighten the room and reduce the glare
options.rationale: The usual first step for his known deficits and tempting here. Cataracts blur the whole field gradually, not one side overnight.

options.text: Have the tray and call bell placed on his right
options.rationale: A sensible adaptation that accepts the change without finding out why it happened.

options.text: Document the change as progression of his cataracts
options.rationale: Cataract change is slow and painless over months.

questions.takeaway: A new or sudden sensory change is never assumed to be the old problem getting worse. Assess it.
questions.strategy: Compare the finding with what his known conditions do. Gradual and whole field does not match sudden and one-sided.

steps.detail: Different from yesterday.
Left side only.
Cataracts and aging do not act this way.

elimination.verdict: Assess him now for other new changes.

questions.stem: A client with hearing loss nodded and said yes throughout insulin pen teaching. The nurse sat facing him in good light and spoke slowly. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Give him the steps in writing to take home
options.rationale: Defensible because written information supports hearing loss. It reinforces the teaching without showing whether he understood.

options.text: Have him show the steps with the pen
options.rationale: Nodding is not understanding. A return demonstration is the only way to evaluate what he took in.

options.text: Repeat the teaching with his better ear toward the nurse
options.rationale: A good technique, but the delivery was already sound and the gap is evaluation.

options.text: Document that the teaching was done and understood
options.rationale: A nod is a social response and many people with hearing loss nod to avoid asking again.

questions.takeaway: With hearing loss, agreement is not evidence. Evaluate teaching by having the client show or explain it back.
questions.strategy: The nurse already communicated well. Ask which nursing process step is still missing.

steps.detail: Facing, lit and slow were all done.
Evaluation.
Supports learning, does not measure it.

elimination.verdict: Have him demonstrate the steps.

questions.stem: A client with Meniere disease follows a low-sodium diet and takes a diuretic. She reports fewer vertigo attacks this month, and says she twice dropped to the floor with no dizziness beforehand. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Reinforce the plan because the attacks have decreased
options.rationale: Fewer attacks is real progress. The two falls show a new and more dangerous problem.

options.text: Teach her to sit down when dizziness begins
options.rationale: Standard teaching for vertigo. These falls came with no warning, so there is nothing to act on.

options.text: Report the falls and add fall precautions
options.rationale: Sudden falls without warning are drop attacks. They mark a serious safety risk that the current plan does not cover.

options.text: Refer her for balance exercises with therapy
options.rationale: Vestibular rehabilitation helps balance and tempts. It does not prevent a sudden drop with no warning.

questions.takeaway: Fewer vertigo attacks does not mean safer. Falls without warning in Meniere disease are drop attacks and change the safety plan.
questions.strategy: The good news comes first in the stem. Read to the end and ask what the falls had in common.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fewer vertigo attacks.
Two falls with no dizziness first.
Sitting when dizzy needs a warning she does not get.

elimination.verdict: Report and add fall precautions.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old who lives alone says food has had no smell or taste since a viral illness. She cooks on a gas stove. Which plan is the priority?

options.text: Suggest stronger seasonings and varied textures
options.rationale: A sound plan for appetite, and it is the tempting choice. It does nothing about a leak or fire she cannot smell.

options.text: Refer her to a dietitian for weight checks
options.rationale: Reasonable follow-up for intake, but weight loss is a slower risk than gas or smoke.

options.text: Encourage eating meals with her neighbors
options.rationale: Helps intake and isolation. It does not address the hazard in her kitchen.

options.text: Install gas and smoke detectors, and date leftovers
options.rationale: Smell is her warning system for gas, smoke and spoiled food. Detectors and dated food replace it.

questions.takeaway: Loss of smell is a safety problem before it is a nutrition problem. Replace the missing warning sense.
questions.strategy: Three options improve eating. The stem adds one detail, a gas stove, that makes safety outrank appetite.

steps.detail: Lives alone, gas stove, cannot smell.
Three address eating. One addresses danger.
Safety comes before comfort and nutrition.

elimination.verdict: Detectors and dated food first.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old with diabetic neuropathy says his feet are always cold in bed and asks for a heating pad. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Provide warm socks and an extra blanket
options.rationale: Warms the feet with no heat source that can burn skin he cannot feel.

options.text: Apply the heating pad on its low setting
options.rationale: Tempting because it honors his request, but he cannot feel a burn developing even on low.

options.text: Soak his feet in warm water before bed
options.rationale: He cannot judge water temperature with his feet, and soaking dries the skin.

options.text: Apply the pad and check his skin hourly
options.rationale: Checking finds a burn after it happens. The safer plan avoids the heat source.

questions.takeaway: When touch is impaired, remove the heat source instead of relying on the client to feel it.
questions.strategy: Ask what protects skin that cannot report pain. Lower heat and more checks still leave the hazard in place.

steps.detail: Reduced sensation in the feet.
Three options apply direct heat.
Socks and a blanket meet the need safely.

elimination.verdict: Warm socks and a blanket.

questions.stem: A 90-year-old resident removes her hearing aids in the dining room, saying the clatter is unbearable, and now eats alone in her room. Which plan is best?

options.text: Serve her meals in her room as she prefers
options.rationale: Respects her choice in the moment, which makes it tempting, but it deepens the isolation the hearing loss started.

options.text: Remind her to keep the aids in at meals
options.rationale: The aids amplify the clatter along with the voices. The reminder does not fix why she takes them out.

options.text: Seat her at a small table away from the kitchen
options.rationale: Lowers background noise so the aids help with speech, and keeps her eating with others.

options.text: Ask the audiologist to fit stronger hearing aids
options.rationale: More amplification makes the background noise louder too.

questions.takeaway: Hearing aids amplify everything. Cut the background noise so the client can stay in the room and in the conversation.
questions.strategy: The problem is the amount of stimuli, not the aids. Choose the option that changes the environment and keeps her social.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Noise is amplified, so she removes the aids.
A reminder and stronger aids leave the clatter.
Eating alone ends the noise and the contact. A quiet table ends only the noise.

elimination.verdict: Small table away from the kitchen.

questions.stem: A withdrawn long-term care resident sits all day beside a television tuned to news she ignores. Her chart notes she taught piano for 40 years. Which plan is best?

options.text: Play piano recordings she chooses each day
options.rationale: Stimuli only help when they mean something to her. Music she picks ties to her life and invites a response.

options.text: Seat her by the nurses' station for more activity
options.rationale: Tempting because it adds people and sound, but more input is not meaningful input and can tip into overload.

options.text: Raise the television volume so she can follow
options.rationale: She is ignoring the program, not straining to hear it. Louder noise adds nothing she values.

options.text: Request a depression evaluation from the provider
options.rationale: Reasonable if withdrawal continues, but the nurse first corrects the lack of meaningful stimuli that can cause it.

questions.takeaway: Deprivation is about the quality of stimuli, not the amount. Choose input that means something to this client.
questions.strategy: The television shows she already has stimulation. Ask which option uses the one personal detail in the stem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Plenty of noise, nothing meaningful.
Louder television and a busy hallway add amount, not meaning.
A nursing measure tied to her history comes before a referral.

elimination.verdict: Piano recordings she chooses.

questions.stem: The nurse advised a 94-year-old bothered by glare to replace bare fluorescent tubes and cover her glossy kitchen table. Which finding best shows the changes worked?

options.text: She says the kitchen feels much cozier now
options.rationale: Pleasant, but it does not show she sees better.

options.text: She keeps the curtains closed all day
options.rationale: She is still avoiding light, and an aging eye needs more light, not less.

options.text: She wears sunglasses while reading indoors
options.rationale: A workaround that tells you glare is still a problem and cuts the light she needs.

options.text: She reads her mail at the table without squinting
options.rationale: A functional outcome at the exact spot that was changed. She can now use her vision there.

questions.takeaway: Judge an environmental change by function: can the client now do the task the glare was blocking?
questions.strategy: Look for what she can do, not how she feels about the room. Two options show she is still dodging light.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Less glare so she can see to do tasks.
Closed curtains and indoor sunglasses mean glare persists.
Reading at the table is measurable.

elimination.verdict: Reads mail at the table without squinting.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old who has trouble seeing while driving at dusk was taught safer driving habits. Which statement shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I put on tinted glasses once the sun starts setting."
options.rationale: Tempting for headlight glare, but tint removes light from an eye that already adapts poorly to the dark.

options.text: "I follow the taillights of the car ahead."
options.rationale: Following closely shortens reaction time when vision is already reduced.

options.text: "I plan my errands so I am home before dusk."
options.rationale: Removes the low light condition altogether, which is the safest adaptation.

options.text: "I keep the dashboard lights turned up bright."
options.rationale: A bright cabin makes the road outside look darker.

questions.takeaway: When dark adaptation is poor, avoid the low light situation instead of trying to see through it.
questions.strategy: Three statements keep him driving in the dark with a trick. One changes when he drives.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Poor vision in low light.
Tint, tailgating and bright dash lights all reduce what he sees or his time to react.

steps.action: Keep the one that avoids the hazard
steps.detail: Daylight driving.

elimination.verdict: Home before dusk.

questions.stem: The nurse taught the son of a 91-year-old with hearing loss how to talk with her. Which observation shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: He repeats the same sentence more slowly each time
options.rationale: Slowing helps, but when a sentence is missed he should rephrase it, not repeat it.

options.text: He touches her arm and waits until she looks up
options.rationale: Gets her attention first so she can use his face and lips from the first word.

options.text: He speaks loudly close to her better ear
options.rationale: Tempting because the better ear matters, but loud speech distorts and she loses his face.

options.text: He answers the nurse's questions on her behalf
options.rationale: Takes her out of the conversation.

questions.takeaway: With hearing loss, get attention and face the person before the first word. Rephrase what is missed.
questions.strategy: Ask which behavior gives her the most cues. Volume and repetition add sound, not understanding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Attention first, face to face, clear normal speech, rephrase.
Repeating and loud speech each break one rule.
She is left out.

elimination.verdict: Touches her arm and waits for eye contact.

questions.stem: A home health nurse visits a 93-year-old with reduced vision and poor balance. Which observations does the nurse identify as hazards to correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A throw rug at the end of the hallway
options.rationale: A loose edge is a trip risk she may not see.

options.text: A raised threshold between the kitchen and hall
options.rationale: Thresholds should be level. She cannot judge the height change.

options.text: A bare bulb reflecting off a waxed floor
options.rationale: Glare washes out what she can see. Light should be bright and diffused.

options.text: Medications kept in the same kitchen drawer
options.rationale: Consistent locations help a person with low vision find things.

options.text: A dark handrail mounted on a pale wall
options.rationale: Sharp contrast makes the rail easy to find.

options.text: Newspapers stacked beside her chair
options.rationale: Clutter in a walking path is a fall hazard.

questions.takeaway: For low vision at home: clear the path, level the floor, cut glare, and keep contrast and consistent placement.
questions.strategy: Judge each item alone. Ask whether it makes the space less predictable or harder to see.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rug, threshold and stacked papers.
Bare bulb on a shiny floor is glare.
Same drawer and a contrasting rail are adaptations.

elimination.verdict: Rug, threshold, glare and clutter.

questions.scenario: A daughter is preparing her home for her mother, who has moderate hearing loss in both ears, wears hearing aids by day and is moving in next week. The daughter lists what she plans to do.
questions.stem: For each plan, indicate whether it supports or does not support the client's safety and communication.

rows.text: A doorbell and smoke alarm that flash a light
rows.rationale: A visual alert replaces a sound she may miss, most of all at night with her aids out.

rows.text: Keeping the television on in the background for company
rows.rationale: Background noise competes with voices and makes her aids less useful.

rows.text: An amplified telephone in her bedroom
rows.rationale: Lets her make and take calls on her own, including a call for help.

rows.text: Calling to her from the next room at mealtimes
rows.rationale: She needs the speaker's face. Go to her and get her attention first.

rows.text: Writing down appointment times and medication changes
rows.rationale: Written information backs up speech for details that must not be misheard.

rows.text: Answering the provider's questions for her at visits
rows.rationale: Saves time, but it removes her from her own care and hides what she did not hear.

questions.takeaway: For hearing loss at home: replace sound alerts with light, amplify the phone, write key details, cut background noise and keep her speaking for herself.
questions.strategy: Test each plan with one question: does it give her another way to get the message, or does it add noise or take her place?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Keep what replaces or boosts sound
steps.detail: Flashing alerts, amplified phone, written notes.

steps.action: Cut what adds noise or distance
steps.detail: Background television and calling from another room.
She stays the one who answers.

elimination.verdict: Supports: flashing alerts, amplified phone, written notes. The other three do not.

questions.stem: A sedated 47-year-old on a ventilator does not respond to voice. The assistive personnel bathes him without speaking to him while discussing his prognosis with a coworker. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Have staff tell him each step before touching him
options.rationale: His ears may still receive sound even though no one can confirm what he perceives. Talking to him gives meaningful input and protects his dignity.

options.text: Turn on the television to give him background orientation
options.rationale: Unselected noise is not meaningful stimulation, and it does not fix the bedside conversation.

options.text: Ask staff to work quietly so he can rest
options.rationale: Tempting because rest matters. Silence during touch removes the only meaningful input he gets.

options.text: Document that he cannot perceive speech
options.rationale: Perception cannot be measured in a sedated client, so the nurse does not assume it is absent.

questions.takeaway: Reception can continue when response is absent. Speak to the unresponsive client as if he hears every word.
questions.strategy: No response tells you about reaction. It tells you nothing certain about reception. Choose the option that assumes he hears.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reception, perception, reaction. Only reaction is visibly missing.
Documenting that he cannot perceive claims something nobody tested.
Quiet removes input. Explanation supplies meaningful input.

elimination.verdict: Explain each step to him before touching.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old stone mason was treated for a chip in his eye and taught eye protection. Which observation at his next visit shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: He wears dark sunglasses while cutting stone
options.rationale: Sunglasses cut glare and ultraviolet light. They leave the sides open and are not impact rated.

options.text: He wears wraparound safety glasses while cutting stone
options.rationale: Impact rated eyewear with side coverage worn during the hazard is the behavior the teaching aimed for.

options.text: He keeps saline in the truck to rinse his eyes
options.rationale: Useful after an exposure. It treats the injury and does not prevent it.

options.text: He looks away when the saw throws chips
options.rationale: Chips travel faster than he can turn.

questions.takeaway: Prevention of occupational eye injury means protective eyewear made for the hazard, worn every time the hazard is present.
questions.strategy: Ask which option prevents the injury and which only responds to it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Saline is response.
Only one covers the sides and resists impact.
Turning away is not protection.

elimination.verdict: Wraparound safety glasses during the task.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old with worsening vision and diabetes has missed three eye appointments. He says, "I know I should go." Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Ask what has kept him from getting to the visits
options.rationale: He already knows the importance. The barrier, such as cost, transportation or time off work, has to be identified before any plan fits.

options.text: Explain again how diabetes damages the retina
options.rationale: He states he knows he should go, so more teaching answers a question he did not ask.

options.text: Book the next available appointment for him
options.rationale: Tempting because it is action. A fourth appointment fails for the same unknown reason.

options.text: Refer him to social services for assistance
options.rationale: May be the right step once the barrier is known.

questions.takeaway: Missed care is often an access problem, not a knowledge problem. Find the barrier before you teach or refer.
questions.strategy: His own words rule out one option. Then ask whether the nurse knows enough to act yet.

steps.detail: He knows he should go, so repeating the teaching adds nothing.
Nobody has asked why he misses visits.
Booking and referral come after the barrier is named.

elimination.verdict: Ask him what gets in the way.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old who plans to become pregnant next year does not know whether she had rubella vaccine as a child. Which plan best protects her baby's hearing and vision?

options.text: Give the rubella vaccine once pregnancy is confirmed
options.rationale: A live vaccine is not given during pregnancy.

options.text: Arrange hearing and vision screening for the newborn at birth
options.rationale: Screening detects a loss after it happens. The question asks for protection.

options.text: Check rubella immunity now and vaccinate before conception
options.rationale: Rubella in pregnancy damages the developing ear and eye. The vaccine is live, so immunity is settled before pregnancy.

options.text: Advise her to avoid sick contacts while pregnant
options.rationale: Helpful, and far less reliable than immunity.

questions.takeaway: Immunization prevents infectious causes of sensory loss. Rubella immunity is confirmed before pregnancy, not during it.
questions.strategy: Two options act on the vaccine at opposite times. Timing decides.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Vaccinate before conception or after pregnancy is confirmed.
Not during pregnancy.
Newborn screening finds a loss. It does not prevent one.

elimination.verdict: Check immunity now and vaccinate before conception.

questions.stem: Staff were asked to keep the belongings of a 72-year-old with severe low vision in fixed places. Which finding best shows the plan is working?

options.text: She calls staff promptly whenever she needs her water
options.rationale: Shows she depends on staff, which is what the plan was meant to reduce.

options.text: A sign over the bed lists where each item belongs
options.rationale: A sign is a step in the plan. It does not show the result for the client.

options.text: She can describe where each of her belongings is usually kept
options.rationale: Tempting. Knowing the usual place does not show the items are actually there.

options.text: After cleaning she finds her call light and water unaided
options.rationale: Finding her own things after the room has been disturbed shows the placement stayed consistent and usable.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate an environmental plan by what the client can do on her own, not by whether staff completed a step.
questions.strategy: Outcome questions ask what the client does. Cross out anything that is a staff action.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A sign is an intervention.
Calling for water is the problem continuing.
Finding the items beats describing them.

elimination.verdict: She finds her call light and water without help.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old with receptive aphasia after a stroke looks at the nurse blankly when told, "It is time to take your morning pills." Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Repeat the sentence more slowly and loudly
options.rationale: Receptive aphasia is a problem understanding language, not hearing it, so volume does not help.

options.text: Give him a written card that says pills
options.rationale: Reading uses the same language comprehension that is impaired.

options.text: Hand him the cup and mime swallowing
options.rationale: He cannot decode spoken or written words, so the message is sent by gesture and demonstration.

options.text: Ask him yes or no questions about the pills
options.rationale: That is the approach for expressive aphasia, where he understands and cannot find words.

questions.takeaway: Receptive aphasia: he cannot understand words. Use gestures, demonstration and short simple cues. Yes or no questions are for expressive aphasia.
questions.strategy: Decide which direction of language is broken. Three options still rely on words.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Understanding, not speaking.
Louder speech, a written card and questions all need comprehension.
Gesture and demonstration.

elimination.verdict: Show him. Hand him the cup and mime the action.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old has lost the left half of the visual field in both eyes after a stroke and is a fall risk. Where does the nurse place the call light and bedside table?

options.text: On his left, so that he must practice scanning to find them
options.rationale: Tempting as rehabilitation. A call light he cannot see fails him the first time he needs it.

options.text: On his right, while teaching him to turn his head left
options.rationale: Safety items go where he can see them now. Scanning toward the blind side is taught so he learns to compensate.

options.text: At the foot of the bed, centered in front of him
options.rationale: Out of reach, and half of it still falls in the lost field.

options.text: On whichever side the staff find most convenient
options.rationale: Placement follows his visual field, not staff workflow.

questions.takeaway: With a visual field loss, put safety items in the intact field and teach scanning toward the lost side.
questions.strategy: Safety before rehabilitation. The call light has to work today.

steps.detail: Right side or left side.
He must be able to see and reach the call light now.
The key still teaches head turning.

elimination.verdict: Intact side, plus scanning practice.

questions.scenario: The charge nurse reviews four clients whose behavior has changed.
questions.stem: For each client, indicate whether the plan should add meaningful stimulation or reduce stimulation.

rows.text: On bed rest for 11 days in a private room, bored, misjudges the time of day
rows.rationale: Restricted environment with poor time judgment is deprivation.

rows.text: In the emergency department hallway for 9 hours, restless, startles at each overhead page
rows.rationale: Constant noise and activity that she cannot filter.

rows.text: Resident with no visitors this month, sits facing a blank wall and is tearful
rows.rationale: Loss of social contact and meaningful input.

rows.text: Chronic pain, hourly checks overnight, picks at the dressing and cannot focus
rows.rationale: Pain plus frequent monitoring is the overload setting.

rows.text: Both eyes patched after surgery, quiet room, reports seeing shapes that are not there
rows.rationale: Removing vision in a quiet room starves the brain of input, and perceptual changes follow.

questions.takeaway: Deprivation shows as boredom, withdrawal and distorted time or perception. Overload shows as restlessness and scattered attention. The plans are opposites.
questions.strategy: Read the setting before the behavior. Isolation, bed rest and patches take input away. Hallways, alarms and hourly checks pile it on.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Private room, no visitors and patched eyes are low input.
Hallway and hourly checks are high input.
Bored or tearful against restless and startled.

elimination.verdict: Add, reduce, add, reduce, add.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old hears better with his right ear than his left. The nurse must teach him about a new medication at the bedside. Which setup does the nurse use?

options.text: Stand at his right side, facing him, at a normal volume
options.rationale: Puts the voice at the better ear and keeps the nurse's face in view, with no shouting.

options.text: Stand at his left side, facing him, at a normal volume
options.rationale: The side is off. The left is his weaker ear, so more words are lost.

options.text: Stand at his right side, speaking from behind his shoulder
options.rationale: The side is right, but he cannot see the nurse's lips and expressions.

options.text: Stand at his right side, facing him, with the voice raised to a shout
options.rationale: The position is right, but shouting raises the pitch and distorts the words.

questions.takeaway: Hearing loss: move to the better ear, stay face to face, speak slowly and clearly, and do not shout.
questions.strategy: All four put the nurse at the bedside. Check three things in each: which ear, whether he can see the face, and the volume.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The stem says the right ear is better. Cut the left side.
Behind the shoulder hides the lips.
Shouting distorts speech.

elimination.verdict: Right side, facing him, normal volume.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel walks a client who is blind and steady on his feet to the dayroom. Which action by the assistive personnel needs correction?

options.text: Offers an arm so the client holds just above the elbow
options.rationale: Correct sighted guide grip. The client holds the guide.

options.text: Walks about half a step ahead of the client
options.rationale: Correct. The guide leads so the client feels turns and stops first.

options.text: Holds the client's upper arm and steers him forward from behind
options.rationale: The client is being pushed. He should hold the guide's arm and follow, so he can feel the guide's movement.

options.text: Says "doorway" before the two of them reach it
options.rationale: Correct. Changes in the path are announced before they arrive.

questions.takeaway: Sighted guide: the client holds your arm just above the elbow and follows half a step behind. You never push or pull from behind.
questions.strategy: This is a needs correction item, so three options are right. Ask in each one who is holding whom and who is in front.

steps.detail: You are looking for the one wrong technique.
In three options the nurse aide leads and the client holds on.
Only one has the aide gripping and steering from behind.

elimination.verdict: Steering him from behind needs correction.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old at home says that when she gets up at night she cannot see for a minute and has stumbled in the hall on the way to the bathroom. Which lighting setup does the nurse recommend?

options.text: A bright bedside lamp switched on, with the hall left dark
options.rationale: The path is unevenly lit. She walks from bright light into a dark hall, which is when she cannot see.

options.text: Night lights along the hall and bathroom, with a pause at each doorway
options.rationale: Gives even low light the whole way and time for the eyes to adjust. The aging pupil dilates slowly.

options.text: Night lights along the hall, with a bare bright bulb in the bathroom
options.rationale: The hall is right, but the bare bright bulb adds glare at the end of the route.

options.text: All lights left off so her eyes stay adjusted to the dark
options.rationale: No light at all. An older pupil cannot open enough to see in the dark.

questions.takeaway: Poor dark adaptation: even lighting along the whole route with night lights, and a pause in doorways. Avoid sudden changes from bright to dark and avoid glare.
questions.strategy: Compare the whole route in each option, from bed to bathroom. The right one has no sudden change in brightness.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No light does not help a pupil that dilates poorly.
Bright to dark, or dim to bare bulb, is the problem she described.
Night lights the whole way plus a pause.

elimination.verdict: Night lights along the whole route and a pause at each doorway.

questions.stem: The daughter of a 75-year-old with low vision will mark the wooden basement stairs her mother uses daily. Which plan does the nurse recommend?

options.text: A brown stripe matched to the wood on the edge of every step
options.rationale: The location is right, but the color gives no contrast, so the edges still blend in.

options.text: A bright yellow stripe on the top and bottom steps only
options.rationale: The color is right, but the middle edges are still unmarked.

options.text: Glossy white paint over the whole surface of every step
options.rationale: One color over the whole tread gives no edge contrast, and gloss adds glare.

options.text: A bright yellow stripe painted on the edge of every step
options.rationale: Sharp contrast on each edge shows where every step ends.

questions.takeaway: Stairs for low vision: sharp contrast, with the edge of every step painted bright yellow.
questions.strategy: Check two things in each plan: is the color a sharp contrast, and is every edge marked?
