options.rationale: A third blind attempt adds pain and uses up veins.

options.text: Tighten the tourniquet and lower the arm
options.rationale: Helps fill veins that are there to find. After two misses with nothing to feel, it is more of the same.

options.text: Ask the provider for an intraosseous line
options.rationale: That route is for emergencies when IV access fails, such as cardiac arrest. Nothing here is an emergency.

questions.takeaway: For difficult access, bring in ultrasound guidance and the vascular access specialist. Repeated blind attempts are not the answer.
questions.strategy: Two options repeat what already failed and one jumps to an emergency route. Look for the step in between.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two, with no vein seen or felt.
Hand vein and a tighter tourniquet are still blind sticks.
Intraosseous access is for emergencies.

elimination.verdict: Ultrasound guided insertion.

questions.stem: On day 6, a client with a nontunneled subclavian catheter is eating, takes all medications by mouth and has had no IV therapy for 2 days. The site is clean. What does the nurse do on rounds?

options.text: Change the dressing to gauze so the site can be seen daily
options.rationale: Gauze hides the site and needs changing every 2 days. It does nothing about a line with no use.

options.text: Flush each lumen and leave the line for possible later use
options.rationale: Keeping a line just in case is the habit the bundle is meant to end. Every extra day adds infection risk.

options.text: Draw blood cultures from the line as a precaution
options.rationale: Cultures are drawn for signs of infection, not as a routine on a clean site.

options.text: Ask whether the catheter can come out today
options.rationale: Daily review of need and prompt removal are part of the bundle. He no longer uses the line.

questions.takeaway: Ask every day whether the line is still needed. A central line that is not being used should come out.
questions.strategy: A clean site makes the line look harmless. The question to ask is whether it has a job, not whether it looks good.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: List what the line is used for
steps.detail: Nothing for 2 days.
Daily review and prompt removal.

steps.action: Cut the options that keep or test it
steps.detail: None of them lowers his risk.

elimination.verdict: Ask about removing the catheter today.

questions.stem: A nurse watches an orientee start a peripheral IV for maintenance fluid on an 87-year-old with thin skin and veins that roll. Which observations show the orientee's technique was correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Chose a 22 gauge catheter
options.rationale: Small, fragile veins take a 22 to 24 gauge, which is enough for maintenance fluid.

options.text: Tied the tourniquet tightly to make the veins stand out
options.rationale: A tight tourniquet bruises thin skin and can burst a fragile vein.

options.text: Held the skin with gentle traction below the site
options.rationale: Gentle traction steadies a rolling vein without tearing the skin.

options.text: Placed the catheter in a vein on the back of the hand
options.rationale: The back of the hand is avoided in older adults. The skin is thin and the veins are fragile there.

options.text: Recorded the skin condition before and after the attempt
options.rationale: Thin skin tears and bruises easily, so its condition is documented around every attempt.

options.text: Listened to the lungs after the fluid had run for a while
options.rationale: Older adults overload easily. Dyspnea, crackles and new confusion are the checks.

questions.takeaway: Older adult IV: 22 to 24 gauge, loose tourniquet, gentle traction, forearm over hand, lower rates, document the skin, watch the lungs and mental status.
questions.strategy: Picture thin skin and fragile veins. Anything forceful or on the back of the hand is wrong for her.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A tight tourniquet.
The back of the hand.

steps.action: Keep the gentle and the watchful
steps.detail: Small gauge, light traction, skin notes, lung checks.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A 68-year-old is to receive maintenance fluid at 25 mL per hour by gravity. To count the slow rate accurately the nurse chooses [[1]].

At 0800 the nurse finds his bag was spiked at 0600 the previous day and is one third full. The nurse [[2]].

His catheter site is covered with a dry, intact gauze dressing dated 2 days ago. The nurse [[3]].

options.text: a microdrip set, 60 drops per mL
options.rationale: At 60 drops per mL, 25 mL per hour is 25 drops per minute, which is easy to count and adjust.

options.text: a macrodrip set, 10 drops per mL
options.rationale: That gives about 4 drops per minute, too few to set accurately.

options.text: a blood administration set
options.rationale: Its filter and large drops are for blood products.

options.text: a secondary piggyback set
options.rationale: A short set for intermittent drugs that attaches to a primary line.

options.text: lets the bag finish, since it is not empty
options.rationale: The limit is time, not volume.

options.text: hangs a new bag now
options.rationale: A container hangs no longer than 24 hours once spiked. This one has hung 26.

options.text: adds a label with today's date
options.rationale: Relabeling hides how long it has hung.

options.text: speeds the rate to empty the bag
options.rationale: That changes the prescribed rate and risks overload.

options.text: leaves it until day 7
options.rationale: Seven days is the interval for a transparent dressing.

options.text: reinforces it with tape
options.rationale: Tape does not replace a dressing that is due.

options.text: changes it today
options.rationale: Gauze is changed every 2 days because the site cannot be seen through it.

options.text: removes it and leaves the site open
options.rationale: An insertion site stays covered.

questions.takeaway: Microdrip, 60 drops per mL, for slow rates. A bag hangs 24 hours at most. Gauze dressings change every 2 days, transparent every 7.
questions.strategy: Each blank has a time or a number behind it. A dressing or bag that looks fine can still be past its limit.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Pick the set by the rate
steps.detail: Slow rates need small drops.

steps.action: Count the hours on the bag
steps.detail: 0600 yesterday to 0800 today is 26 hours.

steps.action: Match the interval to the dressing
steps.detail: Gauze 2 days, transparent 7.

elimination.verdict: Microdrip; new bag now; change it today.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old with a hemoglobin of 6.7 g/dL will receive packed red blood cells. Which setup does the nurse prepare?

options.text: 18 gauge catheter, blood set with filter, primed with 5% dextrose in water
options.rationale: The priming fluid is off. Dextrose in water hemolyzes red cells.

options.text: 18 gauge catheter, blood set with filter, primed with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: An 18 gauge catheter, a filtered blood set and 0.9% sodium chloride only are the three parts of the blood setup.

options.text: 18 gauge catheter, standard set with no filter, primed with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: The tubing is off. Blood runs through a blood administration set with a filter.

options.text: 18 gauge catheter, blood set with filter, primed with lactated Ringer's
options.rationale: The priming fluid is off. Only 0.9% sodium chloride runs with blood.

questions.takeaway: Blood setup: 18 to 20 gauge catheter, blood administration set with a filter, primed with 0.9% sodium chloride only.
questions.strategy: The catheter is the same in all four. Compare the tubing and the priming fluid, one at a time.

steps.detail: All four use an 18 gauge catheter, so the gauge decides nothing.
Dextrose in water and lactated Ringer's are both wrong with blood.
A set with no filter is not a blood set.

elimination.verdict: Filtered blood set primed with 0.9% sodium chloride.

questions.stem: The nurse checks four clients receiving blood products. Which finding requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Plasma thawed 6 hours ago, now infusing
options.rationale: Plasma is infused within 24 hours of thawing, so 6 hours is inside the limit.

options.text: Cryoprecipitate thawed 2 hours ago, now infusing
options.rationale: Cryoprecipitate is infused within 6 hours of thawing, so 2 hours is inside the limit.

options.text: Red blood cells issued 2 hours ago, half infused
options.rationale: Red cells finish within 4 hours of issue. Half done at 2 hours is on schedule.

options.text: Red blood cells issued 5 hours ago, still infusing
options.rationale: Each unit of red cells is completed within 4 hours of issue. At 5 hours the unit is past its limit and bacterial growth is a risk.

questions.takeaway: Time limits: red cells within 4 hours of issue, plasma within 24 hours of thawing, cryoprecipitate within 6 hours of thawing.
questions.strategy: Each option is a product and a time. Match each time against that product's limit.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Red cells 4 hours, plasma 24 hours, cryoprecipitate 6 hours.
6, 2 and 2 hours are inside their limits.
5 hours is over the 4 hour limit for red cells.

elimination.verdict: Red cells still running 5 hours after issue.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old is prescribed 1,000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride over 10 hours by gravity. The tubing delivers 20 drops per mL. Which rate does the nurse set?

options.text: 33 drops per minute
options.rationale: 1,000 mL times 20 drops per mL, divided by 600 minutes, is 33 drops per minute.

options.text: 100 drops per minute
options.rationale: This is the mL per hour. It would be the drop rate only with 60 drops per mL tubing, and here it runs the bag in about 3 hours.

options.text: 17 drops per minute
options.rationale: This is the rate for 10 drops per mL tubing. With this tubing the bag would take about 20 hours.

options.text: 25 drops per minute
options.rationale: This is the rate for 15 drops per mL tubing. With this tubing the bag would take about 13 hours.

questions.takeaway: Drops per minute equals volume in mL times the drop factor, divided by time in minutes. 1,000 times 20 divided by 600 is 33.
questions.strategy: Write the formula first, then put in the drop factor printed on this tubing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 10 hours is 600 minutes.
1,000 mL times 20 is 20,000 drops.
20,000 divided by 600 is 33.

elimination.verdict: 33 drops per minute.

questions.stem: The nurse checks the IV setups of four clients at the start of the shift. Which finding requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Transparent dressing dated 4 days ago, dry and intact
options.rationale: A transparent dressing is changed every 7 days, so day 4 is fine.

options.text: Bag of lactated Ringer's spiked 10 hours ago
options.rationale: A container hangs no longer than 24 hours once spiked. Ten hours is inside the limit.

options.text: Continuous primary tubing labeled 10 days ago
options.rationale: Administration sets are changed every 96 hours. Tubing in use for 10 days is far past that and is a source of infection.

options.text: Gauze dressing changed yesterday, dry and intact
options.rationale: A gauze dressing is changed every 2 days, so one day is fine.

questions.takeaway: Intervals: tubing every 96 hours, bag no longer than 24 hours, transparent dressing every 7 days, gauze every 2 days.
questions.strategy: Each option is an item and its age. Compare each age with that item's change interval.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 96 hours, 24 hours, 7 days, 2 days.
4 days, 10 hours and 1 day are all inside.
10 days of use for tubing with a 96 hour limit.

elimination.verdict: The tubing labeled 10 days ago.

questions.stem: On the 3rd of the month the nurse places a new transparent dressing over a clean, dry subclavian central line site. Which date for the next routine change does the nurse record?

options.text: The 4th, one day after placement
options.rationale: The interval is too short. Each extra dressing change opens the site without need.

options.text: The 5th, two days after placement
options.rationale: Two days is the interval for a gauze dressing. This dressing is transparent.

options.text: The 17th, fourteen days after placement
options.rationale: The interval is too long. A transparent dressing left 14 days is twice past its limit.

options.text: The 10th, seven days after placement
options.rationale: A transparent dressing is changed every 7 days, sooner only if it becomes wet, loose or soiled.

questions.takeaway: A transparent dressing is changed every 7 days. A gauze dressing is changed every 2 days.
questions.strategy: Name the dressing type first. The type sets the number.

steps.detail: Transparent, over a clean and dry site.
7 days.
The 10th.

elimination.verdict: The 10th, seven days after placement.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old will receive one unit of packed red blood cells over 3 hours. Which vital sign schedule does the nurse follow?

options.text: Baseline, 15 minutes after the start, every 30 to 60 minutes, at completion
options.rationale: Baseline first, a check at 15 minutes when severe reactions tend to appear, then every 30 to 60 minutes and at the end.

options.text: Baseline, 1 hour after the start, every 30 to 60 minutes, at completion
options.rationale: The first check is too late. Most severe reactions appear in the first 15 minutes.

options.text: 15 minutes after the start, every 30 to 60 minutes, at completion
options.rationale: The baseline is missing. Without it, a change at 15 minutes cannot be recognized.

options.text: Baseline, 15 minutes after the start, then at completion only
options.rationale: The middle checks are missing. A 3 hour unit needs vital signs every 30 to 60 minutes.

questions.takeaway: Transfusion vital signs: baseline, at 15 minutes, every 30 to 60 minutes, and at completion.
questions.strategy: Look for the schedule with all four parts. Each wrong option drops or moves one part.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Baseline, 15 minutes, every 30 to 60 minutes, completion.
One moves the first check to 1 hour, one has no baseline, one has no middle checks.

elimination.verdict: The schedule with all four parts.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old needs 3 weeks of an infusion with an osmolarity of 1,100 mOsm/L. Which access does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Short forearm catheter, 20 gauge, with the site checked often
options.rationale: The device is off. Peripheral veins take solutions below 900 mOsm/L, and frequent checks do not change that.

options.text: Midline catheter with the tip below the axilla
options.rationale: The tip is still peripheral. A midline takes solutions below 600 mOsm/L.

options.text: PICC with the tip position confirmed by chest x-ray
options.rationale: A solution above 900 mOsm/L needs a central tip, and a PICC is confirmed by x-ray before use.

options.text: Subcutaneous infusion into abdominal tissue
options.rationale: The route is off. Subcutaneous infusion is for slow isotonic fluid.

questions.takeaway: Above 900 mOsm/L goes central. A midline stops at 600 mOsm/L because its tip is peripheral.
questions.strategy: Ask where each device's tip ends. Only a central tip can take 1,100 mOsm/L.

steps.detail: 1,100 mOsm/L is above the peripheral limit.
Forearm vein, below the axilla, lower superior vena cava, tissue.
The PICC.

elimination.verdict: PICC, confirmed by x-ray.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old has a midline catheter in the right upper arm, placed 5 days ago. Which new prescription does the nurse question?

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride at 75 mL per hour
options.rationale: An isotonic fluid is suited to a midline.

options.text: Continuous norepinephrine infusion through the midline
options.rationale: A midline is not used for continuous vasopressors or vesicants. If the drug leaks at a peripheral tip it destroys tissue, so it needs central access.

options.text: A nonvesicant antibiotic every 8 hours for 2 weeks
options.rationale: A midline takes nonvesicants and can stay up to 4 weeks.

options.text: Lactated Ringer's 500 mL over 2 hours
options.rationale: An isotonic fluid is suited to a midline.

questions.takeaway: A midline is peripheral: nonvesicants only, below 600 mOsm/L, up to 4 weeks. No vesicants, parenteral nutrition or continuous vasopressors.
questions.strategy: The question asks for the one to question. Sort the four into isotonic or nonvesicant on one side and vasopressor on the other.

steps.detail: Below the axilla, in a peripheral vein.
Two isotonic fluids and a nonvesicant antibiotic inside 4 weeks.
Norepinephrine needs a central line.

elimination.verdict: The continuous norepinephrine.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old crash victim is bleeding heavily and needs rapid fluid resuscitation. He has a dialysis fistula in the left arm. Which access does the nurse start?

options.text: 16 gauge catheter in the right forearm
options.rationale: Trauma and rapid resuscitation call for a 14 to 16 gauge catheter, and the right arm has no fistula.

options.text: 16 gauge catheter in the left forearm
options.rationale: The site is off. The arm with a dialysis fistula is avoided.

options.text: 22 gauge catheter in the right forearm
options.rationale: The gauge is off. A 22 gauge is for fragile or small veins and cannot deliver fluid fast enough.

options.text: 24 gauge catheter in the right hand
options.rationale: The gauge is off. A 24 gauge is the smallest catheter and gives the slowest flow.

questions.takeaway: Gauge runs backward. Trauma and rapid resuscitation need 14 to 16 gauge. The fistula arm is not used.
questions.strategy: Two things decide this: the size of the catheter and the arm. Rule out by each in turn.

steps.detail: Heavy bleeding needs 14 to 16 gauge. That removes 22 and 24.
The left arm has the fistula.

elimination.verdict: 16 gauge in the right forearm.

questions.stem: An 85-year-old in hospice with mild dehydration and no usable veins is prescribed hypodermoclysis. Which setup is correct for this client?

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride into abdominal tissue at 200 mL per hour
options.rationale: The rate is off. Subcutaneous fluid runs at about 1 mL per minute at most, which is 60 mL per hour.

options.text: 3% sodium chloride into abdominal tissue at 50 mL per hour
options.rationale: The fluid is off. Hypodermoclysis uses isotonic fluid, and 3% is hypertonic.

options.text: 10% dextrose in water into thigh tissue at 50 mL per hour
options.rationale: The fluid is off. 10% dextrose is hypertonic.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride into thigh tissue at 50 mL per hour
options.rationale: Isotonic fluid, a listed site and a rate under 1 mL per minute.

questions.takeaway: Hypodermoclysis: isotonic fluid into the abdomen, thigh or scapular tissue at no more than about 1 mL per minute.
questions.strategy: Check three things in each option: the fluid, the site and the rate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 3% sodium chloride and 10% dextrose are hypertonic.
200 mL per hour is more than three times 60 mL per hour.
Abdomen and thigh are both acceptable.

elimination.verdict: 0.9% sodium chloride into thigh tissue at 50 mL per hour.

questions.stem: A confused 81-year-old has 0.9% sodium chloride infusing by pump through a forearm catheter. Which plan for checking the site does the nurse use?

options.text: The nurse inspects the site once each shift
options.rationale: The interval is too long. A confused client may not report pain or swelling for hours.

options.text: The nurse inspects the site every 1 to 2 hours
options.rationale: The site is inspected every 1 to 2 hours for redness, swelling and pain, and a confused client cannot be relied on to report them.

options.text: Assistive personnel assess the site every 1 to 2 hours
options.rationale: The person is off. Assistive personnel report what they see, and assessing the site stays with the nurse.

options.text: The nurse inspects the site whenever the pump alarms
options.rationale: The trigger is off. A pump alarms late, after tissue is already swollen.

questions.takeaway: Inspect an infusing peripheral site every 1 to 2 hours. The nurse assesses, and the pump does not watch the site.
questions.strategy: Each option names who checks and how often. Both have to be right.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Assessment belongs to the nurse.
Once a shift and only on alarm leave long gaps.
He is confused and may not report symptoms.

elimination.verdict: The nurse, every 1 to 2 hours.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel cares for a client who has a PICC in the left arm. Which action by the assistive personnel needs correction?

options.text: Covers the PICC with a waterproof cover before the shower
options.rationale: Correct. The dressing is kept dry, and a shower with a waterproof cover is allowed.

options.text: Tells the nurse the dressing edge looks damp
options.rationale: Correct. The assistive personnel reports and the nurse assesses and changes a wet dressing.

options.text: Wraps the blood pressure cuff on the left upper arm
options.rationale: No blood pressure cuff goes on the arm with a PICC. Cuff pressure can damage the catheter and the vein.

options.text: Takes the temperature and reports 38.2 C to the nurse
options.rationale: Correct. Fever above 38 C is reported because it can mean a line infection.

questions.takeaway: PICC arm: no blood pressure cuffs and no blood draws on that arm. Keep the dressing clean, dry and intact.
questions.strategy: You are looking for the wrong action. Three options protect the line or report a finding.

steps.detail: Needs correction means find the unsafe action.
Reporting a damp dressing and a fever are both right.

steps.action: Find the action on the PICC arm
steps.detail: The cuff on the left arm.

elimination.verdict: The cuff on the PICC arm.

questions.stem: A client's central line was found open and has now been clamped. He is short of breath with chest pain. Which position does the nurse use?

options.text: Left side with the head lowered
options.rationale: Left side with the head down traps the air in the right atrium, away from the lungs.

options.text: Right side with the head lowered
options.rationale: The side is off. On the right side the air can move on toward the lungs.

options.text: Left side with the head raised 45 degrees
options.rationale: The head position is off. With the head up, air rises out of the right atrium.

options.text: Flat on the back with the head lowered
options.rationale: The side is off. Without the left side turn the air is not held in the right atrium.

questions.takeaway: Air embolism: clamp, then left side with the head down, 100% oxygen and rapid response.
questions.strategy: There are two parts to the position: which side, and head up or down.

steps.detail: Left.
Down.
Only one has left side and head lowered.

elimination.verdict: Left side, head lowered.

questions.stem: A student cares for a client with a hemodialysis catheter in the chest and a 20 gauge forearm catheter. An IV antibiotic is due. Which action by the student needs correction?

options.text: Scrubs the forearm catheter's connector for 15 seconds
options.rationale: Correct. The hub is scrubbed for at least 15 seconds before each access.

options.text: Prepares to flush the dialysis catheter and give the dose through it
options.rationale: A hemodialysis catheter is for dialysis only and is handled by dialysis staff. It is not used for routine IV drugs or blood draws.

options.text: Checks the forearm site for redness and swelling first
options.rationale: Correct. The site is assessed before it is used.

options.text: Flushes the forearm catheter before and after the dose
options.rationale: Correct. The line is flushed before and after medications.

questions.takeaway: A hemodialysis catheter is for dialysis only: no routine IV access and no blood draws.
questions.strategy: Three actions involve the forearm catheter and one involves the dialysis catheter.

steps.detail: Find the wrong action.
Three use the forearm catheter correctly.
The dialysis catheter is not for medications.

elimination.verdict: Giving the dose through the dialysis catheter.

questions.scenario: The charge nurse rounds on six clients with vascular access and checks each setup.
questions.stem: For each setup, indicate whether it is correct or needs correction.

rows.text: Two licensed nurses match the blood label to the client's ID band at the bedside
rows.rationale: The two nurse check is done at the bedside, against the ID band, with two identifiers.

rows.text: An implanted port accessed with a standard straight hypodermic needle
rows.rationale: A port is accessed only with a noncoring (Huber) needle. A standard needle cores the septum so it cannot reseal.

rows.text: A new forearm catheter placed above the site of yesterday's infiltration
rows.rationale: A new site goes proximal to an earlier puncture or infiltration.

rows.text: A short catheter in a foot vein of an adult who walks in the hall
rows.rationale: Leg and foot veins are avoided in adults.

rows.text: A 22 gauge catheter for maintenance fluid in an 88-year-old with fragile veins
rows.rationale: 22 to 24 gauge is used for older adults with fragile or small veins.

rows.text: A new catheter placed in the same vein below a site removed for phlebitis
rows.rationale: Sites below a prior phlebitis or infiltration are avoided, because the fluid flows up through the damaged vein.

questions.takeaway: Port: noncoring needle only. New sites go above an old one, not below. No leg veins in adults. 22 to 24 gauge for fragile veins.
questions.strategy: Judge each row on its own. Ask which single specification is being tested: the needle, the site, the gauge or the check.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Above the old site is right. Below it is wrong.
A port needs a noncoring needle. A 22 gauge suits fragile veins.
Adult leg and foot veins are avoided.

elimination.verdict: Correct, needs correction, correct, needs correction, correct, needs correction.

questions.stem: A carpenter arrives with a nail fragment protruding from his right eye. He is in pain and asks the nurse to pull it out. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Shield the eye without touching the object
options.rationale: A protruding object is never removed by the nurse. Protecting it from movement prevents more damage until the eye care provider arrives.

options.text: Irrigate the eye with saline to clear debris
options.rationale: Right for a surface foreign body and tempting here. Irrigation can move a penetrating object.

options.text: Apply a pressure patch over the eye
options.rationale: Pressure on a penetrated eye can push out its contents.

options.text: Remove it gently and cover the eye with gauze
options.rationale: Only the eye care provider assesses and removes it.

questions.takeaway: A penetrating eye injury is left alone and protected. Only the eye care provider removes the object.
questions.strategy: Three options put force or fluid on the eye. One protects it.

steps.detail: Protruding means penetrating, not surface.
Removal, irrigation and pressure.
A shield with no contact.

elimination.verdict: Shield the eye and leave the object in place.

questions.stem: A client with open-angle glaucoma has used latanoprost nightly for 6 months. Which statement indicates the treatment goal is being met?

options.text: "My eyes feel comfortable and never ache."
options.rationale: Tempting, but open-angle glaucoma is silent, so comfort tells you nothing about the optic nerve.

options.text: "My side vision is starting to come back."
options.rationale: Lost vision does not return. This statement shows a wrong expectation.

options.text: "My field test is unchanged from last time."
options.rationale: The goal is to prevent further damage. A stable visual field is exactly that.

options.text: "My pressure is normal, so I use drops as needed."
options.rationale: Treatment is lifelong and daily. Stopping lets the pressure climb again.

questions.takeaway: Glaucoma treatment succeeds when nothing more is lost. It does not restore vision and it does not depend on how the eye feels.
questions.strategy: Comfort sounds like success. In a painless disease, the only evidence is a measurement that has not worsened.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Prevent further damage, not restore vision.
Vision returning and drops as needed.

steps.action: Compare comfort with a stable test
steps.detail: This disease never hurt, so comfort proves nothing.

elimination.verdict: The unchanged field test.

questions.stem: A very nearsighted client awaiting scleral buckling for a retinal detachment wants to walk to the lounge to read. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Walk with him to the lounge and offer an arm for guidance
options.rationale: Tempting because it prevents a fall, but walking and reading both move the eye and head and can extend the detachment.

options.text: Keep him resting with head still and the eye patched
options.rationale: Before surgery, head movement and activity are restricted and a patch reduces eye movement.

options.text: Bring a large print book to his bedside chair
options.rationale: Keeps him in the room, but reading moves the eye back and forth.

options.text: Raise the lighting so he can read in bed
options.rationale: Good for low vision in general. Here the problem is eye movement, not light.

questions.takeaway: Before retinal detachment repair, the priority is to stop the detachment from spreading: limit activity and head movement and patch the eye.
questions.strategy: Three options help him read safely. Ask whether he should be reading or walking at all.

steps.detail: More retina can detach before surgery.

steps.action: Notice three options keep him reading
steps.detail: Reading means eye movement.
Safe walking is still activity he should not have.

elimination.verdict: Rest, head still, eye patched.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old's daughter sorts his morning and evening pills into a blue box and a green box. He took the evening pills this morning. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Have the daughter give every dose herself
options.rationale: Solves the error by removing his independence when a simpler fix exists.

options.text: Add a bright fluorescent light over the pill boxes
options.rationale: More light helps aging eyes, but fluorescent glare makes it worse and blue still looks like green.

options.text: Switch the boxes to violet and blue
options.rationale: Blues, greens and violets are the colors aging eyes separate least well.

options.text: Label the boxes in large high contrast print
options.rationale: Aging eyes lose blue and green discrimination, so the cue must be print and contrast, not color.

questions.takeaway: Never teach an older adult medications by color, especially blue, green or violet. Use large print, contrast and shape.
questions.strategy: More light is a real need in older eyes, so that option pulls. The error here came from two colors he cannot tell apart.

steps.action: Find the cause of the error
steps.detail: Blue and green look alike to him.

steps.action: Cut the option that repeats the cause
steps.detail: Violet and blue.
Labels keep him independent; the daughter taking over does not.

elimination.verdict: Large high contrast labels.

questions.stem: The clinic nurse has four clients waiting. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: A client with open-angle glaucoma whose pressure today is 26 mmHg
options.rationale: Elevated and needs attention, but this is a chronic, slow problem that will not change in the next hour.

options.text: A contact lens wearer with a painful red eye and a hazy cornea
options.rationale: The cornea has no blood supply of its own, so a possible corneal infection is an emergency.

options.text: A client with cataracts who reports worse glare when driving
options.rationale: Gradual and expected. Safety teaching can wait.

options.text: A client 1 month after LASIK who sees halos at night
options.rationale: A known complication that is not an emergency.

questions.takeaway: Sudden and painful with a hazy cornea outranks any slowly progressive eye problem, even one with an abnormal number.
questions.strategy: The pressure of 26 is the only number on the page, which makes it look like the priority. Acute beats chronic.

steps.detail: Three are gradual or expected.
26 is open-angle range and chronic.
Painful red eye with a hazy cornea.

elimination.verdict: The contact lens wearer.

questions.stem: Two days after cataract surgery a client calls the clinic. Which report indicates recovery is not progressing as expected?

options.text: "The eye feels a little scratchy."
options.rationale: Mild scratchiness is expected early.

options.text: "I still can't see sharply out of that eye."
options.rationale: Best vision takes 4 to 6 weeks, so blurry vision on day 2 is expected.

options.text: "I could see better yesterday than I can today."
options.rationale: Vision should improve steadily. A drop from one day to the next is a vision loss to report now.

options.text: "I bent to pick up a shoe before I remembered."
options.rationale: Bending raises eye pressure and needs reteaching, but one slip with no symptoms is not a failing recovery.

questions.takeaway: After cataract surgery, vision that is imperfect is expected. Vision that is getting worse is not.
questions.strategy: Two options mention poor vision. One is slow improvement and the other is a decline.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Scratchiness.
Not sharp yet versus worse than yesterday.
A teaching need without any symptom.

elimination.verdict: Vision worse today than yesterday.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old who is legally blind, lives alone and prepares her own meals receives her lunch tray. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Describe where each item sits and let her touch it
options.rationale: Describing in detail and allowing touch lets her eat on her own, as she does at home.

options.text: Stay and feed her to prevent spills and burns
options.rationale: Tempting as the safest choice, but she manages meals alone at home and feeding her removes independence she has.

options.text: Ask assistive personnel to cut and feed the meal
options.rationale: Delegation is allowed, but it is still more help than she needs.

options.text: Cut the food and butter the bread for her
options.rationale: Kindly meant and less than feeding her, but she prepares her own meals at home and can do this once she knows where things are.

questions.takeaway: For vision loss: speak normally, describe in detail, allow touch. Give the least help that keeps the patient safe.
questions.strategy: Feeding her looks like the safety answer. The detail that she lives alone and prepares her own meals tells you she already feeds herself.

steps.detail: She lives alone and prepares her own meals, so she eats without help.
Both do the task for her.
Preparing her food is still doing it for her.

elimination.verdict: Describe the tray and let her touch it.

questions.stem: A machinist felt something strike his eye while grinding steel. No object is visible, and an MRI of the orbits is prescribed. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Irrigate the eye with saline before the scan
options.rationale: Right for a surface foreign body, but a high speed metal fragment may have penetrated, and irrigation is not for that.

options.text: Send him and tell the technologist about the grinding
options.rationale: Tempting because the information is passed on. He should not reach the scanner at all.

options.text: Check his acuity and proceed if it is normal
options.rationale: Normal acuity does not rule out a small metal fragment inside the eye.

options.text: Hold the scan and report the metal exposure
options.rationale: MRI is contraindicated when a metal fragment is suspected. X-ray or CT is used instead.

questions.takeaway: Suspected metal in the eye means no MRI. The magnet can move the fragment and cause more injury.
questions.strategy: Three options end with him in the scanner. The stem already told you why that is unsafe.

steps.detail: Grinding steel means metal.

steps.action: Cut what sends him to the scanner
steps.detail: Irrigating first, telling the technologist and checking acuity all end in MRI.
Hold and report so X-ray or CT is ordered.

elimination.verdict: Hold the scan and report the metal.

questions.stem: A client had a laser peripheral iridotomy for angle-closure glaucoma this morning. Which finding best indicates the procedure was effective?

options.text: Eye pressure 16 mmHg with the pain gone
options.rationale: The iridotomy reopens drainage, so pressure falls into the normal range and the pain goes with it.

options.text: No nausea since the antiemetic was given
options.rationale: Tempting, but the drug explains this. It says nothing about the pressure.

options.text: Client resting quietly in a darkened room
options.rationale: Quiet may be relief or may be sedation. It does not measure anything.

options.text: Eye redness slightly less than on arrival
options.rationale: A good sign that lags behind and is too soft to judge the procedure.

questions.takeaway: Judge a treatment by the thing it was meant to change. For angle closure that is the pressure, measured.
questions.strategy: Several findings look like improvement. Ask which one could only come from the iridotomy working.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Blocked drainage and high pressure.
The antiemetic and the dark room.
16 is inside both normal ranges.

elimination.verdict: Pressure 16 mmHg with pain relieved.

questions.stem: A client with open-angle glaucoma starts timolol eye drops. Which statements show the teaching was understood? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I will press the inner corner of my eye after each drop."
options.rationale: Punctal occlusion keeps the drug in the eye and limits absorption into the body.

options.text: "I can stop the drops once my pressure reading is normal."
options.rationale: The pressure is normal because of the drops. Treatment is lifelong.

options.text: "I will use them every day even when my eyes feel fine."
options.rationale: Open-angle glaucoma has no symptoms to guide dosing, so strict adherence is what protects the nerve.

options.text: "New glasses will sharpen what the glaucoma took away."
options.rationale: Vision lost to glaucoma is nerve damage and is not corrected by lenses.

options.text: "If I skip a few days I will feel it and restart."
options.rationale: Rising pressure in open-angle glaucoma is silent, so there is nothing to feel.

questions.takeaway: Glaucoma drops are lifelong and daily. Punctal occlusion limits systemic effects, and lost vision does not return.
questions.strategy: Judge each statement alone. Any statement that treats glaucoma as something he can feel or reverse is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pressing the inner corner after each drop.
Daily use without symptoms.
Stopping, feeling it and regaining vision all assume the disease is reversible or noticeable.

elimination.verdict: A and C.

questions.stem: The nurse assesses an 88-year-old who has had poor intake for 3 days. Which finding most needs follow up?

options.text: Eyes that look sunken and dull in the orbits
options.rationale: Expected with age related loss of orbital fat, so not a reliable hydration sign in an older adult.

options.text: Sclera with a dull yellow tint
options.rationale: Common in older adults. Eye appearance is not used to judge jaundice at this age.

options.text: Dry furrowed tongue with scant dark urine
options.rationale: These are reliable signs of fluid deficit and fit 3 days of poor intake.

options.text: Eyes that feel gritty and dry
options.rationale: Reduced tear production is an expected aging change.

questions.takeaway: Do not use the sclera or eye appearance to judge hydration or jaundice in older adults. Look at the mouth and the urine.
questions.strategy: The eye findings look alarming. In an 88-year-old they are the least trustworthy data.

steps.detail: Three options rest on eye appearance.
Eye appearance misleads in older adults.

steps.action: Take the finding outside the eye
steps.detail: Tongue and urine.

elimination.verdict: Dry furrowed tongue with scant dark urine.

questions.stem: A client with a corneal infection from contact lens wear completes discharge teaching. Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I'll use the drops until the pain is gone."
options.rationale: The full antibiotic course is finished even after symptoms stop.

options.text: "I'll wear glasses until I'm told it has healed."
options.rationale: No contact lenses until the cornea is fully healed, and healing is confirmed by the provider.

options.text: "I'll put my lenses back in once the redness clears."
options.rationale: Tempting because it waits for improvement, but a clear looking eye is not a healed cornea.

options.text: "I'll save the leftover drops for next time."
options.rationale: Leftover drops mean the course was not finished.

questions.takeaway: Corneal infection teaching: finish the antibiotics and keep contacts out until the cornea is fully healed, not just until it looks better.
questions.strategy: Two options delay the contacts. One uses the client's own judgment and one uses the provider's exam.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stopping when pain ends and saving leftovers.
Redness clearing versus confirmed healing.
Symptoms fade before the cornea is whole.

elimination.verdict: Glasses until told it has healed.

questions.stem: A client going home with a corneal ulcer is prescribed antibiotic drops every hour for the first 24 hours. He asks to skip the night doses so he can sleep. Which response is best?

options.text: "Use two drops at bedtime and two when you wake."
options.rationale: Doubling a dose does not replace the steady level that hourly dosing gives.

options.text: "I will ask whether an ointment can cover the night."
options.rationale: Tempting because it respects his need for sleep. The first 24 hours call for hourly dosing as prescribed.

options.text: "Restart the hourly schedule in the morning."
options.rationale: Leaves the infection untreated for hours when vision is at risk.

options.text: "Set an alarm, because the hourly drops continue overnight."
options.rationale: The cornea has no blood supply of its own, so the drops are its only defense and the first day is the critical one.

questions.takeaway: A corneal infection is an emergency. Antibiotic drops are often hourly for the first 24 hours, day and night.
questions.strategy: Sleep is a comfort need. Weigh it against what a gap in dosing can cost.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Corneal infection can take vision quickly.

steps.action: Cut the options that leave a gap
steps.detail: Double doses and restarting in the morning.
An ointment request delays a schedule that matters tonight.

elimination.verdict: The hourly drops continue overnight.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old with cataracts has stopped driving at night and can no longer read her pill labels. She asks if she should wait until they are worse. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: "Surgery is timed by how it limits daily life."
options.rationale: Surgery is the only treatment and is done when ADLs are affected. Night driving and reading labels are ADLs.

options.text: "Stronger glasses and brighter light may be enough for now."
options.rationale: Reasonable early on and tempting as the conservative choice. Her daily function is already limited, so it is past that point.

options.text: "Surgery is done once the pupil turns bluish white."
options.rationale: A mature cataract is not the trigger. Function is.

options.text: "Eye drops can slow the clouding while you wait."
options.rationale: No drop treats a cataract. That belongs to glaucoma.

questions.takeaway: Cataract surgery is timed by function, not by how the lens looks. When ADLs are affected, it is time.
questions.strategy: The conservative option would be right for a client who is still functioning. Two details in the stem say she is not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No night driving, cannot read labels.
Drops and waiting for a white pupil.
Fine before ADLs are affected, not after.

elimination.verdict: Surgery is considered now because ADLs are affected.

questions.scenario: A telephone triage nurse takes six calls from adult clients about their eyes.
questions.stem: For each report, indicate whether the nurse arranges an immediate evaluation or provides routine teaching.

rows.text: A 47-year-old now holds the menu at arm's length to read it
rows.rationale: Presbyopia is expected from the 40s on.

rows.text: A 57-year-old has had a painless gray shadow over one eye since waking
rows.rationale: Sudden and painless with a curtain suggests retinal detachment. Painless does not mean minor.

rows.text: An 80-year-old cannot see for a minute after walking into a dark room
rows.rationale: Poor dark adaptation is an aging change. Teach night lights and pausing in doorways.

rows.text: A client 5 days after scleral buckling woke with sudden sharp pain in that eye
rows.rationale: Sudden pain after retinal surgery is reported immediately.

rows.text: A client 3 weeks after LASIK has dry eyes and halos at night
rows.rationale: Known complications of LASIK that are not emergencies.

rows.text: A 62-year-old has sudden severe pain in a red eye with blurred vision
rows.rationale: Sudden pain, redness and vision loss fit angle-closure glaucoma, a medical emergency.

questions.takeaway: Sudden is never aging. Gradual changes get teaching; sudden changes get seen, with or without pain.
questions.strategy: Ask one question of each row: did this come on suddenly? Do not let the absence of pain lower the urgency.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three are gradual or expected after a procedure.
A sudden shadow is still an emergency.
Sudden pain is on the report list.

elimination.verdict: Routine, immediate, routine, immediate, routine, immediate.

questions.stem: At 0800 a client's pupils were 3 mm, equal and brisk. At 1200 the right is 3 mm and the left is 6 mm and sluggish. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Recheck the pupils in 30 minutes for a trend
options.rationale: Tempting, but the nurse already has a baseline and a change. Waiting adds delay, not information.

options.text: Notify the provider of the change now
options.rationale: A new unequal, sluggish pupil is a change from a documented baseline and is reported right away.

options.text: Document the sizes and continue routine checks
options.rationale: Recording size in mm is right. Stopping there treats a new finding as stable.

options.text: Ask if his pupils have always been unequal
options.rationale: Some people do have a small lifelong difference. The 0800 exam already shows these were equal.

questions.takeaway: Record pupil size in mm every time so that a change is obvious. A new unequal or sluggish pupil is reported now.
questions.strategy: Two options gather more data. The 0800 baseline in the stem already answers both of them.

steps.detail: Equal at 0800, unequal at 1200.
History and recheck are answered by the baseline.
A new change needs action.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider now.

questions.stem: A landscaper has tearing and light sensitivity after debris blew into his eye. The fluorescein exam shows a speck on the surface with no penetration. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Lift the speck off with a dry cotton swab
options.rationale: A dry swab can scratch the cornea.

options.text: Shield the eye and wait for the eye surgeon
options.rationale: The right move for a penetrating object and tempting as the cautious choice. The exam showed the speck is on the surface.

options.text: Start IV antibiotics and a tetanus booster
options.rationale: These are the steps before surgery for a penetrating injury.

options.text: Irrigate the eye with sterile saline
options.rationale: A surface foreign body is treated with a fluorescein exam and then saline irrigation.

questions.takeaway: Surface foreign body: fluorescein exam, then saline irrigation. Penetrating object: leave it, protect it, get the eye care provider.
questions.strategy: Leaving it alone is the rule for a penetrating injury. One phrase in the stem tells you this is not one.

steps.detail: On the surface, no penetration.
Shielding and IV antibiotics belong to a different injury.
Saline does not scratch.

elimination.verdict: Irrigate with sterile saline.

questions.nursesNote: Health fair screening. 64-year-old Black man with type 2 diabetes. Mother used daily eye drops for "pressure". Says he has clipped door frames with his shoulder lately. Sees halos around streetlights. Denies eye pain. Reads the 20/20 line with each eye. Uses reading glasses for small print. Tonometry 27 mmHg in both eyes.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that support referring this client for glaucoma evaluation.

segments.text: 64-year-old Black man with type 2 diabetes
segments.rationale: African American over 40 is a risk group, and diabetes raises risk.

segments.text: Mother used daily eye drops for "pressure"
segments.rationale: A family history of glaucoma.

segments.text: Says he has clipped door frames with his shoulder lately
segments.rationale: Peripheral vision is lost first, and he may not notice it as a vision problem.

segments.text: Sees halos around streetlights
segments.rationale: Halos around lights are listed with open-angle glaucoma.

segments.text: Denies eye pain
segments.rationale: Open-angle glaucoma is painless, so this neither supports nor rules it out.

segments.text: Reads the 20/20 line with each eye
segments.rationale: Central acuity stays normal until late. A normal result here is falsely reassuring, not a reason to refer.

segments.text: Uses reading glasses for small print
segments.rationale: Presbyopia, expected at his age.

segments.text: Tonometry 27 mmHg in both eyes
segments.rationale: Above normal and inside the 22 to 32 open-angle range.

questions.takeaway: Open-angle glaucoma hides behind a normal Snellen result and no pain. Risk group, family history, side vision loss and pressure are what find it.
questions.strategy: The 20/20 acuity and absent pain make him sound healthy. Neither one tests the part of vision glaucoma takes first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Age and race, diabetes, family history.
Bumping door frames, halos, pressure of 27.

steps.action: Leave the normal and the expected
steps.detail: No pain, 20/20, reading glasses.

elimination.verdict: Risk profile, family history, door frames, halos and tonometry.

questions.stem: A client with open-angle glaucoma and COPD started timolol drops 2 weeks ago. Intraocular pressure fell from 28 to 17 mm Hg. He mentions new wheezing on the stairs. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document that the treatment goal is being met
options.rationale: Tempting because the pressure is now normal. The new wheeze is an unexpected finding that the pressure reading does not cancel.

options.text: Reteach punctal occlusion and recheck him next month
options.rationale: Tempting because punctal occlusion does cut systemic absorption. It is teaching for an actual breathing problem that the prescriber needs to hear about today.

options.text: Report the wheezing to the prescriber before the next dose
options.rationale: The deciding detail is new wheezing in a client with COPD on a beta blocker drop. The drug is reaching his lungs, and breathing outranks a good pressure reading.

options.text: Advise using his rescue inhaler before each eye drop
options.rationale: Treats the symptom and keeps giving the cause. Changing how he uses another drug is not the nurse's call.

questions.takeaway: A beta blocker eye drop can act on the lungs and heart. A good eye pressure does not make the plan effective if the drop causes wheezing.
questions.strategy: Two results are in the stem. One is expected and good. Ask which one is new and belongs to breathing.

steps.detail: Pressure 17 is the goal. Wheezing is new.

steps.action: Link the wheeze to the drug
steps.detail: Timolol is a beta blocker and he has COPD.
Reteaching is slower than reporting an actual airway effect.

elimination.verdict: Report the wheezing before the next dose.

questions.stem: The clinic nurse has four clients waiting. Each problem began or was noticed this morning. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: Very nearsighted client with a painless shadow at one edge of vision
options.rationale: The quiet one is the urgent one. A new painless shadow in a nearsighted client suggests the retina is detaching, and it spreads while he waits.

options.text: Client 1 day after cataract surgery with a scratchy eye and vision not yet sharp
options.rationale: Sounds like a surgical problem and is expected on day 1. Mild scratchiness and vision that is not yet sharp are normal, with no pain or sudden loss.

options.text: Client with a corneal abrasion who has tearing and marked light sensitivity
options.rationale: The most uncomfortable client. Tearing and photophobia are expected with an abrasion that is already diagnosed.

options.text: Client with open-angle glaucoma whose side vision has narrowed since the last visit
options.rationale: Tempting because vision is being lost. This is slow, chronic loss that a short wait will not change.

questions.takeaway: Painless does not mean minor. A new shadow or curtain is acute and can progress, so it outranks expected discomfort and chronic loss.
questions.strategy: Three clients have findings that fit what they already have. Find the one whose finding is new and unexplained.

steps.detail: Day 1 cataract scratchiness and blur, abrasion tearing and photophobia.
Open-angle glaucoma loss is gradual.
New shadow in a nearsighted eye.

elimination.verdict: The nearsighted client with the new shadow.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old on a dim medical unit received a first dose of an anticholinergic 2 hours ago. She now reports brow pain, halos around the night light and nausea. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the prescribed as-needed antiemetic and reassess
options.rationale: Tempting because nausea is the complaint she wants fixed. Here nausea is a sign of rising eye pressure, so treating it alone delays the real problem.

options.text: Check visual acuity in each eye with a chart
options.rationale: Tempting as assess first. The stem already gives the cue cluster, and a chart reading in a dim room will not change what must happen next.

options.text: Offer a cool cloth and darken the room further
options.rationale: A comfort measure for headache. Dim light dilates the pupil more and can worsen a blocked drainage angle.

options.text: Notify the provider now and hold the next dose
options.rationale: The deciding detail is a pupil dilating drug plus dim light followed by eye pain, halos and nausea. That cluster means a suddenly blocked drain, which is an emergency.

questions.takeaway: Eye pain with halos and nausea after a dilating drug or dim light is angle closure until proven otherwise. Recognize it and escalate.
questions.strategy: First decide what the three symptoms add up to and what happened 2 hours ago. Then pick the action that matches that problem, not the loudest symptom.

steps.detail: Brow pain, halos, nausea, dim room, anticholinergic.
Sudden rise in eye pressure.
Antiemetic and cool cloth do not lower pressure.
Enough is known to call.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider now and hold the next dose.

questions.stem: Three days after cataract surgery, a client says vision is sharper each day and the eye itches a little. He adds that a few new floaters and one flash appeared last night. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document steady improvement and confirm the next visit
options.rationale: Tempting because acuity is improving and itching is expected. New floaters and a flash are not part of normal recovery.

options.text: Arrange for him to be examined today
options.rationale: The deciding detail is new floaters with a flash of light. They warn of a retinal tear even while central vision is getting better.

options.text: Reinforce no bending, lifting or straining
options.rationale: Correct teaching after cataract surgery and worth repeating. It does not address a finding that needs an eye examination.

options.text: Ask him to call if a curtain appears
options.rationale: Tempting because a curtain is the classic sign. Waiting for it means waiting for the detachment to progress.

questions.takeaway: Improving sharpness can hide a new problem. New floaters or flashes after eye surgery need a same day examination.
questions.strategy: The stem gives good news first and the important detail last. Judge the recovery by the worst new finding, not the average.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sharper vision and mild itching.
Floaters and a flash.
A curtain is a late sign.

elimination.verdict: Arrange an examination today.

questions.stem: A client who is legally blind and walks steadily was shown the route to the bathroom once on admission. At 0200 she wants to walk there alone and refuses the bedpan. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Turn on the bed alarm and ask her to call each time
options.rationale: Tempting as a fall precaution. It restricts a client who can walk and does nothing to build safe independence.

options.text: Place a commode at the bedside for the night
options.rationale: Tempting because it shortens the distance. It changes her environment without orienting her to it and avoids the route she must learn.

options.text: Walk with her offering an elbow and describe the route again
options.rationale: The deciding detail is one orientation only. She is able to walk, so the least restrictive safe action is to guide and reorient until she can do it alone.

options.text: Clear the path and let her go while watching from the door
options.rationale: Respects her wish and tempts for that reason. One walk through is not enough for her to know the route in the dark.

questions.takeaway: For vision loss, give the least help that keeps the client safe: orient, describe, guide by the elbow, then step back as she learns the room.
questions.strategy: Safety and independence both matter here. Look for the option that serves both instead of trading one for the other.

steps.detail: Fall safety and least restrictive care.
Alarm and commode limit her.
She has had only one orientation.

elimination.verdict: Guide her by the elbow and describe the route again.

questions.stem: Four days after cataract surgery, a client says he has not had a bowel movement since the operation and now feels the urge. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Advise him to bear down gently with the urge
options.rationale: Any bearing down raises pressure inside the healing eye.

options.text: Tell him this is expected and will resolve
options.rationale: Constipation may be common, but waiting leads to straining.

options.text: Request a stool softener and warn against straining
options.rationale: Treats the constipation now and protects the eye from a pressure rise.

options.text: Advise extra fiber and more fluids over the next week
options.rationale: Good long-term advice and tempting, but he has the urge now and will strain today.

questions.takeaway: After eye surgery, anything that makes the client strain raises eye pressure. Prevent the strain.
questions.strategy: Connect the bowel complaint to the eye. The best option deals with today's risk, not next week's.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Link the cue to the surgery
steps.detail: Straining raises eye pressure.
Bearing down and waiting.
Fiber works in days. He needs relief now.

elimination.verdict: Stool softener and no straining.

questions.stem: A client with a bacterial infection in both eyes was taught to use the prescribed antibiotic drops. Which statement shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I use the bottle marked left only in my left eye."
options.rationale: Separate bottles keep organisms from one eye out of the other.

options.text: "I stop the drops once both eyes look clear."
options.rationale: The full course is completed even when the eyes look better.

options.text: "I wipe the dropper tip with a tissue between eyes."
options.rationale: Tempting because it sounds clean, but wiping contaminates the tip.

options.text: "I do the better eye first with the same bottle."
options.rationale: Order does not protect a shared bottle from contamination.

questions.takeaway: Both eyes infected means one bottle per eye and the full course.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that keeps the two eyes completely separate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Separate bottles, finish the course.
Clear eyes are not the end point.
Wiping or ordering still shares one tip.

elimination.verdict: A labeled bottle for each eye.

questions.stem: One week after LASIK, a 29-year-old reports dry, gritty eyes and halos around headlights. She has no pain and reads without glasses. How does the nurse evaluate this?

options.text: Possible angle-closure glaucoma needing emergency care
options.rationale: Halos make this tempting, but angle closure brings sudden pain and vision loss, and she has neither.

options.text: Known effects of the surgery to review at follow-up
options.rationale: Dry eyes and halos are recognized after LASIK, and her vision is good.

options.text: A failed correction that will need repeating
options.rationale: She reads without glasses, so the correction is working.

options.text: A corneal infection that needs antibiotic drops
options.rationale: Infection brings pain and a hazy cornea.

questions.takeaway: Halos mean different things in different clients. After LASIK with no pain and clear vision, they are a known effect.
questions.strategy: Use what is absent. No pain and good acuity rule out the emergencies.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dry eyes, halos, no pain, clear vision.
Angle closure and infection both hurt.
She sees without glasses.

elimination.verdict: Known effects; review at follow-up.

questions.stem: After a dilated eye examination, a 52-year-old says he will drive straight back to work, where he reads blueprints. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Wait 15 minutes here, then you can drive."
options.rationale: Dilation lasts hours, not minutes.

options.text: "You may drive if you wear your regular glasses."
options.rationale: Glasses do not correct the blur and light sensitivity from dilated pupils.

options.text: "Rinse your eyes with saline to clear the drops."
options.rationale: The drug has already been absorbed. Rinsing does not reverse it.

options.text: "Arrange a ride and wear sunglasses until it wears off."
options.rationale: Dilated pupils cannot limit light or focus up close for several hours.

questions.takeaway: Dilating drops leave the client light sensitive and blurred for hours. Plan the ride and the sunglasses before he leaves.
questions.strategy: Ask what a dilated pupil cannot do. The answer covers both driving and his close work.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Glare and blurred near vision for hours.
Fifteen minutes, glasses and rinsing do not shorten it.

steps.action: Pick the option that covers safety
steps.detail: A ride and sunglasses until it wears off.

elimination.verdict: Ride home and sunglasses.

questions.stem: At an annual visit, a 60-year-old woman whose sister has glaucoma has an eye pressure of 25 mmHg. She has no pain and says her vision is fine. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Refer her for a prompt glaucoma evaluation
options.rationale: The reading is in the open-angle range and she has a family history. Damage is silent, so she needs an eye care visit soon.

options.text: Send her to the emergency department now
options.rationale: An emergency would be sudden pain, redness and vision loss with a higher pressure.

options.text: Recheck the pressure at next year's visit
options.rationale: Tempting because she feels fine, but open-angle glaucoma takes side vision without symptoms.

options.text: Teach her to report halos or eye pain
options.rationale: By the time symptoms appear the nerve damage is permanent.

questions.takeaway: A raised pressure with no symptoms is the usual picture of open-angle glaucoma. It needs referral, not an emergency response and not a wait.
questions.strategy: Two options overreact or underreact. Match the urgency to a silent, slowly damaging problem.

steps.detail: Above normal, below the emergency picture.
No pain, no vision loss.
No symptoms does not mean no damage.

elimination.verdict: Prompt referral.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old with type 2 diabetes and hypertension has clear vision and asks how to protect his eyesight. Which teaching is the priority?

options.text: Wear sunglasses that block ultraviolet light outdoors
options.rationale: True for cataract prevention and tempting, but his largest risks are his two diseases.

options.text: Control glucose and blood pressure, with yearly exams
options.rationale: These are his major modifiable risks, and yearly exams find damage before he notices it.

options.text: Rest your eyes every 20 minutes at the computer
options.rationale: Eases eyestrain. It does not protect the retina.

options.text: Return for an eye exam if vision blurs
options.rationale: Waiting for symptoms misses early, treatable damage.

questions.takeaway: For a client with diabetes and hypertension, disease control plus scheduled exams protects vision more than any eye-specific habit.
questions.strategy: Several options are true. Ask which one targets the risk factors named in the stem.

steps.detail: Diabetes and hypertension.
Damage comes before blur.
Sunglasses and rest help less than controlling the diseases.

elimination.verdict: Control both diseases and get yearly exams.

questions.stem: After retinal detachment repair with a gas bubble, a client prescribed face-down positioning is found asleep on his back at 0300. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Let him sleep and reposition him at breakfast
options.rationale: Tempting because sleep matters, but the bubble only presses on the repair in the prescribed position.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees
options.rationale: Not the position the surgeon prescribed.

options.text: Wake him and help him back to face-down
options.rationale: The bubble holds the retina in place only when he is positioned as prescribed.

options.text: Call the surgeon to report the position change
options.rationale: The nurse can correct this now. A call adds delay without changing the fix.

questions.takeaway: After retinal repair, the surgeon's positioning is the treatment. Restore it as soon as you find it lost.
questions.strategy: The nurse already knows the prescribed position, so the next step is to act, not to wait or report.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Position keeps the bubble against the repair.
Breakfast is hours away.
The correction is within the nurse's role.

elimination.verdict: Wake him and reposition.

questions.stem: A client with open-angle glaucoma says she never misses her nightly drops. Which finding suggests the adherence teaching was not effective?

options.text: Eye pressure is 18 mmHg at this visit
options.rationale: Within the normal range.

options.text: She keeps the bottle beside her toothbrush
options.rationale: Tying the drop to a nightly habit supports adherence.

options.text: She presses the inner corner after each drop
options.rationale: Correct technique that limits systemic absorption.

options.text: Her one month bottle was last refilled 9 weeks ago
options.rationale: The supply has lasted more than twice as long as it should, so doses are being missed.

questions.takeaway: Check adherence with objective data such as refill dates, not only with what the client reports.
questions.strategy: The stem asks for the finding that does not fit. Three options show good habits or a good result.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Looking for evidence of a problem.
Routine placement and inner corner pressure.
A one month bottle should not last 9 weeks.

elimination.verdict: The late refill.

questions.stem: A client with glaucoma is learning to instill one drop each of two prescribed eye medications. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Release one drop into the pocket without touching the eye
options.rationale: The tip stays off the eye and lashes so the bottle stays clean.

options.text: Wait several minutes, then instill the second medication
options.rationale: Spacing keeps the second drop from washing out the first.

options.text: Wash the hands
options.rationale: Clean hands come before touching the eye area or the bottle.

options.text: Close the eye gently and press the inner corner
options.rationale: Keeps the drug on the eye and out of the bloodstream.

options.text: Tilt the head back and pull the lower lid down
options.rationale: Forms the pocket that will hold the drop.

questions.takeaway: Clean hands, make a pocket, drop without touching, press the inner corner, then wait before the next drug.
questions.strategy: Anchor the first and last steps, then order the middle by what must exist before the drop can go in.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hand washing first, second drug last.
Pocket, drop, then inner corner pressure.

elimination.verdict: Wash, pocket, drop, press, wait.

questions.scenario: A retired teacher reports that over the past year vision in both eyes has grown blurry, colors look faded and oncoming headlights make night driving hard. She has no eye pain and her side vision is full. She has stopped reading and recently missed a curb.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Refer her for an eye examination
options.rationale: The diagnosis is confirmed with an ophthalmoscope, slit lamp and acuity testing.

options.text: Review home lighting and trip hazards with her
options.rationale: She has already missed a curb. Safety is addressed while she waits for care.

options.text: Keep her on bed rest with the eye patched
options.rationale: That is care before retinal detachment repair.

options.text: Advise that stronger glasses will correct it
options.rationale: Clients often blame their glasses, but a clouded lens is treated with surgery.

options.text: Cataracts
options.rationale: Painless, gradual blur with faded colors and trouble driving at night.

options.text: Open-angle glaucoma
options.rationale: That takes side vision first, and hers is full.

options.text: Retinal detachment
options.rationale: That is sudden, with flashes, floaters or a curtain.

options.text: Angle-closure glaucoma
options.rationale: That is sudden and painful.

options.text: Ability to read and manage daily activities
options.rationale: Surgery is timed by the effect on daily life.

options.text: Visual acuity at each visit
options.rationale: Tracks how far the clouding has progressed.

options.text: Eye pain rating every shift
options.rationale: Cataracts are painless.

options.text: Pupil size every hour
options.rationale: Not relevant to a slowly clouding lens.

questions.takeaway: Gradual, painless blur with faded color and night driving trouble points to cataracts. Refer, keep her safe, and track function.
questions.strategy: Use two cues to sort the conditions: speed of onset and pain. Then use side vision to separate cataract from glaucoma.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gradual and painless removes detachment and angle closure.
Full fields argue against open-angle glaucoma.
Referral and home safety.

elimination.verdict: Cataracts; refer and make home safe; monitor function and acuity.

questions.stem: After 4 months of latanoprost in the right eye, a client's pressure is 15 mmHg. The right iris is browner with longer lashes. She has no pain, redness or vision change. How does the nurse evaluate this?

options.text: A reaction that requires stopping the drops
options.rationale: Stopping lets the pressure rise and nerve damage resume. The change is cosmetic.

options.text: An expected drug effect, with the goal met
options.rationale: Prostaglandin drops can darken the iris and lengthen lashes in the treated eye. The pressure is within normal range.

options.text: A sign that the drops are being overused
options.rationale: The effect occurs at the normal dose.

options.text: Inflammation that needs an urgent eye exam
options.rationale: Tempting because the eye looks different. She has no pain, redness or vision change.

questions.takeaway: Prostaglandin eye drops lower pressure and can permanently darken the iris and lengthen lashes. Expected, so the drops continue.
questions.strategy: Ask two things: is the treatment goal met, and is the new finding harmful or only different?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 15 mmHg is within the normal range.
No pain, redness or vision change.
Known effect of this drug class.

elimination.verdict: Expected effect. Goal met, drops continue.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old with a wood splinter penetrating the eye is being prepared for surgery. The eye is shielded and IV antibiotics are running. Which information does the nurse obtain next?

options.text: The fluorescein staining pattern of his cornea
options.rationale: Staining means instilling dye and handling an eye already known to be penetrated. It adds nothing before surgery.

options.text: The date of his last tetanus immunization
options.rationale: A penetrating wound from wood carries tetanus risk, and a booster is given before surgery if he is due.

options.text: Whether he wears contact lenses
options.rationale: Does not change what is done before surgery for a penetrating injury.

options.text: His intraocular pressure by tonometry
options.rationale: Tonometry presses on the eye and is not done on a penetrating injury.

questions.takeaway: Before surgery for a penetrating eye injury: shield, imaging by X-ray or CT, IV antibiotics and tetanus status.
questions.strategy: Two things are already done. Ask what remains on the preoperative list that does not touch the eye.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Shield and antibiotics.

steps.action: Cut anything that touches the eye
steps.detail: Fluorescein staining and tonometry.
Tetanus booster status.

elimination.verdict: Ask about his last tetanus booster.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old fishing guide whose mother had cataract surgery at 60 asks what he can do now to protect his eyes. Which teaching is the priority?

options.text: Have his eye pressure measured every 6 months
options.rationale: Pressure screening looks for glaucoma and does nothing to slow lens changes.

options.text: Use lubricating drops before and after work
options.rationale: Comfort for dry eyes. It does not protect the lens.

options.text: Begin yearly eye exams now rather than waiting until age 40
options.rationale: Tempting because exams matter. An exam finds a cataract, and sunglasses reduce the exposure that causes one.

options.text: Wear ultraviolet blocking sunglasses whenever outdoors
options.rationale: Chronic sun exposure is a modifiable cause of cataract, and his work exposes him daily.

questions.takeaway: Ultraviolet protection lowers the risk of cataract and ocular melanoma. Prevention acts on the exposure. Screening only finds the result.
questions.strategy: He asked what he can do to protect his eyes. Separate the options that prevent from the ones that detect.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Daily sun on the water.
Pressure checks and exams detect.
Ultraviolet light and the lens.

elimination.verdict: Ultraviolet blocking sunglasses outdoors.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old reports burning, gritty eyes that are worse by evening. Her corneas are clear, there is no discharge and her vision sharpens when she blinks. Which plan does the nurse suggest?

options.text: Lubricating eye drops through the day
options.rationale: Tear production falls with age. Clear corneas and vision that clears with blinking fit dry eye.

options.text: Same day evaluation for a corneal infection
options.rationale: An infected cornea is hazy and painful, usually with discharge. Hers is clear.

options.text: Warm compresses and antibiotic ointment
options.rationale: There is no sign of infection to treat.

options.text: Resting the eyes with both lids patched
options.rationale: Patching removes her vision, raises fall risk and does not replace tears.

questions.takeaway: Reduced tears are a normal aging change. Burning and grittiness with a clear cornea and no discharge are treated with lubrication.
questions.strategy: Check the cornea first. Clear and no discharge takes infection off the table.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clear cornea, no discharge.
Vision clears when tears spread.
Patching both eyes of an older adult.

elimination.verdict: Artificial tears.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old had laser photocoagulation last week to seal a small retinal tear. Which finding best shows the treatment was effective?

options.text: She has had no eye pain since the procedure
options.rationale: Retinal tears and detachment are painless, so the absence of pain says nothing.

options.text: Her reading vision is sharper than before
options.rationale: Sealing a tear protects vision. It is not expected to improve focus.

options.text: No new floaters or flashes, and full side vision
options.rationale: The laser was meant to stop the tear from becoming a detachment, so the absence of detachment signs is the outcome.

options.text: Her eye pressure measures 19 mmHg
options.rationale: A normal pressure relates to glaucoma, not to the retina staying attached.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate retinal tear treatment by the absence of detachment signs: no flashes, no new floaters, no curtain. Pain is not part of this condition.
questions.strategy: Recall what a detachment feels like. An outcome can only be judged by a symptom the condition actually produces.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sudden, painless flashes, floaters, curtain.
It was never painful.
No progression to detachment.

elimination.verdict: No flashes, no new floaters, full visual field.
