questions.stem: A client is going home after cataract removal by phacoemulsification. Which instructions does the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wear dark glasses outdoors
options.rationale: The eye is light sensitive after surgery.

options.text: Sleep on the side of the operated eye
options.rationale: Lying on that side puts pressure on the eye.

options.text: Lift nothing heavier than 10 lb
options.rationale: Heavy lifting raises eye pressure.

options.text: Expect your final vision by the end of the first week
options.rationale: Best vision arrives at about 4 to 6 weeks.

options.text: Report sudden pain or loss of vision at once
options.rationale: Signals bleeding, infection or raised pressure.

questions.takeaway: After cataract surgery: dark glasses, avoid anything that raises eye pressure, report sudden pain or vision loss, and expect best vision at 4 to 6 weeks.
questions.strategy: Sort each option by one question: does it raise pressure in the eye or protect it?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No heavy lifting.
Sudden pain or vision loss.
Lying on the operated side and a one week timeline.

elimination.verdict: A, C and E.

questions.scenario: A client is going home after scleral buckling with a gas bubble for a retinal detachment. The nurse listens to what the client and her husband plan to do.
questions.stem: For each statement, indicate whether the discharge teaching was effective or needs more teaching.

rows.text: "My husband will read the mail to me this week."
rows.rationale: Reading and close work are avoided for the first week because of the rapid eye movements.

rows.text: "I will keep my head in the position the surgeon showed me."
rows.rationale: Position keeps the bubble against the repair.

rows.text: "I will fly to my sister's on Friday while I rest."
rows.rationale: Gas expands at altitude and raises eye pressure. No air travel until the surgeon clears it.

rows.text: "I will ask my son to carry the laundry baskets."
rows.rationale: Avoids lifting and straining that raise eye pressure.

rows.text: "If my vision dims suddenly I will mention it at my checkup."
rows.rationale: A sudden vision change is reported immediately.

questions.takeaway: After retinal repair: hold the prescribed position, no reading for a week, nothing that raises eye pressure, no flying with a gas bubble, and report sudden changes at once.
questions.strategy: Test each statement against two rules: protect the repair from pressure and movement, and report sudden change now.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reading, lifting and flying.
As the surgeon prescribed.
Sudden change cannot wait for a checkup.

elimination.verdict: Effective, effective, more teaching, effective, more teaching.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews tonometry readings for four clients in the eye clinic. Which finding requires the nurse to intervene now?

options.text: 12 mmHg in a client who uses nightly glaucoma drops
options.rationale: Inside the normal range. The drops are working.

options.text: 16 mmHg in a client the day after a laser iridotomy
options.rationale: Inside the normal range after the procedure.

options.text: 38 mmHg in an eye that became painful and red an hour ago
options.rationale: Far above normal with sudden pain and redness. This is the angle closure pattern, a medical emergency.

options.text: 19 mmHg in a client who reports dry, gritty eyes
options.rationale: Inside the normal range. Dry eyes are a comfort problem.

questions.takeaway: Normal intraocular pressure is about 10 to 20 mmHg. Angle closure runs 30 mmHg and above with sudden pain and a red eye.
questions.strategy: Sort the numbers first. Three sit inside 10 to 20 mmHg, so the symptoms attached to them do not make them urgent.

steps.detail: 12, 16 and 19 mmHg are normal.
38 mmHg is well above 30.
Sudden pain and redness confirm an emergency.

elimination.verdict: 38 mmHg with a painful red eye.

questions.stem: A nurse instills a prescribed glaucoma drop for a seated 72-year-old. Which technique does the nurse use?

options.text: Head tilted back, client looking up, drop placed in the lower lid pocket
options.rationale: Looking up moves the cornea away, and the pocket holds the drop.

options.text: Head tilted back, client looking up, drop placed on the center of the cornea
options.rationale: The position is right, but a drop on the cornea stings and makes the client blink it out.

options.text: Head tilted back, client looking down, drop placed in the lower lid pocket
options.rationale: The gaze is off. Looking down brings the cornea under the dropper.

options.text: Head upright, eyes closed, drop placed at the inner corner of the lids
options.rationale: The site is off. A drop on closed lids does not reach the pocket reliably.

questions.takeaway: Eye drops: head back, look up, pull the lower lid down to make a pocket, and drop into the pocket, not onto the cornea.
questions.strategy: Compare gaze and landing site in each option.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Up, not down.
The lower lid pocket, not the cornea or closed lids.
Looking up, into the pocket.

elimination.verdict: Head back, looking up, drop in the lower lid pocket.

questions.stem: A client with asthma starts timolol eye drops. The nurse teaches a step to limit how much drug reaches the bloodstream. Which technique does the nurse teach?

options.text: Close the eye gently and press the outer corner by the temple for 30 to 60 seconds
options.rationale: The time is right, but the tear duct opening is at the inner corner.

options.text: Close the eye gently and press the inner corner by the nose for 30 to 60 seconds
options.rationale: Punctal occlusion blocks the tear duct, so less beta blocker drains to the nose and is absorbed.

options.text: Close the eye gently and press the inner corner by the nose for 2 to 3 seconds
options.rationale: The site is right, but a few seconds is too short to keep the drug out of the duct.

options.text: Squeeze the eye tightly shut and rub the lid for 30 to 60 seconds
options.rationale: Squeezing and rubbing push the drop out of the eye and do not block the duct.

questions.takeaway: Punctal occlusion: after the drop, close the eye gently and press the inner corner by the nose for 30 to 60 seconds to limit systemic absorption.
questions.strategy: Two things decide it: where the finger goes and for how long.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Inner corner by the nose, where tears drain.
30 to 60 seconds, not a few seconds.
The eye is closed gently.

elimination.verdict: Inner corner by the nose for 30 to 60 seconds.

questions.stem: A client has two different glaucoma eye drops, one drop each, both due at 0800 in the same eye. Which schedule does the nurse use?

options.text: First drug at 0800, second drug immediately after it
options.rationale: The second drop washes the first out of the pocket.

options.text: First drug at 0800, two drops of the second drug at about 0805
options.rationale: The wait is right, but the dose is off. One drop is prescribed, and the pocket cannot hold a second one.

options.text: First drug at 0800, second drug held until 1200
options.rationale: The prescribed time is off. Both are due at 0800, and a 5 minute gap is all that is needed.

options.text: First drug at 0800, second drug at about 0805
options.rationale: A wait of about 5 minutes lets the first drop absorb before the second arrives.

questions.takeaway: Wait about 5 minutes between two different eye drops in the same eye.
questions.strategy: Both are due at 0800, so look for the smallest gap that still keeps the two drops from mixing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The second drop rinses out the first.
Two drops was not ordered.
Four hours changes the schedule.

elimination.verdict: First at 0800, second at about 0805.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old going home after cataract surgery lives alone and asks what she can do herself this week. Which activity does the nurse approve?

options.text: Carry a 25 lb bag of pet food from the car
options.rationale: The weight is over the 10 lb limit.

options.text: Carry an 8 lb bag of groceries held at waist height
options.rationale: Under the 10 lb limit and done upright, so it does not raise intraocular pressure.

options.text: Bend at the waist to lift an 8 lb laundry basket from the floor
options.rationale: The weight is fine, but bending forward raises pressure in the eye.

options.text: Push hard to move a heavy dresser a short distance
options.rationale: Straining raises pressure in the eye even with nothing lifted.

questions.takeaway: After cataract surgery avoid what raises intraocular pressure: bending, lifting more than 10 lb and straining.
questions.strategy: Ask of each activity: is it over 10 lb, does it involve bending, does it involve straining?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 25 lb is over the limit.
Bending at the waist is restricted.
Pushing a dresser is straining.

elimination.verdict: An 8 lb bag carried upright.

questions.stem: Three days after scleral buckling for a retinal detachment, a client describes his routine at home. Which statement needs correction?

options.text: "I keep my head the way the surgeon showed me."
options.rationale: Correct. Positioning follows the surgeon's instructions.

options.text: "I take the stool softener so I do not strain."
options.rationale: Correct. Straining raises pressure in the eye.

options.text: "I spend the afternoons reading and doing crossword puzzles."
options.rationale: Reading and close work are avoided for the first week. They cause rapid eye movements.

options.text: "I will call at once for sudden pain or pain with nausea."
options.rationale: Correct. These are the findings to report immediately.

questions.takeaway: After retinal detachment repair: position as the surgeon orders, avoid what raises intraocular pressure, and no reading or close work for the first week.
questions.strategy: It is day 3, inside the first week. Look for an activity that makes the eyes jump back and forth.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: You want the statement that is wrong.
Day 3 is inside the first week.
Reading and crosswords.

elimination.verdict: Reading and crossword puzzles in the first week.

questions.stem: A nursing student is about to check a client's pupil response to light. Which setup does the nurse tell the student to use?

options.text: Dim the room, bring the light in from the side, and watch both pupils
options.rationale: A dim room lets the pupils open first. Light from the side tests one eye, and both pupils are checked for the direct and consensual response.

options.text: Brighten the room, bring the light in from the side, and watch both pupils
options.rationale: The room is off. Pupils already constricted by bright light show little change.

options.text: Dim the room, hold the light straight ahead between the eyes, and watch both pupils
options.rationale: The direction is off. Light from the front reaches both eyes and the client focuses on it.

options.text: Dim the room, bring the light in from the side, and watch only the lit pupil
options.rationale: This leaves out the consensual response in the other pupil.

questions.takeaway: Pupil light check: dim the room, bring the light in from the side, watch the lit pupil (direct), then the other pupil (consensual).
questions.strategy: Check room light, direction of the beam, and which pupils are watched.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dim, so the pupils start open.
From the side, one eye at a time.
Both the direct and the consensual response.

elimination.verdict: Dim room, light from the side, watch both pupils.

questions.stem: Before charting PERRLA for a 55-year-old, the nurse checks accommodation. Which technique does the nurse use?

options.text: Client looks at a far object, then at a finger held at arm's length
options.rationale: The near target is too far away to make the eyes converge and the pupils constrict.

options.text: Client looks at a far object while a light is brought in from the side
options.rationale: This tests the reaction to light, not accommodation.

options.text: Client looks at a finger 10 to 15 cm from the nose with one eye covered
options.rationale: The far to near shift is missing, and with one eye covered convergence cannot be seen.

options.text: Client looks at a far object, then at a finger 10 to 15 cm from the nose
options.rationale: Shifting from far to near should make the pupils constrict and the eyes turn in.

questions.takeaway: Accommodation: the client looks far away, then at a finger 10 to 15 cm from the nose. The pupils constrict and the eyes converge.
questions.strategy: Accommodation needs two things: a shift from far to near, and a near target that is truly near.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 10 to 15 cm, not arm's length.
A finger, not a light.
Far first, then near, with both eyes open.

elimination.verdict: Far object, then a finger 10 to 15 cm from the nose.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old arrives at the occupational clinic seconds after a liquid drain cleaner splashed into his left eye. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Irrigate the eye with water or saline for 1 to 2 minutes, then check acuity
options.rationale: The fluid is right, but the time is far too short to remove the chemical.

options.text: Irrigate the eye with water or saline at once for at least 15 minutes
options.rationale: The chemical keeps burning until it is washed out, so irrigation comes before anything else.

options.text: Check visual acuity with the chart, then irrigate for at least 15 minutes
options.rationale: The duration is right, but testing first lets the chemical keep burning.

options.text: Patch the eye firmly and have him wait for the eye care provider
options.rationale: Patching holds the chemical against the eye.

questions.takeaway: Chemical eye burn: irrigate right away with water or saline for at least 15 minutes, before assessment.
questions.strategy: This is one of the few times you act before you assess. Then check the duration.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Irrigate first, test vision after.
At least 15 minutes.
It traps the chemical.

elimination.verdict: Irrigate at once for at least 15 minutes.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews visual acuity results for four clients to decide who meets the definition of legally blind for a low vision services referral. Which client qualifies?

options.text: 20/200 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left, wearing glasses
options.rationale: The better eye is 20/40, so the definition is not met.

options.text: 20/200 in both eyes without glasses and 20/50 with glasses
options.rationale: The corrected value counts, and 20/50 does not meet the definition.

options.text: 20/70 in the better eye while wearing glasses
options.rationale: Reduced vision, but not 20/200 or worse.

options.text: 20/200 in the better eye while wearing glasses
options.rationale: Legal blindness is 20/200 or worse in the better eye with correction.

questions.takeaway: Legally blind means 20/200 or worse in the better eye with correction.
questions.strategy: Three parts must all be true: 20/200 or worse, in the better eye, with glasses on.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 20/70 is not enough.
The better eye decides, not the worse one.
The value with glasses counts.

elimination.verdict: 20/200 in the better eye with glasses.

questions.stem: Ten days after cataract surgery, a client has no pain and sees a little better each day, but says his vision is still not sharp. Which response by the nurse is correct?

options.text: "Your vision should have been sharp within 48 hours of surgery."
options.rationale: The time is off. This wrongly tells him the surgery failed.

options.text: "Your best vision is expected about 4 to 6 months after surgery."
options.rationale: The time is off by months and delays his expectations for no reason.

options.text: "Your best vision is expected about 4 to 6 weeks after surgery."
options.rationale: Steady improvement with no pain at 10 days is on course.

options.text: "Stop the dark glasses so the eye adjusts to light sooner."
options.rationale: Dark glasses are part of postoperative care and do not slow recovery.

questions.takeaway: After cataract surgery, best vision is reached at about 4 to 6 weeks. Sudden pain or vision loss is reported at once.
questions.strategy: The stem gives improving vision and no pain, so nothing needs reporting. Only the time frame is being tested.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Improving and painless.
48 hours is too early and 4 to 6 months is too late.
4 to 6 weeks.

elimination.verdict: Best vision at about 4 to 6 weeks.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old who wears glasses for distance needs a corrected visual acuity check with the Snellen chart. Which setup does the nurse use?

options.text: Standing 20 feet from the chart, glasses on, one eye covered at a time
options.rationale: Corrected acuity is measured at 20 feet with glasses on, each eye on its own.

options.text: Standing 10 feet from the chart, glasses on, one eye covered at a time
options.rationale: The distance is off. The first number of the result is the 20 foot testing distance.

options.text: Standing 20 feet from the chart, glasses off, one eye covered at a time
options.rationale: A corrected acuity is ordered, so the glasses stay on.

options.text: Standing 20 feet from the chart, glasses on, both eyes open throughout
options.rationale: A weaker eye is hidden when the stronger eye reads for both.

questions.takeaway: Snellen chart: 20 feet away, each eye tested separately, with glasses on for corrected acuity. 20/20 is normal.
questions.strategy: Three things can vary: the distance, the glasses and whether an eye is covered. The stem says corrected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 20 feet.
Corrected means glasses on.
One at a time.

elimination.verdict: 20 feet, glasses on, one eye at a time.

questions.stem: The nurse observes a student instill antibiotic drops in a client's right eye. Which action by the student needs correction?

options.text: Checks the label and which eye before opening the bottle
options.rationale: Correct first step.

options.text: Rests the dropper tip on the lower lashes to steady it
options.rationale: A tip that touches the lashes or eye is contaminated and carries organisms back into the bottle.

options.text: Pulls the lower lid down to form a pocket
options.rationale: Correct. The drop goes into the pocket.

options.text: Asks the client to close the eye gently afterward
options.rationale: Correct. Gentle closing keeps the drop in, with no squeezing or rubbing.

questions.takeaway: The dropper tip never touches the eye, lid or lashes.
questions.strategy: Three steps follow the standard sequence. Look for the one where the bottle touches the client.

steps.detail: You want the wrong step.
Check the label, make a pocket, close gently.
The tip rests on the lashes.

elimination.verdict: Resting the dropper tip on the lashes.

questions.stem: A client who is legally blind and hears normally receives a dinner tray. Which statement by the nurse helps him most to feed himself?

options.text: "Your chicken and your coffee are right there in front of you."
options.rationale: Names the items but gives no location he can use.

options.text: "Your chicken is over on this side and your coffee is up there."
options.rationale: "This side" and "up there" depend on seeing where the nurse points.

options.text: "YOUR CHICKEN IS AT 6 O'CLOCK. YOUR COFFEE IS AT 2 O'CLOCK."
options.rationale: The description is right, but his hearing is normal. A raised voice treats vision loss as hearing loss.

options.text: "Your chicken is at 6 o'clock and your coffee is at 2 o'clock."
options.rationale: Clock positions tell him exactly where each item is on the tray.

questions.takeaway: Vision loss: speak normally and describe objects in detail. For a tray, give each item a clock position.
questions.strategy: Check two things: does the statement give a location he can use without sight, and is the voice normal?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only clock positions work without sight.
The stem says he hears normally.
Clock positions in a normal voice.

elimination.verdict: Clock positions in a normal voice.

questions.scenario: A 41-year-old welder arrives in the emergency department with a thin metal fragment protruding from his left eye. The team prepares him for surgery.
questions.stem: For each action, indicate whether it is a correct setup or needs correction.

rows.text: A rigid shield placed over the eye without touching the fragment
rows.rationale: Protects the eye and keeps anything from pressing on the object.

rows.text: A pressure patch taped firmly over the eye and fragment
rows.rationale: Pressure pushes the object deeper and can force eye contents out.

rows.text: Saline irrigation of the eye to wash the surface
rows.rationale: Irrigation is for a surface foreign body. It is not used with a penetrating object.

rows.text: CT scan of the orbits requested
rows.rationale: X-ray or CT is the preferred imaging.

rows.text: MRI of the orbits requested
rows.rationale: A metal fragment can move in the magnet and cause further injury.

rows.text: IV antibiotics started and tetanus booster given before surgery
rows.rationale: Both are given before surgery to prevent infection.

questions.takeaway: Penetrating eye injury: never remove or press on the object, no irrigation, X-ray or CT and never MRI with metal, and IV antibiotics plus tetanus booster before surgery.
questions.strategy: For each row ask two questions: does it press on or move the object, and does it bring metal near a magnet?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The pressure patch and the irrigation.
MRI with a metal fragment.
Shield, CT, antibiotics and tetanus.

elimination.verdict: Correct: shield, CT, antibiotics with tetanus. Needs correction: pressure patch, irrigation, MRI.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old on day 6 of contact isolation now believes it is 1990. Vital signs and glucose are normal. Her hearing aids are in a drawer and the blinds are closed. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Request a prescription for a sitter at the bedside
options.rationale: A sitter adds supervision but does not treat the cause the stem already shows.

options.text: Complete a full cognitive screening tool
options.rationale: Tempting because assessment usually comes first. The stem already gives the cause, and a screen done without her hearing aids would only measure what she cannot hear.

options.text: Insert her hearing aids and open the blinds
options.rationale: Physical causes are already checked and the cues point to sensory deprivation. Restoring meaningful input is the least restrictive fix.

options.text: Ask the provider about a dementia evaluation
options.rationale: New confusion after days of isolation is not labeled dementia before a reversible cause is corrected.

questions.takeaway: New confusion in isolation with normal vital signs and hearing aids in a drawer is sensory deprivation until proven otherwise. Give the input back first.
questions.strategy: The stem hands you the assessment. When the cause is already visible, the next step is to fix it.

steps.detail: Normal vital signs and glucose, aids in a drawer, blinds closed, six days alone.

steps.action: Notice the assess option is late
steps.detail: A cognitive screen without hearing aids gives a false result.
Hearing aids and daylight cost nothing and treat the cause.

elimination.verdict: Insert the hearing aids and open the blinds.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with poorly controlled diabetes has used antibiotic ear drops for external otitis for 7 days. Which finding requires immediate follow-up?

options.text: Deeper, worsening ear pain with new drainage
options.rationale: Worsening pain and drainage in a client with diabetes suggests necrotizing otitis spreading into bone, which can be fatal.

options.text: Pain when the tragus is pressed
options.rationale: This is the expected sign of external otitis and does not show spread.

options.text: A plugged feeling with muffled hearing on that side
options.rationale: Canal swelling causes temporary hearing loss. It is expected while the canal heals.

options.text: A request to resume wearing earbuds
options.rationale: This needs teaching to keep earbuds out for 7 to 10 days. It is not a sign of a complication.

questions.takeaway: External otitis should improve on drops. Worsening pain in a diabetic or immunocompromised client means possible necrotizing otitis.
questions.strategy: Three findings are expected for swimmer's ear. Look for the one moving in the wrong direction in a high risk client.

steps.detail: Tragus pain and a plugged ear belong to the diagnosis.
Diabetes is why the stem mentions it.
Worse after 7 days of treatment is the red flag.

elimination.verdict: Deeper, worsening pain with new drainage.

questions.stem: A client is going home after a tympanoplasty. Which statement indicates a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I will keep my mouth open if I have to sneeze."
options.rationale: Correct. It keeps pressure off the repair.

options.text: "My husband will carry the laundry baskets."
options.rationale: Correct. Lifting is straining.

options.text: "I will dab my nose and not blow it."
options.rationale: Correct. Nose blowing pushes pressure into the middle ear.

options.text: "I fly out to see my daughter this weekend."
options.rationale: Air travel changes middle ear pressure and can disrupt the graft, so it is avoided until the surgeon clears it.

questions.takeaway: After ear surgery, avoid anything that changes middle ear pressure: straining, nose blowing and air travel.
questions.strategy: You are looking for the wrong statement. Ask which plan puts pressure on the repair.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Needs more teaching means find the error.
Open mouth sneeze, no lifting, no nose blowing.
A flight.

elimination.verdict: The flight this weekend.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old roofer newly diagnosed with Meniere disease has had three vertigo attacks this month. He plans to return to work tomorrow. Which plan is most important?

options.text: Start a low sodium diet and limit caffeine
options.rationale: Tempting because it is the core long term teaching. It reduces attacks over time but does not protect him on a roof tomorrow.

options.text: Arrange work off ladders until attacks are controlled
options.rationale: An attack on a roof or ladder could kill him, and attacks are not yet controlled, so the safety risk is addressed first.

options.text: Begin vestibular rehabilitation exercises with a therapist
options.rationale: Balance exercises help over weeks and do not prevent an attack.

options.text: Discuss surgical options with the provider
options.rationale: Surgery is a last resort after lifestyle and drug therapy fail.

questions.takeaway: In Meniere disease, safety comes before education. No ladders or driving while attacks are uncontrolled.
questions.strategy: All four are real parts of Meniere care. His job and his plan for tomorrow decide which one cannot wait.

steps.action: Find the detail that tips it
steps.detail: He is a roofer and goes back tomorrow.
Diet lowers attack frequency slowly.
Surgery is not first line.

elimination.verdict: Keep him off ladders and roofs.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old resident has seemed to ignore staff for a week. He reports itching and fullness in the right ear and turns his left ear toward speakers. Which problem does the nurse suspect first?

options.text: Cerumen impaction
options.rationale: One sided fullness, itching and hearing loss over a short time fit a blocked canal, the most common and most correctable cause in older adults.

options.text: Worsening presbycusis
options.rationale: Tempting because of his age. Presbycusis is gradual and affects both ears, and it does not cause itching or fullness.

options.text: Early dementia
options.rationale: Unheard words can look like inattention. The ear symptoms point to hearing, not cognition.

options.text: Sensory overload
options.rationale: Overload causes restlessness and scattered attention from too much stimulation, which the stem does not describe.

questions.takeaway: Before blaming age or cognition, look in the ear. One sided fullness and itching in an older adult suggests impacted cerumen.
questions.strategy: Age makes presbycusis the reflex answer. One sided and itchy does not fit it.

steps.detail: One ear, a week, fullness, itching.
Gradual and bilateral does not match.
Wax explains every cue.

elimination.verdict: Cerumen impaction.

questions.stem: A parent reports that a 4-year-old pushed a dried bean into the ear an hour ago. A standing order allows ear irrigation for foreign bodies. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Irrigate gently with body temperature water
options.rationale: Tempting because the technique is correct and an order exists. Water makes a bean swell and wedge tighter.

options.text: Instill mineral oil and wait before removal
options.rationale: Oil is used to suffocate a live insect. It does not help with a bean.

options.text: Soften it with ear drops, then irrigate
options.rationale: That is the plan for cerumen. Drops and water both add fluid to a bean.

options.text: Leave it and arrange removal by the provider
options.rationale: Vegetable matter expands with water, so irrigation is withheld and the provider removes it.

questions.takeaway: Never irrigate vegetable matter. It swells with water and locks itself in the canal.
questions.strategy: An order and perfect technique do not make an action safe. Ask what the object is made of.

steps.detail: A dried bean is vegetable matter.
Good technique cannot fix the wrong procedure.

steps.action: Send it to the right person
steps.detail: Manual removal by the provider.

elimination.verdict: No irrigation. The provider removes it.

questions.stem: The nurse receives four call lights at once. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: Client with otitis media whose severe pain stopped suddenly an hour ago
options.rationale: Tempting because it is unexpected and means the eardrum likely perforated. It must be reported, but the pressure is released and the client is not in immediate danger.

options.text: Client one day after tympanoplasty asking for a pain medication
options.rationale: Postoperative pain is expected and can wait a few minutes.

options.text: Client with Meniere disease standing at the sink who says the room began spinning
options.rationale: The client is upright during an attack and can drop without warning. An actual, immediate fall risk comes first.

options.text: Client on gentamicin asking when the trough level will be drawn
options.rationale: A question about a scheduled lab is stable and can wait.

questions.takeaway: Ear disorders are balance disorders. A client who is standing as vertigo starts is the one about to be injured.
questions.strategy: Two clients have unexpected changes. Ask which one can be hurt in the next minute.

steps.detail: Expected pain and a lab question.
Perforation has already happened. The fall has not.
Get the client seated or into bed now.

elimination.verdict: The standing client with Meniere disease.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old at a blood pressure check mentions he woke yesterday unable to hear from his left ear. His wife says his hearing has been fading for years. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Schedule a routine audiology screening
options.rationale: Tempting because audiometry is the most reliable hearing test. A routine appointment treats a sudden change as if it were gradual.

options.text: Report the change to the provider today
options.rationale: Sudden one sided loss is never assumed to be aging and needs same day evaluation.

options.text: Teach him about hearing aid styles
options.rationale: Devices are for established loss after the cause is known.

options.text: Reassure the couple that presbycusis progresses with age
options.rationale: Presbycusis is gradual and bilateral. This explanation dismisses a new finding.

questions.takeaway: New or sudden changes are not assumed to be age related. Sudden loss in one ear is reported the same day.
questions.strategy: The wife's comment pulls you toward aging. The words woke yesterday and left ear pull you back.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Years of fading is old. Overnight in one ear is new.

steps.action: Check the timing of each option
steps.detail: Routine screening is too slow.
It explains away the cue.

elimination.verdict: Report it to the provider today.

questions.stem: A competitive swimmer was treated for external otitis and returns for follow-up. Which statement shows the prevention teaching was effective?

options.text: "I went back to the pool once the pain eased on day 3."
options.rationale: Water is avoided for 7 to 10 days, not until the pain eases.

options.text: "I wear my earbuds at practice to keep the water out."
options.rationale: Sounds protective, but earbuds are one of the causes and are avoided during healing.

options.text: "I use the leftover drops after every swim."
options.rationale: Leftover antibiotic drops are not a prevention plan.

options.text: "I stopped cleaning my ears with cotton swabs."
options.rationale: Swabs injure the canal skin, which is a listed cause of external otitis.

questions.takeaway: External otitis is prevented by protecting the canal skin: no swabs or hairpins, and no water or earbuds for 7 to 10 days during treatment.
questions.strategy: Ask which statement removes a cause of the problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Trauma from swabs, earphones, water.
Pain easing is not healing.
Earbuds irritate the canal.

elimination.verdict: No more cotton swabs.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old who takes aspirin for arthritis tells the clinic nurse that both ears started ringing this week. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Ask how much aspirin she takes each day
options.rationale: The stem does not give the dose. Tinnitus can signal too much aspirin, so the nurse gathers that cue before anything else.

options.text: Suggest a sound machine to mask the ringing at night
options.rationale: Tempting because masking is real tinnitus care. It covers a symptom whose cause has not been looked for.

options.text: Tell her to stop all aspirin until the ringing clears
options.rationale: Changing a drug regimen is the provider's decision and the amount taken is still unknown.

options.text: Schedule a hearing test for next month
options.rationale: Testing may follow, but a month's delay ignores a possible drug cause.

questions.takeaway: When a new symptom appears, check the medication list before anything else. Aspirin and NSAIDs are ototoxic.
questions.strategy: Here the assessment has not been done. No dose is given, so you ask before you act.

steps.detail: How much aspirin is unknown.
Masking hides a warning sign.
Stopping a drug is not the nurse's call.

elimination.verdict: Ask how much aspirin she takes each day.

questions.stem: A veteran with chronic tinnitus and a normal workup says the ringing is worst in his silent bedroom and keeps him awake. Which intervention does the nurse suggest?

options.text: Wear foam earplugs to bed
options.rationale: Tempting because it sounds protective. Blocking outside sound makes the internal ringing more noticeable.

options.text: Ask the provider for a nightly sleeping pill
options.rationale: Sedation does not address the tinnitus and is not the first approach.

options.text: Run a fan or sound machine at the bedside
options.rationale: Background noise masks the ringing, which is worst in silence.

options.text: Avoid all background noise during the day
options.rationale: Silence is his trigger. Ear protection is for loud noise, not ordinary sound.

questions.takeaway: Tinnitus is managed, not cured: masking with background sound, retraining therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you when it is worst. Pick the option that changes that condition.

steps.detail: A silent room.
Earplugs and avoiding sound.
A fan or sound machine.

elimination.verdict: A fan or sound machine at the bedside.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel shouts each instruction to a newly admitted 92-year-old, who winces. The assistive personnel says residents that age cannot hear. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Coach the assistive personnel to lower the pitch instead
options.rationale: The right technique for hearing loss and tempting. It still assumes a loss no one has assessed.

options.text: Request a referral for audiometry
options.rationale: A test is not needed before a simple bedside check.

options.text: Post a hearing impairment sign above the bed
options.rationale: Labels him with a deficit that has not been found.

options.text: Assess how well the resident hears normal speech
options.rationale: Hearing loss is not assumed in an older adult. The wince suggests he hears well, and the nurse confirms it.

questions.takeaway: Do not assume every older adult has hearing loss. Assess each person, then match the communication plan to what you find.
questions.strategy: Three options act as if the hearing loss is real. Check what the stem actually shows.

steps.detail: He winces at the volume.
Age alone was the reason for shouting.
Normal speech first.

elimination.verdict: Assess his hearing with normal speech.

questions.stem: A camper arrives at urgent care frantic, reporting buzzing and movement in the ear. A live insect is visible in the canal. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Instill oil into the canal as prescribed
options.rationale: Oil suffocates the insect so it stops moving and can be removed safely.

options.text: Irrigate the canal with body temperature water
options.rationale: Tempting because irrigation removes many objects. A live insect is never irrigated.

options.text: Shine a light at the ear to draw it out
options.rationale: This is unreliable and leaves the insect moving against the eardrum.

options.text: Ask about past ear surgery and infections
options.rationale: Useful history before irrigation. The insect is already seen, and it is killed first.

questions.takeaway: Live insect in the ear: oil first to kill it, then removal. Never irrigate a live insect.
questions.strategy: The canal has already been inspected. The question is which fluid goes in.

steps.detail: A live insect is visible.
Water makes a live insect struggle.
Oil, then removal.

elimination.verdict: Instill oil.

questions.stem: A client with Meniere disease has followed a low sodium diet and taken a diuretic for 2 months. Which finding best indicates the plan is effective?

options.text: Hearing in the affected ear has returned to normal
options.rationale: Meniere disease is progressive, and treatment is not expected to restore hearing.

options.text: She has had no falls since she stopped driving
options.rationale: Tempting because safety matters. This shows her precautions work, not that the diet and diuretic are controlling the disease.

options.text: She had two vertigo attacks this month, down from eight
options.rationale: Diet and diuretics reduce endolymph volume, so fewer attacks is the outcome they target.

options.text: Her blood pressure is lower than at diagnosis
options.rationale: The diuretic lowers blood pressure, but that is not the goal of this plan.

questions.takeaway: Meniere treatment aims at fewer and milder vertigo attacks. It does not bring back lost hearing.
questions.strategy: Match the outcome to what the treatment acts on: fluid in the inner ear.

steps.detail: Less endolymph, fewer attacks.
No falls reflects not driving.
Hearing does not return to normal.

elimination.verdict: Two attacks this month, down from eight.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old with presbycusis has impacted cerumen removed from both ears. Afterward he hears the nurse better but still misses words in conversation. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Repeat the irrigation to remove remaining wax
options.rationale: Tempting because hearing is still reduced. The stem says the wax is out, and more irrigation cannot fix a nerve problem.

options.text: Document that the procedure did not work
options.rationale: It did work. The correctable part of his loss improved.

options.text: Request a referral for audiometry
options.rationale: The conductive part is fixed. The remaining sensorineural loss needs formal testing and a device.

options.text: Teach him to use softening drops every day
options.rationale: Routine drops address wax, which is no longer the cause of what remains.

questions.takeaway: Mixed loss: clearing the canal fixes the conductive part only. What remains is sensorineural and needs audiology.
questions.strategy: Partial improvement tells you there were two problems. Treat the one that is left.

steps.detail: Better, not normal.
Presbycusis is sensorineural.
Audiometry is the most reliable measure.

elimination.verdict: Refer for audiometry and hearing aid evaluation.

questions.stem: A client who is deaf and communicates by sign language and lip reading needs discharge teaching about a new medication. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Arrange a qualified interpreter through interpreter services
options.rationale: Effective communication is a legal and ethical duty, and interpreter services provide it.

options.text: Sit facing the client in good light
options.rationale: He reads lips, so he must see the nurse's face clearly.

options.text: Provide the instructions in writing
options.rationale: Written information supports what is taught and can be reread at home.

options.text: Ask the client's teenage son to sign the instructions
options.rationale: Convenient, but a family member may leave out or change medical information.

options.text: Raise the voice so he can catch more words
options.rationale: Shouting distorts lip movement and does not help a client who is deaf.

options.text: Have the client explain the plan back through the interpreter
options.rationale: A nod is not understanding. Explaining it back confirms the teaching worked.

questions.takeaway: For a client who is deaf: interpreter services, face to face in good light, written material, and confirm understanding. Not family, not volume.
questions.strategy: A family member who signs is the convenient choice, which makes the son tempting. Ask who is accountable for accuracy.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Louder does not help lip reading.
Accuracy and privacy are at risk.

steps.action: Keep what lets him see, read and confirm
steps.detail: Interpreter, light, writing, explaining back.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, F.

questions.scenario: A 34-year-old has had a cold for 4 days. He woke with throbbing right ear pain, muffled hearing and a temperature of 38.4 C. Moving the pinna does not change the pain. The provider notes a red, bulging eardrum.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Give the prescribed oral antibiotic and analgesic
options.rationale: Antibiotics treat the infection and analgesics treat the pressure pain.

options.text: Irrigate the right ear canal with warm water
options.rationale: Irrigation is never done when otitis media is suspected because it can spread infection.

options.text: Apply mild heat and encourage rest
options.rationale: Mild heat and rest are the comfort measures for otitis media.

options.text: Teach him to avoid earbuds and water for 7 to 10 days
options.rationale: This is the plan for external otitis, where the canal skin is inflamed.

options.text: External otitis
options.rationale: External otitis hurts when the pinna or tragus is moved. His pain does not change.

options.text: Acute otitis media
options.rationale: A cold, deep throbbing pain, fever, muffled hearing and a bulging eardrum fit a middle ear infection.

options.text: Cerumen impaction
options.rationale: Wax causes fullness and hearing loss without fever or a bulging eardrum.

options.text: Meniere disease
options.rationale: Meniere disease causes vertigo and tinnitus. It does not cause fever or a bulging eardrum.

options.text: Ear pain level and any new drainage
options.rationale: Sudden pain relief with drainage means the eardrum has perforated and must be reported.

options.text: Temperature
options.rationale: Falling fever shows the antibiotic is working.

options.text: Pain when the tragus is pressed
options.rationale: This tracks external otitis, not a middle ear infection.

options.text: Daily sodium intake
options.rationale: Sodium matters in Meniere disease, not in otitis media.

questions.takeaway: Otitis media is deep pressure pain behind a bulging eardrum after a cold. Treat with antibiotics, analgesics, heat and rest, and watch for sudden pain relief with drainage.
questions.strategy: The pinna finding sorts the two infections. Once you choose middle ear, the external ear actions and checks drop out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No pain with movement rules out external otitis.

steps.action: Match actions to the middle ear
steps.detail: Oral drugs, heat and rest. No irrigation.
Temperature, pain and drainage.

elimination.verdict: Acute otitis media; antibiotic with analgesic, heat and rest; pain with drainage, temperature.

questions.scenario: A client is one day past a right stapedectomy. The nurse reviews the morning findings.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is expected with safety measures or must be reported to the surgeon.

rows.text: Feels dizzy when he first stands up
rows.rationale: Vertigo is common after stapedectomy. The nurse assists with walking.

rows.text: Right side of the mouth droops when he smiles
rows.rationale: The facial nerve runs close to the surgical site, so new facial weakness is reported at once.

rows.text: Hearing in the right ear is muffled
rows.rationale: Hearing improves in about 4 to 6 weeks.

rows.text: Temperature 38.6 C with yellow drainage on the dressing
rows.rationale: Fever with purulent drainage suggests infection, a postoperative priority.

questions.takeaway: After stapedectomy, dizziness and muffled hearing are expected. Facial weakness and signs of infection are not.
questions.strategy: Ask of each row: is this the surgery healing, or the surgery being harmed?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Vertigo and delayed hearing.
Facial droop means possible cranial nerve VII injury.
Fever with yellow drainage.

elimination.verdict: Expected, report, expected, report.

questions.stem: A client with Meniere disease is in bed with the side rails up, call light in reach and lights dimmed. She is still spinning and has vomited twice. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Give the prescribed antiemetic and antivertigo drugs
options.rationale: The deciding detail is that every safety measure is already in place. The actual problem left is the vertigo and vomiting, so treat it.

options.text: Stay at the bedside and reassess her fall risk
options.rationale: Tempting because safety usually comes first. Safety is already secured, and reassessing adds nothing while she keeps vomiting.

options.text: Encourage sips of oral fluids to replace what she has lost
options.rationale: Fluid loss matters after vomiting. She cannot keep fluids down until the nausea is controlled.

options.text: Review the low sodium diet while she rests
options.rationale: Useful prevention teaching for later. A client in an acute attack cannot learn.

questions.takeaway: In an acute vertigo attack, make her safe, then treat the symptoms. Once safety is done, do not keep repeating it.
questions.strategy: Check what the stem says is already done. The next step is whatever problem is still untreated.

steps.detail: Rails, call light, dim lights, in bed.
Spinning and vomiting.
Fluids and teaching wait for symptom control.

elimination.verdict: Give the prescribed medications.

questions.stem: A client on day 8 of IV gentamicin says his ears started ringing today and he feels off balance when he turns. The next dose is due now. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the dose and report the symptoms on rounds
options.rationale: Tempting because the infection still needs treating. Another dose adds to damage that can become permanent.

options.text: Hold the dose and notify the prescriber
options.rationale: The deciding detail is new ringing plus imbalance on an ototoxic drug. Those are the early warning, and the nurse acts before the next dose goes in.

options.text: Do a whisper test before deciding about the dose
options.rationale: Tempting as assess first. He has already reported the cues, and a normal whisper test would not make the dose safe.

options.text: Give the dose slowly and teach him to rise carefully
options.rationale: Addresses the fall risk and keeps giving the cause. Slowing the infusion is not a fix the nurse can assume.

questions.takeaway: New tinnitus, hearing change or dizziness on an ototoxic drug means stop and report before the next dose.
questions.strategy: The assessment is already in the stem. Ask whether more data would change what you do with the dose in your hand.

steps.action: Link the cues to the drug
steps.detail: Gentamicin is ototoxic.
The dose is due now.
Harm continues with each dose.

elimination.verdict: Hold the dose and notify the prescriber.

questions.stem: The nurse has four clients with ear problems. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: Client the morning after stapedectomy who is dizzy when turning the head
options.rationale: Dizziness looks worrying and is expected early after ear surgery. Safety measures cover it.

options.text: Client with external otitis who has pain when the pinna is pulled
options.rationale: Painful and expected. Pain with movement of the pinna is how external otitis presents.

options.text: Client with otitis media who has new tender swelling behind the ear
options.rationale: The quiet finding is the unexpected one. Swelling and tenderness over the mastoid mean infection is spreading from the middle ear.

options.text: Client with Meniere disease who is spinning and vomiting in bed
options.rationale: The most dramatic client. Vertigo and vomiting are the expected attack, and she is already in bed.

questions.takeaway: Dizziness after ear surgery, pain with external otitis and vertigo with Meniere disease are expected. Redness, swelling or pain behind the ear is reported.
questions.strategy: Match each finding to its condition. Three fit. The one that does not fit its diagnosis is first.

steps.detail: Postoperative dizziness, pinna pain, Meniere vertigo.
Otitis media should not cause swelling behind the ear.
Vomiting in bed is unpleasant and expected.

elimination.verdict: The client with otitis media and mastoid swelling.

questions.stem: An older adult has ear fullness and visible cerumen. A standing order allows irrigation. He mentions the same ear drained fluid after an infection last month. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Irrigate with body temperature water aimed at the canal wall
options.rationale: Correct technique and the usual answer for cerumen. Recent drainage suggests the eardrum may not be intact, and water could enter the middle ear.

options.text: Instill softening drops now and irrigate tomorrow
options.rationale: Tempting because softening first is standard. Drops and irrigation both go through a possible perforation.

options.text: Irrigate gently and stop if he reports dizziness
options.rationale: Stopping for dizziness is right during a safe irrigation. It does not make this one safe to start.

options.text: Hold the irrigation until the eardrum is examined
options.rationale: The deciding detail is drainage after an infection last month. A possible perforation means nothing goes into the canal until the eardrum is seen.

questions.takeaway: A standing order covers the usual client. Recent ear drainage or a possible perforation means no irrigation and no drops until the eardrum is checked.
questions.strategy: Three options put fluid in the ear. Ask what one detail in the history makes any fluid unsafe.

steps.detail: Three options instill fluid.
Drainage after infection last month.
Possible perforation rules out all three.

elimination.verdict: Hold the irrigation until the eardrum is examined.

questions.stem: A client on day 2 of antibiotics for otitis media says the severe ear pain stopped suddenly overnight. He found drainage on the pillow and wants to stop the medicine. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: The pain relief shows the antibiotic is working well
options.rationale: Tempting because relief looks like success. Sudden relief with drainage means the eardrum ruptured, not that the infection cleared.

options.text: Keep the ear dry, finish the antibiotic and be examined
options.rationale: The deciding detail is sudden relief plus drainage. Pressure released through a perforation, so the infection still needs treatment and the eardrum needs a look.

options.text: Rinse the ear canal gently to clear the drainage
options.rationale: Tempting to clean the ear. Nothing is flushed into an ear with a likely perforation.

options.text: Stop the antibiotic if you stay pain free for a full day
options.rationale: Fits his wish and the lack of pain. Stopping early leaves the infection partly treated.

questions.takeaway: Ear pain that stops suddenly with drainage is a perforation. It looks like improvement and still needs the full antibiotic course, a dry ear and an examination.
questions.strategy: Ask how the pain went away. Gradual relief is the drug working. Sudden relief with drainage is something else.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sudden relief, drainage, day 2.
The eardrum perforated.

steps.action: Cut options that add fluid or stop treatment
steps.detail: Irrigation and stopping early are both unsafe.

elimination.verdict: Keep the ear dry, finish the antibiotic and be examined.

questions.stem: An older adult has muffled hearing in the right ear. A tuning fork on the forehead is louder on the right, where bone conduction outlasts air. What does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Referral for a cochlear implant evaluation
options.rationale: Implants are for sensorineural loss. These results point to a conductive problem.

options.text: A review of his drugs for ototoxic agents
options.rationale: Tempting for any new hearing loss, but ototoxic drugs damage the inner ear and sound would be louder in the good ear.

options.text: Teaching that the loss is likely permanent
options.rationale: Conductive loss is often correctable.

options.text: An otoscopic exam for wax or fluid
options.rationale: Sound louder in the poor ear with bone better than air means something is blocking sound, such as cerumen or fluid.

questions.takeaway: Weber louder in the bad ear and bone better than air means conductive loss. Look for a blockage that can be removed.
questions.strategy: Decide the type of loss first. Three options belong to sensorineural loss and one to conductive.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Louder in the affected ear, bone beats air: conductive.
Implant, ototoxic drugs and permanence fit nerve damage.
Look in the canal.

elimination.verdict: Otoscopic exam for wax or fluid.

questions.stem: A nurse with a high-pitched voice is teaching a client with presbycusis in a quiet, well-lit room. Facing him, she sees he still misses many words. Which change is best?

options.text: Speak in a lower tone at the same volume
options.rationale: High frequencies are lost first with aging, so a lower pitch is easier for him to hear.

options.text: Raise her voice so each word carries
options.rationale: Louder speech distorts sound and raises pitch further.

options.text: Move closer and speak into his ear
options.rationale: Speaking into his ear hides her face and lips, which give visual cues to anyone with hearing loss.

options.text: Switch to written instructions instead
options.rationale: Writing is a useful supplement and tempting, but the simplest fix to the missed cue is her pitch.

questions.takeaway: Presbycusis takes high-pitched sounds first. Lower the pitch, not the distance or the volume.
questions.strategy: The stem has already fixed light, noise and position. The one cue left is her voice.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Quiet, lit, face to face.
A high-pitched voice.
Shouting distorts and speaking into the ear hides her face.

elimination.verdict: Lower the pitch.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old with profound sensorineural hearing loss in both ears says that after 3 months her hearing aids make sounds louder but no clearer. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Encourage a longer trial with the aids
options.rationale: Tempting because adjusting takes time, but 3 months is a fair trial and aids help nerve loss least.

options.text: Request a cochlear implant evaluation
options.rationale: An implant bypasses the damaged cochlea and stimulates the nerve directly.

options.text: Ask the audiologist to raise the gain
options.rationale: More volume does not add clarity when the cochlea is damaged.

options.text: Suggest a personal sound amplifier instead
options.rationale: An amplifier does less than the aids she already has.

questions.takeaway: Hearing aids amplify. When the cochlea itself is damaged and aids do not help, the next option is a cochlear implant.
questions.strategy: Three options are more amplification. Her complaint is clarity, which amplification cannot fix.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sensorineural, profound.
Louder but not clearer.
Longer trial, more gain and an amplifier.

elimination.verdict: Cochlear implant evaluation.

questions.stem: An adult had a tube placed in the eardrum for recurrent otitis media. Which statement shows the home care teaching was effective?

options.text: "I rinse the ear in the shower to keep it clean."
options.rationale: Water can pass through the tube into the middle ear.

options.text: "I can swim again once the pain is gone."
options.rationale: The opening remains while the tube is in place, with or without pain.

options.text: "I keep water out of that ear when I bathe."
options.rationale: The tube is an open path to the middle ear, so the ear is kept dry.

options.text: "I blow my nose hard to keep the tube open."
options.rationale: Forceful blowing pushes secretions toward the middle ear.

questions.takeaway: A tube in the eardrum is an open door to the middle ear. Keep water out.
questions.strategy: Picture the tube as a hole. Any statement that sends water or pressure through it is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A direct opening to the middle ear.
Rinsing and swimming.
Hard nose blowing.

elimination.verdict: Keeps the ear dry.

questions.stem: On day 3 of treatment for external otitis, a call center worker is free of pain and asks to resume wearing her in-ear headset. Which response is best?

options.text: "With the pain gone, the headset is safe to wear."
options.rationale: Pain relief comes before the canal skin has healed.

options.text: "Wear it if you wipe it with alcohol each day."
options.rationale: Tempting, but a clean earpiece still rubs and traps moisture in an inflamed canal.

options.text: "Wear it for short calls and remove it between them."
options.rationale: Any in-ear wear irritates the canal during healing.

options.text: "Leave it out for 7 to 10 days and use a speaker."
options.rationale: Earpieces are a cause of external otitis, so the canal is left alone while it heals.

questions.takeaway: Anything worn in the canal can cause or prolong external otitis. Keep the canal empty and dry for 7 to 10 days.
questions.strategy: Three answers put the earpiece back in under some condition. Feeling better is not the same as healed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Earpieces and moisture irritate the canal.
Pain free, cleaned or brief use all return the irritant.
A speaker lets her work.

elimination.verdict: No in-ear headset for 7 to 10 days.

questions.stem: A client on IV furosemide is prescribed IV tobramycin for an infection. Which assessment is most important before the first antibiotic dose?

options.text: Baseline hearing and any ringing or dizziness
options.rationale: Both drugs are ototoxic. A baseline lets the nurse recognize the first change.

options.text: Daily weight and any ankle edema
options.rationale: Tempting because it tracks the diuretic, but it does not address the new combined risk.

options.text: Blood pressure lying and standing
options.rationale: Useful with a diuretic. It is not the risk the new drug adds.

options.text: Lung sounds and oxygen saturation
options.rationale: General assessment that does not target the drug pairing.

questions.takeaway: A loop diuretic plus an aminoglycoside doubles the ototoxic risk. Establish a hearing and balance baseline before the first dose.
questions.strategy: Ask what the two drugs have in common. The priority assessment follows that shared risk.

steps.detail: Loop diuretic and aminoglycoside.
Both can damage the inner ear.
Hearing, ringing and balance.

elimination.verdict: Baseline hearing and balance.

questions.stem: A client with disabling Meniere disease in the left ear is scheduled for a labyrinthectomy. Which statement shows she understands the expected outcome?

options.text: "My hearing should return once the pressure is drained."
options.rationale: That confuses this surgery with a decompression, and hearing is not restored.

options.text: "The spinning should stop, but that ear will be deaf."
options.rationale: Removing the labyrinth ends the vertigo and causes total hearing loss on that side.

options.text: "The ringing and the hearing loss will both go away."
options.rationale: Hearing is lost, not regained.

options.text: "The attacks will continue but should be milder."
options.rationale: Tempting as a modest hope, but the purpose is to stop the vertigo.

questions.takeaway: Labyrinthectomy is a trade: vertigo stops and hearing on that side is gone. The client must be able to state both.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that names the benefit and the cost together.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stops vertigo, removes hearing.
Two statements expect hearing to improve.
Milder attacks is not the aim.

elimination.verdict: No more spinning, deaf in that ear.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old salesman with moderate hearing loss refuses a hearing aid, saying clients will think he is old. He has begun avoiding meetings. Which response is best?

options.text: "Hearing aids are so small now that no one will notice."
options.rationale: Tempting because it is reassuring, but it argues with the worry instead of hearing it.

options.text: "Avoiding meetings will only hurt your career."
options.rationale: A warning adds pressure and closes the conversation.

options.text: "Tell me more about what worries you at work."
options.rationale: Opens his concern so the plan can be built around what matters to him.

options.text: "Many people your age wear them without a problem."
options.rationale: Dismisses his feeling by comparing him with others.

questions.takeaway: When a client refuses a device because of what it means to him, explore the meaning before you sell the device.
questions.strategy: Three responses try to change his mind. One invites him to say more.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Fear of looking old in front of clients.
Both brush the feeling aside.
It pressures him.

elimination.verdict: Ask him to tell you more.

questions.nursesNote: Follow-up visit, day 10 of amoxicillin for acute otitis media of the left ear. Temperature 36.9 C. Reports ear pain 0 of 10 since day 4. Follows conversation in the waiting room without asking for repeats. Provider notes the eardrum is pearly gray and no longer bulging. Reports a low-pitched hum in the left ear that is unchanged. States the ear still feels full. Has 2 doses left and plans to take them.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that show the treatment has been effective.

segments.text: Temperature 36.9 C
segments.rationale: Fever has resolved.

segments.text: Reports ear pain 0 of 10 since day 4
segments.rationale: Pressure pain is gone.

segments.text: Follows conversation in the waiting room without asking for repeats
segments.rationale: He follows conversation without asking for repeats, so the conductive hearing loss that otitis media causes is not present.

segments.text: Provider notes the eardrum is pearly gray and no longer bulging
segments.rationale: The eardrum has returned to normal with no fluid behind it.

segments.text: Reports a low-pitched hum in the left ear that is unchanged
segments.rationale: Low-pitched tinnitus is a sign of the infection and has not improved.

segments.text: States the ear still feels full
segments.rationale: Fullness suggests fluid or pressure remains.

segments.text: Has 2 doses left and plans to take them
segments.rationale: Good adherence, but it is not an outcome of treatment.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate otitis media by the signs it caused: fever, pain, hearing and the eardrum. Adherence is a behavior, not an outcome.
questions.strategy: For each finding ask: is this a sign of the infection that has gone away?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: List the signs otitis media causes
steps.detail: Fever, pain, hearing loss, bulging eardrum, tinnitus.
Temperature, pain, hearing, eardrum.

steps.action: Leave what persists or is not an outcome
steps.detail: Hum, fullness, remaining doses.

elimination.verdict: Temperature, pain, hearing and eardrum.

questions.stem: An older adult with ear fullness and visible cerumen has a prescription for a ceruminolytic followed by irrigation. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Irrigate with body temperature water aimed at the canal wall
options.rationale: Warm water and an indirect stream reduce dizziness and protect the eardrum.

options.text: Ask about past eardrum perforation, drainage or ear infection
options.rationale: Irrigation is unsafe if the eardrum may not be intact or infection is present.

options.text: Reassess hearing and ask about dizziness
options.rationale: Evaluates the result and the client's tolerance.

options.text: Instill the ceruminolytic drops and allow time for softening
options.rationale: Softened wax comes out with less force.

options.text: Inspect the returned solution and the canal for cerumen
options.rationale: Confirms the wax is out.

questions.takeaway: Screen for contraindications, soften, irrigate gently, inspect, then reassess hearing.
questions.strategy: Safety screening comes before any fluid goes in, and evaluation comes last.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rule out perforation and infection.
Soften, then irrigate.
Inspect, then reassess hearing.

elimination.verdict: Screen, soften, irrigate, inspect, reassess.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old's routine exam shows a dull, slightly retracted eardrum. She has no pain or fever and her hearing is unchanged. Her daughter asks if she needs antibiotics. How does the nurse interpret the finding?

options.text: An early middle ear infection
options.rationale: Infection brings pain, fever, redness and then bulging.

options.text: Fluid behind the eardrum that needs drainage
options.rationale: Fluid would muffle her hearing, and it is unchanged.

options.text: An expected change in the eardrum with age
options.rationale: The eardrum loses elasticity and can look dull and retracted. Without pain, fever or hearing change there is nothing to treat.

options.text: A sign of wax pressing on the eardrum
options.rationale: Tempting in an older adult. The eardrum was visible, so the canal is not blocked.

questions.takeaway: A dull, retracted eardrum in an older adult with no symptoms is an aging change. Treat the client, not the appearance.
questions.strategy: Three symptoms are absent. Each one removes an option.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No pain or fever removes infection.
Unchanged hearing removes fluid.
The eardrum was seen, so wax is not blocking it.

elimination.verdict: Expected age related change.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old machinist has reduced hearing in the right ear. The tuning fork on his forehead is louder in the left ear, and air conduction outlasts bone in both. What does the nurse do next?

options.text: Ask about noise exposure and ototoxic drugs
options.rationale: Sound heard better in the good ear with air still greater than bone points to sensorineural loss, so the causes of nerve damage are explored.

options.text: Prepare to irrigate the right ear canal
options.rationale: Irrigation is for a blockage, and these results do not fit a conductive loss.

options.text: Inspect the right canal for impacted wax
options.rationale: Tempting as the simplest cause. Wax would make the fork louder in the right ear and bone greater than air.

options.text: Teach him how to clear the ears when flying
options.rationale: Addresses pressure in the middle ear, which is a conductive problem.

questions.takeaway: Weber louder in the better ear with air greater than bone means sensorineural loss. Look for noise, drugs and aging, not for a blockage.
questions.strategy: Three options chase a blockage. Decide the type of loss first and see which option fits it.

steps.detail: Louder in the good ear.
Air still beats bone.
Inner ear and nerve causes.

elimination.verdict: Ask about noise and ototoxic drugs.

questions.stem: One week after getting his first hearing aid, a 70-year-old says restaurants are unbearably loud and he wants to return it. Which suggestion is best?

options.text: Wear it all day so that he adjusts faster
options.rationale: An aid amplifies background noise, so more hours of it in the first weeks is likely to make him give up sooner.

options.text: Turn the volume down low in every setting
options.rationale: Low enough to tolerate a restaurant is too low to help him hear speech.

options.text: Save it for the places where he most needs to hear well
options.rationale: Tempting as a compromise. Those are the noisy places, and occasional use never lets him adapt.

options.text: Wear it a few hours daily in quiet rooms first
options.rationale: An aid amplifies everything, including background noise. The brain adjusts with short sessions in quiet settings first.

questions.takeaway: A new hearing aid amplifies background noise. Start in quiet settings for short periods and increase gradually.
questions.strategy: Two options are all or nothing. Look for the gradual one.

steps.detail: Background noise, not the aid itself.
All day at once, or only for demanding places.
Quiet first, short periods, then longer.

elimination.verdict: Short periods in quiet, then build up.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old's hearing aid whistles whenever she turns her head. She hears the nurse well and the battery is new. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Replace the battery again
options.rationale: A weak battery makes the aid quiet or silent, and this one is new.

options.text: Reseat the aid snugly in the ear canal
options.rationale: Whistling is feedback from sound leaking around a loose fit. Movement of her head shifts the aid.

options.text: Turn the volume up to cover the whistle
options.rationale: Higher volume increases feedback.

options.text: Send the aid for repair
options.rationale: Reasonable if simple checks fail. Fit and wax are checked first.

questions.takeaway: A whistling hearing aid means feedback: poor fit, wax in the canal or volume set too high. Check the fit first.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you when it happens: with head movement. Ask what moves when the head moves.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New battery, hears well.
Head movement loosens the fit.
Simple check before repair.

elimination.verdict: Reseat the aid.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old surfer has right ear pain and a plugged feeling. He flinches when the nurse pulls the pinna to look in, and the canal is swollen. Which treatment does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Antibiotic and steroid ear drops
options.rationale: Pain on moving the pinna with a swollen canal is external otitis, which is treated topically.

options.text: Oral antibiotics for 10 days
options.rationale: Tempting because ear infection suggests pills. Oral antibiotics are for middle ear infection, where moving the pinna does not hurt.

options.text: Irrigation of the canal with warm water
options.rationale: Water worsens an inflamed canal, and he is to keep the ear dry.

options.text: A ceruminolytic twice a day
options.rationale: The plugged feeling comes from swelling.

questions.takeaway: Pain with movement of the pinna or tragus places the problem in the external canal. Topical drops, heat for comfort, keep it dry.
questions.strategy: One cue separates outer from middle ear: what happens when the pinna is moved.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Movement hurts, so the canal is the source.
Skin of the canal takes topical drugs.
A wet canal is the cause.

elimination.verdict: Topical antibiotic and steroid drops.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old veteran completed 3 months of tinnitus retraining therapy. Which report best shows the therapy was effective?

options.text: "The ringing is quieter on days when I take ibuprofen."
options.rationale: NSAIDs can cause tinnitus, and this credits a drug rather than the therapy.

options.text: "It still rings, but I sleep and work without noticing much."
options.rationale: The therapy aims to make the sound less intrusive. Function has returned even though the sound remains.

options.text: "I keep my house silent so the ringing does not get any worse."
options.rationale: Silence makes tinnitus more noticeable. Background sound is what helps.

options.text: "I am waiting for the therapy to make the ringing stop."
options.rationale: Tempting as a goal. The therapy does not remove the sound, so this shows the wrong expectation.

questions.takeaway: Tinnitus management is judged by function: sleep, work and distress. The goal is to live with the sound, not to silence it.
questions.strategy: Ask what the therapy can actually deliver. Reject any report that measures it by silence.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Less intrusion, not a cure.
Waiting for the ringing to stop.
Silence and NSAIDs.

elimination.verdict: The sound remains and no longer runs his day.

questions.stem: During a vertigo attack, a 36-year-old with Meniere disease lies still with nystagmus. Blood pressure is 158/94 mmHg and pulse is 108 beats per minute. An hour ago they were 122/76 and 80. How does the nurse respond?

options.text: Request an antihypertensive for the blood pressure
options.rationale: Treats a number that is expected to fall on its own, in a client who is already at risk of falling.

options.text: Sit her upright to help lower the pressure
options.rationale: Movement worsens vertigo and vomiting. She stays still.

options.text: Call the rapid response team for the change
options.rationale: Tempting because the change is abrupt. It has a known cause, and the stem gives no other sign of instability.

options.text: Keep her safe and recheck when the attack eases
options.rationale: Blood pressure, pulse and respirations can rise during an acute attack. They are rechecked once the vertigo settles.

questions.takeaway: Vital signs can rise during a Meniere attack. Expected for the condition, so protect from falls and reassess after the attack.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the change is expected for this condition at this moment. Expected findings are monitored.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Tie the change to the attack
steps.detail: Normal an hour ago, raised during vertigo.
Sitting her up worsens the attack.
Recheck when it eases.

elimination.verdict: Safety now, recheck after the attack.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old with Meniere disease has completed 8 weeks of vestibular rehabilitation. Which finding best shows the therapy was effective?

options.text: She turns her head while walking without touching the wall
options.rationale: Vestibular rehabilitation trains balance, so steady walking with head movement is the outcome.

options.text: She reports that the ringing in her affected ear is much softer
options.rationale: Tinnitus is not what the exercises treat.

options.text: She avoids turning her head when she walks
options.rationale: Tempting as caution. Avoiding head movement is the compensation the therapy is meant to replace.

options.text: Her hearing test is unchanged from 8 weeks ago
options.rationale: Hearing reflects the disease course and not balance training.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate vestibular rehabilitation by balance: steady gait with head movement and fewer near falls.
questions.strategy: Match the outcome to what the therapy trains. Balance therapy is measured by balance.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Balance.
Tinnitus and hearing.
Turning the head steadily against avoiding head turns.

elimination.verdict: Steady walking while turning her head.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old is scheduled for a cochlear implant. Which statement shows she understands what to expect?

options.text: "My hearing will be normal once the surgical site heals."
options.rationale: The device does not restore normal hearing.

options.text: "The implant will repair the damaged part of my inner ear."
options.rationale: It bypasses the damaged cochlea and does not repair it.

options.text: "I will not need lip reading once the device is turned on."
options.rationale: Tempting. Visual cues stay useful while she learns the new signal.

options.text: "I will need training to make sense of the new sounds."
options.rationale: The implant sends signals straight to the nerve, and the brain has to learn to interpret them through rehabilitation.

questions.takeaway: A cochlear implant bypasses the cochlea and stimulates the nerve. Hearing is not normal afterward, and audiologic rehabilitation is part of the treatment.
questions.strategy: Three statements promise a finished result. One describes work still to do.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Normal, repaired, no more lip reading.
Bypass, not repair.
Learning to interpret new sounds.

elimination.verdict: She expects training after the implant.
