rows.rationale: The question is whether nerve or muscle is the source.

rows.text: Daily checks of blood flow in the brain arteries after a bleed
rows.rationale: It measures cerebral blood flow at the bedside and can be repeated.

rows.text: Unresponsive after a cardiac arrest; the team asks whether the brain is active
rows.rationale: Brain electrical activity is what an EEG records.

rows.text: Foot drop after a leg injury; the team asks if the nerve is working
rows.rationale: EMG evaluates nerve and muscle disorders.

questions.takeaway: Match the test to the question: EEG for brain electrical activity, EMG for nerve and muscle, transcranial Doppler for cerebral blood flow.
questions.strategy: For each patient ask what the team wants to know: electricity, nerve and muscle, or blood flow.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Staring spells and brain activity after arrest.

steps.action: Find the nerve and muscle questions
steps.detail: Hand wasting and foot drop.
Brain arteries after a bleed.

elimination.verdict: EEG, EMG, Doppler, EEG, EMG.

questions.stem: A patient eating breakfast says, "My face feels strange." Yesterday's cranial nerve check was normal. Which findings does the nurse report? Select all that apply.

options.text: The left corner of the mouth stays down during a smile
options.rationale: New facial asymmetry.

options.text: Both eyebrows rise evenly when the patient looks up
options.rationale: Equal movement of the upper face is a normal finding.

options.text: Pupils are 3 mm, equal and brisk
options.rationale: Normal size, equal and reactive.

options.text: The patient coughs after swallowing a sip of juice
options.rationale: A sign of aspiration risk. The patient also stays NPO.

options.text: Both eyes follow the nurse's finger in every direction
options.rationale: Normal eye movement.

options.text: The voice sounds wet and gurgly after drinking
options.rationale: Fluid is sitting at the airway. This is a swallowing problem.

questions.takeaway: A basic cranial nerve check covers pupils, eye movement, facial symmetry and swallowing. Report whatever differs from baseline.
questions.strategy: Judge each finding alone against yesterday's normal check. Do not expect a set number of correct options.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Equal brisk pupils, full eye movement and even eyebrows.
The mouth is unequal. The eyebrows are even.
Cough and wet voice threaten the airway.

elimination.verdict: A, D, F.

questions.stem: After a fall, a 66-year-old opens his eyes only to nail bed pressure, makes moaning sounds with no words and pulls his hand away from the pressure. Which Glasgow Coma Scale score does the nurse record?

options.rationale: The verbal part is off. Moaning with no words is sounds (2). A score of 3 needs actual words.
Eyes open to pain (2), sounds only (2) and withdrawing from the pressure (4) add up to 8.
The eye part is off. A score of 3 is opening to voice, and he opens only to pressure.
The motor part is off. Pulling away from the pressure is withdrawal (4). A score of 3 is abnormal flexion of the arms to the chest.

questions.takeaway: GCS: eyes 4 spontaneous, 3 voice, 2 pain, 1 none. Verbal 5 oriented, 4 confused, 3 words, 2 sounds, 1 none. Motor 6 obeys, 5 localizes, 4 withdraws, 3 flexion, 2 extension, 1 none.
questions.strategy: Score each part on its own from the stem, then add. Do not start from the total.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Opens only to nail bed pressure is 2, which removes the option with E3.
Moans without words is sounds, 2, which removes V3.
Pulling away is withdrawal, 4, not flexion, 3.

questions.stem: The nurse checks the pupils of four patients admitted after head injuries. Which finding requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Both pupils 3 mm, round, constricting briskly to light
options.rationale: Inside the normal 2 to 6 mm range, equal, round and brisk.

options.text: Both pupils 4 mm, round, constricting briskly to light
options.rationale: Inside the normal range with a brisk reaction.

options.text: Both pupils 6 mm, round, constricting briskly to light
options.rationale: Large, which is the trap, but 6 mm is still inside the 2 to 6 mm range, and the pupils are equal and brisk.

options.text: Both pupils 5 mm, round, constricting sluggishly to light
options.rationale: The reaction is off. The size is inside 2 to 6 mm, but a sluggish reaction is an early warning of pressure on cranial nerve III.

questions.takeaway: Normal pupils are 2 to 6 mm, equal, round and brisk. Record size in millimeters. Sluggish is an early warning; fixed dilated or pinpoint is late.
questions.strategy: Hold each option against two specifications: size within 2 to 6 mm and a brisk reaction. The largest pupil is not automatically the abnormal one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 3, 4, 5 and 6 mm are all inside 2 to 6 mm, so size removes no one.
Three are brisk. One is sluggish.

elimination.verdict: 5 mm and sluggish. Report it.

questions.stem: A patient found slumped in a chair does not respond to a normal voice, a loud voice or a gentle shake of the shoulder. Which stimulus does the nurse use next?

options.text: Squeeze the trapezius muscle
options.rationale: The next step in the order: voice, loud voice, gentle shake, then a trapezius squeeze or nail bed pressure.

options.text: Call the patient's name again in a normal voice
options.rationale: The sequence is off. A normal voice was the first step and has already failed, so repeating it gives no new information.

options.text: Shake both shoulders with more force
options.rationale: The stimulus is off. After a gentle shake the order moves to pressure, not to rougher shaking.

options.text: Chart the patient as unresponsive to all stimuli
options.rationale: The sequence is cut short. A pressure stimulus has not been tried, so no response cannot be recorded yet.

questions.takeaway: Order of stimuli: normal voice, loud voice, gentle shake, then trapezius squeeze or nail bed pressure. Least noxious first, and move up only when there is no response.
questions.strategy: List what has been tried in the stem and pick the next rung, not a lower one and not the end.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Normal voice, loud voice and gentle shake are done.
A normal voice again goes down the ladder.
Unresponsive cannot be charted before pressure is tried.

elimination.verdict: Trapezius squeeze.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old with fever and a stiff neck is being prepared for a lumbar puncture. A CT scan showed no mass. Which preparation does the nurse carry out?

options.text: Empty bladder, lying prone with a pillow under the hips
options.rationale: The position is off. Prone does not open the spaces between the lumbar vertebrae.

options.text: Full bladder, lying on the side with knees drawn to the chest
options.rationale: The bladder specification is off. The patient empties the bladder before the test.

options.text: Empty bladder, lying on the side with knees drawn to the chest
options.rationale: Bladder emptied, side lying, knees to chest. The curled spine opens the space for the needle.

options.text: Empty bladder, lying on the side with both legs straight
options.rationale: The leg position is off. Straight legs leave the lumbar spine flat and the spaces narrow.

questions.takeaway: Lumbar puncture: empty the bladder, side lying with knees to the chest. It is not done when increased ICP is suspected, and you watch for headache after.
questions.strategy: Compare the options one specification at a time: bladder, then body position, then legs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three say empty. Full is the odd one and is wrong.
Side lying is taught. Prone is not.
Knees to chest, not straight.

elimination.verdict: Empty bladder, side lying, knees to chest.

questions.stem: A nursing student checks the pupils of a drowsy patient admitted with a headache. Which action by the student needs correction?

options.text: Brings the penlight in from the side of each eye
options.rationale: Correct technique. Light from the side shows the reaction without the patient focusing on the light.

options.text: Watches the other pupil for constriction as well
options.rationale: Correct. The untested pupil should constrict too, which is the consensual response.

options.text: Records the size of each pupil in millimeters
options.rationale: Correct. Size is documented in millimeters so the next check can be compared.

options.text: Leaves the bright overhead exam light on while testing
options.rationale: The room lighting is off. The light reaction is tested in a dim room, because bright light has already constricted the pupils.

questions.takeaway: Test pupils with the room dim and the penlight brought in from the side. The tested pupil constricts and so does the other one. Record size in millimeters.
questions.strategy: The stem asks for the wrong action. Three options are correct technique.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: You are looking for the one error.
Side approach, both pupils watched and millimeters are all taught.
Bright room lighting hides the reaction.

elimination.verdict: The overhead light. Dim the room.

questions.stem: A patient says the left hand "feels clumsy." Both hand grips are equal. Which test setup does the nurse use to find subtle arm weakness?

options.text: Arms straight out, palms up, eyes closed, held for 20 to 30 seconds
options.rationale: The pronator drift setup. A weak arm drifts down and turns palm in.

options.text: Arms straight out, palms up, eyes open, held for 20 to 30 seconds
options.rationale: The eyes are off. With eyes open the patient sees the drift and corrects it.

options.text: Arms straight out, palms up, eyes closed, held for 3 seconds
options.rationale: The time is off. A few seconds is too short for a subtle weakness to show.

options.text: Arms resting on the lap, palms up, eyes closed, held for 20 to 30 seconds
options.rationale: The arm position is off. Supported arms cannot drift.

questions.takeaway: Pronator drift: arms straight out, palms up, eyes closed for 20 to 30 seconds. It finds weakness too subtle for a grip test.
questions.strategy: All four share palms up. Compare the three things that change: arm position, eyes and time.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Resting on the lap removes the test.
Open eyes let the patient correct.
3 seconds is too short. 20 to 30 seconds is taught.

elimination.verdict: Arms out, palms up, eyes closed, 20 to 30 seconds.

questions.stem: The nurse checks four patients who are about to leave the unit for neurologic tests. Which preparation requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: EEG: hair washed last night with no styling products applied
options.rationale: Correct preparation. Clean hair with no gel lets the electrodes make contact.

options.text: MRI: a medicated skin patch left in place on the upper arm
options.rationale: The screening is off. Patches are on the MRI screening list with pacemakers and implants and are dealt with before the scanner.

options.text: CT with contrast: allergy history and creatinine reviewed
options.rationale: Correct preparation. Allergy and kidney function are checked before contrast.

options.text: Lumbar puncture: bladder emptied before positioning
options.rationale: Correct preparation. The bladder is emptied first.

questions.takeaway: MRI: screen for metal, pacemakers, implants and skin patches. EEG: clean hair, no gels. CT with contrast: allergy and creatinine. Lumbar puncture: empty bladder.
questions.strategy: Match each test to its own preparation and find the one that was skipped.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: EEG and hair, contrast and kidneys, lumbar puncture and bladder all fit.
A patch going into the MRI scanner was not screened.

elimination.verdict: The patch before MRI.

questions.stem: A patient with a breathing tube opens her eyes when her name is spoken and moves her hand to the nurse's hand during a trapezius squeeze. How does the nurse record the Glasgow Coma Scale?

options.text: E2 Vt M5 = 7t
options.rationale: The eye part is off. Opening to her name is to voice (3), not to pain (2).

options.text: E3 Vt M4 = 7t
options.rationale: The motor part is off. Reaching to the nurse's hand is localizing (5). Withdrawal (4) is pulling away.

options.text: E3 Vt M5 = 8t
options.rationale: Eyes to voice (3), verbal recorded as t because of the tube, and localizing (5).
The verbal part is off. She cannot speak around the tube, so verbal is recorded as t, not scored as oriented.

questions.takeaway: An intubated patient cannot be scored for speech, so verbal is recorded as t: E3 Vt M5 = 8t. Reaching to the stimulus is localizing (5); pulling away is withdrawal (4).
questions.strategy: Score eyes and motor from the stem, and treat the tube as the answer to the verbal part.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Verbal is t. The option with V5 is out.
To voice is 3.
Hand goes to the squeeze, so localizes, 5.

elimination.verdict: E3 Vt M5 = 8t.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews Glasgow Coma Scale scores for four patients on a neurology unit. Which patient does the nurse report to the provider immediately?

options.text: Score of 11 yesterday and 11 today
options.rationale: Low but steady. No change from this patient's baseline.

options.text: Score of 15 one hour ago and 13 now
options.rationale: A drop of 2 or more points is reported at once, and this one happened within an hour.

options.text: Score of 13 this morning and 14 now
options.rationale: The score is rising, which is improvement.

options.text: Score of 9 for the past three days
options.rationale: The lowest number here, which is the trap. It is unchanged, so it is less urgent than a new drop.

questions.takeaway: Trend beats a single score. A GCS drop of 2 or more points is reported immediately. A steady 9 is less urgent than 15 falling to 13 in an hour.
questions.strategy: Read each option as a direction: steady, up or down. The lowest number is not the answer.

steps.detail: Two are steady, one is up, one is down.
15 to 13 is 2 points in one hour.

elimination.verdict: 15 to 13. Call now.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old with diabetes reports that his toes feel numb. Which setup does the nurse use to test light touch?

options.text: Eyes open, limbs touched in random order, patient points to each spot
options.rationale: The eyes are off. With eyes open the patient sees the touch and the test shows nothing.

options.text: Eyes closed, each limb touched in the same order from toes up, patient points to each spot
options.rationale: The order is off. A fixed order lets the patient predict the next touch.

options.text: Eyes closed, limbs touched in random order, nurse asks "do you feel this?" each time
options.rationale: The cue is off. The question tells the patient a touch just happened.

options.text: Eyes closed, limbs touched in random order, patient points to each spot
options.rationale: Eyes closed, random order and the patient shows where the touch was, so the answer cannot be guessed.

questions.takeaway: Light touch: eyes closed, touch each limb in random order and have the patient point to the spot. Then touch both sides at once and compare.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option gives the patient a clue. Find the clue: sight, pattern or the nurse's question.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Eyes open fails.
A fixed order fails.
Asking each time fails.

elimination.verdict: Eyes closed, random order, patient points.

questions.stem: An 85-year-old with decreased touch sensation cannot change position alone in bed. The nurse reviews the plan of care. Which entry needs correction?

options.text: Check the bath water with a thermometer before bathing
options.rationale: Correct. The patient cannot feel water that is too hot.

options.text: Inspect both feet and use supportive shoes when up
options.rationale: Correct. Injuries on numb feet go unnoticed.

options.text: Reposition the patient every 4 hours while in bed
options.rationale: The interval is off. A patient with decreased sensation who cannot move alone is repositioned hourly.

options.text: Ask the patient to describe any pain in detail
options.rationale: Correct. Pain perception changes with age, so a detailed description is needed.

questions.takeaway: With decreased touch sensation: thermometer for bath water, watch the feet, supportive shoes, and reposition hourly if the patient cannot do it alone.
questions.strategy: Three entries protect skin the patient cannot feel. One leaves it under pressure too long.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: You want the wrong entry.
Hourly is taught. Every 4 hours is far outside it.

elimination.verdict: Every 4 hours. Change to hourly.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old's pupils are equal, round and brisk to light. To finish the PERRLA check, which test and expected result does the nurse use?

options.text: Patient looks at a far object, then at a near finger; eyes converge and pupils constrict
options.rationale: Accommodation: far to near, the eyes turn in and the pupils get smaller.

options.text: Patient looks at a far object, then at a near finger; eyes converge and pupils dilate
options.rationale: The expected result is off. Pupils constrict for near vision.

options.text: Patient looks at a near finger, then at a far object; eyes converge and pupils constrict
options.rationale: The direction is off. Convergence and constriction happen moving from far to near.

options.text: Penlight brought in from the side of each eye; both pupils constrict
options.rationale: The test is off. This is the light reaction, which the stem says is already done.

questions.takeaway: Accommodation, the A in PERRLA: the patient looks from far to near, the eyes converge and the pupils constrict.
questions.strategy: Two options are the same test with opposite results, and two reverse or replace the test.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The light check is already done.
Far to near.
Constrict, not dilate.

elimination.verdict: Far to near, converge and constrict.

questions.stem: A patient with Guillain-Barré syndrome has leg weakness that reached the thighs today. Which entry in the plan of care does the nurse question?

options.text: Assess breathing effort with each neurologic check
options.rationale: Correct. The weakness can reach the breathing muscles.

options.text: Neurologic checks once every 8 hours
options.rationale: The interval is off. Ascending Guillain-Barré needs neurologic checks every hour.

options.text: Compare leg strength on the right and left sides
options.rationale: Correct. Movement is always compared side to side.

options.text: Report weakness that moves above the thighs
options.rationale: Correct. Upward movement is the change that threatens breathing.

questions.takeaway: Ascending Guillain-Barré syndrome and acute spinal cord injury: neurologic checks every hour, because the weakness can reach the breathing muscles.
questions.strategy: The weakness moved today, so the plan must be able to catch the next move.

steps.detail: You want the entry that does not fit.
Every 8 hours cannot catch weakness that is rising within a day.

elimination.verdict: Once every 8 hours. It should be hourly.

questions.stem: A patient with new slurred speech is NPO. The nurse needs to check the gag reflex before a swallow screen is arranged. Which technique does the nurse use?

options.text: Touch the back of the tongue with a tongue blade
options.rationale: The gag reflex is tested with a tongue blade at the back of the tongue. No gag means aspiration risk.

options.text: Touch the tip of the tongue with a tongue blade
options.rationale: The site is off. The tip of the tongue does not trigger a gag.

options.text: Give a sip of water and watch for coughing
options.rationale: The tool is off. The patient is NPO, and swallowing is not tested in a patient who is NPO.

options.text: Stroke the lips with a cotton swab
options.rationale: The site and tool are off. Touching the lips does not test cranial nerves IX and X.

questions.takeaway: Gag reflex (cranial nerves IX and X): tongue blade to the back of the tongue. Absent gag means aspiration risk. Never test swallowing with water in a patient who is NPO.
questions.strategy: Find the option that reaches the back of the mouth without putting anything down the throat.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: NPO rules out sips.
Lips and tongue tip are too far forward.

elimination.verdict: Tongue blade, back of the tongue.

questions.scenario: A nurse watches a new graduate do a focused neurologic assessment on a drowsy 68-year-old admitted after a fall.
questions.stem: For each action, indicate whether it is correct or needs correction.

rows.text: Charts the pupils as "small and equal"
rows.rationale: Pupil size is documented in millimeters so the next nurse can compare.

rows.text: Puts in the patient's hearing aids before asking orientation questions
rows.rationale: A patient who cannot hear the question is not confused. Aids go in first.

rows.text: Applies nail bed pressure as the first stimulus to wake the patient
rows.rationale: The order starts with a normal voice. Pressure comes last, only if voice and a gentle shake fail.

rows.text: Charts the Glasgow Coma Scale as E3 V4 M6 = 13
rows.rationale: The parts and the total are both recorded.

rows.text: Tests light touch on the right arm and right leg only
rows.rationale: Sensation is always compared right against left.

rows.text: Asks different orientation questions than the ones charted last shift
rows.rationale: Questions are varied so the patient is not repeating memorized answers.

questions.takeaway: Pupils in millimeters, voice before pressure, both sides compared, aids in first, GCS charted as parts plus total, orientation questions varied.
questions.strategy: Judge each row against the taught technique on its own. Do not look for a pattern in the column.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: "Small" is not a measurement.
Pressure is the last stimulus, not the first.
One side tested means nothing to compare.

elimination.verdict: Needs correction, correct, needs correction, correct, needs correction, correct.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with atrial fibrillation was neurologically intact at 1400. Which finding at 1500 requires immediate follow up?

options.text: A mild headache that eased after acetaminophen
options.rationale: A headache that responds to a mild analgesic is not the sudden severe headache of a bleed.

options.text: Briefly unsure of the date after waking from a nap
options.rationale: Tempting because confusion is a stroke sign, but it clears on waking and is not sudden and persistent.

options.text: Sudden double vision and veering to one side
options.rationale: Sudden balance and eye changes are stroke signs from the back of the brain. Atrial fibrillation is an embolic source.

options.text: Hand tremor present since admission
options.rationale: Unchanged from baseline, so it is not a new deficit.

questions.takeaway: Stroke is not only face, arm and speech. Sudden balance or vision change in a patient with an embolic source is a stroke until proven otherwise.
questions.strategy: Look for the finding that is both new and sudden. Face and arm are not the only places a stroke shows up.

steps.detail: The tremor has not changed.
The headache and the grogginess both cleared.
Double vision plus veering is balance and eyes.

elimination.verdict: Sudden double vision and veering. Call the stroke alert.

questions.stem: A patient with right hemiplegia finished an alteplase infusion 6 hours ago and cannot get out of bed. Which measure to prevent venous thromboembolism should the nurse include?

options.text: Apply sequential compression devices to both lower legs
options.rationale: Mechanical prevention carries no bleeding risk during the 24 hours when anticoagulants are held.

options.text: Request a prescription for subcutaneous enoxaparin
options.rationale: The usual choice for an immobile patient, but no anticoagulants for 24 hours after a clot buster and until a follow up CT.

options.text: Place pillows under both knees
options.rationale: Pressure behind the knee slows venous return and raises clot risk.

options.text: Keep the legs still until the follow up CT
options.rationale: Immobility is the cause of the problem, so position changes continue.

questions.takeaway: For 24 hours after a clot buster, prevent clots mechanically. Anticoagulants and antiplatelets wait for the follow up CT.
questions.strategy: Two options prevent clots. The 6 hour mark decides which one is safe right now.

steps.detail: Knee pillows and keeping still both slow venous flow.
Enoxaparin and compression devices both work.

steps.action: Use the time in the stem
steps.detail: 6 hours is inside the 24 hour no anticoagulant window.

elimination.verdict: Sequential compression devices.

questions.stem: Two days after a left hemisphere stroke, a patient cannot name objects, coughs when drinking water, cries without warning and has a flaccid right arm. Which problem does the nurse address first?

options.text: Inability to name common objects
options.rationale: A real communication need, but it does not threaten the airway.

options.text: Coughing when drinking water
options.rationale: Coughing with thin liquids signals aspiration, which threatens the airway.

options.text: Crying without warning
options.rationale: Emotional lability is expected after stroke and needs explanation, not urgent action.

options.text: Flaccid right arm
options.rationale: Needs support on a pillow to protect the shoulder, which can follow airway protection.

questions.takeaway: After a stroke, the swallow problem outranks the language, mood and mobility problems because it threatens the airway.
questions.strategy: All four are real stroke problems. Rank them with airway, breathing and circulation.

steps.detail: Language, mood and limb function are not airway.
Coughing on water means the airway is not protected.

elimination.verdict: Coughing with water. Stop oral intake and rescreen the swallow.

questions.stem: A patient with increased ICP has gurgling secretions in the upper airway and an SpO2 of 90%. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Suction right away until the airway sounds clear
options.rationale: Tempting because airway is first, but prolonged suctioning without oxygen deepens hypoxia and raises ICP.

options.text: Hold suctioning and reposition to avoid raising the ICP
options.rationale: Suction only when needed is the rule. Gurgling with an SpO2 of 90% is when it is needed.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed so the secretions can drain out
options.rationale: A flat or head down position blocks venous drainage and raises ICP.

options.text: Give oxygen, suction briefly, then give oxygen again
options.rationale: The airway must be cleared. Oxygen before and after limits the hypoxia and ICP spike that suctioning causes.

questions.takeaway: With high ICP, suction only when needed, keep it brief and give oxygen before and after. Hypoxia itself raises ICP.
questions.strategy: Two options both clear the airway. Choose the one that also protects the brain from low oxygen.

steps.detail: Gurgling with a low SpO2 means yes.

steps.action: Cut the position that raises ICP
steps.detail: Head of bed stays up.

steps.action: Pick the safer way to suction
steps.detail: Brief, with oxygen on both sides.

elimination.verdict: Oxygen, brief suction, oxygen.

questions.stem: Six days after a subarachnoid hemorrhage, a patient who was alert becomes confused with a new left arm drift. The headache is unchanged. The findings are most consistent with which problem?

options.text: Vasospasm reducing blood flow to brain tissue
options.rationale: New ischemic deficits between days 4 and 14 without a new headache fit arteries clamping down after the bleed.

options.text: Rebleeding from the aneurysm into the subarachnoid space
options.rationale: A rebleed would bring a sudden severe headache. This headache is unchanged.

options.text: Hypoglycemia mimicking a stroke
options.rationale: Can cause confusion, but a one sided drift on day 6 after a bleed points to the vessel.

options.text: Expected recovery pattern after the hemorrhage
options.rationale: A new deficit is never expected recovery and needs to be reported now.

questions.takeaway: After a subarachnoid hemorrhage, new confusion or weakness on days 4 to 14 means vasospasm until proven otherwise. Report it immediately.
questions.strategy: Use the day and the headache. Day 6 with no new headache separates spasm from a rebleed.

steps.action: Cut the option that calls a new deficit normal
steps.detail: New drift is a change.
Rebleed brings sudden worst headache. Spasm brings new ischemia.
Day 6 sits inside days 4 to 14.

elimination.verdict: Vasospasm.

questions.stem: A patient with an ischemic stroke had a BP of 192/114 and received IV labetalol. Which finding indicates the patient is now ready for alteplase?

options.rationale: The diastolic is under the limit but the systolic is still above 185.
Both numbers are below 185/110, the limit before a clot buster.
The systolic is under the limit but the diastolic is still above 110.
The systolic has fallen the most, which makes it tempting. The diastolic is still above 110.

questions.takeaway: Before a clot buster both numbers must be below 185/110. One number in range is not enough.
questions.strategy: Check each option against both halves of 185/110.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 186 is not below 185.
112 and 114 are not below 110.
178 is below 185 and 100 is below 110.

questions.stem: The nurse taught a patient with left homonymous hemianopsia to scan. Which observation at lunch indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: The patient eats what the family moved to the right side
options.rationale: Tempting because the meal is eaten, but the family compensated and the patient did not scan.

options.text: The patient says the vision seems better today
options.rationale: A report of feeling better does not show the skill being used.

options.text: The patient asks staff to describe what is on the tray
options.rationale: Relies on others instead of scanning.

options.text: The patient turns the head left and finishes the whole tray
options.rationale: Turning toward the lost field and finding the food there shows the patient is scanning independently.

questions.takeaway: Scanning is effective when the patient turns the head toward the lost field without being set up by someone else.
questions.strategy: The goal was a patient behavior. Pick the option where the patient does the work.

steps.detail: Saying the vision is better is not a demonstration.
In one the family moved the food. In the other the patient turned the head.

steps.action: Match the outcome to the teaching
steps.detail: The teaching was scanning.

elimination.verdict: Turns the head left and finishes the tray.

questions.stem: A patient with an ischemic stroke was not a candidate for a clot buster. BP is 196/98 and the neuro status is unchanged. Labetalol is prescribed PRN for systolic pressure above 220. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the labetalol to bring the pressure below 180/105
options.rationale: 180/105 is the limit after a clot buster, which makes this tempting. This patient did not receive one.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed flat to reduce the pressure
options.rationale: Lying flat does not treat the BP and reduces venous drainage from the head.

options.text: Hold the labetalol and continue the neuro checks
options.rationale: Without a clot buster, BP is allowed to run high to keep the injured brain perfused. 196 is under the prescribed limit.

options.text: Call the provider to request a lower labetalol threshold
options.rationale: The threshold is deliberate. A sudden drop in pressure can starve the tissue around the stroke.

questions.takeaway: After an ischemic stroke with no clot buster, a high BP is tolerated to protect perfusion. The strict 180/105 limit belongs to the 24 hours after a clot buster.
questions.strategy: Three options try to lower the pressure. Check the stem for whether a clot buster was given and what the prescription says.

steps.detail: No clot buster means the 180/105 limit does not apply.
Labetalol is for systolic above 220. This is 196.

steps.action: Ask what the pressure is doing
steps.detail: It is pushing blood to tissue that can still be saved.

elimination.verdict: Hold the labetalol and keep monitoring.

questions.stem: Thirty hours after a stroke, a previously calm patient becomes restless and pulls at the IV line. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the prescribed PRN sedative for agitation
options.rationale: Sedation hides the LOC changes the nurse needs to track.

options.text: Assess LOC, pupils and oxygen saturation
options.rationale: New restlessness is the earliest sign of rising ICP and can also mean hypoxia, so the cause must be found first.

options.text: Apply hand mitts to protect the IV line
options.rationale: Tempting for safety, but it restrains a symptom without finding its cause and is not the least restrictive step.

options.text: Dim the lights and reduce noise in the room
options.rationale: A good measure for ICP, but it comes after finding out why the patient changed.

questions.takeaway: New restlessness in the first 72 hours after a stroke is a neurologic change. Assess before you sedate, restrain or settle.
questions.strategy: Nothing in the stem has been assessed yet. The behavior is a cue, not a diagnosis.

steps.detail: Calm to restless is a change in LOC.
Sedatives and mitts treat the behavior only.
Dimming the lights can wait a minute.

elimination.verdict: Assess LOC, pupils and oxygen saturation.

questions.stem: The nurse observes assistive personnel caring for a patient with a flaccid left arm and left sided neglect. Which action requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Approaching the patient from the right side
options.rationale: Looks wrong because the left is neglected, but approaching from the unaffected side is what the patient can attend to.

options.text: Putting the left arm into the sleeve first
options.rationale: Dressing the affected side first is correct.

options.text: Pulling the patient up by the left arm
options.rationale: Pulling on a flaccid arm can injure the shoulder.

options.text: Resting the left arm on a pillow
options.rationale: Supporting a flaccid arm protects the joint.

questions.takeaway: Never pull on a flaccid arm. Support it on a pillow and teach assistive personnel to do the same.
questions.strategy: You are looking for the unsafe action. One correct action is written to look wrong.

steps.detail: Find the one action that harms.
Affected sleeve first and a pillow under the arm are right.
Approaching from the unaffected side is taught practice.

elimination.verdict: Pulling by the flaccid arm.

questions.stem: A wife is upset that her husband, 4 days after a right hemisphere stroke, burst into laughter when told sad family news. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Request a depression screening because his mood is changing
options.rationale: Tempting because poststroke depression is real, but abrupt mismatched laughter is lability, not low mood.

options.text: Advise the family to hold back upsetting news until he recovers
options.rationale: Isolates the patient and does not explain the behavior.

options.text: Tell her the laughter shows he is coping well with the news
options.rationale: Kind, and wrong. The laughter is not a sign of coping. It is a stroke effect he cannot control.

options.text: Explain that stroke can cause emotions that do not match his mood
options.rationale: Sudden laughing that does not fit the situation is emotional lability. The family needs it explained.

questions.takeaway: Emotional lability is sudden laughing or crying that does not match the mood. Explain it to the family so they do not take it personally.
questions.strategy: Mismatched and sudden are the tipping words. Depression is sustained, not a burst.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: The laughter is not coping. He cannot control it.
Withholding news does not help the family understand.
A burst that does not fit is lability.

elimination.verdict: Explain emotional lability to the wife.

questions.stem: A patient with facial droop and arm drift had a glucose of 54 mg/dL and received IV dextrose. The glucose is now 118 mg/dL and both deficits persist. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Recheck the glucose in 15 minutes before doing anything further
options.rationale: Tempting after treating hypoglycemia, but 118 is corrected and waiting costs brain tissue.

options.text: Give a snack to keep the glucose up
options.rationale: A facial droop means aspiration risk, so nothing goes by mouth until a swallow screen.

options.text: Continue the stroke alert and prepare for CT
options.rationale: The mimic is corrected and the deficits remain, so this is treated as a stroke and the clock is running.

options.text: Cancel the stroke alert because the glucose was the cause
options.rationale: If glucose were the cause, the deficits would have cleared.

questions.takeaway: Treat hypoglycemia first, then reassess. Deficits that outlast a normal glucose are a stroke until imaging says otherwise.
questions.strategy: The reassessment is already done. The glucose is normal and the deficits are not.

steps.detail: 118 is corrected.
Droop and drift did not clear.

steps.action: Cut the delays and the oral intake
steps.detail: Waiting loses time and a snack risks aspiration.

elimination.verdict: Continue the stroke alert and go to CT.

questions.stem: A patient arrives 1 hour after sudden aphasia began. Which history finding does the nurse report to the stroke team first?

options.text: Takes aspirin 81 mg every day with breakfast
options.rationale: Tempting because it affects bleeding, but daily aspirin does not decide eligibility the way an anticoagulant does.

options.text: Took a dose of apixaban this morning
options.rationale: A recent anticoagulant dose raises bleeding risk and can rule out a clot buster.

options.text: Has had hypertension for 10 years
options.rationale: A risk factor that explains the stroke but does not change the next decision.

options.text: Stopped smoking 2 years ago
options.rationale: Background history that can wait.

questions.takeaway: With last known well already inside the window, the next urgent history is medications, especially anticoagulants.
questions.strategy: The time is already known. Ask which remaining fact could stop the treatment.

steps.detail: Hypertension and smoking do not change the next hour.
Aspirin is an antiplatelet. Apixaban is an anticoagulant.
A same day anticoagulant dose decides candidacy.

elimination.verdict: The apixaban dose this morning.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a patient going home after a TIA. Which statement indicates the teaching was understood?

options.text: "If the numbness returns, I will take an extra aspirin and rest."
options.rationale: Returning symptoms mean call 911. Aspirin could worsen a bleed.

options.text: "If symptoms come back and clear, I will tell my provider at my next visit."
options.rationale: Symptoms that clear are still an emergency.

options.text: "I can stop the clopidogrel once my BP is normal."
options.rationale: The antiplatelet and the BP drug do different jobs.

options.text: "I will take my clopidogrel and BP pills even though I feel normal."
options.rationale: A TIA is a warning. Prevention continues when symptoms are gone.

questions.takeaway: After a TIA, feeling normal is not the end of treatment. Antiplatelets and BP control continue. Any return of symptoms means 911.
questions.strategy: Three statements treat the TIA as finished. One treats it as a warning.

steps.action: Cut the statements that delay care
steps.detail: Resting and waiting for the next visit both delay.

steps.action: Cut the one that stops a drug
steps.detail: A normal BP does not replace an antiplatelet.

steps.action: Keep the one that continues prevention
steps.detail: Feeling normal does not change the plan.

elimination.verdict: Keeps taking clopidogrel and BP pills.

questions.stem: Thirty five minutes into an alteplase infusion, a patient reports a new severe headache and nausea. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Stop the alteplase infusion
options.rationale: A new severe headache with nausea during a clot buster suggests bleeding in the brain. Stopping the drug is the one action that limits the harm.

options.text: Give the PRN antiemetic and analgesic
options.rationale: Treats the symptoms as discomfort and lets the drug keep running.

options.text: Repeat the neuro check and BP
options.rationale: Assessment is usually first, which makes this tempting. The cue is already enough to act on, and the check follows within the minute.

options.text: Call the provider and await orders
options.rationale: The call is required and comes right after the infusion is stopped. Waiting for orders leaves the drug running.

questions.takeaway: During a clot buster, a new severe headache, nausea or vomiting means stop the infusion, then notify and expect a head CT.
questions.strategy: Three options are things the nurse will do. Ask which one stops the harm while the others happen.

steps.detail: New severe headache and nausea during alteplase point to bleeding.
The cue is already in hand. More assessment while the drug infuses adds harm.
Stop, then call, then reassess and prepare for CT.

elimination.verdict: Stop the infusion first.

questions.stem: A patient reports seeing two of everything since a stroke and misjudges the cup when reaching for it. Which intervention should the nurse include?

options.text: Place all items on the patient's right side
options.rationale: This fits a patient who has lost the left half of the visual field. This patient sees the whole field, doubled.

options.text: Teach turning the head side to side to scan
options.rationale: Scanning helps with hemianopsia and is tempting as the usual vision teaching. It does not remove a double image.

options.text: Patch one eye and alternate it every 2 to 4 hours
options.rationale: Covering one eye removes the second image. Alternating the patch keeps both eyes in use.

options.text: Keep the room dim and limit visual stimulation
options.rationale: Light is not the problem, and a dim room adds a fall risk.

questions.takeaway: Match the aid to the vision problem. Double vision gets an alternating eye patch. A lost half field gets scanning and items placed in the intact field.
questions.strategy: Two options treat a lost visual field. Decide whether this patient has lost part of the view or sees it twice.

steps.detail: Two of everything is double vision, not a missing field.
Items to one side and head scanning both treat hemianopsia.

steps.action: Pick what removes the second image
steps.detail: One eye covered gives one image.

elimination.verdict: Alternating eye patch.

questions.stem: A patient with increased ICP had a GCS of 11 and was restless. The nurse raised the head of the bed, kept the head midline and spaced care. Which findings 1 hour later indicate the interventions are effective? Select all that apply.

options.text: GCS of 14
options.rationale: A rising GCS shows LOC is improving, the best sign that ICP is coming down.

options.text: Resting quietly and waking easily to voice
options.rationale: The restlessness is gone and the patient still arouses easily, so this is calm and not stupor.

options.text: Pupils equal and briskly reactive
options.rationale: Brisk equal pupils show the brainstem is not being compressed.

options.text: Heart rate 52 with BP 182/68
options.rationale: A slow pulse with a wide pulse pressure is part of the Cushing triad, a late sign of worsening.

options.text: Quiet and responding only to pain
options.rationale: Quiet because of a deeper LOC is deterioration.

options.text: New vomiting without nausea
options.rationale: Vomiting is a sign of rising ICP.

questions.takeaway: Judge ICP care by the neuro status. Quiet is only good news when the patient still wakes easily.
questions.strategy: Two options describe a quiet patient. Check how easily each one wakes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: GCS 14 and easy to wake are better. Responding only to pain is worse.

steps.action: Read the vital signs as a pattern
steps.detail: Slow pulse with a wide pulse pressure is a late warning.
Brisk pupils are good. New vomiting is not.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C.

questions.scenario: A 66-year-old finished an alteplase infusion 3 hours ago. BP is 188/106. She failed the bedside swallow screen. Neuro status is unchanged from baseline.
questions.stem: For each prescription or action, indicate whether the nurse should implement it or question it at this time.

rows.text: Aspirin 81 mg by mouth now
rows.rationale: No antiplatelets for 24 hours after a clot buster and until a follow up CT shows no bleeding.

rows.text: Insert a urinary catheter to measure output
rows.rationale: Catheters are avoided until the patient is stable because of bleeding risk.

rows.text: Neuro checks and vital signs every 30 minutes
rows.rationale: After the first 2 hours, checks are every 30 minutes for the next 6 hours.

rows.text: Notify the provider about the BP
rows.rationale: 188/106 is above the 180/105 limit after a clot buster.

rows.text: Insert a nasogastric tube for medications
rows.rationale: She failed the swallow screen, but tubes wait until she is stable. Other routes are used.

rows.text: Keep NPO
rows.rationale: A failed swallow screen means nothing by mouth.

questions.takeaway: For 24 hours after a clot buster: frequent neuro checks, BP below 180/105, no tubes, no catheters and no antiplatelets.
questions.strategy: Ask of each row whether it could cause bleeding. If it punctures, scrapes or thins the blood, question it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Aspirin, a catheter and a nasogastric tube.

steps.action: Check the BP against the limit
Match the check frequency to the hour
steps.detail: Hour 3 falls in the every 30 minutes period.

elimination.verdict: Question aspirin, catheter and tube. Implement the checks, the BP report and NPO.

questions.scenario: A 54-year-old with hypertension and cocaine use arrives 50 minutes after a sudden severe headache. He has vomited twice and had a brief seizure in triage. He is drowsy but follows commands. BP 212/118.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Prepare the patient for an immediate noncontrast CT
options.rationale: CT detects bleeding fast and must come before any treatment decision.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and keep the head midline
options.rationale: Helps venous blood drain from the skull while ICP is at risk.

options.text: Prepare the alteplase infusion
options.rationale: He is inside the time window, which makes this tempting, but a clot buster in a bleed is harmful.

options.text: Give aspirin by mouth
options.rationale: Worsens bleeding. A drowsy patient who is vomiting also takes nothing by mouth.

options.text: Hemorrhagic stroke
options.rationale: Sudden headache, vomiting, a seizure, falling LOC, hypertension and cocaine use all point to a bleed.

options.text: Embolic ischemic stroke
options.rationale: Sudden onset fits, but LOC is usually preserved and seizures and headache are not typical.

options.text: Transient ischemic attack
options.rationale: His symptoms are severe and continuing, not resolving.

options.text: Hypoglycemia
options.rationale: A mimic worth checking, but it does not explain a sudden severe headache.

options.text: Level of consciousness
options.rationale: The earliest sign that ICP is rising.

options.text: Pupil size and reaction
options.rationale: Sluggish pupils are an early ICP sign and fixed pupils a late one.

options.text: Bowel sounds
options.rationale: Not affected by this problem.

options.text: Daily weight
options.rationale: Useful for fluid balance over days, not for a bleed in the first hour.

questions.takeaway: Headache, vomiting, seizure and falling LOC point to a bleed. Being inside the time window never replaces the CT.
questions.strategy: The 50 minutes is there to pull you toward a clot buster. Decide the type of stroke before you decide the treatment.

steps.action: Name the problem from the cues
steps.detail: Headache, vomiting, seizure, drowsy, cocaine.
Alteplase and aspirin.
LOC and pupils show rising ICP.

elimination.verdict: Hemorrhagic stroke; CT and head of bed up; LOC and pupils.

questions.stem: A restless patient with increased ICP has the head of the bed at 30 degrees, the head turned sharply right and clear lungs. A bath, a turn and suctioning are due. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Do the bath and turn together so the patient can then rest
options.rationale: Clustering care is the usual way to protect rest, which makes this tempting. With high ICP, back to back care raises the pressure.

options.text: Suction now to keep the airway clear, then let the patient rest
options.rationale: Airway sounds like the priority, but the lungs are clear. Suctioning without need spikes ICP.

options.text: Place the head midline and space the care activities apart
options.rationale: A turned neck blocks venous drainage from the skull, and spacing care keeps the pressure from climbing. Both fit the cues given.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed to improve blood flow to the brain
options.rationale: Tempting as a perfusion fix. Lying flat reduces venous drainage and raises ICP.

questions.takeaway: High ICP reverses the clustering rule. Keep the head midline, suction only when needed and space care out.
questions.strategy: Two usual rules, cluster care and airway first, both point to wrong options here. Check each against a stem detail.

steps.detail: Clear lungs mean there is nothing to suction.
Clustering is the rule that flips with high ICP.
A sharply turned head is a fixable cause of restlessness and pressure.

elimination.verdict: Head midline and space the care.

questions.stem: A man went to bed well at 2200 and spoke normally to his wife at 0500. At 0700 she found him unable to speak. They arrived at 0740. Which time is reported as last known well?

options.text: 0500, when he last spoke normally to his wife
options.rationale: Last known well is the last time someone saw him at baseline. That sets the treatment clock.

options.text: 0700, when his wife found him unable to speak
options.rationale: Tempting because it is when the stroke was noticed. Found time is not onset time and would overstate the window.

options.text: 2200, when he went to bed feeling well
options.rationale: The safe answer when a patient wakes with symptoms and nobody saw him overnight. Here the wife saw him normal at 0500.

options.text: 0740, when he arrived in the emergency department
options.rationale: Arrival starts the door to needle clock, not the treatment window.

questions.takeaway: Last known well is the last time the patient was seen normal. Not when he was found and not always bedtime.
questions.strategy: Three times are defensible. Walk the timeline and stop at the last moment a witness saw him at baseline.

steps.detail: It measures the hospital, not the stroke.
Symptoms began at some point before 0700.
The 0500 conversation is a witnessed normal.

elimination.verdict: Report 0500 as last known well.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients on a stroke unit. Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: Hemorrhagic stroke with a headache rated 6, unchanged since admission
options.rationale: A headache is expected with a bleed and it has not changed.

options.text: Left hemisphere stroke, unable to speak and crying in frustration
options.rationale: Aphasia is expected with left hemisphere damage. The patient needs support soon, not first.

options.text: Right hemisphere stroke, ignoring the left side, bed alarm sounding twice
options.rationale: A real safety risk and very tempting. Impulsivity and neglect are expected, and the alarm is doing its job while the nurse sees the new deficit.

options.text: TIA awaiting discharge, trouble finding words again for 10 minutes
options.rationale: Returning symptoms after a TIA may be a stroke in progress, and treatment is time limited. This is the only new deficit.

questions.takeaway: A TIA is a warning. When the symptoms come back, the clock has started and that patient goes first.
questions.strategy: Safety and a new deficit compete here. Ask which problem gets worse by the minute if the nurse is elsewhere.

steps.detail: Headache with a bleed and aphasia with a left stroke are expected.
It is a potential harm with an alarm already in place.
New, sudden and time limited.

elimination.verdict: See the TIA patient whose symptoms returned.

questions.stem: A patient passed a swallow screen yesterday. At breakfast the assistive worker reports a wet, gurgly voice and a cough after each sip of juice. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Have the assistive worker thicken the juice and continue the meal
options.rationale: Thickened liquids may be the eventual plan, which tempts. That decision follows a new swallow evaluation, not a guess during a meal.

options.text: Stop the meal, keep NPO and request a swallow evaluation
options.rationale: A wet voice and coughing with sips are signs of aspiration now. Yesterday's passed screen no longer describes this patient.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 90 degrees and feed more slowly
options.rationale: Upright positioning lowers risk in a patient who can swallow safely. It does not fix a swallow that is failing.

options.text: Suction the mouth, then resume with the chin tucked down
options.rationale: Clears what is in the mouth and treats a technique that has not been prescribed as safe.

questions.takeaway: A passed screen is a snapshot. Wet voice or coughing with intake means stop, nothing by mouth and a new evaluation.
questions.strategy: Three options keep feeding with an adjustment. The deciding detail is that the cues are happening now, whatever yesterday's result was.

steps.action: Weigh the old result against today's cues
steps.detail: Today's wet voice and cough win.
Three continue oral intake and one stops it.
Aspiration is an airway problem.

elimination.verdict: Stop the meal, NPO and request a swallow evaluation.

questions.stem: A patient arrives 40 minutes after sudden right arm weakness began. The airway is clear, glucose is 110 mg/dL and the neuro check is charted. Alteplase is being considered. Which action is next?

options.text: Obtain an actual weight to calculate the alteplase dose
options.rationale: Needed before the drug is given and quick to do. It is not what decides whether the drug can be given at all.

options.text: Perform the swallow screen so aspirin can be given
options.rationale: The screen is required before anything by mouth. No antiplatelet or clot buster is given until bleeding is ruled out.

options.text: Take the patient for the noncontrast CT scan
options.rationale: Airway, glucose and the neuro check are done. Imaging to rule out a bleed is the step that every treatment decision waits on.

options.text: Repeat the full neuro assessment to confirm the deficit
options.rationale: Tempting as assess first. The assessment is already charted and repeating it spends treatment time.

questions.takeaway: Once airway, glucose and the neuro check are done, the scan is next. Nothing that dissolves or prevents clots is given before a bleed is ruled out.
questions.strategy: List what the stem says is already done, then pick the step everything else waits on.

steps.detail: Airway, glucose and neuro check.
It adds no new information.
Weight and swallow screen matter only after the scan shows no bleed.

elimination.verdict: Go to CT now.

questions.stem: A patient with left sided neglect after a right hemisphere stroke is being moved to a new room. Which arrangement does the nurse plan?

options.text: Bed placed so the left side faces the door
options.rationale: Staff and visitors would arrive in the space the patient ignores, which startles and isolates.

options.text: Bed placed so the right side faces the door
options.rationale: The unaffected side faces the door, so people approach where the patient is aware of them.

options.text: Call light clipped at the left hand for practice
options.rationale: Tempting as retraining, but a safety device belongs where the patient will find it.

options.text: Phone and water kept on the left bedside table
options.rationale: Needed items placed in the neglected space go unused.

questions.takeaway: With neglect, approach from the unaffected side and keep it facing the door. Cue scanning of the neglected side during care, not with safety items.
questions.strategy: Two options mirror each other. Decide which side the patient is aware of.

steps.detail: Right, after a right hemisphere stroke.
Call light, phone and water would be missed.
Right side toward the door.

elimination.verdict: Right side faces the door.

questions.stem: The nurse taught dressing skills to a patient with left arm weakness and left sided neglect. Which observation indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: Guides the left arm into the sleeve first
options.rationale: Dressing the affected side first is the technique taught, and it makes the patient attend to that side.

options.text: Puts the right arm into the sleeve first
options.rationale: Tempting because it uses the strong arm, but it leaves the weak arm hard to dress.

options.text: Waits for the spouse to button the shirt
options.rationale: Shows dependence, not use of the skill.

options.text: Wears the shirt with the left sleeve empty
options.rationale: The neglected side was left out, so the teaching has not worked.

questions.takeaway: For weakness with neglect, the affected side is dressed first and the patient is taught to touch and use both sides.
questions.strategy: Look for the behavior that includes the affected side without help.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The spouse is doing the task.
An empty left sleeve is neglect.
Affected side first.

elimination.verdict: Left arm into the sleeve first.

questions.stem: Alteplase 101 mg is prescribed for a patient with an ischemic stroke who weighs 112 kg. CT shows no bleeding. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give 10 mg as a bolus and infuse 91 mg
options.rationale: Correct method of 10% then the rest, applied to a total that is too high.

options.text: Recalculate using the ideal body weight
options.rationale: The dose is based on actual weight.

options.text: Infuse the full dose over 2 hours by pump
options.rationale: Slowing the infusion does not correct a total above the limit.

options.text: Clarify the prescribed dose with the provider
options.rationale: 0.9 mg/kg gives 100.8 mg, but the total dose is capped at 90 mg, so the prescription is clarified before any drug is given.

questions.takeaway: Alteplase is 0.9 mg/kg of actual weight with a maximum of 90 mg. 10% is a bolus over 1 minute and the rest runs over 60 minutes.
questions.strategy: The arithmetic checks out, which is the trap. Check the total against the maximum dose.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Maximum 90 mg.

steps.action: Drop options that give or reshape the wrong total
steps.detail: Bolus split, slower rate, ideal weight.

elimination.verdict: Clarify the dose before giving it.

questions.stem: A patient returns to the unit after a carotid stent placement. Which finding does the nurse report immediately?

options.text: Hoarse voice with swelling on that side of the neck
options.rationale: Neck swelling with hoarseness means pressure near the airway, so it is reported at once.

options.text: Headache rated 3 that eased with acetaminophen
options.rationale: Tempting because headache is on the report list, but that is a severe headache. This one is mild and relieved.

options.text: Feels tired and wants to sleep but wakes easily
options.rationale: Easy waking shows level of consciousness is intact.

options.text: Tenderness with no swelling at the groin site
options.rationale: Expected at a puncture site when there is no swelling or bleeding.

questions.takeaway: After a carotid stent report severe headache, change in level of consciousness, weakness, severe neck pain, neck swelling, hoarseness or trouble swallowing.
questions.strategy: Three findings are mild or expected. Look for the one that involves the airway.

steps.detail: Site tenderness and tiredness with easy waking.
Mild and relieved.
Hoarseness with neck swelling.

elimination.verdict: Hoarseness with neck swelling.

questions.stem: The nurse taught the spouse of a patient going home after a stroke what to do if symptoms return. Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I will give an aspirin and then call the clinic."
options.rationale: Tempting because aspirin prevents clots, but a bleed cannot be ruled out at home and the clinic is not emergency care.

options.text: "I will drive straight to the stroke center."
options.rationale: Fast, but 911 brings assessment on the way and alerts the stroke team.

options.text: "I will call 911 and note the time it started."
options.rationale: Calling 911 and noting the time gives the team what it needs to decide on treatment.

options.text: "I will let my spouse rest and recheck in an hour."
options.rationale: Waiting uses up the time in which treatment is possible.

questions.takeaway: Time in BE FAST means call 911 and record when the person was last normal. No aspirin at home, no waiting, no driving in.
questions.strategy: Three statements act quickly. Pick the one that also protects the treatment decision.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An hour of rest is an hour lost.
The stroke type is unknown.
911 is faster to care and the time is recorded.

elimination.verdict: Call 911 and note the time.

questions.stem: A patient had an NIHSS score of 13 before a clot buster. Which finding 2 hours after the infusion best indicates the treatment was effective?

options.text: Blood pressure is now 148/84
options.rationale: Shows the pressure is within the limit after the drug, not that brain tissue has recovered.

options.text: NIHSS score is now 5
options.rationale: A lower score means fewer deficits, so blood flow has been restored to threatened tissue.

options.text: No bleeding at the IV sites
options.rationale: Shows the absence of a complication, which is safety and not effectiveness.

options.text: Sleeping and hard to wake
options.rationale: Tempting as rest after a hard day. A lower level of consciousness is a decline.

questions.takeaway: The NIHSS is a trend tool. Higher is worse and 0 is normal, so a falling score after treatment means improvement.
questions.strategy: Separate signs that the drug worked from signs that it did no harm.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hard to wake is worse.
Blood pressure in range and no bleeding.
13 down to 5.

elimination.verdict: NIHSS now 5.

questions.stem: At a clinic visit 3 weeks after a TIA, a patient's blood pressure is high. The patient says, "I ran out of pills. The pharmacy is two bus rides away." Which action is best?

options.text: Review how the pills lower the risk of stroke
options.rationale: Tempting because teaching is a nursing action, but the patient has shown no knowledge gap.

options.text: Ask the provider about adding a second drug
options.rationale: The current drug has not failed. It has not been taken.

options.text: Stress that missed doses can lead to a stroke
options.rationale: A warning does not shorten the trip to the pharmacy.

options.text: Ask about transportation and arrange delivery
options.rationale: The stated barrier is access, so the plan addresses access.

questions.takeaway: Check basic needs such as transportation, food and housing before you assume a patient needs more teaching or more medication.
questions.strategy: Use the patient's own words. They name the barrier, and only one option addresses it.

steps.detail: Distance to the pharmacy.
Knowledge is not the gap.
The first one was not taken.

elimination.verdict: Ask about transportation and arrange delivery.

questions.stem: A patient with a large stroke is at risk for increased ICP. The patient has a temperature of 38.4 C, hard stools and frequent visitors. Which interventions does the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give the prescribed stool softener
options.rationale: Straining raises pressure in the chest and then in the skull.

options.text: Give the prescribed acetaminophen for the fever
options.rationale: Fever adds to secondary brain injury, so temperature is kept normal.

options.text: Keep the room dim and limit visitors to short stays
options.rationale: Noise and stimulation cause agitation, which raises ICP.

options.text: Place pillows under the knees with the hips sharply flexed
options.rationale: Sharp hip flexion raises chest pressure and blocks venous outflow from the head.

options.text: Have the patient cough forcefully every hour
options.rationale: Tempting as routine lung care. Coughing spikes ICP, so it is not scheduled.

questions.takeaway: To hold ICP down: no straining, no fever, quiet dim room, no sharp hip or neck flexion, no unneeded coughing or suctioning.
questions.strategy: Ask of each option whether it raises pressure in the chest or agitates the patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fever, hard stools and visitors each have an intervention.
Blocks venous drainage.
Spikes the pressure.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C.

questions.nursesNote: Day 2 after a right hemisphere ischemic stroke, no clot buster given. 1400: needs each request repeated before following it; followed requests the first time at 1000. Reports a new headache. Vomited once without nausea. Left pupil reacts more slowly than the right. Left arm weakness unchanged from admission. Blood pressure 172/94, unchanged since admission. Heart rate 82 and regular. Respirations 16 and even.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that suggest intracranial pressure is rising.

segments.text: needs each request repeated before following it
segments.rationale: A decline in level of consciousness from 1000, the earliest sign.

segments.text: Reports a new headache
segments.rationale: An early sign of rising pressure.

segments.text: Vomited once without nausea
segments.rationale: Vomiting, often without warning, is an early sign.

segments.text: Left pupil reacts more slowly than the right
segments.rationale: A sluggish pupil is an early warning that the third cranial nerve is being pressed.

segments.text: Left arm weakness unchanged from admission
segments.rationale: The known stroke deficit. It has not changed.

segments.text: Blood pressure 172/94, unchanged since admission
segments.rationale: Tempting because the number is high. It is unchanged and is tolerated when no clot buster was given.

segments.text: Heart rate 82 and regular
segments.rationale: Normal. A slow pulse would be a late sign.

segments.text: Respirations 16 and even
segments.rationale: Normal. Irregular breathing would be a late sign.

questions.takeaway: Early signs of rising ICP are a drop in level of consciousness, headache, vomiting and a sluggish pupil. Vital sign changes come late, so normal vital signs do not reassure.
questions.strategy: Highlight what is new since the last check. Unchanged findings and normal vital signs stay unmarked.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Slower to follow requests, new headache, vomiting, slower pupil.
Arm weakness and blood pressure are unchanged.

steps.action: Do not wait for vital signs
steps.detail: They change late.

elimination.verdict: Repeated requests, headache, vomiting, sluggish left pupil.

questions.stem: A patient began nimodipine after a subarachnoid hemorrhage. Which finding on day 12 best indicates the medication has been effective?

options.text: The blood pressure has stayed lower than on admission
options.rationale: Tempting, since the drug can lower blood pressure. That is a side effect, not the goal.

options.text: The patient reports the headache is now mild
options.rationale: A good sign for comfort. It does not show the arteries stayed open.

options.text: No new confusion or limb weakness since admission
options.rationale: Nimodipine is given to prevent vasospasm on days 4 to 14. No new deficits means brain tissue stayed perfused.

options.text: The follow up CT shows no new bleeding
options.rationale: That speaks to rebleeding, which this drug does not prevent.

questions.takeaway: Nimodipine after a subarachnoid bleed prevents vasospasm. It worked if no new confusion or weakness appears through day 14.
questions.strategy: Ask what the drug is for in this patient. Then pick the finding that measures that purpose, not a side effect.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Prevent vasospasm and new ischemia.
Lower blood pressure is not the goal.
Headache and rebleeding are different outcomes.

elimination.verdict: No new confusion or weakness.

questions.stem: A patient with an ischemic stroke is drowsy but wakes to voice. The airway and lungs are clear and the oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Apply oxygen to bring the saturation to 95% or higher
options.rationale: Low oxygen dilates brain vessels, raises ICP and extends the injury. Oxygen is given when the saturation is below 95%.

options.text: Suction the airway to stimulate a deeper breath
options.rationale: The airway is clear, and suctioning raises ICP.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed flat to improve blood flow
options.rationale: Flat positioning slows venous drainage from the head and adds aspiration risk.

options.text: Recheck the saturation in 15 minutes, since it is still above 90%
options.rationale: Tempting, because 90% is the usual line. For an injured brain the line is 95%.

questions.takeaway: After a stroke, give oxygen when the saturation is below 95%. Hypoxia is a cause of secondary brain injury.
questions.strategy: The number looks acceptable on a medical unit. Ask what target applies to a brain that has lost blood flow.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clear, so suction has no purpose.
Below 95% is treated.
Waiting leaves the brain short of oxygen.

elimination.verdict: Apply oxygen.

questions.stem: A patient finished an alteplase infusion 3 hours ago. Which finding does the nurse report immediately?

options.text: Blood pressure of 174/98
options.rationale: Below the 180/105 limit for the first 24 hours.

options.text: Urine that has turned red in the last hour
options.rationale: Blood in the urine is a sign of bleeding, the major concern after a clot buster.

options.text: NIHSS score of 6, down from 9
options.rationale: A falling score means the deficits are improving.

options.text: A dime sized bruise at the old IV site in the left arm
options.rationale: Minor bruising at a puncture site is watched. It is not active bleeding.

questions.takeaway: After a clot buster, watch every site for bleeding: brain, puncture sites, urine and the GI tract. Blood in the urine is reported at once.
questions.strategy: Check each number against its limit and each change against its direction. One option is new bleeding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lower is better.
A small old bruise against new red urine.

elimination.verdict: Red urine.

questions.stem: The day after an ischemic stroke with no clot buster given, a patient's neurologic status is unchanged. Which finding requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Blood pressure of 168/94
options.rationale: Without a clot buster, a high pressure is allowed in order to keep the brain perfused.

options.text: Temperature of 37.4 C
options.rationale: Within normal limits.

options.text: Blood glucose of 262 mg/dL
options.rationale: High glucose is a cause of secondary brain injury and is kept in a normal range.

options.text: Sleeping, and wakes when his name is spoken
options.rationale: Waking easily to voice is an acceptable level of consciousness.

questions.takeaway: After a stroke, keep temperature, glucose, oxygen and fluids normal. Blood pressure is the one value allowed to run high.
questions.strategy: The blood pressure is the distractor built to catch you. Ask which abnormal value harms the brain if left alone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Temperature and easy waking.
No clot buster, so 168/94 is tolerated.
Glucose well above range.

elimination.verdict: Glucose of 262 mg/dL.

questions.stem: The nurse helped a wife who cares for her husband at home after a stroke make a plan to prevent caregiver strain. Which statement at the next visit indicates the plan is working?

options.text: "I do everything for him so that he does not get tired."
options.rationale: She is taking on more, and he is losing practice at self care.

options.text: "I have stopped my book club so I can stay with him."
options.rationale: Giving up her own activities is a sign of strain.

options.text: "I am sleeping less, but I am learning to manage."
options.rationale: Tempting because she sounds positive. Lost sleep shows the load is too heavy.

options.text: "My sister stays two afternoons a week while I go out."
options.rationale: She is using respite and keeping time for herself.

questions.takeaway: Caregiver teaching is effective when the caregiver takes regular breaks and uses respite, not when she does more.
questions.strategy: Three statements show her giving something up. One shows her getting help.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Breaks and respite for the caregiver.
More tasks, no club, less sleep.
Someone else covers so she can leave.

elimination.verdict: Her sister covers two afternoons.

questions.stem: A patient received alteplase 26 hours ago. This morning's follow up CT shows no bleeding and the swallow screen is passed. Aspirin is prescribed. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the aspirin as prescribed
options.rationale: Both conditions are met: 24 hours have passed and the follow up CT shows no bleeding.

options.text: Hold the aspirin until 48 hours have passed
options.rationale: The wait after a clot buster is 24 hours, and delay leaves him without stroke prevention.

options.text: Ask the provider to confirm the order first
options.rationale: Tempting after a clot buster. The nurse already has the two facts that make the dose safe.

options.text: Hold the dose and check for bruising first
options.rationale: Bleeding checks continue, and they are not a reason to hold a dose the CT has cleared.

questions.takeaway: Antiplatelets start after a clot buster once 24 hours have passed and a follow up CT shows no bleeding.
questions.strategy: The stem gives every safety check already done. When the conditions are met, the right action is to give the drug.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 26 hours, past the 24 hour hold.
No bleeding.
Swallow screen passed.

elimination.verdict: Give the aspirin.

questions.stem: The nurse taught stroke prevention to a 55-year-old who smokes and has hypertension and high cholesterol. Which statement indicates a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I will check my blood pressure at home and keep a log."
options.rationale: Blood pressure control is the core of prevention.

options.text: "I will start a daily aspirin on my own this week."
options.rationale: Aspirin is used when appropriate, which means the provider decides. It carries a bleeding risk.

options.text: "I will keep taking the cholesterol pill every night."
options.rationale: Cholesterol management is part of the plan.

options.text: "I set a quit date and asked about nicotine patches."
options.rationale: Smoking cessation is part of the plan.

questions.takeaway: Stroke prevention is aspirin when appropriate, blood pressure control, cholesterol management and smoking cessation. Aspirin is not self started.
questions.strategy: You are hunting for the wrong statement. Three match the plan and one adds a drug without the provider.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that needs correcting.
Pressure log, cholesterol pill, quit date.
Aspirin on his own.

elimination.verdict: Starting aspirin on his own.

questions.stem: A patient with dysphagia after a stroke has followed the diet set by the speech language pathologist for 2 weeks. Which finding best indicates the nutrition plan is effective?

options.text: Daily weights are steady and the prealbumin has risen
options.rationale: Weight and prealbumin are the measures of nutritional status.

options.text: The lungs are clear and the temperature is normal
options.rationale: Tempting, but this shows that aspiration was prevented. It says nothing about nutrition.

options.text: The patient finishes every tray, with some coughing
options.rationale: Coughing during meals means the diet is not safe.

options.text: The patient says the food tastes better this week
options.rationale: Enjoyment helps intake and is not a measure of nutrition.

questions.takeaway: Judge a dysphagia nutrition plan by daily weight and prealbumin. Clear lungs answer a different question.
questions.strategy: Match the finding to the goal named in the stem. Two options are good news about something else.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Nutrition.
Clear lungs measure aspiration.
Coughing at meals.

elimination.verdict: Steady weight, prealbumin up.

questions.stem: CT shows no bleeding in a 63-year-old who arrived 75 minutes after sudden left arm weakness began. Alteplase is prescribed. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Confirm the blood pressure is below 185/110
options.rationale: The pressure must be under this limit before the drug is started.

options.text: Give 10% of the dose as a bolus over 1 minute
options.rationale: The dose starts with a small bolus.

options.text: Run the rest of the dose over 60 minutes by pump
options.rationale: The remainder follows the bolus as a timed infusion.

options.text: After the infusion ends, do neurologic checks every 15 minutes for 2 hours
options.rationale: Bleeding risk is highest early, so checks stay frequent.

options.text: Change the neurologic checks to every 30 minutes for 6 hours
options.rationale: Checks are spaced out only after the first 2 hours pass without change.
