questions.takeaway: Clot buster sequence: pressure below 185/110, 10% bolus, the rest over 60 minutes, checks every 15 minutes for 2 hours after, then every 30 minutes for 6 hours.
questions.strategy: Put the safety check before the drug, the bolus before the infusion, and the closest monitoring before the wider spacing.

steps.detail: Pressure below 185/110 before any drug.
Bolus over 1 minute, then the 60 minute infusion.
Every 15 minutes for 2 hours, then every 30 minutes.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

questions.stem: A patient with a left hemisphere stroke has right arm weakness, halting speech and cannot read the menu. He understands what is said and is easily frustrated. Which interventions does the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give one step directions in short sentences
options.rationale: Simple language lowers the load on a damaged language center.

options.text: Keep a communication board within his reach
options.rationale: It gives him another way to express needs.

options.text: Speak in a louder voice so the words are clear
options.rationale: He understands what is said, so volume is not the problem. Slow down; do not raise the volume.

options.text: Keep the same daily routine and allow extra time
options.rationale: Structure and time reduce frustration.

options.text: Finish his sentences when he pauses
options.rationale: Rushing or speaking for him adds to the frustration.

options.text: Read the menu choices aloud to him
options.rationale: He understands speech, so hearing the choices replaces the reading he lost.

questions.takeaway: Left hemisphere stroke: short one step directions, a board, a steady routine, extra time. Speak slowly, never loudly, and do not finish sentences.
questions.strategy: Ask of each option whether it gives him another way in or out for language, or whether it takes over for him.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Expression and reading are lost. Understanding is kept.
Short directions, board, routine, reading aloud.
Louder speech and finishing sentences.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, F.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old's alteplase infusion ended 3 hours ago. The nurse sets the monitor's upper blood pressure alarm. Which limit does the nurse use?

options.rationale: The limit is off. This is a clinic screening number, and lowering pressure this far is not the goal after a stroke.
The limit is off. This is the ceiling for starting the drug, not for the 24 hours after it.
After the clot buster the pressure is kept below 180/105 for 24 hours, and the provider is called above it.

options.text: 220 systolic
options.rationale: The limit is off. This applies to a patient who did not receive a clot buster.

questions.takeaway: Blood pressure and the clot buster: below 185/110 before it, below 180/105 for 24 hours after it. With no clot buster, up to about 220 systolic is allowed.
questions.strategy: Three of the numbers are real stroke limits. Place each one in its own phase.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The drug is finished, so this is the after phase.
185/110 is before, 220 is no drug, 180/105 is after.

questions.stem: Four patients arrive with sudden one sided weakness and a CT scan that shows no bleeding. Which patient is inside the standard time window for alteplase?

options.text: Wife saw the weakness begin 2 hours ago while they were talking
options.rationale: Last known well is 2 hours ago, inside the 4.5 hour window.

options.text: Found with weakness 1 hour ago; last seen normal 10 hours ago
options.rationale: The clock is off. Time runs from last seen normal, 10 hours, not from when he was found.

options.text: Woke with weakness 30 minutes ago; went to bed normal 9 hours ago
options.rationale: The clock is off. Last known well is bedtime, 9 hours ago.

options.text: Weakness began 7 hours ago while watching television
options.rationale: The time is off. 7 hours is past the 4.5 hour window.

questions.takeaway: Standard window for the clot buster: within 4.5 hours of last known well. The clock starts at the last normal moment, not when symptoms were found.
questions.strategy: Rewrite each option as hours since last known well, then compare with 4.5.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 2, 10, 9 and 7 hours.
Only 2 hours is inside 4.5.

elimination.verdict: The patient whose wife saw it start 2 hours ago.

questions.stem: Alteplase 72 mg is prescribed for an 80 kg patient with an ischemic stroke. A second nurse has verified the dose. Which setup does the nurse use?

options.text: 7.2 mg bolus over 1 minute, then 64.8 mg over 30 minutes by pump
options.rationale: The infusion time is off. The remainder runs over 60 minutes.

options.text: 7.2 mg bolus over 1 minute, then 64.8 mg over 60 minutes by pump
options.rationale: 10% of 72 mg as a bolus over 1 minute and the remaining 90% over 60 minutes by pump.

options.text: 36 mg bolus over 1 minute, then 36 mg over 60 minutes by pump
options.rationale: The bolus is off. It is 10% of the dose, not half.

options.text: 72 mg over 60 minutes by pump with no bolus
options.rationale: The bolus is missing. 10% is given first over 1 minute.

questions.takeaway: Alteplase: 0.9 mg/kg of actual weight, maximum 90 mg. 10% as a bolus over 1 minute, the rest over 60 minutes by pump.
questions.strategy: Work out 10% of the dose first, then check the time on the remainder.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 10% of 72 is 7.2 mg. Two options have it.
60 minutes, not 30.

elimination.verdict: 7.2 mg over 1 minute, then 64.8 mg over 60 minutes.

questions.stem: A patient's alteplase infusion ended 1 hour ago. Which action by the new nurse caring for the patient needs correction?

options.text: Checks the IV and puncture sites for bleeding
options.rationale: Correct. Bleeding is the major concern after a clot buster.

options.text: Compares each neurologic check with the one before
options.rationale: Correct. A new or worse deficit can mean bleeding in the brain.

options.text: Keeps the patient NPO until the swallow screen
options.rationale: Correct. Nothing by mouth before the screen.

options.text: Sets the next neurologic and vital sign check for 1 hour from now
options.rationale: The interval is off. Checks are every 15 minutes during the infusion and for 2 hours after it.

questions.takeaway: After alteplase: neurologic and vital sign checks every 15 minutes during the infusion and for 2 hours after, every 30 minutes for the next 6 hours, then hourly to 24 hours.
questions.strategy: Place the patient on the schedule first: 1 hour after the infusion is still the 15 minute phase.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: You want the wrong action.
1 hour after is inside the first 2 hours.
Hourly is the schedule for much later.

elimination.verdict: The 1 hour gap. It should be 15 minutes.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with a large stroke is restless and has increased ICP. Which position does the nurse use?

options.text: Head of bed at 30 degrees, head midline, hips only slightly bent
options.rationale: Head up 30 degrees with the neck neutral and no sharp hip flexion lets venous blood drain from the skull.

options.text: Head of bed at 30 degrees, head midline, knees raised so the hips are sharply bent
options.rationale: The hip angle is off. Sharp hip flexion raises chest pressure and blocks venous outflow.

options.text: Head of bed at 30 degrees, chin tucked to the chest on two pillows
options.rationale: The neck position is off. Neck flexion blocks the veins that drain the head.

options.text: Bed flat, head midline, hips only slightly bent
options.rationale: The head of bed angle is off. Flat removes the help gravity gives to venous drainage.

questions.takeaway: Increased ICP: head of bed up per protocol, often 30 degrees, head midline and neutral, no sharp hip or neck flexion.
questions.strategy: Check three points on each option: bed angle, neck, hips. One of them is wrong in each distractor.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Flat is out.
Chin to chest is out.
Sharp flexion is out.

elimination.verdict: 30 degrees, midline, hips nearly straight.

questions.stem: The nurse plans breakfast care for four patients on a stroke unit with one assistive worker. Which assignment is correct?

options.text: Give sips of water to a thirsty patient who is waiting for the swallow screen
options.rationale: The timing is off. Nothing by mouth, including water, before the screen.

options.text: Feed a patient who passed the nurse's swallow screen this morning
options.rationale: The nurse screened and the patient passed, so feeding can be delegated.

options.text: Do the swallow screen on a patient admitted overnight with a stroke
options.rationale: The person is off. The swallow assessment belongs to the nurse and is not delegated.

options.text: Feed pureed food to a new patient whose swallow has not been screened
options.rationale: The timing is off. A softer texture does not replace the screen.

questions.takeaway: NPO until the swallow screen: no food, fluids or medications. The nurse screens. Assistive personnel may feed only after the screen is passed.
questions.strategy: For each patient ask two things: has the nurse screened the swallow, and who is being asked to do what?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut anything by mouth before a screen
steps.detail: Water and pureed food both go.
A screen is not an assistive task.

elimination.verdict: Feed the patient who passed the screen.

questions.stem: A patient with an ischemic stroke and a risk for increased ICP has an oxygen saturation of 93% on room air. The airway is clear. Which plan does the nurse follow?

options.text: Keep the patient on room air until the saturation falls below 90%
options.rationale: The cutoff is off. Oxygen is started when the saturation is below 95%.

options.text: Keep the patient on room air until the saturation falls below 88%
options.rationale: The cutoff is off, and by more. Low oxygen dilates brain vessels and raises ICP.

options.text: Apply oxygen and keep the saturation at 95% or higher
options.rationale: Oxygen is given when the saturation is below 95% to prevent hypoxia and secondary brain injury.

options.text: Lay the bed flat and recheck the saturation in 1 hour
options.rationale: The position and the wait are both off. Flat raises ICP and the low reading goes untreated.

questions.takeaway: Stroke and increased ICP: give oxygen if the saturation is below 95%. Low oxygen and high carbon dioxide dilate brain vessels and raise ICP.
questions.strategy: The usual 90% floor does not apply to an injured brain. Use the stroke number.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It is below 95%.
Both room air options wait for a lower number.

elimination.verdict: Oxygen to 95% or higher.

questions.stem: The nurse checks four patients with increased ICP at the start of the shift. Which finding requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Head of bed at 30 degrees with the head midline
options.rationale: Correct position for venous drainage.

options.text: Stool softener given with the morning medications
options.rationale: Correct. It prevents straining, which raises ICP.

options.text: Bath finished and the turn left until after a rest period
options.rationale: Correct. Care is spaced, not clustered.

options.text: Suctioned every hour on a set schedule, lungs clear
options.rationale: The schedule is off. Suctioning spikes ICP, so it is done only when needed, with oxygen before and after.

questions.takeaway: With increased ICP, suction only when needed and oxygenate before and after. Space care out. Do not cluster procedures.
questions.strategy: Three options lower pressure in the skull. One raises it on a timer.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: You want the wrong setup.
Position, stool softener and spacing all lower ICP.
Routine suction with clear lungs is not needed.

elimination.verdict: Scheduled hourly suction.

questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes is going home after a TIA and asks what blood glucose range to aim for. Which range does the nurse teach?

options.text: 40 to 70 mg/dL
options.rationale: The range is too low. Hypoglycemia causes confusion, slurred speech and weakness that look like a stroke.

options.text: 100 to 180 mg/dL
options.rationale: The glucose goal after a TIA is 100 to 180 mg/dL.

options.text: 200 to 260 mg/dL
options.rationale: The range is too high. High glucose adds to brain injury.

options.text: 250 to 300 mg/dL
options.rationale: The range is too high, and by more.

questions.takeaway: After a TIA the glucose goal is 100 to 180 mg/dL. Both low and high glucose cause secondary brain injury, and low glucose mimics a stroke.
questions.strategy: The brain is hurt by both extremes, so look for the middle range.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Below 70 is hypoglycemia.
Two options sit above 200.

elimination.verdict: 100 to 180 mg/dL.

questions.stem: A patient with an ischemic stroke who did not receive a clot buster had a blood pressure of 228/116. After IV labetalol, which reading requires the nurse to intervene?

options.rationale: A small, gradual fall to under 220 systolic. Pressure is allowed to run high to keep the brain perfused.
Still a gradual fall and still high enough to perfuse the brain.
Lower, reached in steps, and still well above the 120 systolic floor.
The drop is too far and too fast. A sudden fall below 120 systolic cuts perfusion to the brain around the stroke.

questions.takeaway: With no clot buster, blood pressure is allowed to run high, up to about 220 systolic. If it is lowered, lower it gradually and avoid a sudden drop below 120 systolic.
questions.strategy: After a stroke the dangerous reading is the low one, not the high one.

steps.detail: Three readings are small steps down.
108 systolic is under the 120 floor.

questions.stem: A patient with left homonymous hemianopsia after a stroke is about to eat lunch. Which setup does the nurse use?

options.text: Tray on the patient's right side, with a cue to turn the head to the left
options.rationale: Food goes in the intact right field, and turning the head brings the lost left side into view.

options.text: Tray on the patient's left side, with a cue to turn the head to the left
options.rationale: The placement is off. The left field is the lost one, so the meal starts out of sight.

options.text: Tray on the patient's right side, with a cue to keep the head still
options.rationale: The cue is off. Without turning the head, everything on the left stays unseen.

options.text: Tray at the midline, with a patch over the right eye
options.rationale: The device is off. A patch is for double vision, and each eye has lost the same half of the field.

questions.takeaway: Homonymous hemianopsia: put food and objects in the intact field and teach turning the head side to side to scan.
questions.strategy: Name the lost side first. Then check where the tray is and what the head is told to do.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Left is lost. Right is intact.
Right side.
Turn the head toward the lost side.

elimination.verdict: Tray on the right, turn the head left.

questions.stem: A patient walks into the emergency department with a facial droop that began suddenly. Which plan by the triage nurse needs correction?

options.text: Check the airway and breathing before anything else
options.rationale: Correct. ABCs come first.

options.text: Ask when the patient was last known to be normal
options.rationale: Correct. Last known well decides whether treatment is possible.

options.text: Finish the full health history, then start the stroke assessment within 45 minutes
options.rationale: The time is off. A patient with a possible stroke is assessed within 10 minutes of arrival, and the history must not delay care.

options.text: Check a fingerstick blood glucose
options.rationale: Correct. Low glucose looks like a stroke and is quick to fix.

questions.takeaway: A patient with a possible stroke is assessed within 10 minutes of arrival. ABCs first. The history must not delay care.
questions.strategy: Three options take minutes. One spends time the brain does not have.

steps.detail: You want the plan to fix.
Airway, last known well and glucose are fast.
45 minutes is far past 10.

elimination.verdict: The 45 minute history.

questions.stem: A patient's alteplase infusion ended 9 hours ago. Neurologic status is unchanged. Which schedule for neurologic and vital sign checks does the nurse follow now?

options.text: Every 15 minutes
options.rationale: The interval is off. This is the schedule during the infusion and for the first 2 hours after.

options.text: Every 4 hours
options.rationale: The interval is too long. Checks stay frequent for the full 24 hours.

options.text: Every hour
options.rationale: From 8 hours after the infusion until 24 hours, checks are hourly.

options.text: Once every shift
options.rationale: The interval is far too long while bleeding is still a risk.

questions.takeaway: After alteplase: every 15 minutes during the infusion and for 2 hours after, every 30 minutes for the next 6 hours, then every hour until 24 hours.
questions.strategy: Add the phases: 2 hours plus 6 hours is 8. At 9 hours the patient is in the third phase.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The 15 and 30 minute phases end at 8 hours.
Hourly until 24 hours.

elimination.verdict: Every hour.

questions.stem: Four patients are seen in a clinic the day after a TIA. Which patient does the nurse identify as having the highest stroke risk over the next few days?

options.text: Age 72, blood pressure 158/94, has diabetes
options.rationale: Three ABCD2 factors: age 60 or older, pressure 140/90 or higher, and diabetes.

options.text: Age 45, blood pressure 118/70, no diabetes
options.rationale: No factor is met: under 60, pressure under 140/90, no diabetes.

options.text: Age 58, blood pressure 132/84, no diabetes
options.rationale: No factor is met: under 60 and pressure under 140/90.

options.text: Age 50, blood pressure 126/80, has diabetes
options.rationale: One factor only, diabetes. Age and pressure are under the cutoffs.

questions.takeaway: ABCD2 after a TIA: Age 60 or older, Blood pressure 140/90 or higher, Clinical features, Duration, Diabetes. A higher score means a higher near term stroke risk.
questions.strategy: Count the factors in each option against the cutoffs: 60, 140/90 and diabetes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three, zero, zero and one.
Age 72 with 158/94 and diabetes.

elimination.verdict: The 72-year-old.

questions.scenario: A 62-year-old arrived 90 minutes after sudden right arm weakness began. The CT scan shows no bleeding and alteplase is prescribed. Blood pressure is 192/112.
questions.stem: For each action by the team, indicate whether it is correct or needs correction.

rows.text: Starts the alteplase bolus while the blood pressure is 192/112
rows.rationale: The pressure must be below 185/110 before the drug. An antihypertensive is given first.

rows.text: Calculates the dose from the actual weight on the bed scale
rows.rationale: The dose is 0.9 mg/kg of actual weight.

rows.text: Hangs the rest of the dose to run by gravity without a pump
rows.rationale: The remainder runs over 60 minutes by pump.

rows.text: Has a second nurse double check the dose
rows.rationale: The dose is double checked.

rows.text: Gives subcutaneous heparin 2 hours after the infusion ends
rows.rationale: No anticoagulants or aspirin for 24 hours and until a follow up CT shows no bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Before alteplase the pressure must be below 185/110. Dose by actual weight, double checked, by pump. No aspirin or anticoagulants for 24 hours.
questions.strategy: Take each row to its number: 185/110, actual weight, pump, 24 hours.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pump, not gravity.
2 hours is far short of 24.

elimination.verdict: Needs correction, correct, needs correction, correct, needs correction.

questions.stem: A client on a Venturi mask at 35% had an SpO2 at goal until being tucked in. It now reads 88% and the blanket covers the mask adapter. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Increase the oxygen flow rate on the flowmeter
options.rationale: Tempting because the saturation fell, but the device is blocked. More flow through covered ports does not restore the set concentration.

options.text: Pull the blanket away from the air entrainment ports
options.rationale: The ports must stay open for a Venturi mask to deliver its exact concentration. Fixing the device is the fastest correction.

options.text: Change to a nonrebreather mask
options.rationale: A step up in device is not needed when the ordered device has a fixable problem.

options.text: Notify the provider of the drop in saturation
options.rationale: Reasonable if the saturation stays low after the device is corrected. The nurse fixes the obvious cause first.

questions.takeaway: When saturation drops on oxygen, check the device before you change the dose. Venturi ports must stay uncovered.
questions.strategy: The stem hands you the cause: the blanket over the adapter. The answer removes that cause.

steps.detail: The drop followed the blanket covering the adapter.
More flow, a new device and a call all skip the simple fix.
Uncover the ports, then recheck the client.

elimination.verdict: Uncover the entrainment ports.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with pneumonia was started on high flow nasal cannula for a respiratory rate of 34 with accessory muscle use. Which finding one hour later best indicates the therapy is effective?

options.text: SpO2 rose from 89% to 95% with continued neck muscle use
options.rationale: Tempting because the number improved. Continued accessory muscle use means the work of breathing has not eased.

options.text: He says the warm humidified air feels more comfortable
options.rationale: Comfort helps him tolerate the device. It does not show better breathing.

options.text: Respiratory rate is 22 and he speaks in full sentences
options.rationale: Slower breathing and full sentences show less work of breathing, which is the reason the device was started.

options.text: He is sleeping and hard to wake for vital signs
options.rationale: A hard to wake client after respiratory distress may be tiring or retaining CO2. This needs follow up.

questions.takeaway: Judge oxygen therapy by the patient, not only the number. Lower rate, easier effort and full sentences mean it is working.
questions.strategy: Two options show improvement. Ask which one answers the problem that started the therapy: the work of breathing.

steps.detail: Rate 34 with accessory muscles.
One is not an outcome. The other is a warning.
A better number with the same effort loses to a slower rate with full sentences.

elimination.verdict: Rate 22 and full sentences.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old at a clinic visit describes several changes in his breathing. Which report requires follow up?

options.text: He needs several hard coughs to clear mucus that one cough used to clear
options.rationale: Tempting because it sounds like trouble clearing the airway. A less effective cough is an expected change with aging. Teach him to stay hydrated and keep moving.

options.text: He slows down on hills that he walked easily ten years ago
options.rationale: Weaker respiratory muscles and a stiffer chest wall lower endurance gradually. A change over ten years fits aging.

options.text: He had three colds this winter and one in most earlier winters
options.rationale: Tempting because the number went up. More infections are expected with aging. Teach vaccination and hand hygiene.

options.text: He added a second pillow this month because lying flat feels stuffy
options.rationale: He describes it mildly, but needing to prop up to breathe is new shortness of breath. New shortness of breath is not normal aging.

questions.takeaway: New or severe shortness of breath is never normal aging. A client may describe it as a small change in habit, such as an extra pillow.
questions.strategy: Do not rank the reports by how bad they sound. Ask which one is recent and which ones built up over years.

steps.action: Match each report to an aging change
steps.detail: Weaker cough, less endurance and more infections are all expected.
Ten years and most winters are gradual. This month is new.
A second pillow because lying flat feels stuffy is shortness of breath when flat.

elimination.verdict: The second pillow. New dyspnea lying flat needs follow up.

questions.stem: A client admitted after 36 hours of vomiting and diarrhea is restless, with cool mottled legs, a blood pressure of 84/50 and an SpO2 of 98% on room air. The findings are most consistent with which problem?

options.text: Tissue oxygen delivery is low because of poor perfusion
options.rationale: Low volume means less blood reaches the tissues. Saturation can be normal while the tissues go without oxygen.

options.text: Air movement into the alveoli is inadequate
options.rationale: Nothing suggests a ventilation problem. The saturation is normal and no breathing difficulty is described.

options.text: Gas exchange across the alveolar membrane is impaired
options.rationale: A diffusion problem lowers the saturation. This client's is 98%.

options.text: The pulse oximeter reading is falsely high
options.rationale: Tempting with cool legs, but poor circulation makes readings low or unreadable. The low pressure explains the picture.

questions.takeaway: A normal SpO2 does not prove the tissues are oxygenated. Hypovolemia cuts perfusion, so oxygen never reaches them.
questions.strategy: Match each finding to ventilation, diffusion or perfusion. Low pressure and mottled skin are blood flow findings.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 98% rules out a ventilation or diffusion problem.

steps.action: Use the fluid loss and pressure
steps.detail: A day and a half of losses with 84/50 means low volume.
Poor circulation does not make a reading falsely high.

elimination.verdict: Poor perfusion from hypovolemia.

questions.stem: A client who received a first dose of an IV antibiotic 5 minutes ago has a harsh high pitched sound on inspiration with retractions above the collarbones. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Auscultate all lung fields from apex to base
options.rationale: The sound and retractions already show upper airway obstruction. A full exam delays help.

options.text: Give the prescribed as needed bronchodilator inhaler
options.rationale: Tempting because the breathing is noisy. A bronchodilator treats wheezes from narrowed lower airways. This harsh inspiratory sound is stridor from the upper airway.

options.text: Stay with the client and call the rapid response team
options.rationale: Stridor with retractions means the airway is closing. The nurse stays, gets help and supports the airway.

options.text: Apply oxygen by nasal cannula and reassess in 5 minutes
options.rationale: Tempting as a breathing action. Oxygen cannot pass a closing airway, and 5 minutes is too long to wait.

questions.takeaway: Stridor and retractions are findings that need immediate intervention. The assessment is done. Get help and protect the airway.
questions.strategy: Two options act and two assess or wait. The stem already gave you the finding that matters, so ask which action deals with a closing airway.

steps.detail: Harsh inspiratory sound plus retractions is an obstructing upper airway.
The assessment that matters is done.
An inhaler and a cannula work below the blockage. Neither opens it.
Stay and call for help.

elimination.verdict: Stay and call rapid response.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old who smokes a pack a day says he is ready to quit and has set a date two weeks away. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Start a nicotine patch today and review progress at his annual visit
options.rationale: Tempting because medication helps. It leaves out counseling, and follow up a year away is far too late.

options.text: Set up counseling now and add medication only if he relapses
options.rationale: Tempting because counseling is half of the plan. The two work best together from the start.

options.text: Give written quit materials and ask him to call with questions
options.rationale: This fits a client who is not ready. He has a quit date.

options.text: Pair counseling with medication and book a visit near the quit date
options.rationale: He is willing, so the nurse assists with medication plus counseling and arranges follow up within the first week after the quit date.

questions.takeaway: For a client who is ready: assist with counseling plus medication, then arrange follow up within the first week after the quit date.
questions.strategy: He has passed Ask, Advise and Assess. The answer should cover Assist and Arrange.

steps.detail: Ready with a date means Assist and Arrange.

steps.action: Cut the plan for an unready client
steps.detail: Written materials only.
One has medication alone, one has counseling alone, one has both with early follow up.

elimination.verdict: Counseling plus medication with a visit near the quit date.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old office clerk has a dry cough and dyspnea that have worsened over a year. He has never smoked and reports no irritants at home or at his current job. Which question is most useful next?

options.text: What kinds of work did you do in earlier years?
options.rationale: Past work is the part of the exposure history still missing. Lung damage can show up decades after a job ended.

options.text: Which tasks at your office make you short of breath?
options.rationale: Tempting because work exposure matters. He has already reported no irritants at his current job.

options.text: Does anyone smoke inside your home?
options.rationale: Secondhand smoke is a real exposure. He has already reported no irritants at home.

options.text: Did you get an influenza vaccine this season?
options.rationale: Worth asking for health promotion. It does not explain symptoms that built over a year.

questions.takeaway: An exposure history covers present work, residence, environment and past work. Past work is the piece most often skipped.
questions.strategy: List what the stem has already cleared: smoking, home and current job. The answer asks about what is left.

steps.detail: No smoking, no irritants at home or at the current job.
Office tasks and smoke in the home repeat cleared ground.

steps.action: Cut the question that cannot explain a year of symptoms
steps.detail: Vaccine status.
Earlier jobs.

elimination.verdict: Ask about past work.

questions.stem: A client wearing dark nail polish has an SpO2 reading of 87% but is breathing easily at 16 with pink lips. The nurse moves the sensor. Which finding indicates the new reading can be trusted?

options.text: The new number is higher than the first reading
options.rationale: A higher number alone does not prove accuracy.

options.text: The displayed pulse rate matches the apical pulse
options.rationale: A pulse rate that matches the heart rate shows the sensor is picking up a real pulse, so the saturation beside it can be trusted.

options.text: The client says the new site feels comfortable
options.rationale: Comfort does not confirm signal quality.

options.text: The low saturation alarm has stopped sounding
options.rationale: An alarm silences at any value above its limit, accurate or not.

questions.takeaway: Correlate the oximeter with the patient. Trust a reading only when the pulse rate on the monitor matches the client's pulse.
questions.strategy: Ask which option checks the signal itself instead of the number or the alarm.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Easy breathing and pink lips do not fit 87%.

steps.action: Cut options about the number, comfort or alarm
steps.detail: None tests signal quality.
Monitor pulse matches apical pulse.

elimination.verdict: Displayed pulse rate matching the apical pulse.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old with pneumonia on 4 L/min has a steady SpO2 of 93%. Her blood pressure fell from 130/78 to 92/54 and her lactate is 3.4 mmol/L. Which problem is the priority?

options.text: Impaired gas exchange
options.rationale: Tempting because pneumonia is a lung problem. Her saturation is steady on low oxygen, so it is controlled for now.

options.text: Activity intolerance
options.rationale: Real, but it does not threaten her life.

options.text: Developing sepsis
options.rationale: A falling pressure with a raised lactate shows infection is affecting perfusion. Preventing sepsis is part of the pneumonia plan.

options.text: Knowledge deficit about pneumonia vaccination
options.rationale: Teaching waits until she is stable.

questions.takeaway: In pneumonia, watch for sepsis as closely as for gas exchange. The problem that is changing outranks the one that is steady.
questions.strategy: Two problems are serious. One is stable on treatment. The other is new and worsening.

steps.detail: Activity and teaching can wait.
93% and steady on 4 L/min.
Pressure falling, lactate up.

elimination.verdict: Developing sepsis.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel reports that a sleeping client's SpO2 reads 86%. The reading was normal two hours ago. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Go to the client and assess breathing and responsiveness
options.rationale: The nurse has only a number. Looking at the client shows whether it is real and how urgent it is.

options.text: Have the assistive personnel raise the head of the bed and recheck
options.rationale: Tempting because sitting up helps most breathing problems. The nurse still has not seen the client, and assessment cannot be delegated.

options.text: Have the assistive personnel move the sensor to another finger
options.rationale: Tempting because a sleeping client's sensor may have slipped. If the reading is real, this spends time the client may not have.

options.text: Call the provider to report the change in the reading
options.rationale: The provider will ask for an assessment the nurse does not have yet.

questions.takeaway: A single reported number is not an assessment. Go to the patient, then act on what you find.
questions.strategy: No assessment data is in the stem. That is the cue that assessment comes first.

steps.detail: Only a reported number.
There is nothing to report yet.
Each could help, but both leave the nurse without an assessment.
The nurse goes to the client.

elimination.verdict: Assess the client now.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches an older adult about seasonal influenza before winter. Which statement by the client indicates the teaching was understood?

options.text: "I had the vaccine, so I do not need to wash my hands as often."
options.rationale: Vaccination reduces risk and severity. Handwashing stays critical.

options.text: "If I get sick, I will rest for three days and call if I am no better."
options.rationale: Antivirals work best within 24 to 48 hours of symptoms. Three days is too late.

options.text: "Influenza comes on slowly, so I will have time to plan."
options.rationale: Influenza has a rapid onset with severe headache, muscle aches and fever.

options.text: "I will call the day symptoms start to ask about antiviral medicine."
options.rationale: Early contact lets treatment start inside the 24 to 48 hour window.

questions.takeaway: Influenza starts fast. Vaccinate, wash hands and call early because antivirals help only if started within 24 to 48 hours.
questions.strategy: Check each statement against one fact: timing. Only one gets the timing right.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A vaccine does not replace handwashing.
Waiting three days misses the window. Calling day one fits it.
Influenza is sudden.

elimination.verdict: Call the day symptoms start.

questions.stem: The nurse auscultates the chest of a client admitted with a productive cough. Which finding requires follow up?

options.text: Soft, low pitched sounds at both lung bases
options.rationale: Vesicular sounds are expected at the bases.

options.text: Loud, high pitched sounds over the right lower lobe
options.rationale: Bronchial sounds belong over the trachea. Heard over a lung field, they suggest consolidation such as pneumonia.

options.text: Medium pitched sounds beside the sternum
options.rationale: Bronchovesicular sounds are expected near the sternum.

options.text: Loud, high pitched sounds over the trachea
options.rationale: Bronchial sounds are expected over the trachea.

questions.takeaway: Location decides whether a breath sound is normal. A tracheal sound heard out over the lung is abnormal.
questions.strategy: Two options describe the same sound in different places. Look closely at the pair.

steps.detail: Soft at bases and medium near the sternum are expected.
Over the trachea is normal. Over a lower lobe is not.

elimination.verdict: Loud, high pitched sounds over the right lower lobe.

questions.stem: A client with COVID 19 on oxygen drops to 90% and becomes breathless whenever bathing, linen change and meals happen back to back. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Cluster care into short blocks with rest periods between them
options.rationale: Spacing activity with rest lowers oxygen demand while keeping her moving.

options.text: Keep her on strict bed rest until discharge
options.rationale: Tempting because activity drops her saturation. Full bed rest removes the mobility she needs and adds risks.

options.text: Schedule three hallway walks a day to build endurance
options.rationale: Mobility matters, but adding exertion now ignores the drop to 90%.

options.text: Complete all care early so she can rest all afternoon
options.rationale: Doing everything at once is what causes the drop.

questions.takeaway: For activity intolerance, balance rest and mobility. Group care, then protect rest between groups to lower oxygen demand.
questions.strategy: The stem says the trouble comes from activities done back to back. The answer changes the spacing, not the amount.

steps.detail: Care done back to back.
Strict bed rest and extra walks.

steps.action: Cut the plan that repeats the trigger
steps.detail: All care at once.

elimination.verdict: Cluster care with rest periods.

questions.stem: A client on a nasal cannula for 4 days has reddened, intact skin over the tops of both ears. The oxygen saturation is at goal. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Remove the cannula for one hour each shift
options.rationale: Stopping prescribed oxygen risks hypoxemia.

options.text: Apply petroleum jelly under the tubing
options.rationale: Petroleum based products are not used with oxygen.

options.text: Pad the tubing over the ears and reposition it
options.rationale: Padding relieves pressure while the ordered oxygen continues.

options.text: Change to a simple face mask
options.rationale: Tempting because it moves the tubing off the ears. It changes the ordered device and adds mask pressure points.

questions.takeaway: Inspect skin under oxygen tubing. Relieve pressure without interrupting the oxygen or changing the order.
questions.strategy: Look for the option that fixes the skin problem and keeps the therapy the same.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No petroleum with oxygen.

steps.action: Cut options that change the therapy
steps.detail: Removing the cannula or switching devices.
Pad and reposition.

elimination.verdict: Pad and reposition the tubing.

questions.stem: A client prescribed a simple face mask at 8 L/min returns from x-ray drowsy. The flowmeter reads 3 L/min. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Change to a nasal cannula at the same 3 L/min
options.rationale: Tempting because 3 L/min suits a cannula. It changes the ordered device and gives less oxygen than prescribed.

options.text: Turn the flow back up to the prescribed 8 L/min
options.rationale: A simple mask needs at least its minimum flow, about 5 L/min, to flush exhaled carbon dioxide out of the mask. Restoring the ordered setting fixes the cause.

options.text: Check the saturation and keep this flow if it is at goal
options.rationale: Tempting as an assessment. Pulse oximetry does not show carbon dioxide, so a good number would not make this flow safe.

options.text: Ask the provider about lowering the oxygen concentration
options.rationale: Drowsiness here comes from rebreathed carbon dioxide at a low flow, not from too much oxygen.

questions.takeaway: A simple mask needs its minimum flow so exhaled carbon dioxide is not rebreathed. Use the ordered device at the ordered setting.
questions.strategy: The stem gives two numbers that disagree: the order and the flowmeter. Fix the mismatch before anything else.

steps.detail: 8 L/min ordered, 3 L/min running.
Drowsiness fits carbon dioxide rebreathed inside the mask.

steps.action: Cut the options that leave the flow low
steps.detail: A cannula, a saturation check and a lower concentration all keep him at 3 L/min or less.
Restore the prescribed flow, then reassess.

elimination.verdict: Return the flow to 8 L/min.

questions.stem: A client with right lower lobe pneumonia has had IV antibiotics and oxygen for 48 hours. Which finding best indicates the gas exchange goal is met?

options.text: Temperature has been normal for 24 hours
options.rationale: Tempting because it shows the infection is responding. It does not measure oxygenation.

options.text: The white blood cell count is trending down
options.rationale: An infection marker, not a gas exchange measure.

options.text: She coughs up less sputum than yesterday
options.rationale: Less sputum can mean improvement or a weaker cough.

options.text: SpO2 stays at 97% on room air while she walks
options.rationale: Holding saturation without oxygen during activity shows adequate gas exchange.

questions.takeaway: Match the evidence to the goal. Gas exchange is judged by oxygenation and breathing, not by infection markers.
questions.strategy: Three options show the infection improving. Only one measures the goal named in the stem.

steps.detail: Gas exchange.
Temperature, white cells and sputum.
Saturation on room air with activity.

elimination.verdict: 97% on room air while walking.

questions.stem: A client is about to have a thoracentesis. Consent is signed and baseline breath sounds are charted. The client mentions taking warfarin last night. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Report the warfarin dose to the provider now
options.rationale: Bleeding risk must be reviewed before a needle enters the chest. The provider needs this now.

options.text: Auscultate the lungs again for a second baseline
options.rationale: Tempting because baseline findings matter. The stem says they are already charted.

options.text: Position the client upright leaning over the bedside table
options.rationale: Correct positioning, but it comes after the bleeding risk is cleared.

options.text: Remind the client not to cough during the procedure
options.rationale: Good teaching that does not address the new risk.

questions.takeaway: Before thoracentesis: verify preparation and consent, review allergies and bleeding risk, get baseline respiratory findings. A new bleeding risk stops the line.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you what is already done. The answer deals with the one item that is not.

steps.detail: Consent and baseline.
An anticoagulant.

steps.action: Cut the steps that proceed anyway
steps.detail: Positioning and teaching assume the procedure goes ahead.

elimination.verdict: Report the warfarin first.

questions.scenario: A 70-year-old with pneumonia had an SpO2 of 84% and a respiratory rate of 30. The nurse applied a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min and raised the head of the bed. Thirty minutes later the nurse reassesses.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is reassuring or requires follow up.

rows.text: Respiratory rate went from 30 to 20
rows.rationale: Slower breathing shows less distress.

rows.text: She now speaks only 2 or 3 words at a time
rows.rationale: Short phrases mean the work of breathing is rising.

rows.text: SpO2 went from 84% to 94%
rows.rationale: The saturation is back above 90%.

rows.text: She was oriented and is now pulling at the mask and confused
rows.rationale: New confusion is a concerning sign of poor oxygenation.

rows.text: The reservoir bag collapses fully with each breath
rows.rationale: A collapsed bag means the device is not delivering high concentration oxygen. Check the flow and the valves.

questions.takeaway: Monitor the response to oxygen with the whole patient: rate, speech, mental status, saturation and the device itself.
questions.strategy: Judge each row alone. One good number does not cancel new confusion or a collapsed reservoir.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 84% and a rate of 30.
Rate and saturation better. Speech and mental status worse.
A nonrebreather bag must stay inflated.

elimination.verdict: Reassuring, follow up, reassuring, follow up, follow up.

questions.stem: A long term care resident whose roommate has COVID 19 has had diarrhea for 2 days and now has a fever, cough and dry mucous membranes. Which actions does the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place the client on the facility's COVID 19 precautions
options.rationale: Preventing transmission is a priority hypothesis, and roommates are exposed.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed
options.rationale: Upright positioning supports ventilation.

options.text: Offer fluids often and track intake
options.rationale: Fever, diarrhea and dry mucous membranes put her at risk for fluid volume deficit.

options.text: Monitor the SpO2 trend and breathing effort
options.rationale: Trends catch deterioration early.

options.text: Wait for a positive test before starting precautions
options.rationale: Tempting because the test confirms the diagnosis. Exposure plus symptoms is enough to start precautions, and waiting exposes others.

options.text: Seat her at her own table in the dining room for meals
options.rationale: Isolation is a real concern, but a shared room spreads infection even at a separate table. Use other ways to connect.

questions.takeaway: GI symptoms can come before respiratory ones in COVID 19. Act on exposure plus symptoms: precautions, positioning, hydration, monitoring.
questions.strategy: Tie each option to a cue in the stem: the exposed roommate, the cough, the fluid loss.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Exposure needs precautions. Cough needs positioning and monitoring. Diarrhea and fever need fluids.
Precautions start on suspicion, before the result.
A shared dining room.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.scenario: A 68-year-old has been on 60% oxygen by mask for 3 days. SpO2 has stayed at 99% to 100%. Today the nurse hears new crackles with decreased breath sounds at both bases. The prescribed goal is an SpO2 of 92% or higher.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Report the findings and ask about lowering the oxygen concentration
options.rationale: The goal is met with room to spare. The lowest effective concentration limits further harm.

options.text: Help the client deep breathe, cough and change position
options.rationale: Deep breaths and movement reopen collapsed alveoli.

options.text: Increase the oxygen to keep the SpO2 at 100%
options.rationale: More oxygen worsens a complication caused by high oxygen.

options.text: Remove the oxygen until the next provider rounds
options.rationale: Stopping oxygen abruptly without an order risks hypoxemia.

options.text: A complication of high concentration oxygen
options.rationale: High oxygen for days washes out the nitrogen that holds alveoli open. New crackles and decreased sounds fit absorption atelectasis.

options.text: Upper airway obstruction
options.rationale: That causes stridor, not crackles at the bases.

options.text: An inaccurate pulse oximeter reading
options.rationale: The reading has been steady, and the lung sounds are the new finding.

options.text: Fluid volume deficit
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario points to fluid loss.

options.text: Breath sounds at the bases
options.rationale: Shows whether the alveoli are reopening.

options.text: SpO2 against the prescribed goal as oxygen is lowered
options.rationale: Confirms the lower concentration still meets 92% or higher.

options.text: Skin turgor
options.rationale: A hydration check that does not track this problem.

options.text: Bowel sounds
options.rationale: Not related to the oxygen complication.

questions.takeaway: A saturation of 100% on high oxygen is not a goal. Use the lowest effective concentration and listen for new crackles.
questions.strategy: Opposite actions are offered: lower the oxygen or raise it. The goal of 92% tells you which way to go.

steps.action: Read the goal against the reading
steps.detail: 92% wanted, 100% delivered for 3 days.

steps.action: Link the new lung findings to the therapy
steps.detail: High oxygen can collapse alveoli.

steps.action: Choose monitoring that tracks the fix
steps.detail: Breath sounds and saturation at the lower dose.

elimination.verdict: Oxygen complication; ask to lower oxygen and deep breathe; breath sounds and SpO2 against goal.

questions.stem: A client given an IV opioid an hour ago is on oxygen by nasal cannula with an SpO2 of 96%. The respiratory rate is 8 and the client is hard to wake. Which action is first?

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and coach deep breathing
options.rationale: Tempting because both help ventilation. A client who is hard to wake cannot follow coaching, so this does not get breaths moving.

options.text: Increase the oxygen flow to give the client a safety margin
options.rationale: Oxygen is not the missing piece. The client is not moving enough air to clear carbon dioxide, and extra oxygen can hide slow shallow breathing.

options.text: Check the oximeter waveform to confirm the reading
options.rationale: A good step when a reading does not match the client. Here the reading is not the concern. Pulse oximetry shows saturation, not ventilation.

options.text: Stimulate the client to breathe and call for help
options.rationale: A rate of 8 with poor arousal is failing ventilation. The nurse acts on the client, not on the number.

questions.takeaway: A normal SpO2 on oxygen does not prove the client is breathing enough. Rate, depth and alertness tell you about ventilation.
questions.strategy: The dramatic number is the reassuring one. Find the quieter findings that disagree with it.

steps.action: Compare the number with the client
steps.detail: 96% does not fit a rate of 8 and poor arousal.

steps.action: Cut the option about the reading
steps.detail: Confirming the waveform tests the oximeter, not the breathing.
The problem is ventilation.
Coaching needs an awake client. Stimulation does not.

elimination.verdict: Stimulate the client and get help.

questions.stem: One hour after a right thoracentesis a client says breathing feels easier. Which finding does the nurse report now?

options.text: Fainter right sided breath sounds, rate up from 18 to 26
options.rationale: Breath sounds should be the same or better after fluid is removed. Fainter sounds with a rising rate suggest a pneumothorax despite the client feeling better.

options.text: A coughing spell lasting several minutes after the procedure
options.rationale: Coughing is common as the lung expands again. It settled, so it is watched.

options.text: Soreness at the needle site rated 3 on a 0 to 10 scale
options.rationale: Expected after a needle through the chest wall.

options.text: A small spot of clear yellow drainage on the dressing
options.rationale: Tempting as a bleeding concern. A small amount of serous drainage is expected.

questions.takeaway: After a thoracentesis, compare breath sounds with the baseline. Feeling better does not rule out a pneumothorax.
questions.strategy: The client's own report points to improvement. Look for the finding that only means something when compared with the baseline.

steps.detail: Mild soreness and a small serous spot.
Common with lung expansion.
Fainter sounds and a climbing rate.

elimination.verdict: Report the fainter right breath sounds and rising rate.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: Pneumonia with a fever of 38.6 C, crackles and rust colored sputum
options.rationale: All three findings are expected with pneumonia.

options.text: COPD with an SpO2 of 91% who is breathing through pursed lips
options.rationale: Looks unstable, and this is a usual picture for a client with chronic lung disease.

options.text: Admitted with loud wheezing that is now quiet, speaking in single words
options.rationale: Wheezing that goes quiet while the client can barely speak means little air is moving. Silent breath sounds are a danger sign, not improvement.

options.text: COVID 19 on 2 L/min with a steady saturation, fatigue and loss of taste
options.rationale: Expected cues with a stable saturation.

questions.takeaway: Quiet is not always better. When wheezing stops and speech shortens, air has stopped moving.
questions.strategy: One client sounds improved. Check that against a second detail before you believe it.

steps.action: Cut findings expected for the condition
steps.detail: Pneumonia and COVID 19 findings fit their diagnoses.
91% with pursed lips is a chronic picture.
Single word speech says the quiet chest is worse.

elimination.verdict: See the client whose wheezing went quiet.

questions.stem: A client with pneumonia who was calm at 0800 is now restless, keeps pulling off the nasal cannula and insists on going home. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the prescribed as needed medication for anxiety
options.rationale: Tempting because the client looks anxious. A sedative could slow breathing in a client who may be hypoxic.

options.text: Check the SpO2 and assess the client's breathing
options.rationale: New restlessness in a client with a lung problem is an early sign of low oxygen until proven otherwise. No assessment has been done yet.

options.text: Stay with the client and reorient to place and situation
options.rationale: A good safety response to confusion. It addresses the behavior and misses the likely cause.

options.text: Ask a family member to sit with the client for safety
options.rationale: Protects the client from a fall and leaves the cause unexamined.

questions.takeaway: New restlessness or confusion in a respiratory client is hypoxia first. Assess oxygenation before you treat behavior.
questions.strategy: Safety and assessment compete. The stem gives a behavior change and no assessment, so find the cause first.

steps.detail: Restlessness plus a removed cannula points to low oxygen.
It treats a symptom and can worsen breathing.
They follow the oxygen check.

elimination.verdict: Check SpO2 and assess breathing.

questions.stem: A client with pneumonia and thick sputum has heart failure and new swelling in both ankles. The client asks how much to drink. Which response is best?

options.text: Aim for 3 liters of water a day to thin the sputum
options.rationale: The usual pneumonia teaching, which makes it tempting. It applies unless fluids are contraindicated, and heart failure with new edema may be that case.

options.text: Limit yourself to 1 liter a day because of the swelling
options.rationale: Recognizes the heart failure, but a restriction is a prescription the nurse does not set.

options.text: Drink whenever you feel thirsty and that will be enough
options.rationale: Gives no goal and ignores both the thick sputum and the edema.

options.text: I will confirm your fluid goal with the provider first
options.rationale: Two conditions pull in opposite directions and the edema is new. The nurse clarifies the goal before teaching a number.

questions.takeaway: Three liters a day for pneumonia comes with a condition: unless contraindicated. Heart failure with new edema means clarify first.
questions.strategy: Two options state opposite amounts with equal confidence. A detail in the stem makes both numbers unsafe to give.

steps.detail: Thick sputum calls for fluids. Heart failure with edema calls for caution.
The nurse cannot pick 3 liters or 1 liter here.
Thirst is not a plan.

elimination.verdict: Confirm the fluid goal with the provider.

questions.stem: A client on a partial rebreather mask has a reservoir bag that flattens completely with each breath. SpO2 has slipped from 95% to 91%. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Change to a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
options.rationale: Tempting because the saturation is falling. It changes the ordered device before the setup fault on the current one is fixed.

options.text: Raise the flow until the bag stays partly inflated
options.rationale: The reservoir on a partial rebreather must stay partly inflated. A bag that collapses means the flow is too low to supply each breath.

options.text: Tighten the mask straps for a closer seal
options.rationale: A leak would not flatten the bag. The cue points to flow, not fit.

options.text: Recheck the saturation in 15 minutes
options.rationale: The cause is visible now. Waiting lets the saturation keep falling.

questions.takeaway: A partial rebreather works only while its reservoir stays partly inflated. A collapsing bag is a flow problem you fix at the flowmeter.
questions.strategy: The bag is the deciding detail. Fix what the device is showing you before you trade it for a bigger device.

steps.detail: The bag flattens fully, so each breath outruns the supply.
Rechecking later leaves the fault in place.
A new device needs an order. More flow corrects the one you have.

elimination.verdict: Raise the flow until the bag stays partly inflated.

questions.stem: Four clients describe their sputum during morning rounds. Which report does the nurse act on first?

options.text: Thick yellow sputum every morning in a long term smoker
options.rationale: A chronic pattern for this client. It needs teaching, not urgent action.

options.text: Rust colored sputum on day 2 of pneumonia treatment
options.rationale: Tempting because the color is striking. Rust colored sputum is expected with pneumonia already under treatment.

options.text: Pink frothy sputum with new breathlessness at rest
options.rationale: Pink frothy sputum points to fluid in the alveoli. With new breathlessness it is an acute change that threatens gas exchange.

options.text: Clear white sputum after a nebulizer treatment
options.rationale: Clear sputum that moves after a treatment is a good result.

questions.takeaway: Sputum color and texture are cues. Pink and frothy means fluid in the lungs and is acted on first; rust colored fits pneumonia.
questions.strategy: Ask which report is new and unexpected for that client. Two of these are that client's usual picture.

steps.detail: Morning sputum in a smoker is long standing.
Rust color belongs to pneumonia. Clear sputum after a nebulizer is the goal.
Pink froth with new breathlessness is fluid in the lungs.

elimination.verdict: Pink frothy sputum with new breathlessness.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old going home on oxygen by nasal cannula lives with a spouse who smokes. Which statement shows the safety teaching was effective?

options.text: "My wife will smoke outdoors, well away from the oxygen."
options.rationale: Oxygen feeds a flame. Smoking stays away from wherever oxygen is in use.

options.text: "I will put petroleum jelly in my nose for dryness."
options.rationale: Petroleum products are not used with oxygen. A water based product is the safe choice.

options.text: "I will turn the flow up a liter when I feel winded."
options.rationale: Tempting because it sounds like self care. Oxygen is a prescribed dose, and new breathlessness is reported.

options.text: "I will take the cannula off when my ears get sore."
options.rationale: Sore ears are padded and the tubing repositioned. The oxygen stays on.

questions.takeaway: Home oxygen safety: no smoking or flames near it, no petroleum products, and the flow stays where it was prescribed.
questions.strategy: Each wrong statement solves a real problem in an unsafe way. Look for the one that removes a hazard.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Would this be safe if he did it tonight?
Petroleum near oxygen, a self adjusted dose, oxygen taken off.
Smoking moves away from the oxygen.

elimination.verdict: Smoking stays outdoors, away from the oxygen.

questions.stem: On postoperative day 1 a client has low pitched snoring sounds over the central airways. Breathing is unlabored. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Request a prescription for a bronchodilator
options.rationale: A bronchodilator treats wheezes from narrowed airways. These sounds are not wheezes.

options.text: Suction the back of the throat
options.rationale: Tempting because secretions are the cause. A client breathing easily can clear them with a cough, which is less invasive.

options.text: Ask about a diuretic for fluid overload
options.rationale: Fluid produces crackles, not low snoring sounds.

options.text: Have the client cough, then listen again
options.rationale: Rhonchi come from secretions in the large airways. If they clear with a cough, the cause is confirmed and treated at once.

questions.takeaway: Match the sound to its cause: rhonchi are secretions, wheezes are narrowed airways, crackles are fluid. Secretions are moved with a cough first.
questions.strategy: Name the sound before you pick the treatment. Three options treat three different sounds.

steps.detail: Low pitched and snoring over large airways is rhonchi.
A bronchodilator is for wheezes and a diuretic is for crackles.
Unlabored breathing means the client can cough.

elimination.verdict: Have the client cough, then listen again.

questions.stem: A client arrives with fever and cough after travel to a region with a newly emerged influenza strain. The route of spread is not yet confirmed. Which precautions does the nurse start?

options.text: Airborne and contact precautions
options.rationale: For pandemic influenza the slides call for contact and airborne precautions until the type and route are known.

options.text: Droplet precautions with a surgical mask
options.rationale: Tempting because this is the usual answer for seasonal influenza. The route here is unknown, so the broader precautions apply.

options.text: Standard precautions until testing returns
options.rationale: Waiting for the test leaves staff and other clients exposed in the meantime.

options.text: Contact precautions with gown and gloves
options.rationale: Covers only part of the possible spread and leaves the air route open.

questions.takeaway: A new influenza strain with an unknown route gets contact and airborne precautions until the type is known. Seasonal influenza is the droplet case.
questions.strategy: The words "newly emerged" and "not yet confirmed" change the answer from the seasonal one you memorized.

steps.detail: The route is not confirmed.
Precautions start on suspicion.
Airborne plus contact covers what droplet or contact alone would miss.

elimination.verdict: Airborne and contact precautions.

questions.stem: A client admitted with pneumonia is coughing up sputum. The first IV antibiotic dose has just arrived, and a sputum culture and a chest x-ray are prescribed. Which does the nurse do first?

options.text: Hang the antibiotic so treatment is not delayed
options.rationale: Tempting because prompt antibiotics matter. A dose given first can keep the organism from growing in the culture.

options.text: Collect the sputum specimen for culture
options.rationale: The client is producing sputum now. A specimen taken before the first dose identifies the organism, and the antibiotic follows right after.

options.text: Send the client for the chest x-ray
options.rationale: The x-ray takes the client off the unit and delays both the culture and the antibiotic.

options.text: Teach coughing and deep breathing exercises
options.rationale: Useful later. It does not come ahead of the culture and the first dose.

questions.takeaway: Cultures come before the first antibiotic dose. Collect the specimen, then start the drug without delay.
questions.strategy: Two options are both right actions. The order is decided by which one spoils the other.

steps.detail: Teaching and the x-ray do not treat or identify the infection.
The antibiotic can ruin the culture. The culture does not delay the antibiotic by more than minutes.
The client is coughing up sputum now.

elimination.verdict: Collect the sputum, then hang the antibiotic.

questions.stem: A drowsy client with a PaCO2 of 61 mm Hg is started on BiPAP. Which finding two hours later best shows the therapy is working?

options.text: SpO2 has stayed at 98% on the machine
options.rationale: Tempting because the number is good. Saturation does not measure ventilation or carbon dioxide.

options.text: Client sleeps soundly and leaves the mask alone
options.rationale: Sleepiness was the problem. Sound sleep could mean the carbon dioxide is still high.

options.text: Mask seal shows no leak around the nose
options.rationale: A good seal is setup, not outcome.

options.text: PaCO2 is 47 mm Hg and the client is alert
options.rationale: BiPAP was started to support ventilation. A falling carbon dioxide with a clearer mind is the direct evidence.

questions.takeaway: Judge a therapy by the problem it was started for. BiPAP supports ventilation, so look at carbon dioxide and alertness, not saturation alone.
questions.strategy: Ask what was wrong at the start: high carbon dioxide and drowsiness. The answer must show both improving.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Carbon dioxide was high and the client was drowsy.
A sealed mask and quiet sleep do not prove ventilation.
SpO2 shows oxygen. PaCO2 shows ventilation.

elimination.verdict: PaCO2 down and the client alert.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old returns one week after his quit date wearing a nicotine patch. Which report requires the nurse to act?

options.text: "I crave one every time I finish my coffee."
options.rationale: Cravings tied to habits are expected in the first weeks and are handled with counseling.

options.text: "I have been short tempered with my family."
options.rationale: Tempting because it sounds like a mood change. Irritability is an expected part of nicotine withdrawal.

options.text: "I smoke two at night with the patch on."
options.rationale: Smoking while on nicotine replacement raises the nicotine level and the risk of stroke and heart attack. The plan needs to change now.

options.text: "I chew sugarless gum most of the afternoon."
options.rationale: A harmless substitute and a sign he is coping.

questions.takeaway: At cessation follow up, cravings and irritability are expected. Smoking while wearing a nicotine patch is a safety problem.
questions.strategy: Three reports are discomforts of quitting. One adds a second source of nicotine.

steps.detail: Cravings, irritability and gum are the usual course.
Cigarettes plus a patch stack the nicotine.
The follow up visit exists to catch this.

elimination.verdict: Smoking with the patch on.

questions.stem: A student auscultates the lungs of a 67-year-old admitted with pneumonia. Which actions by the student give reliable findings? Select all that apply.

options.text: Works from the apices down to the bases
options.rationale: The slides teach apex to base so no area is skipped.

options.text: Listens to the whole right side, then the whole left
options.rationale: Sounds are compared at matching spots, left against right, before moving down.

options.text: Stays on each spot for a full breath in and out
options.rationale: Some sounds are heard only in one phase of the breath.

options.text: Places the stethoscope over the gown for warmth
options.rationale: Cloth adds noise and muffles sound. The stethoscope goes on skin.

options.text: Compares each spot with the same spot on the other side
options.rationale: The client's other lung is the best reference for what is normal for him.

questions.takeaway: Auscultate on bare skin, apex to base, side to side at matching spots, through a full breath at each one.
questions.strategy: Two options describe opposite ways of moving across the chest. Only one of them compares symmetric areas.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Apex to base is correct.
Matching spots side to side, not one whole side at a time.
Skin, and a full breath at each spot.

elimination.verdict: Apex to base, a full breath at each spot, compared side to side.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old is scheduled for a bedside thoracentesis this morning. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Confirm signed consent, allergies and bleeding risk
options.rationale: First. If any of these is a problem the procedure does not start.

options.text: Record baseline breath sounds, rate and SpO2
options.rationale: Done before the needle so there is something to compare with afterward.

options.text: Help the client stay still while the needle is in
options.rationale: Movement during the procedure risks injury to the lung.

options.text: Compare breath sounds and breathing with the baseline
options.rationale: A change from baseline is how a pneumothorax is caught early.

options.text: Teach which breathing symptoms to report later
options.rationale: Last. A pneumothorax can show up after the client leaves your care.

questions.takeaway: Thoracentesis: verify preparation and safety, get a baseline, support the client during, compare with baseline after, then teach what to report.
questions.strategy: Place the two anchors first: nothing happens before the safety check, and teaching for later comes last.

steps.detail: Consent, allergies and bleeding risk decide whether it goes ahead.
You cannot compare with a baseline you never took.
Keep still, compare, then teach.

elimination.verdict: Verify, baseline, support, compare, teach.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A 44-year-old with heavy menstrual bleeding has a hemoglobin of 7.1 g/dL, clear lungs and an SpO2 of 99%. She is breathless climbing one flight of stairs. Her tissues are short of oxygen because [[1]].

That evening her temperature is 39.1 C and she is breathless at rest. The fever worsens her dyspnea because it [[2]].

The most useful nursing plan tonight is to [[3]].

options.text: air is not reaching her alveoli
options.rationale: Her lungs are clear and her saturation is 99%, so ventilation is working.

options.text: too little hemoglobin is available to carry oxygen
options.rationale: The hemoglobin she has is fully loaded. There is simply not enough of it, so less oxygen reaches the tissues.

options.text: oxygen cannot cross the alveolar membrane
options.rationale: A diffusion problem would lower the saturation. Hers is 99%.

options.text: her pulse oximeter is reading falsely high
options.rationale: Nothing in the case interferes with the sensor. The reading is true and still does not show how much oxygen is carried.

options.text: raises the amount of oxygen her tissues use
options.rationale: A higher metabolic rate raises demand while her carrying capacity stays low.

options.text: narrows her lower airways
options.rationale: Fever does not cause bronchoconstriction.

options.text: lowers the oxygen in the room air she breathes
options.rationale: Inspired oxygen has not changed.

options.text: blocks her drive to breathe
options.rationale: Fever speeds breathing. It does not depress it.

options.text: coach pursed lip breathing every hour
options.rationale: Her airways are open and her blood is saturated. A breathing technique adds no carrying capacity.

options.text: raise the oxygen until the SpO2 reads 100%
options.rationale: One more point of saturation adds almost nothing when hemoglobin is the limit.

options.text: lower the fever and space her activity with rest
options.rationale: The nurse cannot add hemoglobin, and can lower demand while the cause is treated.

options.text: encourage walking in the hall to build endurance
options.rationale: Exercise raises oxygen demand she cannot meet right now.

questions.takeaway: A normal SpO2 shows the hemoglobin is full, not that there is enough of it. With low carrying capacity, lower the demand.
questions.strategy: Walk the oxygen path: air in, across the membrane, carried by blood. Find the one link the data show is weak.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clear breath sounds and 99% rule out ventilation and diffusion.
Hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL is the carrier shortage.
Supply cannot be raised at the bedside, so cut demand.

elimination.verdict: Too little hemoglobin, higher demand from fever, lower the fever and rest.

questions.stem: During an intake, a 52-year-old with a morning cough says he has smoked a pack a day since college. He has not been asked about quitting. What does the nurse do next?

options.text: Offer to request a nicotine patch prescription today
options.rationale: Assist comes after the nurse knows he is willing. Offering it now skips two steps.

options.text: Schedule a follow up call for next week
options.rationale: Arrange is the last step and has nothing to follow up yet.

options.text: Tell him clearly that quitting would help his cough
options.rationale: Advise. Tobacco use has been asked about, so the next step is a clear, personal message to quit.

options.text: Ask how ready he is to set a quit date
options.rationale: Tempting, and it is the step after this one. Readiness is assessed after he has heard the advice.

questions.takeaway: The 5 As run in order: ask, advise, assess, assist, arrange. Once you know he smokes, advise before you measure readiness.
questions.strategy: Place the stem in the sequence. He was asked and answered. Pick the very next step, not a later one.

steps.detail: Ask is done.
A patch and a follow up call belong to assist and arrange.
Advice comes before readiness.

elimination.verdict: Advise him to quit, tied to his cough.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old father who vapes was taught about protecting his newborn. Which statement shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I only vape in the car when the baby is not with me."
options.rationale: Residue settles on the seats and the car seat, so the baby is still exposed later.

options.text: "I vape outside, then change my shirt and wash my hands."
options.rationale: He understands that residue on clothing and skin reaches the baby, and he is removing it.

options.text: "Vapor is just water, so the nursery is the only room I avoid."
options.rationale: Aerosol carries nicotine and irritants, and it travels through the home.

options.text: "I open the windows wide and run a fan when I vape inside."
options.rationale: Ventilation thins the aerosol and leaves residue on surfaces.

questions.takeaway: Thirdhand smoke is the residue left on clothes, skin and surfaces. Going outside is not enough if the residue comes back in.
questions.strategy: Three statements keep the exposure near the baby in some form. Look for the one that removes it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Car, home and nursery plans all leave residue behind.
Changing the shirt and washing hands takes it off.

elimination.verdict: Outside, then change and wash.

questions.stem: A client with pneumonia had sharp pain on inspiration, a grating sound over the left lateral chest and shallow breathing. The nurse gave an analgesic and taught splinting. Which finding shows the plan worked?

options.text: He rates the pain 2 of 10 while resting quietly
options.rationale: Tempting. The pain score is better, and it says nothing about whether he can now expand his lungs.

options.text: The grating sound is no longer heard on the left
options.rationale: A rub that vanishes can mean fluid has collected between the pleural layers, so it is not proof of improvement.

options.text: He sleeps for two hours without waking
options.rationale: Rest is welcome and does not show deeper breathing.

options.text: He breathes deeply and sounds reach both bases
options.rationale: The goal of treating pleuritic pain is full lung expansion, and this shows it.

questions.takeaway: Pain relief for pleuritic pain is a means. The outcome is deep breathing that keeps the bases open.
questions.strategy: Ask what the pain was preventing. The best evidence is that the prevented thing now happens.

steps.detail: Shallow breathing was the risk.
A low score and sleep do not show expansion.
Silence can mean effusion.

elimination.verdict: Deep breaths with sounds to the bases.

questions.stem: A client returned from bronchoscopy 90 minutes ago and asks for water. Which finding shows it is safe to offer sips?

options.text: He gags when the back of his throat is touched
options.rationale: The topical anesthetic has worn off and the airway is protected again.

options.text: He is awake and tells the nurse the correct date
options.rationale: Alertness shows the sedation is clearing. The throat can still be numb.

options.text: His SpO2 is 96% on room air
options.rationale: Good oxygenation does not show he can protect his airway while swallowing.

options.text: His voice is hoarse and he reports a sore throat
options.rationale: Expected after the scope and unrelated to swallowing safety.

questions.takeaway: After bronchoscopy the client stays NPO until the gag reflex returns. Awake is not the same as protected.
questions.strategy: The danger is aspiration through a numb throat. Pick the finding that tests the throat itself.

steps.detail: A numbed throat lets fluid into the airway.
Orientation and SpO2 do not test the throat.
A returned gag reflex.

elimination.verdict: The gag reflex is back.

questions.stem: Two hours after a needle lung biopsy a client is lightheaded. The pulse rose from 78 to 108, breath sounds are equal and the dressing is dry. Which problem does the nurse suspect first?

options.text: Pneumothorax on the biopsy side
options.rationale: A real risk after this procedure. Equal breath sounds make it less likely right now.

options.text: Bleeding inside the chest
options.rationale: A rising pulse with lightheadedness is early blood loss, and a dry dressing does not rule out bleeding the nurse cannot see.

options.text: Lingering effect of the sedation
options.rationale: Sedation slows the pulse and makes a client drowsy. It does not raise the rate by 30.

options.text: Anxiety about the biopsy results
options.rationale: Possible, and never the first explanation for a new tachycardia after an invasive procedure.

questions.takeaway: After lung biopsy watch for two things: pneumothorax and bleeding. A climbing pulse with equal breath sounds points to bleeding.
