options.text: Apply a zinc oxide barrier cream after cleaning
options.rationale: A barrier keeps moisture and stool off the skin.

questions.takeaway: Protect at risk skin: clean promptly without scrubbing, pat dry, apply a barrier, check every 2 hours. Never massage reddened areas or use donut cushions.
questions.strategy: Three of these ideas feel caring and add force to fragile skin: rubbing, scrubbing and a ring of pressure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Massage, scrubbing and the donut.
Frequent checks and a barrier cream.
Two remain, and that is acceptable.

elimination.verdict: B and E.

questions.scenario: A 41-year-old started allopurinol 2 weeks ago. Today the skin is dusky red and painful, with blisters and sheets of peeling over about 35% of the body surface. The mouth has erosions. The next allopurinol dose is due now.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Withhold the allopurinol and notify the provider
options.rationale: Stopping the causative drug is the first step. Nothing else works while it continues.

options.text: Anticipate transfer to a burn unit or ICU
options.rationale: Skin loss over 30% behaves like a major burn and is usually managed in a burn unit or ICU.

options.text: Give the dose with an antihistamine
options.rationale: Treats it as hives and keeps giving the trigger.

options.text: Open the blisters to relieve pressure
options.rationale: Breaks the remaining barrier and raises infection risk.

options.text: Apply warm compresses to the red areas
options.rationale: Heat dilates vessels and adds fluid loss and pain.

options.text: Toxic epidermal necrolysis
options.rationale: A drug triggered reaction with mucosal erosions and more than 30% of the body surface involved.

options.text: Stevens-Johnson syndrome
options.rationale: The same process, involving less than 10% of the body surface.

options.text: Urticaria
options.rationale: Hives are raised, itchy wheals. They do not blister, peel or erode the mouth.

options.text: Contact dermatitis
options.rationale: Follows the shape of what touched the skin and spares the mouth.

options.text: Intake and urine output
options.rationale: Open skin loses fluid and electrolytes the way a burn does.

options.text: Body temperature
options.rationale: Lost skin cannot hold heat, and fever may signal infection.

options.text: Serum uric acid
options.rationale: Tracks the gout the drug was treating, which is not the current threat.

options.text: Blood glucose
options.rationale: Nothing in this picture points to a glucose problem. Fluid and heat loss are the threats.

options.text: Pupil size
options.rationale: Eye care matters here, and it means lubricating and protecting the surface, not checking pupils.

questions.takeaway: SJS and TEN are the same drug reaction sorted by body surface: under 10% is SJS, over 30% is TEN. Stop the drug first, then support like a burn.
questions.strategy: Let the percentage name the condition. Then treat the skin as a lost barrier: fluid leaves, heat leaves, organisms enter.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 35% is over 30%.
A new drug 2 weeks ago, and a dose due now.

steps.action: Monitor what a lost barrier costs
steps.detail: Fluid and temperature.

elimination.verdict: Withhold the drug, notify the provider and anticipate burn level care; TEN; intake and output, temperature.

questions.stem: A restless client on bed rest shifts position often without help. Both elbows and heels have shiny, abraded skin from rubbing against the sheets. Which plan addresses the cause?

options.text: Cover elbows and heels with foam dressings
options.rationale: The damage is friction from rubbing, so a protective layer between skin and linen removes the cause.

options.text: Increase turning to every hour
options.rationale: Tempting. Turning relieves pressure, and this client already moves a great deal.

options.text: Apply zinc oxide to both areas
options.rationale: Barrier cream protects from moisture, which is not the problem here.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees for comfort
options.rationale: A higher head of bed adds sliding and shear.

questions.takeaway: Name the force before you pick the fix: friction needs a protective surface, pressure needs offloading, moisture needs a barrier.
questions.strategy: Each option treats a different force. Find the one in the stem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rubbing is friction.

steps.action: Cut the pressure and moisture fixes
steps.detail: Turning, zinc oxide.
Head of bed at 45.

elimination.verdict: Foam dressings over elbows and heels.

questions.stem: A client on a nasal cannula for 3 days says the tops of both ears are sore. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply moisturizer behind both ears
options.rationale: Treats before looking, and lotion does not relieve pressure.

options.text: Lift the tubing and inspect the skin under it
options.rationale: Devices cause pressure injuries, and soreness is an early cue. The nurse must see the skin before choosing padding or repositioning.

options.text: Change to a face mask
options.rationale: Tempting because it moves the tubing. It changes oxygen delivery, needs a prescription, and puts straps on new skin.

options.text: Explain that soreness from the tubing is expected at first
options.rationale: Dismisses an early warning of tissue damage.

questions.takeaway: Oxygen tubing, tubes, stockings and collars all cause pressure injuries. Soreness under a device means look under it.
questions.strategy: The stem gives a symptom and no skin findings yet.

steps.detail: Only a report of soreness.
Lotion, mask.
Lift and inspect.

elimination.verdict: Lift the tubing and inspect the skin.

questions.stem: A sacral pressure injury is completely covered by yellow slough. A student plans to chart it as stage 3 because no bone is visible. Which response by the nurse is correct?

options.text: "Agreed. No bone means it cannot be stage 4."
options.rationale: Bone could lie under the slough.

options.text: "Chart it as stage 2 until the base is seen."
options.rationale: Slough is not present in stage 2, so this is already full thickness.

options.text: "Probe through the slough with an applicator to find the depth."
options.rationale: Tempting as a way to get the answer. Forcing through necrotic tissue causes harm and still does not show the base.

options.text: "The base is hidden, so the depth cannot be confirmed yet."
options.rationale: When slough or eschar obscures the wound bed, the extent of tissue loss cannot be determined until it is removed.

questions.takeaway: You stage what you can see. A covered base is unstageable until the slough or eschar is gone.
questions.strategy: Ask whether anyone can see the wound bed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The base is fully covered.
Stage 2 and stage 3 both assume a depth.
Probing through slough.

elimination.verdict: The depth cannot be confirmed yet.

questions.stem: A client with toxic epidermal necrolysis over 35% of the body is receiving IV fluids. Which finding best indicates fluid replacement is adequate?

options.text: The open areas look moist and shiny
options.rationale: Moist wound surfaces reflect the skin loss, not the client's volume.

options.text: Urine output is 50 mL per hour
options.rationale: Large skin loss means large fluid loss. Steady urine output shows the kidneys are being perfused.

options.text: The client asks for water less often
options.rationale: Thirst is subjective and does not measure circulating volume.

options.text: Weight is 2 kg above admission
options.rationale: Tempting as proof fluid went in. A rapid gain suggests excess, not balance.

questions.takeaway: Skin is the barrier against fluid loss. When a large area is lost, urine output tells you whether replacement is keeping up.
questions.strategy: Pick the measure of perfusion, not of comfort or of fluid given.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fluid loss through open skin.
Thirst.
Rapid weight gain.

elimination.verdict: Urine output of 50 mL per hour.

questions.stem: A client in a group home was treated for head lice this morning. Which statement by the client indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "The itching will stop tonight, so I will know it worked."
options.rationale: Itching can last after treatment and does not prove success.

options.text: "I can share my brush again once my hair is dry."
options.rationale: Lice spread on shared combs, brushes and hats.

options.text: "I will comb out the nits with a fine comb and wash my bedding in hot water."
options.rationale: Nits stay glued to the hair shaft after treatment, and lice survive off the host for about 2 days, so combing and hot laundering finish the job.

options.text: "I will shampoo with it every day this week to be sure."
options.rationale: Tempting thoroughness. Overuse irritates the scalp and is not how the product is prescribed.

questions.takeaway: Lice treatment has three parts: the product, combing out the nits, and hot washing of linens and clothing. Nothing that touches the hair is shared.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that deals with what the product leaves behind: nits and linens.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It spreads lice.

steps.action: Cut symptom based proof and overuse
steps.detail: Itch lingers, and daily treatment irritates the scalp.
Nits combed out, bedding washed hot.

elimination.verdict: Comb out the nits and wash bedding in hot water.

questions.stem: A client who walks independently has a Braden score of 17. The lowest subscale is moisture, from urinary incontinence several times a day. Which plan best targets this client's risk?

options.text: Order a powered pressure redistributing overlay for the bed
options.rationale: Tempting for any at risk score. Mobility and activity are good, so pressure is not the main driver.

options.text: Start a toileting schedule and apply a barrier cream
options.rationale: The subscale shows moisture is the problem. Keeping skin dry and protected addresses it directly.

options.text: Turn the client every 2 hours in bed
options.rationale: A walking client already shifts weight.

options.text: Request a dietitian consult for protein
options.rationale: Useful if nutrition were the low subscale.

questions.takeaway: The Braden total tells you who is at risk. The subscales tell you what to do about it.
questions.strategy: Match the intervention to the lowest subscale.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Moisture.
Overlay, turning.
Nutrition.

elimination.verdict: Toileting schedule and barrier cream.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches the AP to protect a bedbound client's heels. Which action by the AP indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: Places a folded pillow directly under both heels
options.rationale: The heels still bear weight on the pillow.

options.text: Rubs lotion into both heels with each turn
options.rationale: Rubbing over a bony prominence damages capillaries.

options.text: Places a pillow under the calves so the heels hang free
options.rationale: Floating the heels removes pressure from them completely.

options.text: Puts thick socks on and tucks the top sheet tightly
options.rationale: Socks do not relieve pressure, and a tight sheet presses the heels down.

questions.takeaway: Float heels: support the calf so the heel touches nothing.
questions.strategy: Ask where the weight rests in each option.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Under the heel still means pressure.
It harms fragile vessels.
Pillow under the calves.

elimination.verdict: Pillow under the calves, heels free.

questions.stem: A client with a stage 4 sacral injury is newly confused. Temperature is 38.9 C, heart rate 118 and blood pressure 88/52. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Give the prescribed acetaminophen and recheck in 1 hour
options.rationale: Treats the number and delays recognition of the cause.

options.text: Change the dressing and measure the wound
options.rationale: Tempting because the wound is the likely source. Wound care can wait behind an unstable client.

options.text: Offer oral fluids every 15 minutes
options.rationale: A confused, hypotensive client needs more than sips.

options.text: Report the findings as possible sepsis now
options.rationale: Fever, tachycardia, hypotension and new confusion with a deep wound point to sepsis, a known complication that needs rapid treatment.

questions.takeaway: Pressure injuries can seed sepsis. Fever with low pressure and new confusion is unstable, and that outranks wound care.
questions.strategy: Unstable beats stable. Find the option that responds to the whole picture.

steps.detail: Fever, fast heart rate, low pressure, confusion.
Acetaminophen, sips.

steps.action: Cut the task that can wait
steps.detail: Dressing change.

elimination.verdict: Report possible sepsis now.

questions.stem: A client with diabetes has itchy lower legs with scratch marks. Fingernails and toenails are long and jagged. Which plan is best?

options.text: File the fingernails and refer to podiatry for toenails
options.rationale: Short, filed nails limit scratch injury. Toenails in diabetes go to podiatry because a small cut can become a serious wound.

options.text: Trim the fingernails and toenails straight across at the bedside
options.rationale: Tempting and efficient. Toenail cutting in diabetes is referred.

options.text: Teach the client to clip the toenails after a warm soak
options.rationale: Clients with diabetes should avoid cutting their own toenails.

options.text: Place mitts on both hands at night
options.rationale: More restrictive than needed when nail care solves the problem.

questions.takeaway: For itching, keep nails short and filed. For diabetes, toenails belong to podiatry.
questions.strategy: Two different nails, two different rules. Find the option that respects both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fingers can be filed.
Toenails are referred.
Mitts.

elimination.verdict: File fingernails and refer toenails to podiatry.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a sacral pressure injury at a scheduled dressing change. Place the nurse's actions in the order they are performed.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene and apply gloves
options.rationale: First. Standard Precautions come before any contact with the wound.

options.text: Remove the old dressing and note the drainage on it
options.rationale: Second. The dressing shows the amount and type of exudate.

options.text: Clean the wound as prescribed
options.rationale: Third. The bed and edges must be visible before measuring.

options.text: Measure length and width, then depth with a cotton tipped applicator
options.rationale: Fourth. Surface first, then depth marked at skin level.

options.text: Probe gently for tunneling and note its clock position
options.rationale: Fifth. Hidden extension is checked after the open wound is measured.

options.text: Apply the new dressing and document, comparing with the last entry
options.rationale: Last. Cover the wound, then record so the trend is clear.

questions.takeaway: Protect, expose, clean, measure what you see, probe what you cannot, then cover and compare.
questions.strategy: You cannot measure what you have not cleaned, and you cannot document a trend until you have numbers.

steps.detail: Hand hygiene and gloves.
Old dressing off, wound cleaned.
Surface, depth, tunnels, then dress and document.

elimination.verdict: Hand hygiene, remove, clean, measure, probe, dress and document.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews admission Braden Scale totals for four clients. Which client does the nurse place on the pressure injury prevention bundle?

options.text: The client with a total score of 13
options.rationale: A total of 16 or less means increased risk, and lower scores mean higher risk.

options.text: The client with a total score of 20
options.rationale: Above the cutoff, so not at increased risk by score.

options.text: The client with a total score of 22
options.rationale: Well above the cutoff.

options.text: The client with a total score of 23
options.rationale: The highest score here, which is the lowest risk.

questions.takeaway: Braden Scale: lower score, higher risk. A total of 16 or less (18 or less in some facilities) means increased risk.
questions.strategy: Decide the direction of the scale first. On Braden, low is bad.

steps.detail: Lower scores mean higher risk.
Only 13 is at or below 16.

elimination.verdict: The client scoring 13.

questions.stem: A client on bed rest with a Braden score of 12 slides down whenever the head is raised. Breathing is easy and no feeding is running. Which prescription does the nurse question?

options.text: Foam dressings over the sacrum and both heels
options.rationale: Appropriate. Foam dressings over bony prominences reduce pressure.

options.text: Dietitian consult for protein and calorie goals
options.rationale: Appropriate. Nutrition goals are part of prevention.

options.text: Head of the bed at 45 degrees while resting
options.rationale: The head of the bed stays at or below 30 degrees to prevent shear, and nothing in the stem requires it higher.

options.text: Repositioning with a lift sheet and two staff
options.rationale: Appropriate. Lifting avoids friction and shear.

questions.takeaway: Keep the head of the bed at or below 30 degrees to prevent shear, unless another need requires it higher.
questions.strategy: You are looking for the order that harms. The stem removes the reasons to sit the client up, and only one option carries a number.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Question means find the unsafe order.
45 degrees is above the 30 degree limit, and this client already slides.

elimination.verdict: Head of the bed at 45 degrees.

questions.stem: The AP has repositioned four clients who must stay off a reddened sacrum. Which client's position does the nurse correct?

options.text: Tilted 30 degrees to the left, foam wedge behind the back
options.rationale: Correct setup. A 30 degree tilt takes weight off the sacrum without loading the hip.

options.text: Turned 90 degrees, lying directly on the right hip
options.rationale: 90 degrees puts full weight on the trochanter and trades one pressure point for another.

options.text: Tilted 30 degrees to the right, pillow between the knees
options.rationale: Correct setup. The tilt is 30 degrees and the knees are padded.

options.text: Tilted 30 degrees to the left, heels clear of the mattress
options.rationale: Correct setup. The tilt is 30 degrees and the heels are floated.

questions.takeaway: Side lying is a 30 degree tilt, not 90 degrees directly on the hip.
questions.strategy: You want the faulty position. Three options share one angle, so look hard at the one that differs.

steps.detail: Correct means fix the unsafe position.
90 degrees loads the trochanter. 30 degrees is taught.

elimination.verdict: The client turned 90 degrees onto the hip.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the night plan an AP wrote for a bedbound client with a low Braden score. Which part of the plan needs correction?

options.text: Turn using a lift sheet with a second staff member
options.rationale: Lifting avoids friction and shear.

options.text: Place pillows between the knees and ankles
options.rationale: Padding between bony surfaces reduces pressure.

options.text: Pat the skin dry after cleaning
options.rationale: Patting without scrubbing protects fragile skin.

options.text: Turn every 4 hours so the client can sleep
options.rationale: Turning is at least every 2 hours. Four hours leaves tissue compressed too long.

questions.takeaway: Turn at least every 2 hours, day and night.
questions.strategy: You are looking for the faulty part. One option carries a number, so check it against the taught interval.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Needs correction.
4 hours is double the 2 hour maximum.

elimination.verdict: Turning every 4 hours.

questions.stem: A client on bed rest has urinary incontinence, wears an absorbent brief and has intact skin. Which plan does the nurse give the AP?

options.text: Check under the brief every 2 hours, clean with mild soap and warm water, pat dry, apply barrier cream
options.rationale: Check at least every 2 hours, clean promptly and gently, pat dry and protect with a barrier cream.

options.text: Check under the brief every 2 hours, clean with mild soap and warm water, scrub dry, apply barrier cream
options.rationale: Scrubbing adds friction to wet, fragile skin.

options.text: Check under the brief every 8 hours, clean with mild soap and warm water, pat dry, apply barrier cream
options.rationale: Eight hours leaves urine on the skin far too long.

options.text: Check under the brief every 2 hours, clean with mild soap and warm water, pat dry, massage any red areas
options.rationale: Reddened areas are never massaged because it damages capillaries.

questions.takeaway: Incontinence care: check under products at least every 2 hours, mild soap and warm water, pat dry, barrier cream. Never scrub or massage red areas.
questions.strategy: The options are the same except one part each. Find the changed part.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 2 hours, not 8.
Pat, not scrub.
Barrier cream, not massage.

elimination.verdict: Every 2 hours, pat dry, barrier cream.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old at risk for pressure injury has dry mucous membranes and no heart or kidney disease. Which daily fluid goal does the nurse set with the dietitian?

options.text: 500 mL per day
options.rationale: Far too little. Dehydrated tissue breaks down and heals poorly.

options.text: 1000 mL per day
options.rationale: Half of the minimum taught.

options.text: 2500 mL per day
options.rationale: Within the 2000 to 3000 mL per day goal for pressure injury prevention.

options.text: 6000 mL per day
options.rationale: Double the upper limit, with a risk of fluid overload.

questions.takeaway: Pressure injury prevention: fluids 2000 to 3000 mL per day unless contraindicated, plus protein and calorie goals.
questions.strategy: The stem rules out the reasons to restrict fluid. Recall the range and pick the value inside it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 2000 to 3000 mL per day.
Only 2500 sits inside.

elimination.verdict: 2500 mL per day.

questions.stem: A hip wound has full thickness skin loss. Fat is visible, the edges are rolled, and a thin strip of slough lies at one edge. No muscle, tendon or bone is seen or felt. How does the nurse stage it?

options.text: Stage 2
options.rationale: Stage 2 is partial thickness with exposed dermis. Fat and slough are not visible.

options.text: Stage 3
options.rationale: Full thickness skin loss with visible fat and no exposed muscle, tendon or bone. Slough may be present.

options.text: Stage 4
options.rationale: Stage 4 needs exposed or palpable fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, cartilage or bone.

options.text: Unstageable
options.rationale: Unstageable means slough or eschar hides the base. Here the fat is seen.

questions.takeaway: Stage by the deepest visible tissue: dermis is stage 2, fat is stage 3, muscle, tendon or bone is stage 4. Unstageable only when slough or eschar hides the base.
questions.strategy: Name the deepest tissue you can see, then ask whether the slough hides the base.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fat.
A thin strip at one edge does not obscure the base.

elimination.verdict: Stage 3.

questions.stem: A client's heel has an unbroken blister filled with clear, straw colored fluid. The skin around it is its usual color. How does the nurse document this finding?

options.text: Deep tissue pressure injury
options.rationale: That is a blood filled blister or persistent deep red, maroon or purple skin.

options.text: Stage 1 pressure injury
options.rationale: Stage 1 is intact skin with nonblanchable erythema and no blister.

options.text: Unstageable pressure injury
options.rationale: No slough or eschar is hiding a wound bed.

options.text: Stage 2 pressure injury
options.rationale: Stage 2 may look like an intact or ruptured serum filled blister.

questions.takeaway: Serum filled blister is stage 2. Blood filled blister or maroon or purple skin is a deep tissue pressure injury.
questions.strategy: The fluid in the blister decides. Clear serum and blood point to different injuries.

steps.detail: Clear and straw colored is serum.
Serum is stage 2. Blood would be deep tissue injury.

elimination.verdict: Stage 2.

questions.stem: The nurse measures a stage 3 sacral injury at a dressing change. Which method does the nurse use to record the depth?

options.text: Cotton tipped applicator to the wound base, marked at skin level, tip to mark measured in cm
options.rationale: Depth is taken with a cotton tipped applicator marked at skin level and measured from tip to mark.

options.text: Ruler laid across the widest part of the opening, measured in cm
options.rationale: That measures width, not depth.

options.text: Cotton tipped applicator slid under the wound edge, marked at the edge, measured in cm
options.rationale: That measures undermining, not the depth of the base.

options.text: Gloved finger placed in the wound and the depth estimated
options.rationale: An estimate cannot be compared from one dressing change to the next.

questions.takeaway: Wound size is length by width by depth in cm or mm. Depth: cotton tipped applicator to the base, mark at skin level, measure tip to mark.
questions.strategy: Ask what each method really measures. Only one measures straight down to the base.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Width, undermining, a guess, and depth.
Applicator to the base, marked at skin level.

elimination.verdict: Applicator to the base, marked at skin level.

questions.stem: A stage 3 sacral injury has thick yellow drainage, new warmth and redness spreading past the wound edge. Which dressing does the nurse discuss with the wound nurse?

options.text: Hydrocolloid dressing
options.rationale: For noninfected stage 2 injuries. It would seal in an infected wound.

options.text: Antimicrobial dressing with silver
options.rationale: Antimicrobial dressings such as silver, honey or chlorhexidine are for infected pressure injuries.

options.text: Transparent film dressing
options.rationale: For noninfected stage 2 injuries, and it absorbs nothing.

options.text: Hydrogel dressing
options.rationale: For noninfected wounds with minimal exudate, and it adds moisture.

questions.takeaway: Infected pressure injury: antimicrobial dressing (silver, honey, chlorhexidine). Hydrocolloid, hydrogel and film are for noninfected wounds.
questions.strategy: The stem describes infection. Three options carry the same limit.

steps.detail: Purulent drainage, warmth and spreading redness.
Hydrocolloid, film and hydrogel.

elimination.verdict: Antimicrobial dressing with silver.

questions.stem: A client has a noninfected stage 2 pressure injury on the heel with a pink, moist bed and scant drainage. Which dressing does the nurse expect the wound nurse to choose?

options.text: Alginate dressing
options.rationale: For stage 3 and 4 injuries with moderate exudate. It would dry a wound with scant drainage.

options.text: Superabsorbent dressing
options.rationale: For heavy exudate.

options.text: Antimicrobial dressing with silver
options.rationale: For infected injuries, and this one is not infected.

options.text: Hydrocolloid dressing
options.rationale: For noninfected stage 2 injuries, and it contours to the heel.

questions.takeaway: Hydrocolloid: noninfected stage 2, contours to heels. Alginate: stage 3 and 4 with moderate exudate. Superabsorbent: heavy exudate.
questions.strategy: Match three things from the stem: the stage, the amount of drainage and whether it is infected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Scant, so cut the absorbers.
None, so cut silver.

elimination.verdict: Hydrocolloid.

questions.stem: A client has negative pressure wound therapy on a sacral wound. Which prescription does the nurse carry out as written?

options.text: Foam left untrimmed over the surrounding skin, sealed with an adhesive sheet, changed every 72 hours
options.rationale: The foam is trimmed to fit inside the wound.

options.text: Foam trimmed to fit the wound, sealed with an adhesive sheet, changed every 14 days
options.rationale: Dressing and tubing are changed every 48 to 120 hours. Fourteen days is far too long.

options.text: Foam trimmed to fit the wound, sealed with an adhesive sheet, changed every 72 hours
options.rationale: Foam fits the wound, the adhesive sheet makes the seal, and 72 hours is within 48 to 120 hours.

options.text: Foam trimmed to fit the wound, covered loosely with dry gauze, changed every 72 hours
options.rationale: Without the adhesive sheet there is no seal and no suction.

questions.takeaway: Negative pressure wound therapy: foam trimmed to fit the wound, adhesive sheet seal, suction to a canister, dressing and tubing changed every 48 to 120 hours.
questions.strategy: Three parts per option: where the foam sits, how it is sealed and how often it is changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: In the wound only.
Adhesive sheet.
48 to 120 hours.

elimination.verdict: Trimmed foam, adhesive seal, every 72 hours.

questions.stem: Ten days after starting allopurinol, a client has painful skin that is blistering and peeling over 40% of the body surface. What does the nurse communicate to the provider?

options.text: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, hold the allopurinol, request burn unit transfer
options.rationale: Stevens-Johnson syndrome is less than 10% of body surface. This is 40%.

options.text: Toxic epidermal necrolysis, hold the allopurinol, request burn unit transfer
options.rationale: More than 30% is toxic epidermal necrolysis. The first step is stopping the drug, and care is often in an ICU or burn unit.

options.text: Toxic epidermal necrolysis, give the next allopurinol dose, request burn unit transfer
options.rationale: The first step is to stop the triggering drug.

options.text: Overlap syndrome, hold the allopurinol, request burn unit transfer
options.rationale: Overlap is 10% to 30% of body surface.

questions.takeaway: Body surface involved: Stevens-Johnson syndrome less than 10%, overlap 10% to 30%, toxic epidermal necrolysis more than 30%. First step: stop the drug.
questions.strategy: Place 40% in the right range first, then check what happens to the drug.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 40% is over 30%.
Held, not given.

elimination.verdict: Toxic epidermal necrolysis, hold the drug, burn unit.

questions.stem: An open abdominal wound healing by second intention is on day 12. The bed is beefy red and moist, and the edges are pulling inward. There is no odor or fever. How does the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Proliferative phase, on schedule
options.rationale: Granulation and contraction belong to the proliferative phase, which runs from about day 4 to 2 to 4 weeks.

options.text: Inflammatory phase, lasting longer than expected
options.rationale: The inflammatory phase is days 1 to 5 and shows redness, warmth, edema and pain, not granulation.

options.text: Maturation phase, earlier than expected
options.rationale: Maturation begins at about 3 weeks and shows a thinner, paler, firmer scar.

options.text: Wound infection, needing a culture
options.rationale: Beefy red, moist tissue with no odor or fever is healthy granulation.

questions.takeaway: Healing phases: inflammatory days 1 to 5; proliferative day 4 to 2 to 4 weeks (granulation, contraction); maturation 3 weeks to 1 year or longer.
questions.strategy: Match the day to the phase, then match the findings to the phase.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Day 12 sits in the proliferative window.
Granulation and contraction fit it.

elimination.verdict: Proliferative phase, on schedule.

questions.scenario: The nurse makes rounds on clients at risk for pressure injury and reviews what staff have set up.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is a correct setup or needs correction.

rows.text: A reddened sacrum left unmassaged while the client is turned off the area
rows.rationale: Reddened areas are never massaged because massage damages capillaries.

rows.text: A client in a chair who is able to stand, assisted to stand and march 5 steps once each shift
rows.rationale: Chair clients who are able stand and march in place 5 steps every hour.

rows.text: Mild soap and warm water used to clean a soiled client, then the skin patted dry
rows.rationale: Skin is cleaned promptly with mild soap and warm water and patted dry without scrubbing.

rows.text: A ring shaped cushion under the buttocks of a client in a wheelchair
rows.rationale: Donut cushions damage capillaries and are never used.

rows.text: Zinc oxide barrier cream applied after cleaning a client who is incontinent
rows.rationale: Zinc oxide, petrolatum and dimethicone are the barrier creams taught.

rows.text: Foam dressings in place over the sacrum and heels of a client on bed rest
rows.rationale: Foam dressings over bony prominences reduce pressure.

questions.takeaway: Never massage reddened areas or use donut cushions; chair clients march 5 steps every hour; mild soap, warm water, pat dry; zinc oxide barrier; foam over bony prominences.
questions.strategy: Judge each row alone against the taught number or device.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 5 steps every hour, not once a shift.
Foam, barrier cream and gentle cleaning are right. A ring cushion is not.

elimination.verdict: Correct, needs correction, correct, needs correction, correct, correct.

skills.title: FSBS/Insulin Administration Check-Off
skills.subtitle: Interpreting the value, recognizing hypoglycemia, insulin types and timing, and injection technique

questions.stem: A 61-year-old's premeal fingerstick reads 312 mg/dL after a week of readings near 150. He has just peeled an orange and his hands were not washed. Sliding scale insulin is ordered. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the sliding scale dose listed for 312 mg/dL
options.rationale: Tempting because the order covers this value. Sugar on the skin can raise the reading, and insulin dosed from a false high can cause a low.

options.text: Wash and dry his hands, then repeat the fingerstick
options.rationale: The value does not fit his trend and the finger was not clean. A clean, dry finger gives a result the dose can be based on.

options.text: Notify the provider of the sudden rise in glucose
options.rationale: Reasonable if a repeat on a clean finger is still high. The nurse confirms the value before reporting it.

options.text: Hold the insulin and recheck before the next meal
options.rationale: This leaves a possible high untreated for hours when a repeat takes one minute.

questions.takeaway: Wash and dry the hands before every fingerstick. A reading that does not fit the client is repeated on a clean, dry finger before insulin is dosed from it.
questions.strategy: The stem gives a number and a reason to doubt it. Settle the doubt before you treat or report.

steps.action: Compare the value with the trend
steps.detail: 312 after a week near 150 does not fit.
Orange juice on unwashed fingers.

steps.action: Cut the actions that trust the number
steps.detail: Dosing and calling both act on a doubtful value.
Waiting until the next meal answers nothing now.

elimination.verdict: Wash, dry and repeat the fingerstick.

questions.stem: A student's first fingerstick on a 76-year-old with cold hands gave too small a drop. After coaching, which action on the second attempt shows the coaching was effective?

options.text: Warms the hand, then punctures the center pad
options.rationale: Tempting because gentle warming is correct. The center pad is more painful, and the side of the fingertip is the taught site.

options.text: Lowers the hand, then squeezes the fingertip for a drop
options.rationale: Lowering the hand is correct. Squeezing is the error to avoid.

options.text: Rewashes the hand, then punctures while it is damp
options.rationale: Washing is correct. The finger must be dry, because water dilutes the sample.

options.text: Lowers the hand, then punctures the side of the fingertip
options.rationale: Letting the hand hang down improves flow, and the side of the fingertip gives a good sample.

questions.takeaway: Poor flow from a cold hand: warm gently or lower the hand, use the side of a dry fingertip, avoid squeezing.
questions.strategy: Each option has two parts. One wrong half spoils the option, so check both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Warming, lowering and washing are all correct first halves.
Center pad, squeezing and a damp finger are each errors.

steps.action: Keep the option with two correct halves
steps.detail: Lowered hand, side of the fingertip.

elimination.verdict: Lowers the hand and punctures the side of the fingertip.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old received regular and NPH insulin in one syringe at 0800. She missed her afternoon snack and is shaky and sweating at 1630. Which explanation guides the nurse's follow-up?

options.text: The NPH is still within its peak
options.rationale: NPH peaks 4 to 12 hours after the dose. At 1630 she is 8.5 hours in, with no snack to cover it.

options.text: The regular insulin is reaching its peak
options.rationale: Tempting because regular insulin is the mealtime insulin. Its peak was 2 to 4 hours after the dose, which ended at 1200.

options.text: The two insulins cancelled each other in the syringe
options.rationale: Mixing regular and NPH is a prescribed practice. It does not cancel either dose.

options.text: The morning dose has worn off entirely
options.rationale: A dose that has worn off would produce a high, not signs of a low.

questions.takeaway: Count the hours from the dose. Regular peaks at 2 to 4 hours. NPH peaks at 4 to 12 hours, so an afternoon low after a morning mix belongs to the NPH.
questions.strategy: Do the clock math for each insulin before you choose. 0800 to 1630 is 8.5 hours.

steps.detail: 0800 to 1630 is 8.5 hours.
Regular peaked from 1000 to 1200. NPH peaks from 1200 to 2000.
Reduced intake at the peak sets up the low.

elimination.verdict: The NPH is still within its peak.

questions.stem: At 0730 a 63-year-old who is eating normally is due regular insulin 6 units before breakfast. His tray comes at 0800. Which actions does the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check his fingerstick glucose before preparing the dose
options.rationale: The current value decides whether insulin is safe to give now.

options.text: Confirm the solution in the vial is clear
options.rationale: Regular insulin is clear. A cloudy vial is not used.

options.text: Roll the vial between the palms before drawing
options.rationale: Rolling is for NPH, a cloudy suspension. Regular insulin is a clear solution that does not need mixing.

options.text: Give the dose now, 30 minutes before the tray
options.rationale: Regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes, so half an hour ahead matches it to the meal.

options.text: Pinch up the skin and insert the needle at 90 degrees
options.rationale: Correct technique that keeps the dose in the subcutaneous tissue.

options.text: Pull back on the plunger to check for blood
options.rationale: Aspiration is not required for subcutaneous insulin.

questions.takeaway: Before regular insulin: check the glucose, confirm the vial is clear, give it 30 minutes before the meal, pinch and insert at 90 degrees without aspirating. Rolling is for NPH.
questions.strategy: Two options are correct habits for a different insulin or a different injection. Judge each against regular insulin given subcutaneously.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Glucose check, clear vial, timing and a pinched 90 degree insertion are all correct.
Rolling mixes a cloudy suspension. Regular insulin is a clear solution.
Not done for subcutaneous insulin.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D and E.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with erratic glucose readings was taught site rotation last week. Which report at today's visit shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I use my abdomen in the morning and my thigh at night."
options.rationale: Tempting because it sounds organized. Moving between regions makes each dose absorb at a different rate.

options.text: "I use the exact same spot so the dose stays predictable."
options.rationale: One region is right, but one spot is not. Rotation within the region protects the tissue.

options.text: "I stay in my abdomen and pick a different spot each time."
options.rationale: One anatomical region with rotation inside it keeps absorption consistent.

options.text: "I move from abdomen to arm to thigh through the week."
options.rationale: This is rotation between regions, which varies absorption dose to dose.

questions.takeaway: One region, a new spot within it each time. Rotating between regions changes absorption and makes readings erratic.
questions.strategy: Three options change something that should stay fixed or fix something that should change. Find the one that keeps the region and moves the spot.

steps.detail: Two options move between regions. They say the same thing.
It keeps the region but never rotates.
Same region, different spot.

elimination.verdict: Stays in the abdomen and picks a different spot each time.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old with type 1 diabetes and influenza calls the clinic. She has taken her insulin and is sipping fluids often. Her glucose has stayed near 270 mg/dL since morning. What does the nurse tell her to do next?

options.text: Test for ketones
options.rationale: A glucose that stays over 240 during illness calls for a ketone test, which shows whether ketoacidosis is developing.

options.text: Keep sipping fluids and recheck in four hours
options.rationale: Tempting because both are sick day rules. She is already doing them. The sustained value over 240 adds a step.

options.text: Skip the next insulin dose until she can eat
options.rationale: Illness raises glucose. Stopping insulin leads to ketoacidosis.

options.text: Drink a glass of juice to keep her strength up
options.rationale: Her glucose is high. Fast-acting carbohydrate is for a low.

questions.takeaway: Sick days: keep taking insulin, check glucose every three to four hours, keep fluids going, test ketones when glucose stays over 240.
questions.strategy: Ask what the stem says she is already doing. The answer is the sick day rule she has not yet followed.

steps.detail: Insulin taken, fluids going.

steps.action: Find the trigger in the stem
steps.detail: Glucose staying over 240.

steps.action: Match the trigger to its rule
steps.detail: Over 240 means ketones.

elimination.verdict: Test for ketones.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old going home on regular 5 units and NPH 15 units in one syringe gives a return demonstration. Which sequence shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: Rolls the NPH, draws NPH to 15, then regular to 20
options.rationale: Right total, wrong order. A syringe holding NPH should not enter the regular vial.

options.text: Rolls the NPH, draws regular to 5, then NPH to 20
options.rationale: Clear before cloudy, with the second insulin drawn to the total of both doses.

options.text: Rolls the NPH, draws regular to 5, then NPH to 15
options.rationale: Right order, but stopping at 15 gives only 10 units of NPH.

options.text: Rolls the regular, draws regular to 5, then NPH to 20
options.rationale: The vial that needs rolling is the cloudy NPH. Drawing it unmixed gives an uneven dose.

questions.takeaway: Roll the NPH, draw regular first, then draw NPH to the total of both doses.
questions.strategy: Check three things in each option: which vial is rolled, which is drawn first, where the plunger stops.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: NPH first is out.
5 plus 15 is 20, so stopping at 15 is out.
The cloudy vial is rolled.

elimination.verdict: Rolls the NPH, draws regular to 5, then NPH to 20.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old with an insulin pump is admitted. Her glucose has climbed from 150 to 320 mg/dL in four hours with ketones present. Lunch was normal. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Have her deliver a correction dose through the pump
options.rationale: Tempting because the glucose is high. If the pump is not delivering, a dose sent through it will not reach her.

options.text: Ask what she ate for lunch
options.rationale: The stem already says lunch was normal. A meal does not explain ketones.

options.text: Inspect the infusion site and tubing
options.rationale: A fast rise with ketones in a pump user points to interrupted delivery, since there is no long-acting insulin on board.

options.text: Recheck the glucose in one hour
options.rationale: Waiting lets ketones build in a client who may be getting no insulin.

questions.takeaway: A pump holds only rapid-acting insulin. Rising glucose with ketones means look for an interruption at the site or in the tubing first.
questions.strategy: Two options treat the high. Ask whether the route for that treatment can be trusted yet.

steps.detail: Fast rise plus ketones means no insulin is arriving.
Lunch was normal.

steps.action: Check the delivery before using it
steps.detail: A correction through a blocked line does nothing.

elimination.verdict: Inspect the infusion site and tubing.

questions.stem: At 1500 a 73-year-old who received NPH at 0700 has a fingerstick glucose of 56 mg/dL. He is alert, shaky and able to swallow. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: First. The glucose is known and under 70, so treatment comes before anything else.

options.text: Recheck the fingerstick glucose in 15 minutes
options.rationale: The recheck number, not how he feels, shows whether the low has resolved.

options.text: Give another 15 to 20 g if the recheck is under 70
options.rationale: Treatment repeats until the glucose is at least 70.

options.text: Review his intake and insulin timing to find the cause
options.rationale: Once he is safe, work out why it happened. He is in the NPH peak.

questions.takeaway: Treat first, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still under 70, then work out why it happened.
questions.strategy: The assessment is already in the stem. Start with treatment and leave the search for a cause until he is above 70.

steps.detail: 56 mg/dL, alert, able to swallow.
No further assessment is needed to act.
Finding the reason does not raise his glucose.

elimination.verdict: Treat, recheck, repeat if needed, then find the cause.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old has sliding scale NovoLog ordered with meals. Her fingerstick at 1100 was 204 mg/dL. Lunch was delayed and the tray is set down at 1235. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Repeat the fingerstick and dose from the new value
options.rationale: The 1100 value is over 90 minutes old. A sliding scale dose is based on the glucose at the time the insulin is given.

options.text: Give the dose listed for the 1100 value now
options.rationale: Tempting because the food is here and the check was done. Her glucose may have changed since 1100, so the dose could be wrong.

options.text: Hold the mealtime dose since the check is outdated
options.rationale: The check is outdated, but the fix is a new check. Holding leaves the meal uncovered.

options.text: Ask the provider for a dose based on the 1100 value
options.rationale: The order already tells the nurse what to give. What is missing is a current value.

questions.takeaway: A sliding scale dose needs a current glucose. If the meal is delayed, repeat the fingerstick when the food arrives and dose from that value.
questions.strategy: Look at the two times in the stem. Ask whether the number still describes the client.

steps.detail: 1100 to 1235 is 95 minutes.

steps.action: Cut the options that use the old value
steps.detail: Dosing from it or calling about it.
Holding skips the meal coverage. A new fingerstick takes a minute.

elimination.verdict: Repeat the fingerstick, then dose.

questions.stem: The nurse gave a 65-year-old Humulin R 8 units at 1130 for a 1200 lunch. At 1200 the kitchen says trays will be 45 minutes late. He is alert with no symptoms. Which action is best?

options.text: Notify the provider that the tray is late
options.rationale: Tempting because a delay that affects the regimen is reported. Calling does not protect him from insulin that is already working.

options.text: Document the delay and check him at 1245
options.rationale: Regular insulin has started working. Waiting until the tray comes leaves him uncovered.

options.text: Give his next dose 45 minutes later
options.rationale: This addresses the next meal, not the insulin already given.

options.text: Check his glucose and get food to him now
options.rationale: Regular insulin starts in 30 to 60 minutes, so he needs food now and a glucose check while intake is delayed.

questions.takeaway: Insulin already given cannot wait for a late tray. Recheck the glucose and bring food to the client.
questions.strategy: The insulin is in. Pick the action that deals with this dose in this client right now.

steps.detail: Given at 1130, regular insulin is active by 1200.
Next dose and a 1245 check do not help now.
Food and a glucose check protect him first. The call can follow.

elimination.verdict: Check his glucose and get food to him now.

questions.stem: A new nurse had a near miss with look-alike insulins last week. Today the order reads Novolin R 4 units before lunch. Which action by the new nurse shows the review was effective?

options.text: Takes the Novolin vial from the client's usual bin
options.rationale: Tempting because the bin is labeled for the client. Location does not confirm which Novolin is in the hand.

options.text: Selects a cloudy Novolin vial and rolls it gently
options.rationale: Rolling is right for NPH. A cloudy vial means this is Novolin N, or a regular vial that should not be used.

options.text: Reads the label for R and confirms the vial is clear
options.rationale: The letter and the appearance are the two checks that separate regular from NPH under one brand name.

options.text: Matches the brand name on the vial to the order
options.rationale: The brand is shared by both insulins. Matching it is how the near miss happened.

questions.takeaway: A shared brand name does not mean a shared insulin. Read the letter and check the appearance: regular is clear, NPH is cloudy.
questions.strategy: Ask which option would catch the wrong vial. Brand and bin location would both let Novolin N through.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Novolin N given for Novolin R.

steps.action: Cut checks that both vials would pass
steps.detail: Brand name and bin location.
Cloudy is not regular insulin.

steps.action: Keep the two checks that differ
steps.detail: The letter R and a clear solution.

elimination.verdict: Reads the label for R and confirms the vial is clear.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old's sliding scale lists regular insulin doses for 151 to 400 mg/dL and gives no instruction above 400. His 1130 fingerstick is 418 mg/dL. He is alert and thirsty. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the dose listed for 351 to 400 mg/dL
options.rationale: Tempting because it is the closest dose on the scale. His value is outside the order, so no listed dose applies.

options.text: Report the value to the provider and get a dose
options.rationale: The order does not cover 418. The nurse assesses him and gets a prescribed dose instead of choosing one.

options.text: Give the top listed dose plus 2 more units
options.rationale: The nurse does not add units without an order.

options.text: Recheck the fingerstick at 1230 before acting
options.rationale: Waiting an hour leaves a high glucose with symptoms untreated and unreported.

questions.takeaway: A sliding scale covers only the values written on it. A glucose outside the scale is reported, and the nurse gives only a prescribed dose.
questions.strategy: Read the order as written. Ask whether it covers this number before you ask which dose is closest.

steps.action: Place the value on the scale
steps.detail: 418 is above the last range.

steps.action: Cut the doses the nurse invents
steps.detail: The top dose and the top dose plus 2 units both lack an order.
He is thirsty and high now.

elimination.verdict: Report the value and get a dose.

questions.stem: At 2100 the nurse prepares insulin glargine for a 75-year-old and sees the solution is cloudy. The client says it looked the same last night and the dose was given. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Discard the vial and obtain a new one for tonight's dose
options.rationale: Glargine is a clear solution. Cloudiness means contamination or degradation, and the basal dose is still due.

options.text: Roll the vial gently and draw up tonight's dose
options.rationale: Tempting because rolling a cloudy vial is correct for NPH. Glargine should never look cloudy.

options.text: Hold tonight's dose and report the vial in the morning
options.rationale: Tempting because it avoids the bad vial. Basal insulin is not skipped, and a new vial solves the problem tonight.

options.text: Draw the dose, since last night's caused no problem
options.rationale: A dose from a degraded vial is unpredictable. One uneventful night does not make it safe.

questions.takeaway: Only NPH and premixes that contain it look cloudy. Glargine is always clear, so a cloudy vial is discarded and replaced.
questions.strategy: Two options reject the vial. Ask which one still gets the client the basal dose.

steps.detail: Glargine is clear.

steps.action: Cut the options that use the vial
steps.detail: Rolling it or drawing from it.

steps.action: Compare the two that reject it
steps.detail: Holding leaves the client without basal insulin. Replacing does not.

elimination.verdict: Discard the vial and get a new one.

questions.scenario: A 64-year-old is going home on Lantus at bedtime and NovoLog with meals. The nurse evaluates his statements after teaching.
questions.stem: For each statement, indicate whether the teaching was understood or needs reinforcement.

rows.text: "I take the NovoLog when my plate is in front of me."
rows.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin starts in 10 to 30 minutes, so it is given with the food.

rows.text: "Lantus has no big peak, so I take it whether or not I eat."
rows.rationale: Lantus is basal insulin with no pronounced peak. It is not matched to meals.

rows.text: "To save a shot, I draw the Lantus and NovoLog in one syringe."
rows.rationale: Lantus is never mixed with other insulins.

rows.text: "If my sugar is 62, I take glucose and check again in 15 minutes."
rows.rationale: Under 70 is treated with fast-acting carbohydrate and rechecked in 15 minutes.

rows.text: "I pull back on the plunger to look for blood before I inject."
rows.rationale: Aspiration is not required for subcutaneous insulin.

questions.takeaway: NovoLog follows food. Lantus does not, and it is never mixed. A low is treated and rechecked in 15 minutes. Subcutaneous insulin is not aspirated.
questions.strategy: Judge each statement alone. Two of them sound careful or efficient and are still wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mealtime insulin follows food. Basal insulin does not.
Long-acting insulin goes in its own syringe.
No aspiration for a subcutaneous injection.

elimination.verdict: Rows 1, 2 and 4 are understood. Rows 3 and 5 need reinforcement.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old jogs after dinner and takes regular insulin before that meal. He has had two evening lows this week after injecting his thigh. Which plan does the nurse suggest for the dinner dose?

options.text: Keep the thigh and inject deeper
options.rationale: Depth is not the issue. The working muscle speeds absorption.

options.text: Use the thigh and massage it before the jog
options.rationale: Massage and exercise both speed absorption, which would add to the lows.

options.text: Inject the abdomen at dinner
options.rationale: The abdomen is not the working limb during a jog, so absorption is not sped by the exercise.

options.text: Skip the dinner dose on jogging days
options.rationale: Tempting because it stops the low. Omitting a prescribed dose is not the nurse's or client's call. The site is the cause.

questions.takeaway: Exercise speeds absorption from the injected limb. Do not inject a limb that is about to work.
questions.strategy: The lows have a pattern in the stem: thigh plus jog. Change the site, not the prescription.

steps.detail: Lows follow thigh injections before a jog.
Massage and a working thigh.
Skipping a dose is not a site fix.

elimination.verdict: Inject the abdomen at dinner.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old had a 0300 glucose of 46 mg/dL followed by a 0700 glucose of 250 mg/dL, so the provider lowered her bedtime NPH. Which result shows the change was effective?

options.text: 0700 glucose 122 mg/dL, no overnight check done
options.rationale: Tempting because the morning value is in range. Without the 0300 value the overnight low could still be there.

options.text: 0300 glucose 58 mg/dL, 0700 glucose 204 mg/dL
options.rationale: Both improved slightly, but she is still low overnight and still rebounding.

options.text: 0300 glucose 52 mg/dL, 0700 glucose 148 mg/dL
options.rationale: The morning value is in range, but the overnight value is still a low.

options.text: 0300 glucose 102 mg/dL, 0700 glucose 136 mg/dL
options.rationale: The overnight low is gone and the morning value is in range, so the rebound has stopped.

questions.takeaway: The problem was the overnight low. The change worked only when the 0300 value is above 70 and the morning value is in range.
questions.strategy: Evaluate the problem that was treated. The dose was lowered to stop a 0300 low, so the 0300 value must be in the answer.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A low at 0300 that rebounded.

steps.action: Cut any option with a 0300 value under 70
steps.detail: 52 and 58 are still lows.

steps.action: Cut the option with no 0300 value
steps.detail: It cannot show the low is gone.

elimination.verdict: 0300 glucose 102 mg/dL, 0700 glucose 136 mg/dL.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old's home list shows Lantus 20 units at bedtime. Tonight's medication record reads Humalog 20 units at bedtime. He ate dinner at 1730. Which action does the nurse take at 2100?

options.text: Give the Humalog with a snack to cover it
options.rationale: Tempting because food makes rapid-acting insulin safer. A snack does not make a questionable order correct.

options.text: Hold the dose and verify the order with the provider
options.rationale: Humalog is rapid acting and given with meals. Twenty units at bedtime that matches his Lantus dose suggests a transcription error, so it is verified first.

options.text: Give the Humalog as written on the record
options.rationale: A large rapid-acting dose with no meal can cause a severe low overnight.

options.text: Give Lantus 20 units, since that matches his home list
options.rationale: Tempting because it is probably what was meant. The nurse does not substitute one insulin for another without an order.

questions.takeaway: Check the insulin type against its usual timing. A rapid-acting insulin ordered at bedtime with no meal is verified before it is given, and the nurse does not substitute.
questions.strategy: Two options give the insulin as written and one swaps it. Ask which option fixes the order itself.

steps.action: Match the insulin to its timing
steps.detail: Humalog follows food. Lantus is the bedtime basal insulin.

steps.action: Cut the options that give Humalog
steps.detail: With or without a snack, the order is still in doubt.
Changing the insulin needs an order.

elimination.verdict: Hold and verify with the provider.

questions.stem: At 0930 a 72-year-old who received regular insulin at 0645 and ate little breakfast snaps at the nurse and refuses his bath. He is awake and answering questions. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Check his fingerstick glucose
options.rationale: New irritability at the peak of regular insulin after a small meal suggests a low. The check takes seconds and directs treatment.

options.text: Give 4 ounces of juice
options.rationale: Tempting because a low is likely. He is awake and stable enough for a quick check. The value has not been measured.

options.text: Return in an hour to offer the bath again
options.rationale: This treats a behavior change in a client on insulin as a mood problem.

options.text: Ask the provider about a sleep aid
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem points to a sleep problem.

questions.takeaway: A behavior change in a client on insulin is a glucose check first, most of all at the insulin's peak with reduced intake.
questions.strategy: No glucose value is in the stem. When the assessment is missing and the client is awake, get the number before you treat.

steps.detail: 0645 to 0930 is inside the 2 to 4 hour peak.
None is given.
A fingerstick is fast and tells you whether juice is needed.

elimination.verdict: Check his fingerstick glucose.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old with type 1 diabetes has a stomach virus and cannot keep food down. Which statement shows the sick day teaching needs to be repeated?

options.text: "I will skip my Levemir until I can eat again."
options.rationale: Basal insulin is not matched to food and is never stopped on sick days. This is the statement that needs correcting.

options.text: "I will hold my Humalog when I cannot eat a meal."
options.rationale: Sounds like skipping insulin, which tempts. Mealtime insulin follows food, so holding it without a meal is correct.

options.text: "I will test for ketones if I stay over 240."
options.rationale: Correct sick day rule.

options.text: "I will check my glucose every four hours tonight."
options.rationale: Correct. Glucose is checked every three to four hours during illness.

questions.takeaway: Rapid acting insulin follows food. Basal insulin does not, and it continues through illness.
questions.strategy: Two statements involve holding insulin. Sort them by which insulin depends on a meal.

steps.detail: You are looking for the wrong statement.
Ketones over 240 and checks every three to four hours are right.
Humalog follows food. Levemir does not.

elimination.verdict: Skipping the Levemir is the error.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old's glucose readings are still erratic two weeks after site teaching. Which report best explains the readings?

options.text: "I stay in my abdomen and use a new spot each time."
options.rationale: Correct rotation within one region. It keeps absorption steady.

options.text: "I pinch the skin and go straight in at 90 degrees."
options.rationale: Correct technique.

options.text: "I rub the spot afterward so it will not bruise."
options.rationale: Massaging the site changes how fast the insulin is absorbed, which makes the readings swing.

options.text: "I skip the bruised spot from last week's injection."
options.rationale: Correct. Bruised tissue is avoided.

questions.takeaway: Do not massage an insulin site. Rubbing changes absorption even when the rotation is correct.
questions.strategy: The rotation sounds fixed. Look for the other habit that changes absorption.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One region, new spot. Correct.
Pinch and 90 degrees. Correct.
Rubbing the site.

elimination.verdict: Rubbing the site explains the swings.

questions.stem: At 1030 the nurse reviews four clients. Which client does the nurse check first?

options.text: Regular insulin at 0715, ate all of breakfast, no symptoms
options.rationale: Tempting because regular insulin is at its peak. A full breakfast and no symptoms make a low less likely.

options.text: Basal insulin at 0800, ate 25% of breakfast, no symptoms
options.rationale: Tempting because of the poor intake. Basal insulin has no pronounced peak and is not matched to meals.

options.text: Rapid-acting insulin with breakfast, glucose 226 mg/dL, reports thirst
options.rationale: A high with thirst is assessed next, after a possible low.

options.text: Regular insulin at 0730, ate half of breakfast, asks for a snack
options.rationale: Regular insulin peaks 2 to 4 hours after the dose, so he is at the peak with reduced intake. Hunger is an early sign of a low.

questions.takeaway: Reduced intake at the insulin's peak is the setup for a low. Hunger is a warning sign, so check the glucose before treating it as a food request.
questions.strategy: Each client has a risk on paper. Find the one with a peak, reduced intake and a symptom together.

steps.detail: A high with thirst follows a possible low.

steps.action: Cut the insulin with no peak
steps.detail: Basal insulin is not matched to meals.

steps.action: Compare the two regular insulin clients
steps.detail: Both are at the peak. One ate fully and has no symptoms. One ate half and is hungry.

elimination.verdict: The client on regular insulin who ate half and asks for a snack.

questions.stem: A client on bedtime NPH has a 0200 glucose of 128 mg/dL and a 0700 glucose of 234 mg/dL. A coworker suggests asking the provider to lower the bedtime NPH. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Agree and request a lower bedtime NPH dose
options.rationale: Tempting because a lower dose fixes a rebound high. A rebound needs an overnight low, and 128 is not low.

options.text: Report both values and that no overnight low occurred
options.rationale: The glucose rose without a low, which is the dawn pattern. The provider needs both values to choose the change.

options.text: Ask for another 0200 check before reporting anything
options.rationale: The overnight value is already in hand. Repeating it delays the report.

options.text: Give a bedtime snack tonight and recheck at 0700
options.rationale: A snack treats an overnight low that did not happen and would raise the morning value.

questions.takeaway: Somogyi is an overnight low that rebounds to a morning high. Dawn rises without a low. The overnight value tells them apart.
questions.strategy: Decide what the 0200 number rules out before you choose what to ask for.

steps.detail: 128 is not a low.
A rise without a low is dawn, so lowering the dose does not fit.
The needed assessment is already done.

elimination.verdict: Report both values. There was no overnight low.

questions.stem: At 1100 a client with a glucose of 262 mg/dL received correction insulin. At 1300 his glucose is 66 mg/dL. He feels fine and says, "Finally, it is down." Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: 66 is under 70, so it is treated now even without symptoms. The correction went too far.

options.text: Document the result as an effective treatment
options.rationale: Tempting because the number fell and he feels well. Effective means 70 to 180, and lower is not better.

options.text: Recheck the glucose in 15 minutes before acting
options.rationale: Tempting because a recheck is part of the rule. The recheck comes after the carbohydrate.

options.text: Hold his next mealtime insulin and notify the provider
options.rationale: Reporting the low is reasonable later. It does not raise his glucose now.

questions.takeaway: Effective glucose treatment lands between 70 and 180 mg/dL. Under 70 is treated first, with or without symptoms.
questions.strategy: The number moved the right way. Check where it stopped.

steps.detail: 66 is below the 70 line.
No symptoms does not cancel the rule.
Treat, then recheck, then report.

elimination.verdict: Treat the low with fast-acting carbohydrate.

questions.stem: After teaching, a 54-year-old stopped injecting into a firm raised area on her abdomen. On unchanged doses her prelunch readings fell from the 230s to the low 70s within a week. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Report the trend so the doses can be reviewed
options.rationale: Insulin absorbs better from healthy tissue, so the same dose now does more. Readings heading toward 70 mean the dose needs review before a low happens.

options.text: Advise going back to the old site for now
options.rationale: The thickened tissue absorbs poorly and unpredictably. It was the cause of the high readings.

options.text: Praise the change and continue the same plan
options.rationale: Tempting because the teaching clearly worked. The plan was built on poor absorption and the trend is still falling.

options.text: Suggest a larger breakfast to offset the insulin
options.rationale: Adjusting food to chase a dose is not the nurse's fix. The dose itself needs review.

questions.takeaway: Thickened injection sites absorb insulin poorly. When a client moves to healthy tissue the same dose works harder, so watch for lows and have the dose reviewed.
questions.strategy: The teaching worked. The question is what the falling numbers mean for a dose that has not changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: From the 230s to the low 70s on the same dose.
The lump caused the problem.
The trend is one step from a low, so someone must review the dose.

elimination.verdict: Report the trend for a dose review.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old on insulin is found unresponsive with a fingerstick glucose of 41 mg/dL. A saline lock is in place. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Squeeze glucose gel inside the cheek
options.rationale: Tempting because it is fast and at hand. An unresponsive client cannot protect the airway, so nothing goes in the mouth.

options.text: Give IV dextrose per the hypoglycemia protocol
options.rationale: Oral treatment is for a client who is alert and can swallow. With IV access in place, dextrose treats the low without an aspiration risk.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and offer juice
options.rationale: Positioning does not make swallowing safe in a client who does not respond.

options.text: Repeat the fingerstick on the other hand
options.rationale: The value fits the client. Repeating it delays treatment.

questions.takeaway: The rule of 15 by mouth is for a client who is alert and can swallow. An unresponsive client gets a route that does not involve the mouth.
questions.strategy: Two options treat the low. The word "unresponsive" decides the route.

steps.detail: An unresponsive client cannot swallow safely.
Gel and juice share the same flaw.
A reading of 41 in an unresponsive client fits.

elimination.verdict: IV dextrose per protocol.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old has NovoLog 4 units scheduled with meals plus a correction scale that starts at 150 mg/dL. Her prelunch glucose is 139 mg/dL and her tray has arrived. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Hold all insulin because the glucose is in range
options.rationale: Tempting because 139 looks fine. The scheduled dose covers the meal she is about to eat, not the current number.

options.text: Give 4 units plus the lowest correction dose
options.rationale: The scale does not start until 150, so no correction is ordered for 139.

options.text: Wait and recheck the glucose after she eats
options.rationale: Rapid acting insulin is given as the food arrives. A reading after the meal cannot be used for a premeal order.

options.text: Give the scheduled 4 units with no correction
options.rationale: The mealtime dose covers the food. The correction dose is added only when the glucose reaches the scale.

questions.takeaway: Scheduled mealtime insulin and correction insulin are two separate orders. A glucose below the scale cancels the correction, not the meal dose.
questions.strategy: Read the order as two parts and answer each part separately.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The tray has arrived, so the scheduled dose is due.
139 is under 150, so no correction.

steps.action: Cut the all or nothing options
steps.detail: Holding everything and adding a correction both ignore one part.

elimination.verdict: Give the scheduled 4 units with no correction.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old on insulin is alert and shaky with a glucose of 60 mg/dL. Lunch is due in 20 minutes. Which does the nurse give?

options.text: Half a cup of regular apple juice
options.rationale: About 15 g of simple sugar with nothing to slow it, so the glucose rises within minutes.

options.text: Peanut butter on whole grain crackers
options.rationale: Tempting because it has carbohydrate and staying power. Fat and protein slow absorption, so it suits the follow up, not the first treatment.

options.text: A small bar of milk chocolate
options.rationale: The fat in chocolate slows the sugar.

options.text: The lunch tray as soon as it arrives
options.rationale: A glucose under 70 with symptoms is treated now, not in 20 minutes.

questions.takeaway: Fast-acting means simple sugar without fat or protein: juice, regular soda or glucose tablets. Fat slows the rise.
questions.strategy: All four contain carbohydrate. Ask which one reaches the blood fastest.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Twenty minutes is too long for a symptomatic low.
Peanut butter and chocolate both carry it.
Juice has nothing to slow it.

elimination.verdict: Half a cup of regular juice.

questions.stem: At 0740 four insulin doses are coming due on the unit. Which dose does the nurse give first?

options.text: Lantus due at 0800 for a client still asleep
options.rationale: Basal insulin is not matched to food, so a few minutes do not matter.

options.text: Novolin R for a client whose tray comes at 0830
options.rationale: Regular insulin goes about 30 minutes before the meal, so this one is due at 0800.

options.text: Humalog for a client whose tray comes at 0815
options.rationale: Rapid acting insulin waits for the food. Given now, it would act before she eats.

options.text: Humalog for a client whose tray was just set down
options.rationale: Rapid acting insulin is given as the meal arrives. Her food is here, so the dose is due this minute.

questions.takeaway: Insulin timing follows the food: rapid acting as the tray arrives, regular about 30 minutes before, basal on the clock.
questions.strategy: For each dose, find the tray. Only one client has food in front of her.

steps.detail: Lantus does not depend on a meal.
Thirty minutes before 0830 is 0800.
Same insulin; only one tray has arrived.

elimination.verdict: Humalog for the client whose tray is here.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old who tests four times a day has sore, calloused finger pads. After teaching, which statement shows it was effective?

options.text: "I skip the bedtime test to rest my fingers."
options.rationale: Dropping a check hides a reading the insulin plan depends on.

options.text: "I use the sides and switch fingers each time."
options.rationale: The sides of the fingertips have fewer nerve endings, and rotating fingers lets each site heal.

options.text: "I keep to one finger so the others can heal up."
options.rationale: Tempting because it spares most fingers. Repeated sticks in one place are what build the callus and soreness.

options.text: "I squeeze the tip hard to get a bigger drop."
options.rationale: Squeezing hurts more and can alter the reading.

questions.takeaway: Puncture the side of the fingertip and rotate fingers. It hurts less and keeps the skin intact for the next check.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that keeps every scheduled test and spreads the punctures out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Skipping a test is not a comfort measure.
It adds pain and can spoil the result.
One finger concentrates the damage. Sides and rotation spread it.

elimination.verdict: Sides of the fingertips, a different finger each time.

questions.stem: The nurse asked an assistive personnel to report any fingerstick under 70 mg/dL at once. Which action by the assistive personnel shows the direction was understood?

options.text: Gives juice for a reading of 63, then tells the nurse
options.rationale: Tempting because the low gets treated. Deciding on treatment belongs to the nurse, who must assess the client first.

options.text: Charts a reading of 63 and reports it after rounds
options.rationale: A low reported late is a low left untreated.

options.text: Uses the call light to report a reading of 63 now
options.rationale: The value reaches the nurse at once and the assistive personnel stays with the client.

options.text: Repeats a reading of 63 twice before telling the nurse
options.rationale: Extra checks delay the report the nurse asked for.

questions.takeaway: An assistive personnel can obtain the fingerstick. The nurse assesses and decides treatment, so a low value is reported immediately.
questions.strategy: The direction had two parts: under 70, and at once. Find the action that meets both without adding anything.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Charting first and repeating first both slow the report.
Giving juice is a treatment decision.
Call light, now, staying with the client.

elimination.verdict: Reports the 63 right away by call light.

questions.stem: At 1100 a 77-year-old who received regular insulin at 0700, before breakfast, has a glucose of 57 mg/dL. After treating him, the nurse reviews the morning. Which findings could explain the low? Select all that apply.

options.text: He left most of his breakfast on the tray
options.rationale: The dose was sized for a full meal that he did not eat.

options.text: He walked the hall for 30 minutes at 0930
options.rationale: Exercise uses glucose, and 0930 is 2.5 hours after the dose, inside the 2 to 4 hour peak.

options.text: The dose was injected into his abdomen
options.rationale: The abdomen is a standard site with steady absorption. It does not explain a low.

options.text: The dose was given 30 minutes before the tray came
options.rationale: That is the correct timing for regular insulin.

options.text: He has had a low grade fever since 0600
options.rationale: Illness tends to raise glucose, not lower it.

options.text: The syringe was drawn 2 units past the ordered mark
options.rationale: More insulin than ordered lowers the glucose further.

questions.takeaway: After a low, work out why: less food, more activity or too much insulin, most of all at the peak of the insulin.
questions.strategy: For each finding ask one question: does this add insulin effect or remove glucose? If neither, leave it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Less eaten than the dose was meant for.
A walk that fell inside the peak of regular insulin.
Two extra units.
A usual site, correct timing and fever do not cause a low.

elimination.verdict: Poor intake, the walk and the overdrawn dose.
