questions.stem: A 51-year-old has a fingerstick glucose due before lunch. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Verify the client's identity with two identifiers
options.rationale: First. The result and any insulin that follows must belong to the right client.

options.text: Check the strip date and have the client wash and dry hands
options.rationale: Supplies and skin are made ready before the puncture so the reading can be trusted.

options.text: Hold the hand below the heart and puncture the fingertip
options.rationale: Lowering the hand improves blood flow so one puncture gives an adequate drop.

options.text: Touch the drop to the strip without squeezing the finger
options.rationale: Squeezing can alter the sample.

options.text: Compare the result with the client and the insulin order
options.rationale: Last. The number is judged against how the client looks and what is ordered.

questions.takeaway: Fingerstick: right client, valid strip, clean dry finger, hand lowered, no squeezing, then interpret the number against the client and the order.
questions.strategy: Anchor the ends first. Identity opens the sequence and interpreting the result closes it.

steps.detail: Nothing is done to an unverified client.
Strip date and clean dry hands.
Hand lowered, no squeezing, then read it against the client.

elimination.verdict: Identify, prepare, puncture, sample, interpret.

questions.scenario: A 29-year-old with type 1 diabetes missed two days of insulin. Her fingerstick glucose is 436 mg/dL. She is drowsy and very thirsty, with dry mucous membranes, deep rapid breathing and abdominal pain.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Test for ketones
options.rationale: High glucose with deep rapid breathing and abdominal pain means ketones are likely, and the result guides treatment.

options.text: Give the prescribed insulin and IV fluids
options.rationale: She lacks insulin and is dry. Both are replaced together.

options.text: Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: That treats a low. Her drowsiness comes from a very high glucose.

options.text: Encourage a walk to bring the glucose down
options.rationale: Her signs point to ketones, and exercise with ketones makes the ketosis worse.

options.text: Hyperglycemia with ketoacidosis
options.rationale: No insulin for two days, a glucose of 436, deep rapid breathing and abdominal pain.

options.text: Hypoglycemia
options.rationale: A low gives sweating and shakiness with a low reading.

options.text: Dawn phenomenon
options.rationale: That is a mild early morning rise in a client who is taking insulin.

options.text: Rebound after a night time low
options.rationale: A rebound follows a low in a client who is taking insulin. She has had no insulin for two days.

options.text: Glucose at the prescribed intervals
options.rationale: Shows the insulin is working and catches a fall that is too fast or too far.

options.text: Level of consciousness and breathing pattern
options.rationale: Drowsiness and deep rapid breathing should ease as the acidosis clears.

options.text: Injection site for bruising
options.rationale: Not the concern in this emergency.

options.text: Appetite at the next meal
options.rationale: Intake matters later, once she is stable.

questions.takeaway: Very high glucose with deep rapid breathing and abdominal pain is ketoacidosis. Check ketones, replace insulin and fluid, and watch the glucose and the brain.
questions.strategy: Drowsiness can come with a high or a low. The number, the dryness and the breathing pattern say which.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 436 mg/dL with dry membranes is high.
Carbohydrate does not belong.
Glucose and mental status.

elimination.verdict: Ketones and insulin with fluids, ketoacidosis, glucose and level of consciousness.

questions.scenario: At 1130 a 59-year-old had a glucose of 318 mg/dL with thirst and frequent urination. The nurse gave the prescribed correction dose of rapid-acting insulin and he ate lunch.
questions.stem: For each finding at 1400, indicate whether it shows the expected response or requires follow up.

rows.text: Glucose is 182 mg/dL
rows.rationale: The glucose has come down and is nowhere near low.

rows.text: Glucose is 326 mg/dL
rows.rationale: No change after the dose. Recheck the technique and the order, and report it.

rows.text: He is sweating and his hands shake
rows.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin is at its peak. Check the glucose now.

rows.text: He reports less thirst and has not voided since noon
rows.rationale: Less glucose is spilling into the urine, so the water loss has slowed.

rows.text: Glucose is 244 mg/dL and he says the thirst is easing
rows.rationale: The value is falling and the symptoms are easing. Rapid-acting insulin is still working, so the nurse keeps monitoring.

questions.takeaway: A correction dose has worked when the glucose falls toward range and the symptoms ease. No change and an overshoot both need action.
questions.strategy: There are two ways to miss: the number did not move, or it moved too far. Anything else is the goal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sweating and shaking hands at the peak of the dose.
326 mg/dL.
182 and 244 mg/dL are both lower than 318 and neither is low.

elimination.verdict: Expected, follow up, follow up, expected, expected.

questions.stem: The nurse must give regular insulin 8 units. The supply drawer has no insulin syringes, only 1 mL tuberculin syringes. The client's tray arrives in 30 minutes. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Draw 0.8 mL in the tuberculin syringe
options.rationale: A tenfold overdose. That volume holds 80 units of U-100 insulin.

options.text: Get an insulin syringe from another unit or pharmacy
options.rationale: Insulin is measured in units on a syringe marked in units. A short delay is safer than converting.

options.text: Draw 0.08 mL in the tuberculin syringe
options.rationale: The arithmetic is right. Measuring units in a syringe marked in mL is the error that causes insulin overdoses.

options.text: Hold the dose and chart that supplies were unavailable
options.rationale: An omitted dose leaves the meal uncovered when the right syringe can be found.

questions.takeaway: Insulin is drawn up only in an insulin syringe marked in units. Never convert a dose to mL at the bedside.
questions.strategy: Two options convert the dose and one skips it. Only one keeps both the dose and the safeguard.

steps.detail: Either volume relies on a decimal point.
The dose is still due.
Use the right syringe.

elimination.verdict: Get an insulin syringe.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old on insulin is found unresponsive with a fingerstick glucose of 38 mg/dL. She has no IV access. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Pour apple juice slowly into her mouth
options.rationale: She cannot protect her airway, so anything by mouth can be aspirated.

options.text: Place glucose gel inside her cheek and wait
options.rationale: Still an oral route in a client who cannot swallow.

options.text: Start an IV line first, then give dextrose by that route
options.rationale: Access may take several attempts while her brain goes without glucose.

options.text: Give glucagon by injection and turn her on her side
options.rationale: It works without a vein or a swallow, and vomiting is common afterward, so she is positioned to protect the airway.

questions.takeaway: Unresponsive and low: nothing by mouth. With no IV, give glucagon by injection and position on the side.
questions.strategy: First rule out every option that needs her to swallow. Then choose the fastest route that remains.

steps.detail: Juice and gel both risk aspiration.
An IV start delays treatment.
Side lying after glucagon.

elimination.verdict: Glucagon and side lying.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old takes glargine at bedtime and aspart with meals. For 4 days the fasting readings were 196 to 214 mg/dL with no night time lows, and readings after meals were at goal. What does the nurse conclude?

options.text: The aspart doses are too small for the meals he eats
options.rationale: Readings after meals are at goal, so the mealtime insulin is doing its job.

options.text: The glargine dose is not covering him overnight
options.rationale: The fasting value reflects basal insulin, and it is the only reading out of range.

options.text: He is rebounding from lows during the night
options.rationale: No lows were found overnight, so there is nothing to rebound from.

options.text: The fasting readings are inaccurate
options.rationale: Four days of consistent values is a pattern, not an error.

questions.takeaway: Fasting glucose reflects the long-acting insulin. Glucose after meals reflects the rapid-acting insulin.
questions.strategy: Match each reading to the insulin working at that hour. Only one insulin is active before breakfast.

steps.action: Find the out of range reading
steps.detail: Fasting only.
Glargine overnight.

steps.action: Use the stem to rule out rebound
steps.detail: No night time lows.

elimination.verdict: The basal dose needs review.

questions.stem: The nurse watches an assistive personnel do morning fingersticks. Which action requires the nurse to step in?

options.text: Carries the meter from one room to the next without wiping it
options.rationale: A shared meter carries blood between clients. It is disinfected after every use.

options.text: Puts on new gloves in each client's room
options.rationale: Correct practice.

options.text: Drops each used lancet straight into the sharps container
options.rationale: Correct practice.

options.text: Checks each client's name band before the puncture
options.rationale: Correct practice.

questions.takeaway: A glucose meter used on more than one client is cleaned and disinfected between clients. Lancets are single use.
questions.strategy: This asks for the unsafe action. Three of the four are steps you want to see.

steps.detail: Look for the error.
Gloves, sharps, identification.
Blood on a shared meter.

elimination.verdict: The meter that is not wiped.

questions.stem: At 1100 the nurse has four tasks waiting. Which one does the nurse give to an experienced assistive personnel?

options.text: Decide whether a client at 148 mg/dL needs correction insulin
options.rationale: Interpreting a value against an order is nursing judgment.

options.text: Show a new client how to rotate injection sites
options.rationale: Teaching stays with the nurse.

options.text: Recheck a client who was treated for a low 15 minutes ago
options.rationale: This client is not yet stable, and the recheck is an evaluation of treatment.

options.text: Obtain the prelunch fingerstick on a stable client
options.rationale: A routine procedure with a predictable result on a stable client, reported back to the nurse.

questions.takeaway: Delegate the routine fingerstick on a stable client. Keep assessment, teaching, evaluation and the unstable client.
questions.strategy: Screen each task for judgment, teaching or instability. The one with none of those can be delegated.

steps.detail: The correction decision.
Site rotation.
The recent low.

elimination.verdict: The routine prelunch fingerstick.

questions.stem: The nurse draws up regular insulin 6 units and sees a large air bubble in the barrel with the plunger at the 6 unit line. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Give the dose, since a little air under the skin is harmless
options.rationale: The air is harmless. The problem is that it takes the place of insulin, so the dose is short.

options.text: Add 1 more unit to make up for the bubble
options.rationale: Guessing at the lost volume makes the dose inaccurate.

options.text: Tap the bubble out, then correct the dose to 6 units
options.rationale: Removing the air and redrawing to the line gives the exact dose.

options.text: Discard the vial and open a new one
options.rationale: The vial is not the problem.

questions.takeaway: An air bubble in an insulin syringe means less insulin than the line shows. Clear it and recheck the dose.
questions.strategy: Ask what the bubble changes. It changes the amount of drug, so the fix must restore the exact amount.

steps.detail: Underdose, not air injury.
Adding a unit is a guess.
Expel air, redraw to 6.

elimination.verdict: Tap out the air and redraw.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old's readings rose from the 140s to the 260s over 5 days on unchanged doses, meals and sites. Which report best explains the rise?

options.text: "I leave the vial on the dashboard between visits to my daughter."
options.rationale: Heat breaks insulin down, so each dose delivers less effect.

options.text: "I keep the vial I am using in the refrigerator door."
options.rationale: Proper storage.

options.text: "I opened this vial about 2 weeks ago."
options.rationale: Within the usual use period after opening.

options.text: "I let the dose warm in my hand before I inject."
options.rationale: Comfort measure that does not weaken the insulin.

questions.takeaway: Insulin exposed to heat or freezing loses strength. When doses and habits are unchanged and glucose rises, check storage.
questions.strategy: Doses, food and sites are ruled out by the stem. Look for the habit that damages the drug itself.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Use what the stem rules out
steps.detail: Dose, meals and sites.
Refrigerator, 2 weeks open and hand warming are fine.
Heat in a car.

elimination.verdict: The dashboard.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old on sliding scale insulin with a prelunch glucose of 296 mg/dL says she will skip lunch to bring it down. After teaching, which statement shows she understood?

options.text: "I will skip lunch and still take my usual insulin."
options.rationale: Mealtime insulin without the meal sets up a low.

options.text: "I will skip both lunch and insulin, then recheck at dinner."
options.rationale: With no insulin the glucose stays high through the afternoon.

options.text: "I will drink juice in place of lunch so I do not go low."
options.rationale: Juice raises a glucose that is already high.

options.text: "I will eat lunch and take the insulin my scale calls for."
options.rationale: Insulin lowers a high glucose. Regular meals with the ordered dose keep it steady.

questions.takeaway: A high reading is treated with the ordered insulin, not by skipping a meal. Skipping meals leads to swings.
questions.strategy: Find the statement that keeps food and insulin together. The others separate them or add sugar.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Insulin alone and food alone both fail.
Juice at 296 mg/dL.
Meal plus the scale dose.

elimination.verdict: Eat and dose by the scale.

questions.stem: At 1700 a student has glargine 16 units and aspart 5 units to give, and plans to draw both into one syringe to spare the client a second injection. What does the nurse tell the student?

options.text: Draw the aspart first, then the glargine
options.rationale: That order is for mixing a short-acting insulin with NPH. Glargine is not mixed at all.

options.text: Draw the glargine first, then the aspart
options.rationale: Order does not matter because the two cannot share a syringe.

options.text: Use two syringes and two separate sites
options.rationale: Glargine cannot be mixed with any other insulin, since mixing changes how it is absorbed.

options.text: Give the aspart now and hold the glargine until 2100
options.rationale: The glargine is due now. The fix is a second syringe, not a new time.

questions.takeaway: Long-acting insulin is never mixed in a syringe with another insulin. Two insulins, two syringes, two sites.
questions.strategy: Two options argue about drawing order. If the mix itself is wrong, both go.

steps.detail: The shared error is one syringe.
The dose is due.
Two injections.

elimination.verdict: Two syringes, two sites.

questions.stem: A client's regular insulin scale reads: 151 to 200 mg/dL, 2 units; 201 to 250, 4 units; 251 to 300, 6 units; 301 to 350, 8 units. The premeal fingerstick is 250 mg/dL. Which dose does the nurse prepare?

options.text: 2 units
options.rationale: This is the dose for 151 to 200 mg/dL, one row too low.

options.text: 4 units
options.rationale: 250 mg/dL is the top value of the 201 to 250 row, so the dose is 4 units.

options.text: 5 units
options.rationale: Splitting the difference between two rows is not on the order. The nurse gives only a dose the scale lists.

options.text: 6 units
options.rationale: This is the dose for 251 to 300 mg/dL. 250 has not reached that row.

questions.takeaway: Read a sliding scale by the row that contains the exact value. A boundary number belongs to the row that lists it, and the nurse never averages rows.
questions.strategy: The value sits on the edge of a row. Find the row that prints the number 250.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 250 is printed in the 201 to 250 row.
5 units is not on the scale.

elimination.verdict: 4 units.

questions.stem: The nurse checks four syringes that a student has prepared for 0730 doses. Which syringe does the nurse have the student discard?

options.text: Novolin R 6 units alone, clear solution
options.rationale: Regular insulin is clear and may be given alone.

options.text: Humulin R 4 units drawn first, then Humulin N to 16 units
options.rationale: Correct mixing. Regular is drawn before NPH and the second insulin is drawn to the total.

options.text: Humalog 5 units alone, clear solution
options.rationale: Rapid acting insulin is clear and may be given alone.

options.text: Levemir 12 units with Novolin R 4 units in one syringe
options.rationale: Levemir is detemir, a long-acting insulin. Long-acting insulin is never mixed in a syringe with another insulin, so this syringe is discarded and two are prepared.

questions.takeaway: Regular and NPH may share a syringe, regular drawn first. Long-acting insulin (Lantus, Levemir) is never mixed with any other insulin.
questions.strategy: Two syringes hold a mix. One mix is a prescribed practice and one is never allowed.

steps.detail: A clear vial of regular or rapid acting insulin given alone is fine.
Regular with NPH is allowed. Long-acting with anything is not.

elimination.verdict: The Levemir and Novolin R syringe.

questions.stem: A client received Novolin R 8 units at 1200 and ate lunch. At 1300 the client is made NPO for a late procedure. Through what time does the nurse plan glucose checks for this dose?

options.text: Through 1400
options.rationale: Two hours after the dose is only the start of the 2 to 4 hour peak.

options.text: Through 1600
options.rationale: This is the end of the peak. Regular insulin keeps working after its peak, for 5 to 8 hours in all.

options.text: Through 2000
options.rationale: Regular insulin lasts 5 to 8 hours. A 1200 dose can act until 2000, and with no food coming the nurse covers the whole duration.

options.text: Through 1200 the next day
options.rationale: A 24 hour duration belongs to long-acting insulin, not regular.

questions.takeaway: Regular insulin: onset 30 to 60 minutes, peak 2 to 4 hours, duration 5 to 8 hours. With no food coming, monitor for the whole duration, not only the peak.
questions.strategy: The question asks how long the dose lasts, not when it peaks. Add the longest duration to the dose time.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The peak ends at 1600. The dose does not.
1200 plus 8 hours is 2000.

elimination.verdict: Through 2000.

questions.stem: At 0730 a new nurse explains the insulin plan for four clients whose breakfast trays come at 0800. Which statement needs correction?

options.text: "The Humulin N I give now will cover this breakfast."
options.rationale: NPH has an onset of 1 to 2 hours and peaks at 4 to 12 hours. It will not be working at 0800, so it does not cover this meal.

options.text: "The Novolin R I give now will be working when the tray comes."
options.rationale: Correct. Regular insulin starts in 30 to 60 minutes and is given about 30 minutes before the meal.

options.text: "The NovoLog waits until the tray is in front of the client."
options.rationale: Correct. Rapid acting insulin starts in 10 to 30 minutes and is given with the food.

options.text: "The Lantus is not timed to the tray."
options.rationale: Correct. Long-acting basal insulin has no pronounced peak and is not matched to meals.

questions.takeaway: NPH: onset 1 to 2 hours, peak 4 to 12 hours, duration 14 to 24 hours. It covers the hours after a meal, not the meal that comes 30 minutes after the dose.
questions.strategy: Put each insulin's onset next to the 30 minutes before the tray. One of them has not started by then.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rapid 10 to 30 minutes, regular 30 to 60 minutes, NPH 1 to 2 hours, long-acting no peak.
NPH has not started at 0800.

elimination.verdict: The Humulin N statement.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old on insulin is alert, swallowing safely and shaky with a fingerstick of 62 mg/dL. The only fast-acting carbohydrate at hand is glucose tablets labeled 4 g each. How many tablets does the nurse give?

options.text: 1 tablet
options.rationale: 4 g is far below the 15 to 20 g needed to raise the glucose.

options.text: 2 tablets
options.rationale: 8 g is about half the amount.

options.text: 10 tablets
options.rationale: 40 g is double the top of the range and pushes the glucose too high.

options.text: 4 tablets
options.rationale: 4 tablets give 16 g, inside the 15 to 20 g range for a glucose under 70 in a client who can swallow.

questions.takeaway: A glucose under 70 mg/dL in an alert client who can swallow gets 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate. Count the grams on the label, then recheck in 15 minutes.
questions.strategy: Turn each option into grams and hold it against 15 to 20 g.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only 16 g falls between 15 and 20 g.

elimination.verdict: 4 tablets, 16 g.

questions.stem: A student gives a 55-year-old's subcutaneous insulin in the abdomen while the nurse observes. Which action by the student needs correction?

options.text: Pinches up a fold of skin before inserting the needle
options.rationale: Correct. The pinch lifts the subcutaneous tissue.

options.text: Slides the needle in at 15 degrees, just under the skin surface
options.rationale: Insulin is given with the skin pinched and the needle inserted at 90 degrees. A 15 degree angle places the dose in the skin, not in the subcutaneous tissue.

options.text: Injects the dose slowly without pulling back on the plunger
options.rationale: Correct. Subcutaneous insulin is injected slowly and is not aspirated.

options.text: Holds the needle in briefly, then withdraws at the same angle
options.rationale: Correct. This lets the full dose stay in the tissue.

questions.takeaway: Subcutaneous insulin: pinch, insert at 90 degrees, do not aspirate, inject slowly, hold briefly, withdraw at the same angle.
questions.strategy: Walk through the injection in order and stop at the step that does not match the taught angle.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pinch, slow injection without aspiration and a brief hold are all taught.
90 degrees is taught. 15 degrees is not.

elimination.verdict: The 15 degree insertion.

questions.stem: A client's premeal regular insulin has been given in the buttock and is acting too slowly to cover meals. The provider asks for the site with the fastest absorption. Which site does the nurse use?

options.text: Abdomen
options.rationale: Absorption is fastest from the abdomen, then the arm, then the thigh, then the buttock.

options.text: Back of the upper arm
options.rationale: Faster than the buttock but second to the abdomen.

options.text: Front of the thigh
options.rationale: Third in the order, only one step faster than the site that is failing.

options.text: The opposite buttock
options.rationale: The same region absorbs at the same slow rate.

questions.takeaway: Absorption by site, fastest to slowest: abdomen, arm, thigh, buttock. Choose one region and rotate within it.
questions.strategy: Recite the order from fastest to slowest and take the first one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The other buttock changes nothing.
Abdomen, then arm, then thigh.

elimination.verdict: Abdomen.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews new insulin prescriptions for four clients who are eating normally. Which prescription does the nurse question?

options.text: NovoLog 4 units with each meal
options.rationale: Correct. Rapid acting insulin is given with meals.

options.text: Humulin R 6 units 30 minutes before breakfast
options.rationale: Correct. Regular insulin is given about 30 minutes before the meal.

options.text: Lantus 14 units with each meal, three times daily
options.rationale: Lantus is a long-acting basal insulin that lasts 20 to 24 hours and is not timed to food. Three doses a day with meals reads like a mealtime insulin order written for the wrong drug, so it is verified.

options.text: Humulin N 18 units once every morning
options.rationale: A usual NPH schedule. It lasts 14 to 24 hours.

questions.takeaway: Check the insulin type against its usual timing. Long-acting insulin lasts 20 to 24 hours and is given on the clock, not with each meal.
questions.strategy: Put each drug's duration next to how often it is ordered. One order repeats a 24 hour insulin three times a day.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: NovoLog with meals and regular 30 minutes before are correct.
NPH once a morning fits. Lantus three times a day with meals does not.

elimination.verdict: Lantus with each meal.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old with type 1 diabetes has a fever and nausea at home and is taking her insulin and sipping fluids. Which monitoring plan does the nurse teach?

options.text: Glucose every 3 to 4 hours; ketones if it stays over 240 mg/dL
options.rationale: This is the sick day schedule: glucose every 3 to 4 hours and a ketone test when the glucose stays over 240.

options.text: Glucose every 3 to 4 hours; ketones if it stays over 400 mg/dL
options.rationale: Right glucose interval. Waiting for 400 lets ketoacidosis develop before anyone tests for it.

options.text: Glucose every 8 hours; ketones if it stays over 240 mg/dL
options.rationale: Right ketone threshold. Eight hours between checks is too long during illness.

options.text: Glucose before meals only; ketones if it stays over 240 mg/dL
options.rationale: She is nauseated and may not eat meals, so checks tied to meals leave long gaps.

questions.takeaway: Sick day monitoring: glucose every 3 to 4 hours, ketones when the glucose stays over 240 mg/dL, insulin and fluids continued.
questions.strategy: Each option pairs an interval with a ketone threshold. Both halves must be right.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Every 3 to 4 hours, not every 8 hours or only at meals.

elimination.verdict: Every 3 to 4 hours, ketones over 240.

questions.stem: At 0910 a new nurse gives 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate to an alert client with a fingerstick of 61 mg/dL. Which part of the new nurse's plan needs correction?

options.text: Give another 15 to 20 g if the next value is under 70
options.rationale: Correct. Treatment repeats until the glucose is at least 70.

options.text: Review the client's intake and insulin timing once stable
options.rationale: Correct. The cause is worked out after the client is safe.

options.text: Recheck the fingerstick at 1010
options.rationale: The recheck is due 15 minutes after treatment, at 0925. An hour leaves a low that may not have resolved unmeasured.

options.text: Hold the mealtime insulin until the glucose is at least 70
options.rationale: Correct. Insulin is not given to a client whose glucose is low.

questions.takeaway: After treating a low, recheck in 15 minutes and treat again if still under 70 mg/dL.
questions.strategy: Find the clock time in the plan and count the minutes from the treatment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0910 to 1010 is 60 minutes.
The recheck interval is 15 minutes, so 0925.

elimination.verdict: The 1010 recheck.

questions.stem: A client has NovoLog 5 units with each meal plus a NovoLog correction scale: 151 to 200 mg/dL, 2 units; 201 to 250, 4 units. The tray is here and the fingerstick is 236. Which dose does the nurse give?

options.text: 4 units
options.rationale: This is the correction alone. The scheduled dose that covers the meal is left out.

options.text: 5 units
options.rationale: This is the scheduled dose alone. The glucose is on the scale, so the correction is also due.

options.text: 7 units
options.rationale: This adds the correction for 151 to 200. A value of 236 is in the next row.

options.text: 9 units
options.rationale: The scheduled 5 units cover the meal and the 4 units from the 201 to 250 row correct the glucose. Both are the same insulin and both are due now.

questions.takeaway: Scheduled mealtime insulin and correction insulin are two orders. When the glucose is on the scale and the meal is present, give both: here 5 plus 4 is 9 units.
questions.strategy: Work the two orders one at a time, then add.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 5 units, because the tray is here.
236 sits in the 201 to 250 row: 4 units.
9 units.

elimination.verdict: 9 units.

questions.stem: The nurse double checks four insulin doses that a student has drawn up from U-100 vials. Which dose requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Regular insulin 5 units drawn to the 0.5 mL line of a tuberculin syringe
options.rationale: Insulin is drawn only in an insulin syringe marked in units. 0.5 mL of U-100 insulin holds 50 units, ten times the dose.

options.text: Regular insulin 5 units drawn to the 5 unit line of an insulin syringe
options.rationale: Correct syringe and correct line.

options.text: NPH insulin 12 units drawn to the 12 unit line of an insulin syringe
options.rationale: Correct syringe and correct line.

options.text: NovoLog 3 units drawn to the 3 unit line of an insulin syringe
options.rationale: Correct syringe and correct line.

questions.takeaway: Insulin is measured in units in an insulin syringe. U-100 means 100 units in 1 mL, so 0.5 mL is 50 units.
questions.strategy: Three options share the same syringe and a line that matches the dose. One uses a syringe marked in mL.

steps.detail: Only one is a tuberculin syringe.
0.5 mL of U-100 is 50 units, not 5.

elimination.verdict: The tuberculin syringe at 0.5 mL.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with cool hands needs a premeal fingerstick glucose. Which setup does the nurse use to obtain the sample?

options.text: Washed, damp finger; side of the tip; hand lowered; no squeezing
options.rationale: One thing is off: the finger is damp. Water dilutes the sample.

options.text: Washed, dry finger; center of the pad; hand lowered; no squeezing
options.rationale: One thing is off: the center pad. The side of the fingertip is the taught site and hurts less.

options.text: Washed, dry finger; side of the tip; hand lowered; no squeezing
options.rationale: Clean and dry gives a true sample, the side of the tip is the site, and lowering the hand improves flow without squeezing.

options.text: Washed, dry finger; side of the tip; hand raised; no squeezing
options.rationale: One thing is off: the hand is raised. Holding it below the heart improves flow in a cool hand.

questions.takeaway: Fingerstick setup: washed and dry finger, side of the fingertip, hand held below the heart, no squeezing.
questions.strategy: Each option has four parts. Read across and find the one part that changes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dry, not damp.
Side of the tip, not the center pad.
Lowered, not raised.

elimination.verdict: Dry finger, side of the tip, hand lowered, no squeezing.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old eats unpredictably. The provider wants a mealtime insulin given only once the tray is in front of her, starting to work within 10 to 30 minutes. Which insulin does the nurse expect to give?

options.text: Humulin R
options.rationale: Regular insulin starts in 30 to 60 minutes and is given about 30 minutes before the meal, before the nurse knows whether she will eat.

options.text: Humalog
options.rationale: Humalog is lispro, a rapid acting insulin. It starts in 10 to 30 minutes and is given as the food arrives.

options.text: Humulin N
options.rationale: NPH starts in 1 to 2 hours and is not a mealtime insulin.

options.text: Lantus
options.rationale: Long-acting basal insulin has no pronounced peak and is not matched to meals.

questions.takeaway: Rapid acting insulin (Humalog, NovoLog): onset 10 to 30 minutes, given just before or with the meal. Regular: onset 30 to 60 minutes, given 30 minutes before.
questions.strategy: The order names an onset. Match the number to the insulin, not the brand name to the brand name.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 10 to 30 minutes is rapid acting.
Humalog is lispro. Humulin R is regular and Humulin N is NPH.

elimination.verdict: Humalog.

questions.scenario: A student prepares and gives regular insulin 6 units with NPH 14 units in one syringe to a 60-year-old, after a premeal fingerstick. The nurse observes each step.
questions.stem: For each action, indicate whether it is correct or needs correction.

rows.text: Rolls the NPH vial gently between the palms before drawing
rows.rationale: NPH is a cloudy suspension and is rolled, not shaken, so the dose is even.

rows.text: Draws the NPH to 14 units, then puts the needle into the regular vial
rows.rationale: Regular is drawn first. A syringe holding NPH should never enter the regular vial.

rows.text: Reads the filled syringe at the 20 unit line
rows.rationale: The second insulin is drawn to the total of both doses: 6 plus 14 is 20 units.

rows.text: Punctures the center of the finger pad for the glucose check
rows.rationale: The side of the fingertip is the site. The center pad is more painful.

rows.text: Picks a new spot in the abdomen, the region used for the last dose
rows.rationale: One region with a new spot each time keeps absorption consistent.

rows.text: Rubs the injection site firmly after withdrawing the needle
rows.rationale: Massaging the site changes how fast the insulin is absorbed.

questions.takeaway: Mixed dose: roll the NPH, draw regular first, draw NPH to the total. Fingerstick on the side of the tip. Rotate within one region and do not massage.
questions.strategy: Judge each step on its own. A right total does not fix a wrong drawing order.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rolling and a total of 20 are right. NPH first is wrong.
Side of the fingertip, same region with a new spot, no rubbing.
